necessary for V. cholerae survival during exposure to acid stress. A screen using thousands of signature-tagged mutants identified 95 mutants attenuated for virulence in the infant mouse model. A subsequent challenge with organic acids revealed that nine genes (cpdA, efp, gshB, hepA, mrsA, nqrA, nqrF, pnp, and recO) were vital for a robust organic ATR (Merrell et al., 2002). Of these nine genes, five (mrsA, recO, gshB, pnp, and cpdA) have the greatest impact on acid stress resistance, as exhibited by mutants with a more than 1000-fold decrease in viability upon acid exposure (Merrell et al., 2002). mrsA encodes a phosphoglucomutase, which functions in maintenance of cell wall– lipopolysaccharide (LPS) structure (Green and Karp, 2004). Diminished cell wall integrity could directly lead to increased influx of damaging organic acids. recO encodes a DNA daughter strand gap repair protein, which presumably is involved in mitigating DNA damage caused by acid stress (Kuzminov, 1999). gshB encodes a glutathione synthetase and plays a role in glutathione synthesis and potassium homeostasis. It has also been shown to be required for acid tolerance in Rhizobium tropici, where the researchers showed that the gshB mutation has a pleiotropic effect. The mutation causes not only increased acid sensitivity but also sensitivity to osmotic and oxidative stresses (Riccillo et al., 2000; see Sections 11 and 10 respectively). The gshB mutant exhibits an inability to control intracellular pH and also accumulates K+ in the cytosol. pnp encodes a polyribonucleotide that is involved in messenger RNA (mRNA) decay and catalyzes nucleotidal transfer reactions (Littauer and Kornberg, 1957). cpdA encodes a cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) phosphodiesterase, which regulates transcription via modulation of cAMP levels within the cell (Amin and Peterkofsky, 1995). Through the concerted action of all of these factors, V. cholerae becomes resistant to exposure to acid stress. It is worth mentioning that V. cholerae previously exposed to mild acid stress (∼pH 5.7) exhibits a more than 1000-fold increase in resistance to high acidity (∼pH 4.5) when compared to a na¨ıve strain (Merrell and Camilli, 1999; Merrell et al., 2002). This suggests that V. cholerae can be primed for subsequent exposure to increasingly acidic conditions within the gastrointestinal tract, and this ultimately allows for efficient colonization of additional hosts (Merrell and Camilli, 1999). In addition to conferring increased acid resistance, initial exposure to acid stress induces a cross-protective effect toward subsequent bile shock (Alvarez et al., 2003). This can be expected since V. cholerae experiences acid shock followed by bile shock as it passes from the stomach to the small intestine, and it illustrates the extent to which this organism has adapted to its particular niche. 

In nature, V. cholerae frequently forms biofilms (see Section 22) upon attachment to chitin-rich surfaces of shellfish and zooplankton (Pruzzo et al., 2008). Like that of other microbes, V. cholerae biofilm formation is controlled by quorum sensing (Schembri et al., 2002; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003; see Section 22). Under conditions of low bacterial density, the primary quorum-sensing regulator, LuxO, inhibits expression of HapR, a negative regulator of both biofilm formation and virulence. In contrast, high bacterial density leads to accumulation of autoinducer CAI-1, which has been shown to directly inhibit LuxO activity (Miller et al., 2002; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003; Zhu et al., 2002). This leads to de-repression of HapR, which can then block biofilm formation and virulence. In the biofilm state, individual cells are protected from myriad environmental insults, including high acidity (Hall-Stoodley and Stoodley, 2005; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003). Zhu and Mekalanos discovered that a hapR mutant formed significantly thicker biofilms than wild-type (WT) V. cholerae, characterized by a 16- fold decrease in biofilm detachment. In addition, they showed that while in the biofilm state, V. cholerae is 1000-fold more resistant to acid shock (pH 4.5). However, when the biofilms were mechanically disrupted, the bacteria were no longer protected from acid exposure, highlighting the importance of the physical biofilm structure and not individual cell physiology in conveying this resistance (Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003). This has profound implications for the relative virulence of V. cholerae when in a biofilm state versus a planktonic state, since the gastric acid barrier must be overcome in order to successfully colonize the host. Further evidence was gleaned from a simple field study where 133,000 individuals living in Bangladesh filtered their drinking water through sari cloth and reduced the incidence of cholera by ∼50% (Colwell et al., 2003). The filtration method was too coarse (>20 μM) to remove planktonic Vibrio cells but was fine enough to filter out zooplankton, most phytoplankton, and biofilm debris (Colwell et al., 2003). It is logical to suspect that the observed decrease in infection was due to removal of free-floating or plankton-associated V. cholerae biofilms, which are inherently more resistant to stomach acids. 

## 17.5.3 Overcoming bile stress

Bile serves a dual function within the host: fat digestion and inhibition of microbial growth. In addition, its alkaline nature helps neutralize stomach acid that enters the small intestine. Fat digestion occurs due to the surfactant nature of bile salts, the major component of bile, which comprise over 6% of its volume (Hall and Guyton, 2011). Bile salts are amphipathic molecules possessing a hydrophobic side that interacts with the globular fat particles and causes the bile salts to envelope the fat particles. The enveloped particles disperse into 14–33 μM triglyceride micelles, which can be digested easier by pancreatic lipase and subsequently absorbed by the villi of the intestinal wall (Hall and Guyton, 2011). The bactericidal effects of bile are manifested through the disruption of various hydrophobic interactions required for proper functioning of the pathogens’ phospholipid bilayer, intra- and extracellular proteins, and nucleic acids (Merritt and Donaldson, 2009; Sytnik et al., 1978). V. cholerae, like other enteric bacteria, has evolved several mechanisms for overcoming bile stress: altered outer membrane permeability, bile salt export, active degradation of bile fatty acids, increased motility, and biofilm 

formation (see Section 22). The transport of hydrophilic solutes into the periplasmic space of V. cholerae is largely mediated by the general diffusion porins OmpU and OmpT. Both proteins form pores in the outer membrane but differ in their selectivity for particular cations, sugars, and β-lactam antibiotics, with OmpU allowing passage of larger sugars and OmpT permiting higher influx of cations and antibiotics (Chakrabarti et al., 1996; Simonet et al., 2003; Wibbenmeyer et al., 2002). V. cholerae’s first line of defense against bile-induced damage is limiting bile entry into the cell through altered expression of OmpU and OmpT (Provenzano et al., 2000; Wibbenmeyer et al., 2002). Upon exposure to deoxycholic acid, a major bile salt, V. cholerae simultaneously increases expression of OmpU and decreases expression of OmpT in a ToxR-dependent manner (Provenzano et al., 2000). As expected, deletion of OmpU but not OmpT results in a significant growth defect in the presence of bile salts (Provenzano and Klose, 2000; Provenzano et al., 2001). Furthermore, expression of OmpT in place of OmpU in an engineered V. cholerae strain causes a 100-fold decline in the ability to colonize infant mouse intestines (Provenzano and Klose, 2000). Although the exact bile resistance mechanism conferred by OmpU is not well understood, it is believed that the smaller pore size (vs. that of OmpT) blocks entry of deoxycholic acid into the periplasm (Duret and Delcour, 2006). Despite the importance of ompU in overcoming bile stress, it seems that another gene, putative phosphoporin vca1008, is also highly important for bile resistance in the El Tor biotype strain (Goulart et al., 2010). When cells are exposed to sodium deoxycholate, phosphoporin expression is enhanced, and, similarly to OmpU, this response requires ToxR (Goulart et al., 2010). vca1008 mutants were 18-fold less effective in intestinal colonization of infant mice versus WT, and, though this is not as dramatic a defect as seen with ompU mutants, it is still substantial. Intriguingly, disruption of vca1008 in the classical strain O395 does not produce this phenotype, suggesting a strain-specific role for this gene in the physiology and pathogenicity of the El Tor serotype (Goulart et al., 2010). When the extracellular bile concentration rises in the duodenum, there is an inevitable influx of bile components into the bacteria. V. cholerae possesses at least three export systems to prevent the accumulation of toxic bile salts within the cell: the resistance–nodulation–division (RND) family efflux systems, the multisubunit cation–proton antiporters (MRP system), and the vceCAB efflux system (Bina et al., 2008; Colmer et al., 1998; Dzioba-Winogrodzki et al., 2009). The RND efflux system is composed of six genes (vexB, vexD, vexF, vexH, vexK, and vexM) encoding plasma membrane-localized transport proteins with overlapping function (Bina et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2012). These genes confer increased resistance to antimicrobial compounds such as detergents, antibiotics, and bile and, due to their functional redundancy, can be mutated individually without adversely affecting the V. cholerae growth rate in bile salts and in in vivo colonization (Bina et al., 2006, 2008). Interestingly, a vexB–vexD double mutant is over 200-fold more susceptible to deoxycholate when compared to the single mutants, yet deletion of the remaining four RND genes in the double mutant background increased deoxycholate sensitivity by only twofold (Bina et al., 2008). This indicates that VexB and VexD are the primary RND pumps involved in bile salt export. Expression of vexB and vexD is negatively regulated by the tetR family transcriptional regulators VexR and BreR, respectively. Bile stimulates increased vexB and vexD expression by binding VexR and BreR, causing them to release from their target promoters (Bina et al., 2008; Cerda-Maira et al., 2008). VexK is also involved in bile resistance, serving an auxiliary function to the VexB and VexD proteins. A triple mutant of vexB, vexD, and vexK exhibited the same deoxycholate sensitivity as the RND null mutant (Bina et al., 2008). This tightly regulated efflux system allows V. cholerae to limit expression of these potentially deleterious membrane pumps to instances when they are required. 

The MRP system of V. cholerae consists of six transmembrane proteins encoded in a single operon (mrpA, mrpC, mrpD, mrpE, mrpF, and mrpG). When the mrp operon was heterologously expressed in an E. coli mutant lacking two Na+–H+ antiporters (NhaA and NhaB), the strain showed enhanced resistance to Na+, which is indicative of functional mrp expression (Dzioba-Winogrodzki et al., 2009). In addition, when this E. coli strain was exposed to increasing concentrations of bile salts (sodium cholate and sodium taurocholate), it exhibited increased growth versus the empty-vector control (Dzioba-Winogrodzki et al., 2009). Although this operon has not been studied in its native bacteria, this evidence strongly suggests that MRP plays a crucial role in protecting V. cholerae during bile exposure. 

The vceCAB efflux system is homologous to the emrAB efflux system of E. coli, but it differs in the requirement for TolC, an outer membrane protein. It appears that vceC encodes a protein that can substitute for TolC, based on a heterologous expression study where expression of vceCAB but not vceAB in a ΔtolC E. coli background conferred increased resistance to deoxycholate (Colmer et al., 1998). The study also found that deletion of vceB in V. cholerae increased sensitivity to deoxycholate fourfold, emphasizing the important role that these genes play in overcoming bile stress. Interestingly, TolC is required in V. cholerae for bile resistance and intestinal colonization despite the presence of a functional vceCAB efflux system (Bina and Mekalanos, 2001). Because TolC serves as the outer membrane pore protein for the RND efflux system, ΔtolC mutants can no longer export substrates via RND efflux and exhibit a 13-fold increase in sensitivity to bile and bile salts (Bina and Mekalanos, 2001). These results suggest that the vceCAB system plays a secondary role to the RND efflux system in survival during bile stress. Nevertheless, the concerted action of all three efflux systems described here allows V. cholerae to resist the effects of bile and efficiently colonize the host small intestine (Figure 17.5.2). 

V. cholerae has developed a means of sensing bile salts in the intestines and using them as signal molecules to activate virulence gene expression (Hay and Zhu, 2015; Yang et al., 2013).

Bile exposure induces several stress response pathways in the bacteria, enhancing its survival. Yang et al. (2013) revealed that taurocholate induces expression of ToxT through TcpP, a transmembrane transcriptional regulator. Upon interaction with this bile salt, TcpP dimerizes and, through direct binding to the promoter element, can stimulate ToxT expression. Once ToxT is produced, it can activate expression of the major virulence factors: CTX and TCP, which are essential for host colonization (Yang et al., 2013). Furthermore, this group showed that other bile salts, including glycocholate and cholate, cause increased expression of the major subunit of TCP (TcpA), strongly suggesting that the pathogen is utilizing these host-derived molecules as cues to alter its gene expression profile to suit a changing environment (Yang et al., 2013). It seems that V. cholerae has co-opted these host-derived factors into its virulence gene regulatory network, thus allowing it to modulate virulence factor production in response to disparate extracellular signals. Although virulence factor production may not directly provide protection against bile, it guards against downstream stressors such as the immune system, which V. cholerae ultimately encounters as the infection progresses. 

Bile contains a substantial amount of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids as well as cholesterol. Whereas bile salts such as taurocholate are known to upregulate virulence gene expression, unsaturated fatty acids such as arachidonic, linoleic, and oleic acid repress expression of the major virulence factors ctxAB and tcpA (Chatterjee et al., 2007). V. cholerae has evolved a clever mechanism of dealing with excess unsaturated fatty acids present in bile: enzymatic degradation and/or assimilation into the phospholipid bilayer (Giles et al., 2011). Unlike E. coli and Salmonella enterica, which under bile exposure fails to incorporate any new phospholipid species into their envelope, V. cholerae produces new bile-derived phospholipid species containing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (Giles et al., 2011). Basic local alignment search tool (BLAST) analyses performed by Giles and colleagues revealed the presence of gene homologs of long-chain fatty acid uptake proteins (FadL and FadD) and acyltransferases (PlsB, PlsC, PlsX, and PlsY) required for the formation of phospholipids from exogenous fatty acids (Giles et al., 2011). One can speculate that, by adopting a phospholipid profile that reflects the fatty acid composition of the surrounding environment, V. cholerae is employing an homeoviscous adaptation to survive membrane stress (see also Section 18). 

V. cholerae can evade the bactericidal effects of bile by increasing its motility and translocating to an area with lower bile concentrations. The increased-motility response to bile is mediated by the NADH–ubiquinone oxidoreductase system, which powers flagellar rotation by generating a sodium-motive force (Krukonis and DiRita, 2003). It has been hypothesized that increased motility might propel the bacteria deep into the mucus lining of the intestine, where bile concentration is lower, and which ultimately is proximal to the preferred colonization site at the surface epithelium (Krukonis and DiRita, 2003; Schuhmacher and Klose, 1999). 

V. cholerae often adopts a biofilm lifestyle, where it is encased in an extracellular matrix largely composed of vibrio polysaccharide (VPS) (Yildiz and Schoolnik, 1999). When in a biofilm, V. cholerae is protected from environmental insults such as antimicrobial compounds and dessication (see Section 22). When V. cholerae encounters bile, it transitions to the biofilm state and, in this way, is protected from bile-induced damage. Treatment with 0.4% crude bile, 0.4% cholate bile salt, or 0.01% deoxycholate bile salt induces, respectively, a fourfold, 4.5-fold, or twofold increase in biofilm formation, respectively. This biofilm induction is fully dependent on the vps loci, as a deletion mutant failed to generate biofilm in response to bile stress (Hung et al., 2006). As expected, the vps mutant is sixfold more susceptible to bile salts than the WT strain. In addition to the vps genes, vps co-regulated protein (vcp) is also upregulated during exposure to bile and is required for the biofilm response (Hung et al., 2006). This biofilm formation likely depends on bile-induced postranscriptional activation of VpsR, but not VpsT (Hung et al., 2006). 

In combination, all of these physiological changes, from physical exclusion of the bile components to an altered growth state, enable V. cholerae to survive and propogate in the bile-rich region of the small intestine. 

## 17.5.4 Overcoming competing bacteria

During intestinal colonization, Vibrio cholerae will inevitably encounter commensal flora that have taken up residence. It is estimated that there are on average 106 commensals/mL of fluid in the small intestine, and, most likely, these bacteria pose a competitive barrier to establishment of V. cholerae in the intestine (Bornside et al., 1966; Gibson and Rastall, 2004; Kalser et al., 1966). V. cholerae benefits from a notably faster growth rate (Mourino-Perez et al., 2003; Nielsen et al., 2010; Rasmussen et al., 2007), which gives it a competitive advantage over the endogenous flora. However, this alone may not be sufficient to overcome these established gut bacteria. A seminal article revealed the importance of a functional type 6 secretion system (T6SS) for V. cholerae colonization (Fu et al., 2013). Through the use of Tn-seq analysis, the group found that deletion of tsiV3, a gene that encodes an immunity protein to the bacteriocidal T6SS effector VgrG3 (an amidase), resulted in a colonization defect during co-infection with the WT strain (Fu et al., 2013). The T6SS is not expressed in vitro, but during in vivo infection V. cholerae upregulates transcript production from at least five T6SS genes, including the effector TseL (a lipase) and its cognate immunity protein, TsiV1 (Dong et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2013). This shows that environmental signals only found during growth in the small intestine are stimulating V. cholerae to activate its T6SS. Whether these signals are host derived or originate from commensal flora is unknown. Most importantly, these data reveal that during in vivo infection, V. cholerae is expressing functional T6SS genes that exert bacteriocidal effects on adjacent bacteria while protecting the pathogen from its own toxic effectors (MacIntyre et al., 2010). 

Commensal bacteria have been shown to influence the duration of V. cholerae infections (Hsiao et al., 2014). Although V. cholerae can efficiently outcompete commensal flora during initial intestinal colonization, it is susceptible to quorumsensing signals (see Section 21) originating from the recovering gut microbiota during the later stages of infection (Hsiao et al., 2014). One commensal, Ruminoccocus obeum, has been shown to increase significantly during V. cholerae infection and directly impact the pathogenicity of V. cholerae (Hsiao et al., 2014). R. obeum synthesizes the AI-2 autoinducer, which is recognized by V. cholerae and leads to downregulation of tcp virulence gene expression. Furthermore, the addition of R. obeum to a V. cholerae–infected mouse reduced the bacterial load of the pathogen by more than 1000-fold when compared to no R. obeum control (Hsiao et al., 2014). The exact mechanism by which V. cholerae responds to R. obeum AI-2 remains to be elucidated; however, we do know that AI-2 acts partly by repressing expression of two virulence activators, AphA and AphB. The observed six- to sevenfold decline in LuxO and HapR levels in the presence of R. obeum is incongruent with known quorumsensing pathways that lead to virulence factor regulation (Hsiao et al., 2014; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003). Regardless, this group found that an additional quorum-sensing transcriptional regulator, VqmA, was upregulated 25-fold in V. cholerae in the presence of R. obeum, and a vqmA mutant exhibited an early competitive advantage in colonization versus WT upon addition of R. obeum (Hsiao et al., 2014). These results suggest that VqmA binds AI-2 and transduces the signal to downregulate virulence gene expression through an uncharacterized pathway. 

The above studies reveal the complex dynamic between V. cholerae and the host microbiota that occurs during infection and how both pathogens and commensals respond to each other, in a constant turf battle for the gut. 

## 17.5.5 Overcoming the host immune system

The final source of stress that V. cholerae encounters during host colonization is the immune system. Several factors are secreted from intestinal epithelial cells and neighboring immune cells in an effort to control proliferation of this pathogen (Figure 17.5.3). 

Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and RNS, respectively) are produced in response to enteric pathogen infection by members of the NADPH oxidase protein family (Fang, 2004), and it is probable that V. cholerae infection induces a similar oxidative burst. ROS and RNS exposure often results in DNA, protein, and membrane damage, which can result in bacterial cell death (see Section 10). V. cholerae has an arsenal of gene

Figure 17.5.3 Vibrio cholerae colonizes the small intestine and encounters commensal flora and immune system components. Exposure induces several stress response pathways in the bacteria, enhancing its survival. The presence of commensal bacteria likely stimulates T6SS expression to inhibit their growth. ROS, RNS, and CAMPs are sensed, and corresponding neutralizing enzymes are produced in response. CTX production blocks dendritic cell maturation to a pro-inflammatory state. products intended to scavenge and detoxify these damaging ROS and RNS species, including OxyR, PrxA, KatB, KatG, and NorR. OxyR, a member of the LysR family of transcriptional regulators, controls the expression of the antioxidant defense system, which is often composed of superoxide dismutase and catalase (Howell et al., 2000; Lizarraga-Partida et al., 2009). An oxyR mutant is hypersensitive to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ both in vitro and in vivo, despite the presence of additional ROS detoxifying enzymes that are independent of the OxyR regulon (Wang et al., 2012). This result emphasizes the fundamental role that this regulon plays in the ROS response. PrxA, a protein divergently transcribed from oxyR, is induced by exposure to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and has been shown to contribute to ROS resistance (Stern et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012). KatB and KatG are catalases that are expressed independently of the OxyR regulon, underscoring the multiple layers of regulation involved in ROS resistance (Wang et al., 2012; see Section 10). Interestingly, when supernatants from WT, but not katB–katG double mutants, are added to cultures of the oxyR strain, growth is restored to that of the WT (Wang et al., 2012). This shows that KatB and KatG are secreted into the supernatant and are likely functioning in trans to detoxify ROS. NorR regulates the expression of RNS detoxification genes hmpA and nnrS, and the presence of all three genes is required for resisting low levels of nitric oxide (NO) stress under microaerobic conditions in vitro. In addition, hmpA and nnrS mutants are defective for prolonged colonization of adult mouse intestines (Stern et al., 2012). Further research on additional genes involved in ROS and RNS resistance is required to garner a more thorough understanding of how V. cholerae copes with oxidative stress during host colonization. 

The innate immune system produces copious amounts of secretory immunoglobulin A (S-IgA), an antibody primarily found in bodily secretions and in the mucus lining of the intestines, to combat pathogenic infections (Fagarasan and Honjo, 2003; Snoeck et al., 2006). S-IgA binds directly to E. coli through interaction between the antibody glycan moeities and the type I pili at the bacterial surface in a mannosesensitive manner (Moshier et al., 1996; Wold et al., 1990). Similarly, S-IgA binds to V. cholerae type IV mannose-sensitive hemagglutinin (MSHA) pili in a nonspecific manner (Hsiao et al., 2006; Watnick et al., 1999). MSHA has been implicated in attachment during V. cholerae biofilm formation, but it appears to serve no useful purpose once the bacteria reach the mucus lining of the intestines (Watnick and Kolter, 1999). 

Because MSHA serves as an anchor point for S-IgA, V. cholerae must decrease MSHA expression once inside the host to evade detection (Hsiao et al., 2006). Indeed, constitutively overexpressed MSHA mutants exhibit severe 1000-fold colonization defects during in vivo competition assays in WT, but not in IgAknockout infant mice. Furthermore, it has been shown that S-IgA–MSHA binding prevents V. cholerae from penetrating the mucus barrier and attaching to the surface epithelium (Hsiao et al., 2006). Lastly, it was demonstrated that MSHA expression is downregulated by the key virulence transcription factor, ToxT (Hsiao et al., 2006). Together, these findings reveal how tight transcriptional regulation of genes necessary for the biofilm lifestyle enables V. cholerae to transition to a pathogenic lifestyle within the human host. 

During infection, immune cells secrete cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs), which are small, positively charged proteins (Reddy et al., 2004). These CAMPs are attracted to the negatively charged lipid A component of LPS and, through direct binding, disrupt the bacterial membrane, resulting in cell death (Reddy et al., 2004). Some enteric bacteria, such as Salmonella enterica, modify the structure of the lipid A domain in response to CAMPs by capping the negatively charged phosphate groups with either phosphoethanolamine or aminoarabinose. This modification masks the surface charge with aminecontaining substituents that ultimately block binding of CAMPs to the bacterial envelope (Trent et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 1999, 2001). A recent publication demonstrated that V. cholerae utilizes a similar strategy to avoid the effects of CAMPs during gut colonization (Hankins et al., 2012). V. cholerae attaches glycine and diglycine residues to its lipid A molecules to mask the negative charge and confer resistance to CAMPs. Furthermore, it has been found that these modifications depend on the presence of three genes involved in the transfer of glycine to LPS: almG, almF, and almE (Hankins et al., 2012). An almG–almF–almE triple mutant is 100-fold more sensitive to the CAMP polymixin B, highlighting the vital role that these genes play in protecting V. cholerae from host-derived CAMPs during infection (Hankins et al., 2012). 

Although the innate immune system plays a prominent role in combating initial V. cholerae infection, the acquired immune system is largely involved in conveying resistance to subsequent infections. B lymphocytes are immune cells that produce antibodies such as IgA and immunoglobulin G (IgG) against invading pathogens (Airoldi et al., 2004). Following pathogen clearing, a subset of these lymphocytes differentiates into memory B cells, which retain the required genetic information to produce antibody specific to that pathogen (Lang, 2009). Upon reexposure to a pathogen, circulating memory B cells allow the immune system to react rapidly by producing highly specific antibody against that pathogen, thus preventing re-infection (Lang, 2009). While V. cholerae infection is rapid, with symptoms manifesting within hours of pathogen ingestion, surviving patients still mount a primary immune response, resulting in the creation of V. cholerae–specific memory B cells (Harris et al., 

2009; Jayasekera et al., 2008). It is currently believed that longterm immunity via the protective mucosal response is mediated by memory B cells in the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) (Glass et al., 1985; Harris et al., 2008). In a study of 39 cholera patients, it was found that all patients had circulating memory B cells specific to cholera toxin B (CTB), toxin–co-regulated pilus major subunit A (TcpA), and LPS (Harris et al., 2009). Furthermore, antigen stimulation elicited memory responses in IgG and IgA production by day 90, with the B cell responses persisting for up to a year (Harris et al., 2009). However, anti-CTB and anti-LPS IgG antibodies alone cannot protect from further infection, which implies that they serve an auxiliary role in suppressing the next round of V. cholerae infection. GALT-mediated antigenspecific IgA secretion is likely the primary means of blocking subsequent V. cholerae colonization of the gut (Levine et al., 1983; Svennerholm et al., 1984a,b). 

Many pathogens such as Chlamydia, Borellia, and enteropathogenic E. coli have evolved mechanisms to subvert the proinflammatory signaling pathways of immune cells in order to escape detection (Diterich and Hartung, 2001; Hauf and Chakraborty, 2003; Le Negrate et al., 2008). V. cholerae also exhibits immunomodulatory behavior during infection (Satchell, 2003). Studies have shown that CTX, the toxin responsible for causing the diarrhoeal symptoms of cholera, also has a direct effect on proinflammatory cytokine production by macrophages and dendritic cell (DC) maturation (Braun et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2002; Cong et al., 2001; Gagliardi et al., 2000). Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) is a major proinflammatory cytokine released by macrophage immune cells in response to toll-like receptor-4 (TLR4) stimulation by bacterial LPS (Medzhitov, 2001). TNFα induces proximal endothelial cells to express chemokines and adhesins, which attract neutrophils and other leukocytes to the infection site. Furthermore, TNFα stimulates macrophage-mediated production of NO to destroy invading pathogens and to signal adjacent cells (Medzhitov, 2001). When administered in vitro to primary macrophages, CTX suppresses expression of TNFα and downstream NO production in response to LPS challenge (Cong et al., 2001). In addition, CTX toxin stimulates expression of the antiinflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 (IL10), which in turn inhibits production of interleukin-12 (IL12). IL12 is produced by macrophages also in response to LPS sitmulation, and its proinflammatory effects include activation of natural killer (NK) cells to degranulate and produce interferon gamma (INFγ) (Medzhitov, 2001). INFγ serves a vital function in stimulating macrophages to produce additional proinflammatory cytokines and amplify localized inflammation (Medzhitov, 2001). Through inhibition of TNFα and IL12-mediated inflammation, V. cholerae can effectively circumvent the lethal effects of the immune response. 

CTX also impacts DC maturation by inducing immature DCs to become IL4-producing cells, which subsequently prime na¨ıve T cells to mature into Th2 cells (de Jong et al., 2002). Under CTX-deficient infection conditions, DCs would normally develop into INFγ-producing cells due to enhanced TNFα production. The INFγ-producing cells would then stimulate na¨ıve T cells to mature Th1 cells (de Jong et al., 2002; Moretta, 2002). These results imply that V. cholerae can directly dictate the fate of host immune cells via CTX production. One can speculate that V. cholerae benefits from this shift from the Th1-mediated cellular immune response to the Th2-mediated humoral response due to decreased macrophage and CD8+ cytotoxic T cell involvement. Further evidence of immune cell involvement in enhancing V. cholerae infection is provided by a recent publication, which shows that neutrophils are required for robust colonization and CTX-induced virulence in adult mice (Queen and Satchell, 2013). 

## 17.5.6 Concluding remarks



Foster JW. 2001. Acid stress responses of Salmonella and E-coli: survival mechanisms, regulation, and implications for pathogenesis. Journal of Microbiology 39: 89–94.

Wang H, Chen SS, Zhang J, Rothenbacher FP, Jiang TT, et al. 2012. Catalases promote resistance of oxidative stress in Vibrio cholerae. PLoS One 7(12): e53383. 



In summary, V. cholerae has amassed a genetic arsenal to help it overcome a plethora of host defenses intended to hamper its infectious lifestyle. This organism serves as the perfect example of a pathogen that has adapted to the various physiological stresses arising from infection of a healthy host. In light of this, there is a continuing need to research additional mechanisms of combating this lethal pathogen, whether through development of effective vaccines and antitoxins or inhibition of virulence factor production.

# Ensemble modeling enables quantitative exploration of bacterial nitric oxide stress networks

Jonathan L. Robinson and Mark P. Brynildsen 

Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA 

## 17.6.1 Introduction

The increasing incidence of antibiotic-resistant infections combined with a deteriorating pipeline of new antibiotics have continued to worsen an already prevalent global health crisis (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2013; Nathan and Cars, 2014; Taubes, 2008). The situation has recently culminated in the White House issuing an executive order to strengthen and coordinate efforts to combat antibiotic resistance (Obama, 2014), which has intensified the search for alternatives to antibiotics. One such class of anti-infectives is antivirulence therapies, which target host–pathogen interactions essential to pathogenesis (Fernebro, 2011). By inhibiting virulence factors such as cell adhesion, toxin production, biofilm formation, detoxification of immune antimicrobials, and quorum sensing, antivirulence therapies fight infection in a manner that limits selective pressure to the host environment and avoids damage to commensal microbiota (Cegelski et al., 2008; Escaich, 2008; Fernebro, 2011). Because resistance derives from selective pressure, agents that inhibit infection without perturbing bacterial growth beyond the host will inherently have slower resistance development than conventional antibiotics (Rasko and Sperandio, 2010). Bacterial defenses against nitric oxide (NO∙), a potent antimicrobial synthesized by the innate immune response (Fang, 2004; Nathan, 1992), have been identified as virulence factors for a number of pathogens (Robinson et al., 2014a), and are thus being explored for the development of new anti-infectives (Bryk et al., 2008; Darwin et al., 2003; Helmick et al., 2005). Compounds that impair bacterial NO∙ response networks could be used to synergize with host-derived NO∙ to prevent infection and/or facilitate immune-mediated clearance. However, known inhibitors of bacterial NO∙ detoxification systems, such as cyanide (Gardner et al., 1998), carbon monoxide (Gardner et al., 2000), and antimycin (Carr et al., 1989), are highly toxic toward humans, thereby precluding their use as antibacterials. Antimicrobial imidazoles have also been shown to inhibit bacterial NO∙ detoxification systems, but their poor permeability into Gram-negative bacteria limits their utility (Helmick et al., 2005). Identification of alternative inhibitors of bacterial NO∙ defense systems is therefore desirable to facilitate antivirulence development. Two complementary approaches to identify such inhibitors are to perform chemical screens to identify compounds with more favorable properties than current agents, or study the bacterial NO∙ stress response to identify other network components that can be targeted to enhance bacterial sensitivity toward NO∙. Although mutants and chemicals can be identified through the use of screens, the mechanisms underlying how genetic and chemical perturbations impact NO∙ defenses may be elusive due to the complexity of NO∙ stress responses. 

NO∙ exposure inhibits, damages, and activates an extensive and diverse collection of biomolecules within bacteria, resulting in systems-level perturbations (Bowman et al., 2011; Toledo and Augusto, 2012). The kinetic competition between reaction targets and microbial NO∙ detoxification and repair systems contribute to a complex reaction network dictating the outcome of NO∙ exposure (Robinson and Brynildsen, 2013). In order to quantitatively study this network, a computational approach is required (Lim et al., 2008; Robinson et al., 2014a). Previously, we demonstrated the ability of kinetic models to capture the dynamics of NO∙ in cultures of E. coli, and accurately predict the influence of environmental and genetic perturbations on the behavior of its NO∙ response network (Robinson and Brynildsen, 2013; Robinson et al., 2014b). With the proven potential to quantitatively interpret and predict NO∙ dynamics and perturbations to the bacterial response network, we hypothesize that these models have the capacity to be used in an ensemble framework for mechanistic dissection of any chemical treatment or genetic mutation. The implementation of an ensemble modeling approach holds promise in enhancing and broadening the scope of quantitative models as tools for extracting therapeutically important information about bacterial NO∙ response networks. By collectively analyzing an ensemble of different network configurations and/or parameterizations, and iteratively reducing the ensemble with model-guided experimentation, the mechanism underlying the effect of a chemical or mutation found to sensitize bacteria toward NO∙ stress could be determined. 

In this chapter, we summarize the current state of the art in modeling bacterial NO∙ stress, and the accomplishments achieved using these models thus far. We then discuss how to implement an ensemble approach with these quantitative models, and its potential to provide mechanistic insight into NO∙-sensitive phenotypes caused by chemical or genetic perturbations. Given the existing studies that have demonstrated the feasibility and utility of using kinetic models to study NO∙ stress in bacteria, we extrapolate that ensemble modeling will be highly successful when applied to the mechanistic dissection of genetic and chemical perturbations to bacterial NO∙ response networks. 

## 17.6.2 Current models of bacterial NO∙ stress

Within bacteria, NO∙ and its reaction products can interact with a wide range of biochemical species, including iron–sulfur ([Fe-S]) clusters, ${ \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } ,$ thiols, DNA bases, hemes, tyrosine residues, and transition metals (Bowman et al., 2011; Toledo and Augusto, 2012), resulting in the inhibition of major cellular processes ranging from aerobic respiration (Stevanin et al., 2000) and TCA cycle function (Richardson et al., 2011) to amino acid biosynthesis (Hyduke et al., 2007) and glycolysis (Mohr et al., 1999). To counter this stress, bacteria have evolved defensive machinery to detoxify NO∙ (Carr et al., 1989; Gardner et al., 1998) and repair NO∙-damaged biomolecules (Spek et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2002). The result is a complex web of reactions that extends to the far reaches of metabolism, transcriptional regulation, and macromolecular biosynthesis (Bowman et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2014a). As such, the dynamics of NO∙ stress are dictated by the kinetics of the reactions that comprise this network, and can be simulated using quantitative models. The use of a kinetic model permits the analysis of dynamic, highly complex cellular networks, where the changes in species concentrations and the timescales of these changes can vary by orders of magnitude. Our previous work has demonstrated that this approach can accurately capture the dynamics of the NO∙ stress network in E. coli, and reveal interesting and important emergent system properties (Robinson and Brynildsen, 2013; Robinson et al., 2014b). 

A kinetic model of the NO∙ biochemical network in E. coli has been constructed and includes processes such as NO∙ autoxidation, thiol nitrosation, DNA base deamination, enzymatic NO∙ detoxification, nitrosylation and repair of [Fe-S] clusters, and reversible inhibition of cytochrome terminal oxidases (Robinson and Brynildsen, 2013). Experimental measurements of [NO∙] dynamics in a culture of NO∙-treated E. coli were in quantitative agreement with simulations, and they validated the model prediction that increasing the rate of NO∙ delivery decreases the utility of NO∙ dioxygenase (Hmp), thus defining a kinetic regime where the major aerobic NO∙ detoxification system in $E .$ coli is dispensable (Robinson and Brynildsen, 2013). More recently, the model has been used to explore the influence of two important design parameters (release rate and total payload) of therapeutics that directly deliver NO∙ to infection sites on the efficacy of NO∙ treatment (Robinson et al., 2014b). Simulations predicted that a faster NO∙ delivery rate would correspond to greater therapeutic efficacy (longer duration of bacterial respiration inhibition) for lower NO∙ payloads, while slower release rates were predicted to be more effective at higher total NO∙ payloads. Experimental measurements of [NO∙] and $[ \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ]$ quantitatively confirmed the model-predicted relationship (Robinson et al., 2014b). Figure 17.6.1 illustrates the use of a kinetic model to capture NO∙ dynamics in a bacterial culture and validate model predictions with experimental measurements. 

Given these accomplishments, models of bacterial NO∙ stress are ready to be put to use in drug and target discovery by providing a framework to mechanistically dissect perturbations that impact the network. The identification of a genetic mutant or small molecule that enhances bacterial NO∙ sensitivity does not necessarily illuminate its mechanism of action. By using a quantitative model, one can interpret the experimental observations in a manner that takes into account the existing knowledge of the governing bacterial NO∙ response network. In cases where the NO∙-sensitizing mutation or chemical is novel, and thus extends beyond the current knowledge base upon which the model was constructed, it will require flexibility in the model to capture the observed phenotype. An approach that has proven effective in accounting for uncertainty in network structure and/or parameterization is ensemble modeling (Alves and Savageau, 2000; Brown and Sethna, 2003; Kuepfer et al., 2007), where an ensemble of different models can be generated to span the breadth of potential mechanisms. 

## 17.6.3 Ensemble modeling enables quantitative exploration of uncertain systems

The use of ensemble modeling allows quantitative analysis of models with a high degree of uncertainty in parameter values (e.g., reaction rates and species concentrations), system components (e.g., metabolites and enzymes), and/or network architecture (e.g., available reactions and their mechanisms) due to scarce or conflicting experimental data (Alves and Savageau, 2000; Battogtokh et al., 2002; Kuepfer et al., 2007). The system can instead be represented by a diversity of models (the ensemble), where each possesses different parameter values and/or network structures. Through an iterative process of in silico predictions and experimental measurements, the confidence and predictive strength of the ensemble increase as it converges to a single mechanism. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/d7bb30249e3f574307f328841e8ae6c5f8469b38fd52acdff971e6e6bb846149.jpg)



Figure 17.6.1 Kinetic modeling can be used to quantitatively capture and predict NO∙ dynamics in bacterial cultures. (a) A hypothetical measured [NO∙] curve (solid blue curve) following NO∙ treatment of a bacterial culture compared with a simulation (dotted black curve) from a kinetic model of the bacterial NO∙ stress network. To the right of the curves is a representative distribution of NO∙ consumption by different network pathways in E. coli, predicted by the model (Autox. and Gas are NO∙ autoxidation in the culture media and loss to the gas phase, respectively, whereas cellular consumption is broken down into Hmp-mediated detoxification, thiol nitrosation, [Fe-S] nitrosylation, and NorV-mediated detoxification). (b) Models can be used to analyze the network in silico, including the prediction of system perturbations such as the deletion of the dominant intracellular NO∙ sink (E. coli’s Hmp in this example). (c) Hypothetical experimental validation (solid green curve) of the model-predicted result (dashed black line) of the network perturbation. Data and simulations shown are purely illustrative; for actual measurements and model simulations, see Robinson and Brynildsen (2013) and Robinson et al. (2014b).


Ensemble generation can be accomplished using a number of different approaches (Alves and Savageau, 2000; Battogtokh et al., 2002; Brown and Sethna, 2003; Hettling and van Beek, 2011). For brevity, we focus on two here: one that is hypothesis driven, and another involving a systematic relaxation of model parameters. In the first approach, competing hypotheses regarding the structure of a particular reaction pathway exist, and therefore, different models can be created to represent each individual hypothesis (Kuepfer et al., 2007; Schaber et al., 2012). In the second approach, a systematic relaxation of model parameters can be performed to yield mechanistically distinct systems. In this case, each member of the ensemble would share the same network architecture but differ in their parameter values (Alves and Savageau, 2000; Rizk and Liao, 2009; Tran et al., 2008). Once the ensemble has been generated, experiments can be performed to reduce the ensemble size and ultimately arrive at a single mechanism that describes the system of interest. 

To begin the reduction process, the ensemble is used to identify conditions in silico that yield substantial disagreement between ensemble members. Conditions promoting large variation among ensemble predictions are ideal for discriminating between possible mechanisms, and are therefore used to guide experimental design. The corresponding experiments are performed, and models whose predictions are in disagreement with the new experimental data are discarded, reducing the ensemble size (Tan et al., 2011). This feedback cycle of guided experimentation and ensemble reduction can be iterated until convergence to a single mechanism is achieved. 

A number of previous studies have implemented ensemble modeling to computationally explore systems where considerable uncertainty existed, or to investigate the robustness of predictions to parameter uncertainty (Battogtokh et al., 2002; Hettling and van Beek, 2011; Jia et al., 2012; Kuepfer et al., 2007; Rizk and Liao, 2009; Tan et al., 2011). For example, Kuepfer and colleagues applied ensemble modeling to evaluate 19 different network structures describing the target-of-rapamycin (TOR) pathway of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Kuepfer et al., 2007). Although the ensemble was not reduced to a single model, the quantification of relative training errors and prediction errors with experimental data narrowed it to seven models whose shared features provided insight into the underlying mechanism, such as the importance of the Tap42p–Tip41p complex formation in signal control (Kuepfer et al., 2007). In the context of modeling metabolic networks, Tran and colleagues generated an ensemble of models of E. coli central metabolism that differed in their dynamics but shared the same steady-state flux and metabolite concentrations (Tran et al., 2008). Their analysis highlights the fact that the path taken (i.e., the order of experiments) to reduce the ensemble does not affect the final model to which the ensemble converges, but can impact the number of experiments required to achieve convergence. More recently, ensemble modeling has been applied to analyze the production of aromatic amino acids in E. coli, where phenotypic data obtained from enzyme overexpressions were used to obtain a reduced ensemble capable of accurately predicting the dynamics and enzymatic bottlenecks of the 3-deoxy-D-arabinoheptulosonate-7-phosphate (DAHP) synthesis pathway (Rizk and Liao, 2009). Hettling and van Beek have used a mathematical model to evaluate two hypothesized roles of creatine kinase (CK) in heart muscle, taking an ensemble approach to account for error associated with experimentally measured parameter values (Hettling and van Beek, 2011). An algorithm that accounts for model “sloppiness” (Brown and Sethna, 2003; Gutenkunst et al., 2007) has been used to generate and analyze an ensemble of parametrically distinct models that can identify confidence intervals not only on parameters, but also on predictions (Hettling and van Beek, 2011). Without reducing the size of the ensemble, the predictions were able to rule out the hypothesis that shuttling of high-energy phosphate groups is an important role of CK in heart muscle (Hettling and van Beek, 2011).

Figure 17.6.2 Flowchart illustrating the application of ensemble modeling to dissect the mechanism underlying a perturbation found to enhance NO∙ sensitivity. (a) A mutation or chemical is identified that impairs bacterial NO∙ detoxification through an unknown mechanism of action, resulting in a perturbed [NO∙] profile. Shown are hypothetical measured [NO∙] curves demonstrating the effect of the perturbation (red curve) to “normal” wild-type (WT) NO∙ consumption dynamics (blue curve). (b) An ensemble of models is generated by releasing parameter constraints and/or varying network structure, and re-optimizing the model to capture the perturbed [NO∙] curve. (c) The ensemble is used to perform in silico analyses to determine which experimental conditions will yield a large variation in dynamics among ensemble members. In this example, predicted hmp (messenger RNA) profiles are illustrated to vary substantially among ensemble members. (d) The corresponding experiment is performed, and models exhibiting incorrect predictions are eliminated from the ensemble. Steps (C) and (D) are iterated until the ensemble has been reduced to a single model, which represents the mechanism underlying the NO∙-sensitizing perturbation. Data and simulations shown are purely illustrative; for actual measurements and model simulations, see Robinson and Brynildsen (2013) and Robinson et al. (2014b). 

## 17.6.4 Prospects of ensemble modeling of NO∙ stress

Given the complexity and breadth of the bacterial NO∙ stress response network, a quantitative model is necessary to study its dynamics as a collective system. Upon discovery of a chemical or mutant that perturbs the NO∙ response network, we hypothesize that an ensemble approach could be used to systematically delineate the mechanism underlying the observed phenotype (Figure 17.6.2). 



in the United States, 2013. http://www.cdc.gov/drugresistance/threatreport-2013/ 



The ensemble could be used to simulate experimentally accessible conditions in silico to rapidly screen for those that result in large variation among ensemble members, facilitating the elimination of mechanisms that are inconsistent with the new data. Through an iterative process, the ensemble is reduced to a single model, representing the mechanism through which the chemical or mutation is perturbing the bacterial NO∙ response network. Knowledge of the mechanism will illustrate how resistance can be obtained and illuminate possible synergies with other strategies, while also providing a deeper understanding of the pathogen’s physiology.

## 17.6.5 Conclusion



Darwin KH, Nathan CF. 2005. Role for nucleotide excision repair in virulence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Infection and Immunity 73(8): 4581–4587. 



Antibiotic resistance is a threat to global health, and it has motivated the search for alternative approaches to conventional antimicrobials (Arias and Murray, 2009; Bush et al., 2011; CDC, 2013; Taubes, 2008). Antivirulence is a promising alternative that targets the host–pathogen interactions essential for establishing infection, such as pathogen defenses against the immune system (Cegelski et al., 2008; Escaich, 2008; Fernebro, 2011). NO∙ is a potent antimicrobial produced by the immune system (Fang, 2004; Nathan, 1992), and NO∙ defense systems are common virulence factors for pathogens (Darwin and Nathan, 2005; Richardson et al., 2006; Robinson et al., 2014a). Disrupting bacterial NO∙ defense networks therefore represents a promising antivirulence approach that could facilitate immune-mediated clearance (Bryk et al., 2008; Darwin et al., 2003; Helmick et al., 2005). Moreover, agents found to sensitize bacteria toward NO∙ could be used synergistically with exogenous NO∙ delivery platforms, which are currently under investigation for the treatment and prevention of antibiotic-resistant infections (Friedman et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2010; Schairer et al., 2012). Because the promiscuous reactivity of NO∙ and its oxidation products yields a highly complex reaction network, it can be difficult to decipher the mechanism underlying a chemical or mutation found to sensitize a pathogen toward NO∙. Kinetic modeling has been shown to quantitatively capture NO∙ dynamics in E. coli cultures, and successfully predict the result of system perturbations or changes in experimental conditions. We hypothesize that the use of an ensemble approach, which has been shown to be effective in handling parameter or network structure uncertainty, could be used with kinetic models of NO∙ stress to delineate the mechanism underlying a chemical or mutant identified to sensitize bacteria toward NO∙. Through an iterative process of in silico ensemble predictions and guided experimentation, the ensemble could be reduced to a single model that describes the mechanism of the NO∙-sensitizing compound or mutation. Furthermore, we assert that ensemble modeling, when coupled with high-throughput mutant or chemical screens that search for enhanced NO∙ sensitivity, will provide a robust platform to identify targets or compounds with antivirulence potential, and their mechanisms of action.
