## Adaptation to cell envelope stress

Randi L. Guest and Tracy L. Raivio 

Department of Biological Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada 

## 18.1.1 Introduction

The bacterial envelope is a particularly important place for signal transduction, since it is the first cellular compartment to encounter environmental changes, and its integrity and function are integral for the survival of the bacterium. Thus, sensors needed for timely and appropriate expression of genes such as virulence factors are present in the envelope, as well as signal transduction pathways important for monitoring, maintaining, and adapting the envelope to environmental parameters that impact its functioning. 

The Cpx envelope stress response is one of several described in the gammaproteobacteria (reviewed in Raivio, 2005; Rowley et al., 2006). While it is becoming evident that there are clear linkages between such responses, they are each believed to monitor some unique aspect of the Gram-negative envelope and mount an appropriate response to perturbations. A large body of evidence recently reviewed in Raivio (2014) indicates that the Escherichia coli Cpx-envelope stress response senses and mediates adaptation to events that result in protein misfolding in the bacterial periplasm. The main arguments in support of this model are twofold. First, the direct overproduction of misfolded, aggregated proteins (as well as a plethora of signals expected to generate misfolded envelope proteins) leads to strong induction of the Cpx response. Second, the expression of a number of genes involved in the secretion, folding, and degradation of envelope proteins is regulated by the activated Cpx response. 

## 18.1.1.1 The Cpx response is activated by misfolded proteins, adhesion, and growth

The Cpx-envelope stress response is regulated by a typical two-component regulatory system (reviewed in Mizuno, 1998; see Section 3) made up of the sensor histidine kinase CpxA in conjunction with the response regulator CpxR. Although the molecular mechanism(s) used by CpxA to sense misfolded proteins is unclear, current data indicate that it involves the periplasmic chaperone CpxP (Thede et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2011), which acts to inhibit the autokinase activity of CpxA (Fleischer et al., 2007) in the absence of inducing signals (Buelow and Raivio, 2005; DiGiuseppe and Silhavy, 2003; Raivio et al., 1999, 2000). This signaling mechanism likely occurs at the periplasmic face of the inner membrane (Tschauner et al., 2014) and involves titration of the periplasmic chaperone CpxP from the CpxA sensing domain by misfolded proteins, followed by the subsequent degradation of CpxP and the aggregated polypeptide(s) (Isaac et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2011). Although this is an appealing model for signal sensing supported by many studies, it should be noted that it is not sufficient to explain Cpx pathway activation. In the absence of cpxP, the Cpx response is only modestly induced, and envelope stress signals lead to further significant activation (DiGiuseppe and Silhavy, 2003; Raivio et al., 1999). Accordingly, additional signaling events, beyond the relief of CpxP inhibition, are involved in turning on the Cpx envelope stress response. This conclusion is supported by the observation that many microbes lack a putative cpxP homolog (De Wulf et al., 2000). 

Another, perhaps distinct, mechanism of CpxA-dependent activation of the Cpx response is mediated by the outer membrane lipoprotein NlpE. Overexpression of NlpE suppresses the toxicity of some aberrantly folded and localized fusion proteins in the envelope by activating expression of the periplasmic protease DegP in a Cpx-dependent fashion (Danese and Silhavy, 1997; Snyder et al., 1995). NlpE is also required to induce the Cpx response upon adhesion to a hydrophobic, abiotic surface (Otto and Silhavy, 2002). It has been proposed that this occurs through a change in the orientation of two independently folded β-barrel domains in NlpE that is instigated by a flexible linker upon adhesion. This event is proposed to allow direct interaction between the C-terminal domain of NlpE and the sensing domain of CpxA to mediate activation of the response (Hirano et al., 2007). At present, it is unclear whether surface activation of the Cpx response by NlpE is related to induction of the pathway by NlpE overexpression, and much remains to be learned about this important input into the pathway. 

In addition to signals that are generated in the envelope, the Cpx response also appears to be activated by undefined cues originating in the cytoplasm and generated by growth, specifically the transition into the stationary phase (DiGiuseppe and Silhavy, 2003; Wolfe et al., 2008). Although CpxR is known to be phosphorylated by the small cellular metabolite and phosphate donor acetyl-phosphate (Danese and Silhavy, 1998; Pogliano et al., 1997; Raivio and Silhavy, 1997), the growth-related activation of CpxR appears to be partly independent of acetylphosphate and may involve posttranslational acetylation events (Lima et al., 2012; Wolfe et al., 2008). Cpx signaling events are covered in detail in Chapter 18.2. 

## 18.1.1.2 The Cpx-envelope stress response regulates events at the inner membrane

The first identified members of the Cpx regulon encode periplasmic chaperones (spy, cpxP, ppiA, and dsbA) and proteases (degP) (reviewed in Dorel et al., 2006; Raivio, 2005, 2014; Raivio and Silhavy, 2001; Vogt and Raivio, 2011) and support the conclusion that the Cpx response is an envelope proteinmisfolding response in E. coli. However, recent in-depth analyses of the Cpx transcriptome in E. coli as well as Haemophilus ducreyi and Vibrio cholerae suggest that adaptation to envelope protein misfolding may be just one element of this response. In fact, chaperones and proteases known to be Cpx regulated in E. coli have not been found to be Cpx controlled in H. ducreyi (Gangaiah et al., 2013). 

Many studies in a variety of organisms demonstrate links between the Cpx envelope stress response and the expression of virulence factors. Although there are exceptions, in many cases activation of the Cpx response appears to downregulate the production of envelope-spanning protein complexes, including virulence determinants. Similarly, Cpx response induction often has a deleterious effect on virulence in animal and tissue culture models of disease, although whether this is attributable to its negative impact on the expression of toxins, pili, and secretion systems remains to be determined. In addition, as our knowledge of the Cpx regulon increases, it has become apparent that certain cellular functions are enriched, including inner membrane processes such as transport and energy generation. Cumulatively, the existing transcriptome work suggests that the Cpx stress response mediates a multipronged approach to envelope stress adaptation, including the downregulated production of many envelope proteins as well as induction of adaptive factors that affect multiple cellular processes. All of these findings have been reviewed recently in Raivio (2014) and Vogt and Raivio (2011) and will not be discussed further here. 

Recent studies have begun to highlight an emerging relationship between the Cpx-envelope stress response, efflux, and metal trafficking. This work suggests that CpxA senses toxic cellular metabolites that may alter metal trafficking and are expelled from the cell at least partly via Cpx-regulated efflux pumps. This chapter will focus on the findings of these studies and how they have expanded our view of Cpx-sensed stresses and the consequent adaptations. 

## 18.1.2 The Cpx-envelope stress response is linked to efflux pump expression and function

Resistance–nodulation–division (RND) efflux pumps are required for the expulsion of noxious substances from within the bacterial cell, including antibiotics and metabolic waste products. These are tripartite protein complexes, consisting of the outer membrane channel TolC, an inner membrane transporter, and a membrane fusion protein. Interestingly, the Cpx-envelope stress response can become activated by mutations in each of these RND efflux pump components. Furthermore, the Cpx response also has been implicated in the positive regulation of efflux pump expression in a number of Enterobacteriacea. 

## 18.1.2.1 Mutation of efflux pump components activates the Cpx-envelope stress response

The first hint that inhibition of efflux may activate the Cpx response was in 2009, when Slamti and Waldor found that a transposon inserted into tolC increased the expression of a cpxP–lacZ fusion in Vibrio cholerae (Slamti and Waldor, 2009). This finding was confirmed in two independent studies investigating the role of the Cpx response in V. cholerae (Acosta et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2014). It has since been shown that mutations in tolC activate the Cpx response in multiple organisms, including E. coli and Sinorhizobium meliloti (Rosner and Martin, 2013; Santos et al., 2010). The reason why mutation of tolC activates the Cpx response is unclear. It is possible that the absence of TolC may destabilize many TolC-dependent transporters, perhaps generating a protein-misfolding signal. However, when tolC was deleted in a strain lacking all nine tolCdependent transporters in E. coli, Cpx activation was unchanged from the tolC single mutant (Rosner and Martin, 2013). Instead, it is believed that endogenously produced toxic metabolites that are normally excreted through TolC accumulate in the cell when tolC is mutated. 

Mutations in four of the RND efflux transporters in E. coli, acrB, acrD, mdtC, and mdtF activate a spy–lacZ reporter gene in a CpxA-dependent fashion to the same extent as the mutation of tolC. This occurs only when all four transporters are inactive, as a single mutation in each transporter had only a moderate effect on spy–lacZ activity (Rosner and Martin, 2013). Likewise, inactivation of all six RND efflux transporters in V. cholerae induces the Cpx response. This was attributed to the inactivation of only two transport systems, VexRAB and VexGH, in this strain (Taylor et al., 2014). As multiple RND efflux pumps must be inactivated to induce the Cpx response, it is possible that these transporters have redundant activities and can efflux the same metabolites. 

Finally, it has been shown that mutation of the membrane fusion protein mtrC activates the Cpx response in H. ducreyi (Rinker et al., 2011). In the absence of MtrC, the RND efflux transporter MtrD may remain active but not associate with MtrE, a homolog of E. coli TolC. This would then lead to an accumulation of toxic metabolites in the periplasm, subsequently inducing envelope stress and activation of the Cpx response (Rinker et al., 2011). 

The identity of the toxic metabolite or metabolites that accumulate and induce the Cpx response in the absence of RND efflux pumps remains unknown. So far, three metabolites have been ruled out: indole, acetate, and ethanol (Rosner and Martin, 2013). Interestingly, addition of iron reduces Cpx activation in a tolC, vexB, or vexH mutant in V. cholerae (Acosta et al., 2015). Multiple iron-chelating metabolites are predicted to accumulate in the absence of TolC, including porphyrins, citrate, and enterobactin (Bleuel et al., 2005; Helling et al., 2002; Ruiz and Levy, 2014; Turlin et al., 2014). Incidentally, accumulation of ironfree enterobactin in the periplasm is predicted to disrupt multiple processes associated with the Cpx response, including motility, cell wall biogenesis, and respiration (Vega and Young, 2014). Recently, our group has found that Cpx activation in the absence of tolC is reduced when genes involved in enterobactin biosynthesis are disrupted (E Court, RL Guest, TL Raivio, unpublished observation). We propose a model whereby the Cpx response is activated by the accumulation of iron-chelating metabolites, such as enterobactin, in the periplasm. It is currently unclear whether iron-free enterobactin can directly activate the Cpx response, or if this indirectly induces envelope stress. 

## 18.1.2.2 The Cpx-envelope stress response regulates the expression of efflux pumps

Activation of the Cpx response has been implicated in resistance to a variety of toxic molecules due to the upregulation of multidrug efflux pump gene expression. In E. coli, resistance to copper, indole, deoxycholate, and the cationic antimicrobial peptide protamine upon activation of the Cpx response has been linked to increased expression of tolC, acrD, and mdtABC (Fung et al., 2013; Hirakawa et al., 2003; Nishino et al., 2010; Slamti and Waldor, 2009; Weatherspoon-Griffin et al., 2014). Upregulation is achieved through a regulatory network that includes the Cpx, Bae, and Mar stress responses. Hirakawa and colleagues have shown that CpxR in conjunction with the response regulator BaeR bind directly to the promoters of acrD and mdtABC to increase their expression (Hirakawa et al., 2005). Conversely, activation of tolC expression appears to occur indirectly through the Mar response. The mar operon consists of three genes, the repressor marR, the activator marA, and marB. In the absence of stress, MarR binds to the mar promoter to keep the response off. Under inducing conditions, toxic molecules bind directly to MarR and prevent interaction with the mar promoter. Toxic molecules that inhibit MarR activity, including indole and copper, can also induce the Cpx response (Cao et al., 2007; Weatherspoon-Griffin et al., 2014; Yamamoto and 

Ishihama, 2005). Shi and colleagues have proposed a model where indole inhibits MarR activity, allowing CpxR∼P to bind directly to the mar promoter and activate the Mar response. MarA then increases the expression of genes involved in resistance to a variety of antimicrobial agents, including tolC and the RND efflux pump acrAB (Weatherspoon-Griffin et al., 2014). 

CpxR∼P has been shown to directly regulate expression of the KpnEF SMR efflux pump in Klebsiella pneumonia, which is involved in resistance to bile, detergents, and various antibiotics (Srinivasan and Rajamohan, 2013). The roles of other stress responses in regulation of this efflux pump remain unknown. 

Interestingly, the regulatory networks present in E. coli do not appear to be conserved in V. cholerae. Like E. coli, activation of the Cpx response in V. cholerae promotes resistance to antimicrobial compounds that are excreted through RND efflux pumps, including bile, thiosulfate, citrate, and ampicillin (Taylor et al., 2014). Moreover, Cpx activity increases expression of tolC, vexAB, and vexG (Acosta et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2014). However, V. cholerae appears to lack the Bae and Mar stress responses (Taylor et al., 2014). Instead, it appears that the Cpx pathway may directly regulate the expression of these RND efflux components (Acosta et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2014). This brings up the interesting possibility that the Cpx response in V. cholerae evolved to perform some of the duties of the Mar and Bae stress responses. 

## 18.1.3 The Cpx-envelope stress response is linked to metals

Numerous studies since the 2000s link the Cpx-envelope stress to metals (see Section 20). Cpx-regulated genes exhibit changes in transcription in the presence of copper, zinc, and iron and have functions demonstrated, or suspected to be involved in, acquisition, efflux, and/or storage of metals. Moreover, the association between the Cpx response and metals occurs across at least three different orders of the gammaproteobacteria, suggesting its conservation. 

## 18.1.3.1 Copper, zinc, and iron lead to changes in Cpx-regulated gene expression

Much evidence supports the conclusion that changes in cellular metal status alter Cpx pathway activity. Ishihama and coworkers provided some of the earliest evidence of this, demonstrating that short exposures to toxic concentrations of copper resulted in elevated expression of the genes encoding known Cpx-regulated periplasmic chaperones, cpxP and spy (Yamamoto and Ishihama, 2005). In addition, they demonstrated that 10 additional copper-induced genes, not previously linked to copper adaptation, were directly controlled by CpxR (Yamamoto and Ishihama, 2005, 2006). Subsequent studies confirmed these findings. Several groups used transcriptomics or reporter genes to show that expression of spy (Srivastava et al., 2014; Yamamoto et al., 2008), ppiA (Pontel et al., 2014), cpxP, degP, and yccA (Kershaw, 2005) are in fact all upregulated by exogenous copper in both rich and minimal medias. 

In addition to copper, other studies suggest that fluctuations in zinc or iron can alter expression of Cpx-regulated genes. Lee and colleagues (Lee et al., 2005) demonstrated elevated expression of numerous Cpx-regulated genes (spy, cpxP, degP, yccA, ppiA, and yncJ) in chemostat cultures exposed to 200 μM zinc sulfate. Similarly, the addition of zinc to zinc-depleted cultures resulted in a sharp and dramatic increase in cpxP expression (Graham et al., 2011). Most recently, the V. cholerae Cpx response was shown to be induced by iron depletion (Acosta et al., 2015). 

Finally, the effect of metals on the Cpx response is not limited to E. coli, but rather impacts gammaproteobacteria derived from at least three different orders. In V. cholerae, CuSO4 was shown to induce expression of cpxP reporter genes (Acosta et al., 2015; Slamti and Waldor, 2009). Similarly, in Shewanella oneidensis, exposure to chromate resulted in elevated transcription of genes encoding putative CpxR and CpxA homologs, together with many genes that share similar functions with the Cpx regulons of E. coli, V. cholerae, and H. ducreyi. These include genes encoding predicted hydrogenases, reductases, transporters, iron-binding proteins, and efflux pumps (Chourey et al., 2008). 

## 18.1.3.2 Cpx-regulated genes play roles in metal trafficking and/or resistance

Consistent with the ability of altered metal concentrations to change Cpx-regulated gene expression, a number of Cpx regulon members play known or predicted roles in metal homeostasis (see Section 20). For example, the Cpx response upregulates the expression of the iron-storing ferritin in E. coli, while downregulating the expression of the EfeUOB ferrous iron transporter (Cao et al., 2007; Price and Raivio, 2009). A further role for the Cpx response in cellular iron trafficking is indicated by the fact that genes encoding iron transport, storage, and metabolism genes are overrepresented in the V. cholerae Cpx regulon (Acosta et al., 2015) and are tightly linked to a putative CpxR homolog in S. oneidensis (Chourey et al., 2008). Finally, the MdtABC efflux pump, which is involved in metal detoxification in numerous microbes (Leblanc et al., 2011; Nishino et al., 2007; Wang and Fierke, 2013), is jointly regulated by the Cpx and Bae envelope stress responses (Raffa and Raivio, 2002). 

Altered expression of the above Cpx-regulated genes, and likely others (discussed further in this chapter), most certainly plays a physiological role in withstanding stresses related to alterations in cellular metal concentrations. The earliest example of this was the finding that a cpxRA mutant displayed sensitivity to copper (Yamamoto and Ishihama, 2006). In another case, a putative S. oneidensis CpxR homolog was shown to be necessary for resistance to chromate (Chourey et al., 2008). In V. cholerae, deletion of cpxR resulted in sensitivity to iron depletion, and this phenotype could be complemented by the addition of exogenous iron (Acosta et al., 2015). Surprisingly, iron was also able to suppress Cpx response induction and the growth phenotypes of cpx mutants in the presence of other inducing cues. Although the reason is not currently understood, this observation suggests a direct connection between metal homeostasis and the Cpx response. 

In this light, it is intriguing that the Cpx signaling protein and chaperone CpxP shares structural homology with other periplasmic proteins that have roles in metal resistance. CpxP shares a “kinked hairpin” alpha-helical structure reminiscent of ZraP and CnrX (Thede et al., 2011). ZraP, like CpxP, is a periplasmic chaperone that also controls the activity of the ZraSR zinc-responsive two-component system. Its chaperone activity and oligomeric state are regulated by zinc binding (Appia-Ayme et al., 2012). CnrX is a periplasmic metal sensor that regulates an extracytoplasmic function sigma factor involved in metal resistance in Cupriavidus metallidurans (Grass et al., 2005; Pompidor et al., 2009). Finally, mutations of the gene encoding the CpxP homolog Spy in E. coli have been shown recently to result in changes in the intracellular concentration of, and sensitivity to, zinc (Wang and Fierke, 2013). Interestingly, CpxP crystallizes in the presence of zinc, and we have shown that mutations affecting Cpx signaling in both E. coli K-12 and enteropathogenic E. coli lead to alterations in zinc resistance and trafficking (JL Wong and TL Raivio, unpublished). 

Although all of the studies described in this section support a role for the Cpx response in adaptation to altered metal concentrations, the nature of the inducing signal that arises, or even which metal species is relevant, is not known. It is known that alterations in one metal species lead to cellular changes in the trafficking and concentrations of others. For example, transcriptome studies make it clear that copper-trafficking and detoxification genes are upregulated in the presence of zinc (Lee et al., 2005), while excess copper leads to changes in transcription of genes impacting zinc and iron metabolism (Pontel et al., 2014). Similarly, elevated copper and zinc concentrations were shown to result in a 6–8-fold increase in the cellular levels of iron (Graham et al., 2011). Accordingly, what aspects of metal excess and limitation may be relevant for the Cpx response are not currently clear. Hopefully, more insight into the molecular mechanisms of Cpx signal transduction will shed light on this area. 

## 18.1.4 Model

It has long been thought that the Cpx-envelope stress response serves to sense and respond to misfolded envelope proteins. This model has been substantiated by the finding that the Cpx regulon includes a number of envelope-localized protein-folding and degrading factors and the fact that overexpression of proteins known to be misfolded is a potent Cpx inducer. However, recent discoveries, highlighted here and in Raivio (2014), have demonstrated a role for the Cpx response in sensing diverse signals related to efflux and metals, together with the regulation of a variety of cellular processes that are not linked clearly to protein folding. How, then, do these findings elucidate our understanding of the Cpx-envelope stress response? 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/2e231fb07a7f69cb2bc2f435f65d044edb82129a52711894ea889e9ba873b039.jpg)



Figure 18.1.1 A model for the role of the Cpx-envelope stress response in sensing and mediating adaptation to changes in metal trafficking and/or respiration. Alterations in cellular metal concentrations, efflux, and/or respiration lead to induction of the Cpx response. In response, phosphorylated CpxR upregulates efflux pump expression and downregulates components of the electron transport chain.


Interestingly, many of the conditions that lead to Cpx activation have been proposed to interfere with electron transport. Enterobactin accumulation in the periplasm may reduce NADH dehydrogenase I activity (Dhamdhere and Zgurskaya, 2010; Vega and Young, 2014). Zinc and copper ions can inhibit the activity of many respiratory enzymes by interfering with iron– sulfur cluster biogenesis, displacing iron in iron–sulfur clusters, or preventing proton-pumping activity (Fung et al., 2013; Kita et al., 1984; Macomber and Imlay, 2009; Schulte et al., 2014). Furthermore, the Cpx response is required for growth under iron-limiting conditions only when bacteria are grown on nonfermentable carbon sources (Acosta et al., 2015). Notably, regulation of respiratory complexes by the Cpx response has been demonstrated in E. coli, Haemophilus ducreyi, and V. cholerae (Acosta et al., 2015; Gangaiah et al., 2013; Guest and Raivio, in preparation; Raivio et al., 2013). All of these observations intimate a link between respiration and the Cpx response. 

This connection is further supported by the observation that, upon transition from aerobic to microaerophilic growth conditions, transcriptome analysis reveals upregulation of iron and copper metal-trafficking functions alongside Cpx-regulated genes (Partridge et al., 2007). Furthermore, inhibition of terminal oxidase activity results in coincident changes in expression of genes involved in respiration, metal trafficking and metabolism, and transport (Davidge et al., 2009). Modeling suggests that CpxR is the responsible transcription factor. It has been suggested that the transition from the use of the aerobic, coppercontaining cytochrome bo oxidase to the microaerophilic, cytochrome bd oxidase may liberate copper into the periplasm, which subsequently stimulates signaling pathways to alter gene expression (Partridge et al., 2007). 

We suggest that Cpx-inducing signals may be generated by perturbing envelope proteins or protein complexes that contain metal or metallated cofactors and/or are directly involved in metal trafficking. The resultant response could involve changes that correct protein-folding problems, metal-trafficking imbalances, and/or the functioning of diverse proteins dependent on inner membrane–localized complexes carrying metalcontaining cofactors (Figure 18.1.1). 

This model is consistent with the established role of the Cpx response in protein folding and accommodates recent observations described in this chapter regarding efflux and metal trafficking. It further provides an explanation for the conserved downregulation of some respiration enzymes and transport functions as well as the diverse phenotypes historically associated with the Cpx response (Raivio, 2014). These include downregulated proton motive-dependent transport (Plate, 1976), the inability to grow on the nonfermentable carbon source succinate (Morris and Newman, 1980), and resistance to aminoglycosides and colicins (Newman et al., 1981; Plate, 1976; Sutton et al., 1982). 

Although we are learning more about the conserved cellular roles of the Cpx response through our study of the inducing signals and the regulon, the outstanding challenge has been, and remains, to understand what the nature of the inducing signal(s) are and how or if they are integrated to control activity of the signaling pathway (see Section 18.1.2 for a current review of what is known). 

## 18.1.5 Significance

Activation or removal of the Cpx response results in changes in virulence and resistance to antibiotics in many pathogens, including antimicrobial peptides, an important aspect of innate immunity (see Raivio, 2014, for a review). Furthermore, a commensal strain of E. coli lacking the Cpx response is unable to colonize the colon (Lasaro et al., 2014). Interestingly, strains carrying mutations in the genes encoding ArcB and RcsB – response regulators that control respiratory and envelope stress adaptation, respectively – are the only other mutants in this study that are similarly defective in colonization of the intestine. These observations suggest a connection between respiration and envelope stress during adaptation to the intestine and indicate an important role for the Cpx-envelope stress response during host infection and colonization. It seems probable that Cpx-regulated changes in metal trafficking are also important for adaptation to stresses encountered in a host organism; in addition to metal sequestration, metal flooding leading to toxicity is an important aspect of innate immunity (Porcheron et al., 2013). New insights into Cpx-signaling events and adaptation will improve our understanding of the fundamental physiological requirements for pathogen and commensal survival alike in the host environment.

# New insights into stimulus detection and signal propagation by the Cpx-envelope stress system

Patrick Hoernschemeyer and Sabine Hunke 

Molecular Microbiology, Biology/Chemistry, University of Osnabrueck, Osnabrueck, Germany 

## 18.2.1 Introduction

Two-component systems (TCSs) provide the main instrument by which bacteria couple environmental changes to adaptation. TCSs employ a phosphorylation cascade from an inner membrane (IM) sensor kinase to a cytosolic response regulator (Hoch, 2000; Stock et al., 2000) (see Section 3). Some TCSs are additionally modulated by an accessory protein, which can be found in the cytosol or the envelope of a bacterial cell (Buelow and Raivio, 2010; Heermann and Jung, 2010; Krell et al., 2010). The envelope of Gram-negative bacteria is composed of the IM, the periplasmic space, and the outer membrane (OM), and it is completed by exposed surface structures such as flagella, secretion systems, and adhesins (Silhavy et al., 2010). 

The Cpx-envelope stress system of Gram-negative bacteria serves as a model for the investigation of stimulus detection, signal propagation, and prevention of unwanted crosstalk in TCS signaling (Hunke et al., 2012; Laub and Goulian, 2007). It detects and responds to envelope perturbations by regulating the expression of chaperones and proteases, envelope proteins, macromolecular surface structures, and other stress systems (Figure 18.2.1; see also Chapter 18.1) (Bernal-Cabas et al., 2014; Bury-Mone et al., 2009; Raivio et al., 2013; Vogt et al., 2014). The Cpx-TCS consists of the sensor kinase CpxA and the response regulator CpxR. Two accessory proteins orchestrate the Cpx-TCS: The periplasmic protein CpxP inhibits the Cpx-TCS in unstressed cells and detects misfolded envelope proteins; the OM lipoprotein NlpE activates the Cpx-TCS during biofilm formation (see Section 22) (Fleischer et al., 2007; Hung et al., 2001; Otto and Silhavy, 2002; Raivio et al., 1999; Snyder et al., 1995; Tschauner et al., 2014). 

Recent reviews summarize the functional role of the Cpx-TCS for Gram-negative bacteria (Raivio, 2014; Vogt and Raivio, 2012). Here, we focus on our current knowledge of how stimuli are integrated and how signal propagation into the cytosol might occur. 

## 18.2.2 Stimulation of the Cpx-TCS

The activity of the Cpx-TCS is modulated by diverse stimuli. These include alkaline pH, salt, depletion of the lipids, attachment to hydrophobic surfaces, acetyl phosphate, a low cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) level, carbon monoxide, metals, indole, alcohols, hormones, the lipopolysaccharide intermediate Lipid II, peptidoglycan, and misfolded proteins (reviewed in Hunke et al., 2012). Since these stimuli induce or reflect protein misfolding, it has been assumed that the Cpx-TCS reacts on misfolded proteins (Raivio and Silhavy, 2001; see Chapter 18.1). However, recently modifications of the cell wall have been found to induce the Cpx-TCS (Evans et al., 2013). Moreover, the Cpx-TCS modulates the expression of genes important for peptidoglycan cross-linking (Bernal-Cabas et al., 2014; Raivio et al., 2013). Thus, it becomes evident that the Cpx-TCS preserves the integrity of the full cell envelope. Thereby, specific stimuli and target gene expression can once in a while be linked. As another example, it is known that acetyl phosphate activates CpxR (Wolfe et al., 2008). A high acetyl phosphate level reflects a high energy status of the cell (Behrends et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2000). Now, it has been shown that activated CpxR inhibits expression of those respiratory chain complexes that act as proton pumps (Raivio et al., 2013). Hence, the Cpx-envelope stress system counteracts energy stress. However, some antibiotics induce crosstalk between CpxA and the oxidative stress response regulator ArcA (see Section 10), resulting in hydroxyl radical formation and finally in bacterial cell death (Kohanski et al., 2008). How these opposite functions of the Cpx-TCS in energy stress response are balanced is not understood (Mahoney and Silhavy, 2013; Raivio et al., 2013).

Figure 18.2.1 Model of the Cpx-TCS. The sensor kinase CpxA is activated by a variety of signals (IN), resulting in the transphosphorylation of the response regulator CpxR. Phosphorylated CpxR modulates the expression of genes (OUT) encoding surface structures and folding factors. Two accessory proteins integrate additional stimuli by modulating the activity of the Cpx-TCS: CpxP (red) inhibits autophosphorylation of CpxA in unstressed cells, detects misfolded envelope proteins, and guides them to degradation by the protease HtrA; and the outer membrane lipoprotein NlpE (green) activates the Cpx-TCS during adhesion.


## 18.2.3 Function of the accessory proteins CpxP and NlpE for stimulus perception

Stimulus perception by the Cpx-TCS is balanced by the accessory proteins CpxP and NlpE. 

The periplasmic CpxP protein inhibits the Cpx-TCS in a negative feedback loop and counteracts extracytoplasmic protein– mediated toxicities (Danese and Silhavy, 1998; Isaac et al., 2005; Raivio et al., 1999). For misfolded proteins derived from the P pilus of uropathogenic E. coli, CpxP appears to act as an adaptor protein for the HtrA protease (Isaac et al., 2005). CpxP inhibits autophosphorylation of reconstituted CpxA, probably by direct interaction between the concave polar surface of CpxP and negatively charged residues on the periplasmic sensor domain of CpxA (Figure 18.2.2) (Fleischer et al., 2007; Tschauner et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2011). This interaction is obstructed by a high NaCl concentration and misfolded pilus subunits (Tschauner et al., 2014). Cumulatively, these studies emphasize a model in which the inhibitory and supporting functions of CpxP are linked for some stimuli: In unstressed cells, CpxP associates with CpxA to shut off the Cpx-TCS. Envelope stress conditions induce the displacement of CpxP from CpxA, resulting in Cpx-TCS activation. 

The OM lipoprotein NlpE (new lipoprotein E), which is characterized as the copper homeostasis protein, CutF, is required to activate the Cpx-TCS in response to surface adhesion independently from CpxP (Gupta et al., 1995; Otto and Silhavy, 2002). Overproduction of NlpE activates the Cpx-TCS and is used as a Cpx-specific activation stimulus (DiGiuseppe and Silhavy, 2003; Snyder et al., 1995). The crystal structure revealed that a NlpE monomer consists of two β-barrel domains that are linked by two β-barrels and that two NlpE monomers form a domain swapped dimer (Figure 18.2.2) (Hirano et al., 2007). In the monomer, the N-terminal lipid anchored β-barrel domain contains a CxxC motive, which is suggested to be involved in copper sensing by oxidation or coordination. It is speculated that Cpx-TCS activation by NlpE might result from tertiary or quaternary structural instability causing direct contact between the C-terminal β-barrel domain of NlpE and CpxA (Hirano et al., 2007). However, how attachment to surfaces induces this structural instability of NlpE, how NlpE bridges the peptidoglycan layer, and how NlpE interacts with CpxA are unknown. 

## 18.2.4 Structural insight into stimulus detection by CpxA

The sequence of CpxA obeys the typical sensor kinase architecture, including an extracytosolic sensor domain in the periplasm, two membrane-spanning transmembrane domains, and the cytosolic effector moiety. The latter is connected to one transmembrane domain and is composed of a HAMP domain that elongates into two helices: the DHp (dimerization and histidine phosphotransfer) domain that is connected through a loop region to the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding CA (catalytic and ATP-binding) domain. For sensor kinases in general, constitution of the homodimer is accomplished by dimerization of each respective DHp domain, establishing a four-helix bundle (Stewart, 2010) (see Section 3). Eventually, autophosphorylation of a conserved histidine in the DHp domain occurs via the CA domain that forms an α/β-sandwich and binds ATP (Ashenberg et al., 2013). 

Investigating the periplasmic sensor domain of CpxA, it soon became evident that the domain posses an important regulatory function in CpxA activation. Amino acid exchanges within the periplasmic domain, as well as the deletion of the entire periplasmic domain (and transmembrane domain), essentially trigger the autokinase activity, leading to the conclusion that an aberrant conformation of the domain leads to a constitutively active CpxA lacking phosphatase activity (De Wulf and Lin, 2000; Keller et al., 2011; Mechaly et al., 2014; Pogliano et al., 1998). 

Kwon et al. solved the truncated periplasmic domain of Vibrio parahaemolyticus of CpxA, comprising amino acid residues 38–173, to a resolution of 2.1 A (Figure 18.2.2) (Kwon ˚ et al., 2012). The obtained structure reveals a globular domain encompassing a five-stranded β-sheet that is surrounded by three alpha-helices. This structure was classified as a PAS (Per–Arnt– Sim) fold that resembles the PAS domains of other sensor kinases, including AbfS, KinD, and LuxQ (Kwon et al., 2012). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/2b01c8c13f63857b3883631c52efd0ea915cd7ed5369dee6da38bfb2ec8e32e0.jpg)



Figure 18.2.2 Structural insight into the Cpx-TCS. Combined in a model of the envelope of a Gram-negative bacterium are the structures of E. coli NlpE (green; PDB accession code 2Z4H) (Hirano et al., 2007), E. coli CpxP (red-gray dimer; PDB 3ITF) (Zhou et al., 2011), the truncated periplasmic domain V. parahaemolyticus CpxA (cyan and blue; PDB 3V67) (Kwon et al., 2012), and the dimeric cytosolic domains of E. coli CpxA (cyan and blue; PDB 4BIV) (Mechaly et al., 2014).


The surface charge distribution of the V. parahaemolyticus CpxA periplasmic domain exposes an overall basic character, distributed over four regions, and two acidic surfaces. The basic surfaces are suggested as ligand recognition sites (for, e.g., Cl− ions). The acidic surfaces (encompassing residues Asp49– Glu151) are thought to be involved in CpxP binding, although no concluding statement can be made due to the use of a truncated periplasmic domain of CpxA (Kwon et al., 2012). However, peptide array analysis demonstrates the importance of negatively charged amino acid residues within the C-terminal region of the periplasmic domain of E. coli CpxA for CpxP binding (E138DNYOLYLIRPASSSQSDEINLLFD162) (Zhou et al., 2011). 

Together, identifying the ligand-binding site as well as unraveling the CpxP binding mode to the periplasmic sensor domain of CpxA still require further studies. 

## 18.2.5 Signal propagation

A milestone in gaining insights into the catalytic mechanism of CpxA was reached by Mechaly et al., who crystallized the cytosolic part of CpxA (amino acid residues 188–457) in different enzymatic conformations (Mechaly et al., 2014). 

The cytoplasmic domain of the CpxA homodimer follows the classical architecture of sensor kinases (Figure 18.2.3; see Section 3). Each monomer contains two elongated coiled-coil helices that comprise the HAMP and DHp domains, whereas the latter is linked to the CA domain. Both coiled-coil helices can be subdivided into α1 and the N-terminal part of α2 (two parallel helices that form the HAMP domain) and the two antiparallel helices α2 and α3 that form the DHp domain. Altogether, these units form a central four-helix bundle within the homodimer. 

It turns out that the homodimer is highly asymmetric concerning the positioning and orientation of the CA domain, as well as concerning the alignment of α3 helices toward each other, creating an overall curved asymmetric structure. This becomes more evident when taking into account that helix α2 contains two kinks at Ser238 and Pro253, allowing for segmental movements of both DHp domains with respect to each other, eventually conferring a different positioning of the CA domains with respect to the four-helix bundle core of the homodimer. Ser238 marks the intersection between the HAMP domain and the DHp domain. At this point, a switch from parallel (HAMP domains) to antiparallel (DHp domains) within the four-helix bundle occurs. The kink at Pro253 is in direct proximity of the phosphorylatable His248. The C-terminal part of α3 is connected to the CA through a short loop. The CA is composed of a two-layer 3α–5β sandwich fold that is typical of the GHKL superfamily and forms an ATP-binding Bergerat fold (Mechaly et al., 2014). 

It is well known that autophosphorylation in HK dimers can be in cis (HK853 from T. maritima, PhoR from S. aureus, and ArcB from E. coli) or in trans (NtrB, AtoS, CheA, and AgrC from E. coli) (Ashenberg et al., 2013). The handedness of the DHp domain is decisive for the determination of cis- or trans-autophosphorylation. A right-handed loop confers trans-autophosphorylation as in EnvZ, whereas a left-handed loop leads to cis-autophosphorylation as in HK853 (Ashenberg et al., 2013; see Section 3). Handedness depends on the loop region at the base of the DHp domain. In the case of CpxA, a right-handed loop connects α2 and α3, suggesting trans-autophosphorylation. Indeed, the CA of CpxA loaded with ATP belongs to a different subunit of the homodimer than the histidine that is in the correct position to be phosphorylated (Mechaly et al., 2014). 

As mentioned in this chapter, the kinks at Ser238 and Pro253 confer segmental mobility of the DHp helices. This is important when the homodimer needs to adapt to different conformations in order to enter different enzymatic modes. Hence, this finding implies segmental movements within the DHp domain in response to physical stress by torsional, rotational, or translational stress that is propagated through the IM to the HAMP domain and finally to the DHp domain. From this, Mechaly et al. stated a model on segmental movements (Figure 18.2.3): The inactive CpxA homodimer comprises a symmetric conformation that is disintegrated upon stimulus detection. This stimulus detection initiates the disintegration of the symmetry of the HAMP domains (α1 and the N-terminus of α2) and leads to movement of segments α2 and α3. The model proposes separate rotations of two individual rigid bodies: (i) α1 and the Nterminus of α2; and (ii) the C-terminus of α2 and α3. In more detail, the C-terminus of α3 of subunit A dislocates from the center of α2 of subunit B. This results in the creation of a large contact interface (∼1200 A˚ 2) for CA of subunit A, which is composed of α3 of subunit A and α2 of subunit B, thus retaining CA of subunit A in a fixed (inactive) conformation. In contrast, and as a result of the same segmental movements on the opposite side of the dimer, the CA of subunit B perceives only small DHp– CA contact interfaces. This leads to greater mobility for this CA, posing the so-called Michaelis complex that displays the autophosphorylation activity. Accordingly, a highly dynamic autophosphorylation is suggested, including only a single phosphorylation per homodimer, which is supported by in vitro experiments that never show thorough phosphorylation of CpxA. As a conclusion, this model proposes that the symmetric state of the homodimer poses a phosphatase-active state, whereas the phosphotransferase state is attributed to the asymmetric state (Mechaly et al., 2014). 

## 18.2.6 Outlook

Recent research allowed first insight into the mechanisms of stimulus perception and propagation by the Cpx-TCS. However, several underlying mechanisms are only poorly understood. It is suggested that NlpE bridges the periplasmic space to activate CpxA (Hirano et al., 2007). This model has similarity to the mechanism of TonB-dependent energy transduction from the IM to the OM to allow for active transport over the OM, although in the opposite direction (Braun et al., 1991; Postle and Larsen, 2007). If this model of bridging the periplasmic space to transduce information from the OM to the IM by the use of an OM-anchored lipoprotein applies, the mechanisms of interaction of NlpE and CpxP with CpxA and how these interactions are coordinated to a final response remain unclear. According to our current working hypothesis, the N-terminal periplasmic PAS domain of CpxA integrates CpxP independent stimuli, and the C-terminal periplasmic region acts as a circuit breaker operated by CpxP.

In addition, unveiling the exact movement of the transmembrane domains will be important to understand the propagation of the signal beyond the membrane and the inflicting effects on the HAMP domains. One possible approach could be the employment of the electron spin resonance technique in order to monitor changes of intermolecular distances of labeled amino acid residues within the homodimer that are located in close proximity to the membrane. This might help to elucidate whether the transmembrane domains move in a piston-like or tilted manner. Solving these questions will help to understand stimulus perception and propagation not only by the Cpx-TCS but by TCS in general.

# Promiscuous functions of cell envelope stress-sensing systems in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii

Vijaya Bharathi Srinivasan and Govindan Rajamohan 

Bacterial Signaling and Drug Resistance Laboratory, Council of Scientific Industrial Research – Institute of Microbial Technology, Chandigarh, India 

## 18.3.1 Introduction

Over the last few years, the foremost problem of multidrug resistance has been responsible for widespread incidences of severe nosocomial infections worldwide (Haley et al., 1985; Vincent et al., 1995). According to the recent World Health Organization (WHO) report on global surveillance of antimicrobial resistance, the incidence of multidrug resistance has been reported at an alarming pace (WHO, 2014). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have included the notoriously drugresistant pathogens Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii in its list of urgent and serious antimicrobialresistant threats for humans (Pendleton et al., 2013; Podschun and Ullmann, 1998). 

K. pneumoniae is an opportunistic pathogen that causes severe illnesses such as septicemia, pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and soft tissue infections, and it has been recognized for over 100 years as a cause of community-acquired pneumonia. The hypervirulent, hyperviscous K. pneumoniae that belongs to the K1 serotype has recently emerged as a cause for pyogenic liver abscesses, sometimes complicated by endophthalmitis or meningitis. It has emerged in Taiwan, Singapore, Korea, and other Asian countries (Daikos and Markogiannakis, 2011; Rapp and Urban, 2012; Wu et al., 2009). Its wide array of drug resistance determinants and its ability to sustain in unfavorable environmental conditions have justifiably propelled the pathogen to the forefront of scientific attention (Perez et al., 2007; Pitout, 2008). K. pneumoniae has emerged as a highly troublesome pathogen for many medical institutions globally, including India (Molton et al., 2013). 

A. baumannii is a Gram-negative, strictly aerobic, nonfermenting, nonfastidious, nonmotile, catalase-positive, oxidasenegative bacteria with a DNA G+C content of 39–47% (Howard et al., 2012). There is an increasing concern regarding the prevalence of this bacterium on abiotic surfaces, especially in intensive care units, where it has been associated with different types of infections such as pneumonia, meningitis bacteremia, urinary tract infections, and others. As determined by the Infectious Diseases Society of America, A. baumannii is one of the “red alert” pathogens that greatly threaten the utility of our current antibacterial armamentarium (Pendleton et al., 2013). 

As for other bacterial pathogens, multidrug resistance is multifactorial, and there are many factors that contribute to different resistance profiles. Multidrug resistance (MDR) in bacteria has been attributed to either intrinsic or acquired mechanisms. The resistance mechanisms in bacteria are diverse and include enzymatic modification of antibiotics, target gene mutation, altered outer membrane permeability, and upregulated multidrug efflux pump activity (Piddock, 2006). One of the major contributing factors to the success of these pathogens as human pathogens is their ability to acquire resistance genes rapidly and persist in the inanimate environment for a long time, with subsequent reactivation upon favorable conditions (MacRitchie et al., 2008). 

Crucial components of the resistant mechanisms are the signaling pathways and proteins that play key roles by recognizing the signals from external and internal cellular environments and switch on or off the target genes to prepare them for antimicrobial assaults. Understanding the global regulatory network and signaling cascade and its components is therefore critical to combat illnesses. Though the functional relevance of protein kinases in bacterial genetics and physiology is increasingly being recognized, two-component systems (TCSs) still remain the predominant intracellular information-processing pathways and are considered as potential drug targets (Stephenson and Hoch, 2002: see Section 3). TCSs, also referred to as twocomponent signal transduction systems, are recognized as a key mechanism through which bacteria perceive and respond to their environment. TCSs are easily identifiable in genomic databases and are present in more than 95% of the bacterial genomes sequenced to date as well as archaea and eukaryotic organisms such as plants and fungi (Gotoh et al., 2010). TCSs comprise a transmembrane sensor histidine kinase protein (HK) and a cytoplasmic transcriptional response regulator (RR). The HK consists of an input domain that senses the environmental stimulus and a cytoplasmic transmitter domain that has kinase activity to convert the external stimulus into an adaptive signal by autophosphorylation at a conserved histidine residue. The phosphorylated histidine transfers the phosphate onto the conserved aspartic acid of the RR, inducing conformational changes in its DNA-binding domain and activating it. The active RR is involved in DNA binding and regulates expression of its downstream genes (Stock et al., 2000: see Section 3). The DNAbinding domain of RR is classified based on its secondary structure, and the winged helix-turn-helix type is the most common RR that belongs to stress-sensing systems (MacRitchie et al., 2008). The OmpR family of regulators is one such example. Although there is a plethora of information available on its physiological relevance, its direct participation in antimicrobial resistance is not yet clearly delineated. 

The MisT2 database (www.mistdb.com) has shown the presence of >466 signaling proteins in the 5,472,672 bp (GC content: 57.4%) genome sequence of the K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044 K1 serotype (Accession no. AP006725.1) (Wu et al., 2009) and >275 signaling proteins in the genome sequence of A. baumannii strain AYE (Iacono et al., 2008). Both these pathogens do harbor members of the OmpR family of regulators; however, their functions in cellular physiology in general and antibiotic resistance in particular have remained completely unexplored. Therefore, in this study, the unknown aspects of the functions of OmpR-type regulators (CpxAR of Klebsiella and RstAB of Acientobacter) are deciphered in the multidrug-resistant model organisms K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii. 

The Cpx envelope stress response is controlled by the TCS ranging from signal integration by the kinase CpxA to the output response by CpxR. CpxA is induced by a variety of envelope stresses and displays different functions, for example in envelope stress response system, pilus assembly, type III secretion, motility and chemotaxis, adherence, and biofilm development (see also Chapters 18.1 and 18.2) (De Wulf and Lin, 2000). Overall, the Cpx system of bacteria is known to be involved in maintenance, adaptation, and protection of the bacterial envelope in response to a variety of stressors, one such environmental attack that pathogenic bacteria such as Klebsiella spp. are exposed to in the pressure of antibiotics. The functional characterization of TCSs in Eschierichia coli has demonstrated that purified RstA protein is transphosphorylated by the cytoplasmic domain of RstB in a phosphotransfer experiment (Yamamoto et al., 2005). RstAB is a member of the OmpR family, and its functions are well characterized in E. coli and Salmonella (Jeon et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2005). RstA-promoted expression of the ferrous iron transporter FeoB under iron-repleted conditions was shown to increase the Fur activity in Salmonella enterica (Joen et al., 2008). BfmRS, an rstAB homolog, from the ompR family has been characterized in A. baumannii and has a role in cell adhesion, biofilm, resistance to serum killing, virulence, and antibiotic susceptibility (Gaddy and Actis, 2009; Liou et al., 2014). Interestingly, the homolog of bfmRS is found in different MDR A. baumannii strains, including A. baumannii AYE; however, its function in these MDR strains has never been examined. Here, we initiated a systematic study to elucidate the biological role of TCSs CpxAR from K. pneumoniae and RstAB from A. baumannii in modulating physiology and antimicrobial resistance. 

## 18.3.2 Materials and methods

Bacterial strains, media, and methods: The two bacterial strains used in this study, K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044 and A. baumannii AYE, were obtained from the National Taiwan University Hospital, Taiwan, and from ATCC, respectively. Bacterial cultures were grown at 37 ◦C with constant shaking (220 rpm) in lysogeny broth (LB) medium or on LB agar (Difco, BD, USA) supplemented with specific antibiotics for mutants (100 μg/ml kanamycin for K. pneumoniae and 400 μg/ml hygromycin for A. baumannii) and complemented constructs (100 μg/ml chloramphenicol for K. pneumoniae and 200 μg/ml zeocin for A. baumannii), and stored at −80 ◦C before use. A standard protocol was used for general molecular biology techniques (Sambrook et al., 1989), while primers were custom-synthesized (Eurofins MWG operons, Germany). 

Construction of isogenic and complemented strains: The cpxAR null mutant ΔcpxAR of K. pneumoniae and complemented construct ΔcpxARΩcpxAR were generated previously (Srinivasan et al., 2012a). A 1363 bp internal fragment from the rstAB operon of A. baumannii (ABAYE3063/ABAYE3064) was amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using ΔrstAB-F (TATGTCGCGAAACCAGTTCAACCACGTG-TATTATTAG) and ΔrstAB-R (TGATCGGATATGAGAAAT-GCTTTTGAATCTTGGCAAG) primers and cloned into a hygromycin cassette containing a pUC4K-derived suicide vector. The recombinant plasmid pUC-rstAB was electroporated into A. baumannii AYE to construct the isogenic mutant ΔrstAB strain. The intact rstAB operon along with its promoter were amplified with FL rstAB-F (TGCGTTTAAT-CACCTGAATTTGACCGGGAGTCGAAGTAAT) and FL rstAB-R (CCTGAGAAGCGGCAAACCTATTTTGGAAC-CTGATGCAACT) and cloned into a zeocin-resistant shuttle vector (Srinivasan et al., 2014). The resulting construct was electroporated into ΔrstAB to obtain the transcomplemented strain ΔrstABΩrstAB. 

Bacterial phenotypic assays: The growth kinetics of K. pneumoniae (wild type (WT), ΔcpxAR, and ΔcpxARΩcpxAR) and A. baumannii (WT, ΔrstAB, and ΔrstABΩrstAB) strains were monitored in LB at different pHs (5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0, 10.0, and 12.0) (Srinivasan et al., 2014). In the growth inactivation assay, cultures at the mid-log phase were inoculated into LB containing ciprofloxacin (0.005 μg/ml) in independent experiments either alone or with efflux pump inhibitors carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP 2.5 μg/ml); 2,4,dinitrophenol (DNP 2.5 μg/ml); verampamil (VER 2.5 μg/ml); or reserpine (RES 2.5 μg/ml) (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) (Srinivasan et al., 2014). Optical densities of a culture with agitation were measured for 10 h at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with shaking using a Bioscreen C automated growth analysis system (Labsystems, Finland) at 600 nm and automatically recorded for each well after every 30 min. The motility assays were carried out as reported before, where LB-grown A. baumannii cultures $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 \mathrm { n m } } = 1 . 0 )$ were inoculated with a toothpick on LB plates with 0.25%, 0.45%, and 0.7% agar and incubated for 10 h at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Srinivasan et al., 2012b). The crystal violet binding assay was carried out as described in Srinivasan et al. (2012b). In the oxidative susceptibility test, small Whatman 3MM paper disks (6 mm) were impregnated with different amounts of hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ (0.131, 0.263, 2.631, 5.262, 7.894, 13.15, 26.31, 52.62, and 78.94 μM) and air-dried as reported before (Hennequin and Forestier, 2009). The cultures were grown to $\mathrm { \mathrm { O D } } _ { 6 0 0 \mathrm { n m } }$ 0.1 and were uniformly spread over an LB agar plate. Next, filter paper disks impregnated with specific concentrations of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ were placed at the center of the agar surface. The diameter of a zone of inhibition was measured (in millimeters) which is a qualitative measure of the inhibitory activity of the compound. The sensitivity of cells to oxidative stress was tested by exposing stationary-phase bacteria diluted in LB medium $\mathrm { \ O D } _ { 6 0 0 \mathrm { n m } }$ 0.2 at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in the presence of 0.07894, 0.7894, 1.5788, 2.3682, and 3.1576 mM $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ for 1 h. Survival was counted by plating the cells onto agar plates before and after exposure to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ , and results were expressed as percentages (see Section 10). Acidified sodium nitrite and sodium nitroprusside (SNP) were used to generate nitrosative stress to check cell growth in the presence of NO-releasing agents as described previously (Srinivasan et al., 2012b). 

Stress challenge assays: The K. pneumoniae (WT, ΔcpxAR, and ΔcpxARΩcpxAR) and A. baumannii (WT, ΔrstAB, and ΔrstABΩrstAB) cells were exposed to different stress challenges at varied concentrations (see Figures 18.3.2 and 18.3.3), and survival was quantified as described previously. The results were expressed as the ratio of the number of colony-forming units obtained from LB cultures containing different concentrations of substrates to the number of colony-forming units obtained from control cultures (LB agar alone). These experiments were performed at least three times (Srinivasan et al., 2012b). 

Antibiotic susceptibility and accumulation assays: The strains in this study were examined for antibiotic resistance by using commercial antibiotic discs (Hi Media, India) as described previously according to the interpretation criteria recommended by the CLSI (Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, 2010). The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of antibiotics was tested using E-strips. The fluorimetric accumulation of substrates and reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) was determined, as described in Srinivasan et al. (2014). Outer membrane proteins were purified, as described in Srinivasan et al. (2012b). 

Gene cloning, expression, Gel shift assays: The respective RR was amplified using gene-specific primers, which contained NdeI and BamHI sites of the pET28C vector to generate an Nterminal ${ \mathrm { H i s } } _ { 6 } – { \mathrm { R R } }$ fusion protein. All clones were confirmed by sequencing and transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3). The RR was purified through Qiagen $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ nitrilotriacetic acid columns. The promoter region was amplified using specific primers and subjected to an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) with purified protein. Briefly, end-labeled (using $[ \gamma - ^ { 3 2 } \mathrm { P } ]$ ATP) PCR products were incubated with increasing concentrations (in a range of 50–500 nM) of protein in binding buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 2 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM DTT, 50 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, and 1 μg of poly(dI⋅dC). The complexes were separated on 5% native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) gels for 2 h. The gel was then dried and exposed to the phosphor screen for image analysis. 

Bioinformatic analysis and statistical analysis: Homology searches, similarities, and identities analysis were performed using the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) server and Simple Modular Architecture Research Tool (SMART; www.smart.embl-heidelberg.de). All data are presented as means plus or minus the standard error of the mean. Statistical analysis was performed on crude data by using a paired Student t-test. p values of <0.05 were considered significant. 

## 18.3.3 Results

## 18.3.3.1 Identification and functional characterization of cpxAR and rstAB: in silico analysis of cpxAR and rstAB

The K. pneumoniae gene KP1 0078 (1374bp, 457aa) was found to exhibit >75% identity with CpxA proteins from other organisms. The KP1 0079 (699bp, 232aa) gene, encoding a 23 kDa protein, exhibited homology to CpxR proteins, the RRs of TCSs in bacteria (Srinivasan et al., 2012a). Upon performing BLAST, the A. baumannii gene ABAYE3063 (1650 bp, 549 aa) exhibited >70% identity (in brackets) with the RstA protein of other Acinetobacter, with the closest homolog being RstB of A. pittii (97%), A. calcoaceticus (97%), A. haemolyticus (86%), A. junii (86%), A. beijerinckii (86%), A. haemolyticus (86%), A. towneri DSM 14962 (79%), A. indicus (77%), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa B136-33 (68%). Structural motifs present in A. baumannii RstB mark it as the sensor–HK component of a TCS (see Section 3). Secondary-structure prediction and comparison to known HK structures indicate that this RstB has a short, cytoplasmic part (amino acids 1–6), followed by a transmembrane helix (amino acids 7–29), residues 30–240 comprise the extracellular region with mixed secondary structures and that probably serve as the sensor, residues 241– 263 forms the second transmembrane helix, and amino acids

264–549 comprise a large cytoplasmic region and other conserved residues and domains are present in its primary sequence. The ABAYE3064 (717 bp, 238 aa) gene encodes a 27.2 kDa protein with homology to OmpR proteins that are the RRs in TCSs. ABAYE3064 exhibits >40% identity to RstA of Enterobacter aerogenes, Salmonella typhimurium, E. coli, Shigella flexneri, Proteus mirabilis, and Yersinia pestis. Comparing A. baumannii RstA to other RRs indicates that this RstA has two domains: an N-terminal signal receiver domain (amino acids 10–118) and a C-terminal effector domain (amino acids 155–231). In the receiver domain, the residue (D51) necessary for phosphoryl transfer from RstA is conserved. An analysis of the primary sequence and the secondary-structure prediction for A. baumannii aligned RstA to the sequence of the receiver domain of the structurally characterized YycF from Bacillus subtilis (Protein Data Bank accession no. 2zwm), which indicates that this domain is 30% identical to that of A. baumannii RstA, suggesting that the structures of the two proteins are likely to be very similar. The C-terminal domain of A. baumannii RstA very likely binds to DNA, given its sequence homology to other effector domains that have this function. A multiple sequence alignment of the OmpR-type proteins clearly showed that they were highly conserved among different bacteria (Figure 18.3.1). 

## 18.3.3.2 Role of Klebsiella cpxAR and rstAB in physiological stress response

Impact on bacterial growth, motility, and biofilm formation In our previous study, we deciphered the involvement of the Cpx signal transduction system in influencing growth in K. pneumoniae. The growth profile of ΔcpxAR was found to be reduced compared to the WT in LB at pH 6.0 and 8.0. The other tested pHs, 3.0 and 12.0, were toxic to both of the cultures (Srinivasan et al., 2012a). The motility and biofilm-forming ability of the cpxAR mutant were found to be diminished (data not shown). Results demonstrate that cpxAR influences the physiological responses in K. pneumoniae.

The other tested pHs, 3.0 and 12.0, were toxic to both cultures. The results demonstrate that rstAB influences growth of A. baumannii. When the cultures were grown in different concentrations of agar for 14 h, WT cells exhibited motility-like behavior around the point of inoculation, and distance of migration was 37 mm (0.25%), 30 mm (0.45%), and 26 mm (0.7%). In contrast, the rstAB mutant cells had slightly impaired motility, and distance of migration was 32 mm (0.25%), 27 mm (0.45%), and 24 mm (0.7%), indicating loss in motility. We found that in vitro biofilm-forming ability of ΔrstAB was ∼1.5-fold less compared to the WT strain. 

## Role of cpxAR and RstAB in stress responses

In our study, we have tested WT, mutant, and complemented strains in the presence of different stress-inducing agents such as bile, NaCl, hydrogen peroxide, and various disinfectants in K. pneumoniae (for CpxAR) and A. baumannii (for RstAB) (Table 18.3.1 and Figures 18.3.2 and 18.3.3). Overall, the results imply a broad-spectrum antimicrobial resistance property of cpxAR and rstAB, which are signal-sensing systems in K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii, respectively.

## 18.3.3.3 Effect of Klebsiella CpxAR and Acinetobacter RstAB in the antibiotic stress response

## Effect on antibiotic susceptibility

Analysis of a disc diffusion assay for K. pneumoniae ΔcpxAB displayed decreased susceptibility toward imipenem, cefepime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefotaxime, and chloramphenicol (data not shown) (Srinivasan et al., 2012a). However, A. baumannii ΔrstAB exhibited decreased susceptibility toward erythromycin, ceftazidime, neomycin, streptomycin, and linezolid (data not shown). The survival abilities of the wild-type, mutant, and complemented strains of K. pneumoniae ΔcpxAB and A. baumannii ΔrstAB were analyzed, and the data obtained revealed that the mutant exhibited decreased ability to withstand the exposure of selected biocides, antibiotics, and structurally unrelated compounds (Figures 18.3.2 and 18.3.3). 

## Effect on drug efflux capability in K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii

The cell envelope is the prime line for most outside stress conditions that may modify envelope components and thus cause an extracytoplasmic stress response. A reduction in the permeation of antibiotics is generally related to a decrease in porin expression or an alteration in the porin structure. To check loss in efflux activity, we examined and analyzed the effect on survival ability for different strains using efflux-based substrates. Overall, the results confirmed that the wild type exhibited higher survival rates compare to the mutant, demonstrating its role in antimicrobial efflux (Figures 18.3.2a and 18.3.3a). 

To distinguish whether there was any loss in efflux pump activity in the cpxAR mutant, the growth profile of WT (K. pneumoniae) and ΔcpxAR was monitored with cefoxolin either alone or with CCCP, an uncoupler known to collapse the membrane energy and block the energy-dependent efflux pump. As expected, a decrease in growth $( 1 . 9 9 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { f o l d } \pm 0 . 0 5 6 ; p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ was observed in the cpxAR mutant. In an independent experiment using benzalkonium chloride, a substantial decrease (2.47- $\mathrm { f o l d } \pm 0 . 0 6 9 ; p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ in growth was observed in the cpxAR mutant in the presence of CCCP, clearly illustrating the contribution of cpxAR in conferring antimicrobial resistance, possibly as a regulator of the efflux pump in K. pneumoniae. Similarly, the growth profile of WT and ΔrstAB was monitored with ceftriaxone either alone or with CCCP, and a decrease in growth $( 1 . 1 7 \mathrm { - f o l d } \pm 0 . 0 1 5 ; p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ ) was observed in the rstAB mutant. Using chlorhexidine, a substantial decrease $( 3 . 4 6 5 \mathrm { - f o l d \pm 0 . 0 7 8 } ;$ $\begin{array} { r }  p < 0 . 0 0 1 \ \end{array}$ in growth observed in the rstAB mutant in the presence of CCCP signifies its role in antimicrobial resistance in A. baumannii. The growth profile of WT and ΔcpxAR or ΔrstAB in the presence of CCCP was equivalent to the growth that was observed in LB alone for the WT and ΔcpxAR or ΔrstAB strains. Additionally, the flourimetric assays further confirmed a loss of efflux activity in the ΔcpxAR and ΔrstAB mutant as compared to WT. 

A reduction in the permeation of antibiotics is generally related to a decrease in porin expression or an alteration in the porin structure. To get an insight, we evaluated the membrane profiles of ΔrstAB and the wild type (A. baumannii). Analysis revealed alterations in both inner and outer membrane fractions of wild type and mutant; however, it was intriguing to note the presence of overexpressed bands in the outer membrane fractions of mutants of varying sizes: ∼26 kDa, ∼39 kDa, and ∼40 kDa, respectively (data not shown). Upon identifying the proteins by MALDI-TOF, it was found that ∼26 kDa matched 100% with CarO (ABAYE0924), ∼39 kDa matched 100% with OmpA (ABAYE0640), and ∼40 kDa matched 100% with AmpC (ABAYE1110). 

## Regulatory role of CpxAR and RstAB in drug resistance

RT-PCR analysis revealed that, compared to WT, expression of efflux pumps such as acrB, acrD, and eefB genes were decreased by threefold, fivefold, and twofold, respectively, in the cpxAR mutant, while there was a marginal increase in expression of the major facilitator-type efflux pump kmrA compared to WT (Srinivasan et al., 2012a). 

Compared to the WT A. baumannii strain, the porin genes carO (ABAYE0924) and ompA (ABAYE0640) showed, respectively, >10-fold and threefold increased expression in ΔrstAB. Our RT-PCR data corroborated well with the altered outer membrane profile that was observed for ΔrstAB. The efflux genes abeM, adeB, and adeJ showed threefold, onefold, and onefold, and ampC beta-lactamases twofold, increased expression respectively in ΔrstAB as compared to WT. Gel shift assays demonstrate that RstA was able to bind to promoters of β-lactamases and efflux pumps. Overall, our results provided evidence for the additional regulatory role of CpxAR or RstAB systems on MDR efflux pumps and porins.

## Effect on virulence in A. baumannii

The Caenorhabditis elegans–A. baumannii infection model was employed to determine the involvement of rstAB in virulence. The WT and mutant strains were examined for their abilities to kill C. elegans. The WT strain displayed 10% and 20% killing at 96 and 120 h, respectively. However, the mutant strain killed only 4% of the worms after 96 h $( p < 0 . 0 1 )$ . The E. coli strain OP50 was used as negative control. Thus, our findings demonstrate that the rstAB mutant kills C. elegans more slowly than the wild-type strain. 

## 18.3.4 Discussion

Numerous outbreaks caused by multidrug-resistant Gramnegative pathogens from different parts of the world are appearing very rapidly (Haley et al., 1985; Vincent et al., 1995). There is an urgent need to develop new anti-infectives. Due to their central role in bacterial virulence regulation and their absence in animals, including humans, TCSs have been suggested as targets for antimicrobials (Stephenson and Hoch, 2002); thus, it is prudent to investigate their role in bacterial physiology in detail (see Section 3). The commonly found TCS in the bacterial kingdom is the OmpR-type regulator, which is known to perform diverse functions, for example modulating expression of the type VI secretion system in Yersinia pseudotuberculosis to maintain intracellular pH homeostasis, regulating motility by positive regulation of flhDC, altering expression of ompC and ompF in enteric bacteria, capsular polysaccharide synthesizing in Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, and phoP in virulence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Hu et al., 2009; Mattison et al., 2002; Ryndak et al., 2008; Santander et al., 2007). CpxAR and RstAB are members of the OmpR family, their functions well characterized in E. coli and Salmonella (Hirakawa et al., 2003a; Hu et al., 2011). In this study, the unknown functions of CpxAR from K. pneumoniae and RstAB from A. baumannii were decoded. The recently sequenced genomic data of K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044, encoding 4992 proteins, revealed the presence of the CpxAR operon in its genome. The operon was disrupted, and our study has elucidated its overall effects on general physiology and on antibiotic and disinfectant resistance in the pleomorphic bacillus K. pneumoniae. 

BfmRS, an rstAB homolog from the ompR family, has been characterized in A. baumannii 19606 (type strain), where it is shown to regulate expression of the CsuA–BABCDE chaperone– usher secretion system required for formation of biofilm structures in this pleomorphic bacillus (Gaddy and Actis, 2009: see Section 22). Liou et al. have recently shown that BfmRS in A. baumannii 17978 (a drug-susceptible strain isolated in France in 1951 from a 4-month-old infant with fatal meningitis; 

Accession no. CP000521) has a role in cell adhesion, resistance to serum killing, virulence, and antibiotic susceptibility (Liou et al., 2014). Interestingly, the homolog of bfmRS is found in the genome of recently sequenced A. baumannii ACICU (an epidemic multidrug-resistant clinical isolate responsible for an outbreak in Rome, Italy, in 2005; Accession no. CP000863), A. baumannii AB307-0294 (obtained from the blood of a patient hospitalized in Buffalo, New York, in 1994; Accession no. CP001172), A. baumannii AB900 (perineal isolate obtained in 2003 from an active-duty military patient at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center (WRNMMC), United States; Accession no. ABXK00000000), A. baumannii AB0057 (MDR bloodstream isolate collected in 2004 from a patient at WRNMMC; Accession no. ABJM01000001), and A. baumannii AYE (an epidemic multidrug-resistant clinical isolate responsible for a nationwide outbreak in France in 2001; Accession no. CU459141). Our study has shown for the first time its unprecedented involvement in biofilm formation, stress response, tolerance to antibiotics and disinfectants, and virulence. In the presence of osmotic and bile challenges, the rstAB mutant exhibited two- to threefold lower survival capabilities than the wild type, and its level of growth in physiological pH was slightly impaired. It is likely, therefore, that the rstAB factor controls functions required for survival of bacteria in the host, where they encounter environmental assaults such as high osmolarity and bile salts. Reactive oxygen species, including $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , superoxide, and hydroxyl radical, are toxic to cells due to their ability to damage DNA and especially proteins containing iron–sulfur clusters or sulfur atoms (see Section 10). In bacteria, many transcription factors have been found to sense the presence of reactive oxygen species and induce antioxidant systems. Evidence for the involvement of the rstAB system in oxidative stress tolerance has been demonstrated in this study. Yamaguchi et al. demonstrated the role of rstAB in β-lactam resistance in E. coli (Hirakawa et al., 2003b). Thirteen RRs present in the E. coli genome, including rstA when overreproduced in a drughypersensitive heterologous host, conferred low-level β-lactam resistance. In this study, we studied the role of rstAB in antibiotic resistance. Increased expression of efflux genes and porins may partly explain the resistant behavior shown by the rstAB mutant; however, detailed studies related to this hypothesis are highly warranted. In spite of regular preventive surface disinfection in clinical settings, inanimate surfaces have often been described as the source for the persistence of multidrug-resistant A. baumannii (Howard et al., 2012). This study provides primary evidence for the participation of rstAB TCSs in mediating disinfectant resistance. Involvement of rstAB in A. baumannii virulence further strengthens the multitasking ability of RstAB. 

## 18.3.5 Conclusions

In summary, our overall study provides, for the very first time, conclusive experimental evidence for the participation of OmpR family regulators in mediating resistance against cellular physiology, stress response, and antimicrobial resistance in multidrug-resistant strains of K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii.
