# Influence of BrpA and Psr on cell envelope homeostasis and virulence of Streptococcus mutans

Zezhang T. Wen1, Jacob P. Bitoun2, Sumei Liao3, and Jacqueline Abranches4 

1Center for Oral and Craniofacial Biology, Department of Comprehensive Dentistry and Biomaterials, and Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Parasitology, Louisiana State University Health Sciences Center, New Orleans, Louisiana, USA 

2Department of Microbiology & Immunology, Tulane University, New Orleans, Louisiana, USA 

3Division of Allergy and Clinical Immunology, Departments of Medicine and Immunology, University of Colorado Denver, Aurora, Colorado, USA 

4Center for Oral Biology, University of Rochester Medical Center, Rochester, New York, USA 

## 18.4.1 Introduction

The oral cavity is a dynamic environment that undergoes frequent and often rapid fluctuations in pH and in the presence of reactive oxygen species (ROS); see Section 10, among other stressors. In the oral cavity, a variety of antibacterial compounds, such as fluoride, hydrogen peroxide, sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and chlorhexidine, come from oral care products (e.g., toothpastes and mouth rinses). On the other hand, many bacteria residing within the oral cavity can also produce hydrogen peroxide and antimicrobial peptides (bacteriocins) (Kuramitsu et al., 2007). Streptococcus mutans, a key etiological agent of human dental caries, lives almost exclusively on the tooth surface in biofilms better known as dental plaque. This bacterium possesses multiple mechanisms to colonize the tooth surfaces and under certain conditions, such as frequent consumption of a sucrose-rich diet, can become numerically significant, leading to carious lesions (Burne, 1998; Hamada and Slade, 1980). S. mutans is known for its ability to survive and adapt to environmental insults, including mounting protective responses in reaction to various stimuli (Burne, 1998; Lemos and Burne, 2008). 

Biofilm regulatory protein A (BrpA) is a protein of 406 amino acid residues with a C-terminal region sharing some similarity to the LytR–CpsA–Psr (LCP) family of proteins (Bitoun et al., 2012a, 2013; Hubscher et al., 2008). LCP proteins are a group of putative membrane-associated proteins widespread in Grampositive bacteria, and limited studies so far have shown that LCP proteins play a key role in cell envelope biogenesis, stress tolerance, biofilm formation (see Section 22), and modulation of expression of proteins involved in these processes (Bitoun et al., 2012a, 2013; Hanson et al., 2011, 2012; Hubscher et al., 2008; 

Wen and Burne, 2002. Wen et al., 2006). The Psr protein also possesses homology to members of the LCP family of proteins, with the highest similarity to the penicillin-sensitive repressor (Psr) proteins (Bitoun et al., 2013). Different from Psr and other members of the LCP family of proteins, however, BrpA possesses an additional domain on its C-terminus of about 100 amino acid residues that is composed of more than 30% serine and threonine. It is therefore possible to target BrpA in drug therapy and/or vaccination as a novel strategy against S. mutans and human dental caries, which is still a major health problem worldwide. Our recent studies have shown that both BrpA and Psr play crucial roles in S. mutans stress tolerance responses and biofilm formation, traits critical to the ability of this bacterium to cause carious diseases (Bitoun et al., 2012a; Wen et al., 2006; Wen and Burne, 2002). Both redundancy and differences in functionality exist between these two paralogs (Bitoun et al., 2013). The expression of BrpA is regulated in response to environmental conditions and cell density (Bitoun et al., 2012a). Consistently, deficiency of BrpA affects expression of genes known to be critical in stress tolerance, cell envelope homeostasis, bacterial adherence, and biofilm formation (Bitoun et al., 2012a; Wen et al., 2006; see Section 22). 

## 18.4.2 Deficiency of BrpA and Psr causes major defects in biofilm formation

Identified via a functional genomics approach, BrpA is shown to have drastic effects in S. mutans biofilm formation; such effects appear to be primarily related to biofilm accumulation and structure and are sucrose independent (Wen and Burne, 2002; Yoshida and Kuramitsu, 2002; see Section 22). In vitro 

studies have used 96-well plates under static conditions and glass slides and hydroxylapatite discs, a commonly used tooth model, under both static and continuous flowing conditions, and the results so far have shown that like the wild type, UA159, the BrpA-deficient mutant, TW14D (formerly TW14), is still capable of binding to the surfaces tested, albeit to a slightly reduced degree, and forms sparse microcolonies of various sizes. Unlike the wild type, however, the deficient mutant has limited ability to accumulate and develop into mature biofilms, especially under continuous flowing conditions (Bitoun et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2006). Unlike the smooth, evenly distributed biofilms of the wild type, the mutant biofilms are thin, loose, and sparse, as revealed by confocal laser-scanning microscopy (CLSM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure 18.4.1) (Bitoun et al., 2012a, 2013; Wen et al., 2006). S. mutans possesses at least three glucosyltransferases, GtfB, GtfC, and GtfD; and, in the presence of sucrose, it can produce copious glucose polymers (Bowen and Koo, 2011; Vacca-Smith and Bowen, 1998). These adhesive glucans (also mutans), along with the Gtf enzymes and glucan-binding proteins, constitute a sucrose-dependent pathway of biofilm formation that plays a central role in S. mutans’ dominance in cariogenic plaque and caries formation (see Chapter 22.3). When sucrose is present in the growth medium, both S. mutans wild type and the BrpA mutants form better biofilms than they do with glucose as the sole carbohydrate source, but the depth of the biofilms formed by the deficient mutants is still less than that of the wild type (Wen et al., 2006; Wen and Burne, 2002; Yoshida and Kuramitsu, 2002). Relative to the parent strain, this mutant also displayed a moderate reduction in capacity to bind to and form biofilms on surfaces coated with human saliva. Consistently, biacore assays have demonstrated a reduction by more than 57% in salivary agglutininmediated whole-cell receptor interaction in the mutant lacking BrpA (Bitoun et al., 2012a).

S. mutans wild type (UA159), BrpA mutant (TW14D), Psr mutant (TW251), and the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant (TW314) were grown in BM medium supplemented with glucose, sucrose, and glucose plus sucrose, and biofilms were grown on hydroxylapatite discs. After 48 h, biofilms were stained with LIVE/DEAD BacLight fluorescent dye and dissected optically using confocal laser-scanning microscopy. Images presented here are representatives of xyz, xz, and yz images (512 × 512) from cultures grown in BM with glucose plus sucrose. Bitoun et al., 2013, Microbiol. 159: 493–506. With permission of SGM.


BrpA deficiency does not have a significant impact on growth rate during planktonic growth. However, relative to the parent strain, the deficient mutant does have a higher tendency to form longer chains that are more than twice the length of the parent strain (Wen and Burne, 2002). Moreover, the deficient mutant also has a higher autolysis rate and decreases viability (Bitoun et al., 2012a, 2013; Wen et al., 2006). CLSM analysis of BrpA-deficient and wild-type biofilms stained with Live/Dead BacLight fluorescent dye revealed that the BrpA mutant had a heightened number of cells stained with red fluorescence (dead cells), and more cell debris can be identified in the mutant biofilms than in the wild type under SEM (Wen et al., 2006). 

Like BrpA, deficiency of Psr causes little effects during planktonic growth but results in major defects in biofilm formation, especially in the presence of sucrose. Unlike the wild type and the BrpA mutant, however, biofilms of the Psr-deficient mutant, TW251, are typically planar, flat, and tight. As revealed by CLSM analysis coupled with Alexa-488-conjugated concanavalin A staining, the BrpA-deficient mutant produces significantly more glucans than the parent strain during growth in a sucrosecontaining medium (Figure 18.4.2) (Bitoun et al., 2012a, 2013). In contrast, the Psr mutant biofilms contain little or no glucans under the same conditions. BrpA and Psr double deficiency appears to be lethal under the conditions studied (Bitoun et al., 2013). A Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant, TW314, was shown to have severe defects in biofilm formation. Interestingly, the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant biofilms also contained a lot more glucans than the wild type (Figure 18.4.2) and the respective BrpA and Psr single mutants. See Section 18.4.7 for more details on the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant. 

## 18.4.3 BrpA and Psr are required for acid tolerance

S. mutans is endowed with a high capacity to withstand acid challenge (aciduricity), one of the most significant virulence attributes of this cariogenic bacterium (see Section 16). In addition, this bacterium is also capable of launching an adaptive acid tolerance response that is characterized by enhanced resistance to lower pH following initial exposure to a sublethal lowpH environment (Burne, 1998; Lemos and Burne, 2008; Quivey et al., 1995a). The role of BrpA in acid tolerance was first observed during growth in broth adjusted to low pH, where the wild-type strain had a final culture optical density $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 \mathrm { n m } } )$ of approximately 0.49 after 48 h and the BrpA-deficient mutant could reach only 0.24, indicative of defects in acid tolerance as a result of BrpA deficiency (Wen et al., 2006). As revealed by acid-killing assays, by incubating the bacterium in a low-pH buffer (pH 2.8) for different time points, BrpA deficiency significantly increases the susceptibility of S. mutans to low pH. Relative to the parent strain, the survival rate of the deficient mutant, TW14D, was 1 log lower when incubated in buffer at pH 2.8 for 45 min (Figure 18.4.3a). To assess the role of BrpA in the acid tolerance response, S. mutans strains were incubated in brain heart infusion (BHI) adjusted to a sublethal pH 5.0 for 1 h prior to the acid-killing assay; such pre-exposure is known to significantly enhance the ability of S. mutans to survive low pH (Figure 18.4.3b). Like wild-type UA159, the BrpA mutant, TW14D, significantly increased its survival rate after initial incubation at pH 5.0 (Figure 18.4.3b). Relative to UA159, however, the survival rate is still significantly lower. These results suggest that BrpA influences acid tolerance in S. mutans, and this effect is mostly related to constitutive acid tolerance rather than mounting an inducible acid tolerance response. Similar results can also be seen with the mutant deficient in Psr, TW251, as highlighted in Figure 18.4.3, indicative of a similar role for Psr in acid tolerance response (Bitoun et al., 2013). Unlike BrpA and Psr single mutants, the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant, TW314, was shown to have lost its ability to launch an adaptive acid tolerance response (Figure 18.4.3b). 

## 18.4.4 BrpA, but not Psr, affects the susceptibility to oxidative stress

Like other oral bacteria, S. mutans must cope with various oxidative stress conditions, including damaging ROS and unfavorable cellular redox potential (Marquis, 1995). ROS, such as ${ \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } } ^ { - }$ , OH, and $\mathrm { R } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ are produced inside the bacterial cells when growing in an aerobic environment. ROS can be fatal if not detoxified promptly, as they cause oxidization of proteins and nucleic acids as well as lipid peroxidation (see Section 10). Recent studies have shown that the presence of oxygen also induces complex changes in the transcriptome of S. mutans, including genes affecting cell envelope biogenesis and stress tolerance (Ahn and Burne, 2007; Ahn et al., 2007). S. mutans lacks a complete respiratory chain and does not normally carry out oxidative phosphorylation (Marquis, 1995). In S. mutans, oxygen metabolism is largely mediated by NADH oxidases (Nox), which reduces oxygen to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ through oxidation of NAD(H) to

This bacterium also lacks catalase but does possess superoxide dismutase (SOD), alkyl hydroperoxide reductase (AhpCF), and peroxide resistance protein (Dpr) (Ajdic et al., 2002; Higuchi et al., 2000; Marquis, 1995; Yamamoto et al., 2000). SOD catalyzes dismutation of superoxide, yielding hydrogen peroxide, which is then reduced by AhpCF and Dpr. These enzymes are believed to play an essential role in ROS detoxification and the oxidative stress response (Higuchi et al., 2000; Jakubovics et al., 2002; Marquis, 1995; Yamamoto et al., 2000; see Section 10). In addition to these classical oxidative stress response genes (details on gene regulation are discussed further in this chapter), BrpA deficiency also influences the susceptibility of S. mutans to oxidative stress. As shown in an in vitro challenge assay using planktonic cultures, the ability of S. mutans to survive hydrogen peroxide challenge at 0.2% (w/v or 58 mM, final concentration) decreases by more than 3 log as a result of BrpA deficiency (TW14, Figure 18.4.4), when compared to the parent strain, UA159. However, no such effects have been observed with the Psr-deficient mutants under these conditions (Bitoun et al., 2013). 

## 18.4.5 BrpA deficiency affects cell division, cell envelope, and the susceptibility of the deficient mutants to cell envelope stressors

The cell envelope is of essential importance for growth, cell morphology, cell division, interaction with the environment, and antimicrobial resistance. S. mutans strains deficient in BrpA have a decreased viability and an increased autolysis rate, suggesting a role for BrpA in cell envelope biogenesis and/or homeostasis. Under the transmission electron microscope (TEM), the BrpA-deficient mutant also has a rougher and fibrous outer surface (peptidoglycan) when compared to the wild type, UA159 (Figure 18.4.5a). Relative to the parent strain, the deficient mutant, TW14D, also tends to form longer chains (Figure 18.4.5b) and exists in biofilms as a chain of fatty Buddha beads (Bitoun et al., 2013). Like BrpA, Psr deficiency also leads to an elevated autolysis rate (Bitoun et al., 2013). However, unlike BrpA, the Psr-deficient mutant possesses no major defects in cell morphology under TEM (Figure 18.4.5a). In contrast, the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant, TW314, displays severe defects in cell division (Figure 18.4.5c) (see Section 19.4.7 for more details). 

Consistently, as shown by a plate-based susceptibility assay, BrpA deficiency significantly reduces the ability of the mutants to survive several cell envelope–active antimicrobial agents and detergents (Bitoun et al., 2012a). Among the antimicrobial agents tested, nisin and bacitracin showed the most significant changes in minimal inhibition concentration (Bitoun et al., 2012a). These two antibiotics interfere with Lipid II cycling, blocking peptidoglycan and cell wall biosynthesis (Breukink and de Kruijff, 2006). In minimal bactericidal concentration, the BrpA-deficient mutant has a ≥1.5-fold reduction in colonyforming units against nisin, chlorhexidine, and SDS (Bitoun et al., 2012a), chemicals that can compromise membrane integrity and are commonly used in oral healthcare products. Taken altogether, these results provide further support for a role for BrpA in regulation of cell envelope biogenesis and homeostasis by S. mutans. However, no such effects were observed with the Psr-deficient mutant (Bitoun et al., 2013). 

## 18.4.6 BrpA deficiency affects virulence in a Galleria mellonella model

Recent studies have shown that a subset of strains of S. mutans, such as OMZ175 (serotype f), are highly invasive and consequently may play a significant role in the development of certain systemic diseases, such as infective endocarditis (Abranches et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 2005). Invasion assays using human coronary artery endothelial cells (HCAECs) (Abranches et al., 2009) revealed that a BrpA deficiency in OMZ175 only slightly reduces the invasion efficiency $\left( \mathinner { p \mathopen { = } 0 . 0 8 9 } \right)$ . The mutant was also analyzed using a Galleria mellonella (wax worm) model for systemic disease. This model is widely used to screen microbial virulence and has been used to investigate a number of bacterial pathogens, including group A streptococci and S. mutans (Kajfasz et al., 2010; Loh et al., 2013). The results showed that the survival rate of worms infected with the BrpA-deficient mutants was significantly higher than that of the infected wildtype strain OMZ175 $( p < 0 . 0 1 )$ (Figure 18.4.6). However, no major differences could be measured when strain UA159 and its BrpA-deficient mutants were compared in the wax worms $( p >$ 0.05) (Bitoun et al., 2012a). In contrast, when the Psr-deficient mutants were analyzed, no differences were observed between the parent strains, OMZ175 and UA159, and their respective Psrdeficient mutants (Bitoun et al., 2013).

## 18.4.7 Double deficiency of BrpA and Psr is lethal

It is apparent that some level of redundancy can be identified in functions of BrpA and Psr in S. mutans’ pathophysiology. To investigate the impact of a BrpA and Psr double deficiency, repeated efforts were made, but failed, to generate this double mutant. Moreover, mutants with allelic replacement of the chromosomal copy of both brpA and psr could only be achieved in the presence of a wild-type copy of the brpA or psr in a shuttle vector. These results suggest that a functional BrpA or Psr is likely required for viability in S. mutans, which is similar to what has been found in Bacillus subtilis, but different from Staphylococcus aureus (Kawai et al., 2011; Over et al., 2011). Characterization of a Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant further revealed that Psr deficiency and BrpA-down expression cause severe defects in cell division and morphology (Figure 18.4.5) (Bitoun et al., 2013). Unlike the wild type and the respective BrpA and Psr single mutants, the Psr-deficient and BrpAdown mutant forms severe clumps in broth, and it exists predominantly in longer chains of dividing cells and cells with multiple septa as observed by TEM and SEM analyses, which further supports a role for BrpA and Psr in cell division and separation. In addition, the amount and frequency of mesosomes were also increased in the BrpA mutant, and especially in the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant, TW314 (Figure 18.4.5c) (Bitoun et al., 2013). The Psr deficiency and BrpA-down expression were shown to further compromise the acid tolerance response in S. mutans, resulting in loss of the ability to mount an adaptive acid tolerance response (Figure 18.4.3b; see Section 16). Characteristically, the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant biofilms formed in the presence of sucrose are loosely bound and patchy, and they contained what appeared to be a plume of microcolonies, with drastic increases in glucans (Figure 18.4.2) (Bitoun et al., 2013). 

## 18.4.8 BrpA expression is regulated in response to environmental conditions

As revealed by promoter mapping and reporter gene fusions, the expression of brpA is differentially regulated under the direction of two different promoters (Bitoun et al., 2012a; Wen et al., 2006). Under the conditions studied so far, brpA can be cotranscribed with its upstream locus, brpB, as a two-gene operon (Bitoun et al., 2012a), while the intergenic region of 344 base pairs also possesses promoter activity (Wen et al., 2006). As shown by luciferase reporter fusion assays, BrpA expression is at its maximum during the early exponential phase (Bitoun et al., 2012a), consistent with our earlier study by Northern blotting (Wen and Burne, 2004). In agreement with a role of BrpA in environmental and cell envelope stress responses, the level of luciferase reporter activity also significantly increases in cells following treatment with hydrogen peroxide, methyl viologen, SDS, chlorhexidine, and various cell envelope antimicrobials at their respective subinhibitory concentrations (Table 18.4.1) (Bitoun et al., 2012a). Efforts were also made to evaluate the impact of pH on BrpA expression, but the results were inconclusive, probably due to the impact of low pH on the luciferase enzyme.

Consistent with its broad role in S. mutans pathophysiology, a deficiency of BrpA causes substantial alterations in the

During the early exponential phase, where brpA transcription is at its maximum, microarray analysis identified 92 genes upregulated and 90 downregulated by a factor of at least 1.5-fold, relative to the wild-type strain UA159 (Bitoun et al., 2012a). In mid-exponential phase cultures, more than 41 genes were identified as up- or downregulated in response to BrpA deficiency (Wen et al., 2006). While distinctive differences exist between the two transcriptional profiles of the early exponential phase and the mid-exponential phase cultures, the breadth of impact of BrpA deficiency on the transcriptional profile is very similar, which includes genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis, carbohydrates and energy metabolism, nucleic acids and DNA metabolism, and molecular chaperones and other cellular processes (Bitoun et al., 2012a). More details on the genes affected in response to BrpA deficiency can be found in our recent articles (see Wen et al., 2006). Those known to play critical roles in S. mutans stress tolerance responses, cell envelope homeostasis, and biofilm formation are listed in Table 18.4.2. 

## 18.4.9.1 Acid and oxidative stress tolerance

It is known that many of the stressors encountered by bacteria in the oral cavity induce DNA damage; in particular, acid and oxidative stresses increase the formation of abasic sites in DNA (see Sections 10 and 16 respectively). Earlier studies by the Quivey group and others showed that DNA repair systems, including recombinant protein RecA, and stress response pathways are directly linked in S. mutans (Lemos and Burne, 2008; Quivey et al., 1995a). In response to BrpA deficiency, recA expression is reduced by more than 2.7-fold in both early and mid-exponential phase cultures; therefore, reduction of RecA is likely a major factor that underlies the compromised acid and oxidative stress tolerance (Bitoun et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2006). Among the downregulated genes is also ropA for Trigger factor, a ribosome-associated peptidyl-prolyl cis–trans isomerase that is highly conserved in most bacteria (Wen et al., 2005). In S. mutans, deficiency of RopA weakens tolerance to acid-killing and oxidative stresses induced by hydrogen peroxide and paraquat. The membrane-associated proton-translocating F-ATPase is known to be the primary determinant that allows S. mutans to maintain intracellular pH homeostasis (Bowden and Hamilton, 1998). It is believed to be the major factor involved in acid tolerance response in this bacterium (Quivey et al., 1995a,b). Interestingly, expression of F-ATPase is increased by more than 2.5-fold in early exponential phase cultures (Bitoun et al., 2012a), but reduced by as much as 5.6-fold in mid-exponential phase cultures (Wen et al., 2006) when compared to the wild type. It is apparent that BrpA deficiency weakens the ability of the deficient mutant to tolerate acid and low pH. Initially, the mutant is able to compensate by increasing F-ATPase expression. However, as the defects in cell envelope and the reduction in expression of genes such as recA continue, the cells would likely fail to keep up the compensatory response (Bitoun et al., 2012a; Wen et al., 2006).

Redox repressor (Rex) in Bacillus subtilis and Streptomyces coelicolor is a transcriptional repressor involved in regulation of oxidative stress and central metabolism in response to intracellular NADH or NAD+ level (Brekasis and Paget, 2003; Pagels et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008). Our recent studies have shown that Rex in S. mutans functions as a repressor and an activator, regulating central fermentation pathways, oxidative stress tolerance, and biofilm formation (Baker et al., 2014; Bitoun et al., 2011, 2012b). Relative to the wild type, Rex deficiency causes major defects in oxidative stress, biofilm formation, and alterations in expression of a large number of genes. In S. mutans, rex is significantly downregulated in response to BrpA deficiency (Bitoun et al., 2011, 2012a). As part of the BrpA regulon, reduction of Rex likely contributes to the weakened oxidative stress responses of the BrpA-deficient mutant as well. 

As detailed in Section 18.4.4, Sod, Nox, and Dpr in oral streptococci have been shown to play major roles in oxidative stress tolerance responses and are highly inducible by oxidative stresses (Derr et al., 2012; Jakubovics et al., 2002; Lemos and Burne, 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2000). Characteristically, sod, nox, and dpr all are elevated in the BrpA mutant (Wen et al., 2006). Upregulation of protective enzymes SOD, Dpr, and Nox may signal oxidative stresses of the BrpA-deficient mutant. In support of this theory, genes for molecular chaperones GroEL, DnaK, and DnaJ and ATPase ClpE can also be identified as upregulated in response to BrpA deficiency. DnaK, DnaJ, and GroEL are involved in protein folding, renaturation, and presentation proteins for degradation, and are known for playing important roles in control of various stress responses (Lemos and Burne, 2008). ClpE ATPase is also a well-known member of the stress regulon in Bacillus spp. and S. mutans (Lemos and 

Burne, 2002). Members of the molecular chaperones and stress regulons are typically upregulated in response to various stresses (Lemos and Burne, 2008). 

## 18.4.9.2 Cell envelope homeostasis and cell division

The bacterial cell wall is a repeating, three-dimensional polymer known as peptidoglycan or murein, consisting of a linear, alternating N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) and Nacetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) motif, cross-linked via peptides appended to MurNAc. Of the genes altered in response to BrpA deficiency, several encode proteins with potential roles in peptidoglycan biosynthesis (Bitoun et al., 2012a). Among them are rgpG for a putative N-acetyl glucosaminyltransferase, murG for a putative undecaprenyl-PP-MurNAc-pentapeptide-UDP-GlcNAc transferase, ddlA for a D-alanine-D-alanine ligase, and murE for a UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase. The exact roles of these gene products remain unclear; however, downregulation of genes involved in peptidoglycan synthesis would have an impact on cell envelope biogenesis and homeostasis, leading to defects in cell envelope integrity. Such defects would likely contribute to altered cell morphology, reduced viability, an elevated autolysis rate, and increased susceptibility to cell envelope antimicrobials and detergents (Bitoun et al., 2012a, 2013; Wen et al., 2006). Cell envelope defects would also likely lead to weakened capacity to survive and respond to environmental insults, and therefore, this feature can partly explain the weakened acid and oxidative stress responses of the BrpA-deficient mutants (Bitoun et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2006). Besides, several genes predicted to encode proteins with important roles in cell division are also affected as a result of BrpA deficiency. Among them are the putative cell division proteins FtsW, FtsQ, and FtsX and the glucose-inhibited division protein GidA. Downregulation of genes for cell division proteins will likely have an effect on cell morphology, which could be in part attributed to the observed long chains in BrpA mutants, especially the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant. 

## 18.4.9.3 Biofilm formation

Biofilm formation is a sequential process that is initiated with bacterial adherence to a surface. It is followed by multiplication and formation of microcolonies. Surface-associated growth also triggers production of extracellular polymeric matrices, which include polysaccharides and deoxyribonucleic acids (environmental DNA (eDNA)) (Bowen and Koo, 2011; Liao et al., 2014; see Section 22). Accumulating data suggest that a series of highly coordinated physiological and biochemical functions are required for the bacterium to form mature biofilms in response to environmental cues (Abranches et al., 2006, 2008; Jefferson, 2004; Stanley and Lazazzera, 2004; Vlamakis et al., 2013; Wen and Burne, 2004; Wen et al., 2006, 2011). In vitro model studies under static and continuously flowing conditions have showed that defects in biofilm formation as a result of BrpA deficiency are mostly related to biofilm accumulation and biofilm development, although moderate reduction in adherence can also be measured. The decreased viability, the reduced acid and oxidative tolerance, and the compromised cell envelope integrity are likely part of the contributing factors to the weakened capacity of the deficient mutant to accumulate and develop mature biofilms. Besides, BrpA deficiency is also shown to affect adhesin P1– and the glucans-mediated bacterial cell–surface and cell–cell interactions. 

Adhesin P1 is part of the sucrose-independent pathway of S. mutans biofilm formation. It mediates high-affinity bacterial adherence to the salivary pellicle via interactions with salivary agglutinin (Crowley et al., 1999). Recently, P1 is also shown to form amyloid, a proteinaceous nanofiber also known to play an important role in bacterial adherence and biofilm formation in Bacillus spp. and several other bacteria (Oli et al., 2012; Romero et al., 2010). The expression of P1 is upregulated in response to BrpA deficiency, as revealed by Western blot analysis, but interestingly, both biofilm formation on saliva-coated surfaces and biacore analysis of the agglutinin-mediated whole cell– receptor interactions showed that the BrpA-deficient mutant has a reduced ability to interact with salivary agglutinins (Bitoun et al., 2012a). Likely, the reduced stability and/or misfolding of P1 are the underlying factors. In support of this theory, several genes encoding components of the Sec translocase were also found altered in BrpA mutants (Table 18.4.2). Alteration in expression of members of the Sec translocon complex, as well as the global defects in cell envelope integrity, will likely influence the function of the translocation machinery. Therefore, the increased P1 expression could be a result of a compensatory reaction to such a compromise, although the underlying mechanism awaits further investigation. In addition, results of Western blotting that showed disproportional increases in density of lower molecular weight bands reactive to antibodies recognizing truncated P1 also suggest a compromise in stability of P1. These results also suggest that BrpA deficiency may affect bacterial adherence and biofilm formation by S. mutans on the tooth surface as well. 

The adhesive glucans, especially the water-insoluble α1,3- linked glucans of GtfB and GtfC, are fundamental in sucroseinduced biofilm formation and cariogenicity of S. mutans (Bowen and Koo, 2011; Vacca-Smith and Bowen, 1998). The GtfD product is soluble and readily metabolized to function as primers for GtfB (Bowen and Koo, 2011). In addition, recent studies by us and others have shown that alterations in glucan structure and/or the ratio of glucans to glucan-binding proteins could have a significant impact on S. mutans’ surface adherence and biofilm formation (Bitoun et al., 2011; Hazlett et al., 1998; Wen et al., 2005). As revealed by DNA microarray analysis and further confirmed by real-time PCR and Western blotting, gtfB was upregulated by 2.4-fold in response to BrpA deficiency, while no significant differences in gtfD and gtfC could be measured between the mutant and the parent strain. These results are consistent with the increased amount of glucans observed for mutant biofilms under CLSM and measured by a colorimetric assay (Bitoun et al., 2013). It is likely that the alteration in GtfB expression will lead to changes in glucan structure and/or the ratio of glucans to glucan-binding proteins, and thus influence surface attachment and biofilm formation by the deficient mutant (Bitoun et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2005). Besides roles in acid and oxidative tolerance responses, as mentioned in this chapter, deficiency of trigger factor RopA in S. mutans also significantly reduces the expression of GtfB and GtfD (Wen et al., 2005). Thus, reduction of RopA expression is also a likely contributor to defects in biofilm formation by the BrpA-deficient mutant. 

## 18.4.9.4 Psr influences different sets of genes

Real-time PCR and Western blot analyses have shown that Psr deficiency also affects gene expression in the deficient mutants. While the exact impact of Psr deficiency on the transcriptional profile is still under investigation, our studies so far also suggest that Psr may influence different sets of genes from BrpA and that other factors are likely involved in BrpA- and Psr-mediated regulations. For instance, Psr deficiency leads to downregulation of the expression of gtfC and gtfD by 3.9- and 3.0-fold, respectively, which is different from BrpA, but consistent with the deficiency of glucans and the reduced biofilm formation by the Psr mutant (Bitoun et al., 2013). Interestingly, opposing effects in gtfB and gtfC expression can also be seen in the Psrdeficient and BrpA-down mutant. Specifically, the Psr-deficient and BrpA-down mutant is featured with increases of gtfB by 16- fold and gtfC by 6.13-fold and a reduction of gtfD by 1.52-fold (Bitoun et al., 2013). Similar patterns can also be seen with genes involved in cell division. However, the details of the underlying mechanism await further investigation. 

## 18.4.10 Summary and future directions

BrpA and Psr are paralogs of the LCP family proteins, but they are different from Psr and other members of the LCP family proteins; BrpA also possesses a serine–threonine-rich C-terminal domain that is seemingly unique to S. mutans (Wen and Burne, 2002). Both BrpA and Psr play an important role in S. mutans pathophysiology, including autolysis, acid tolerance response, and biofilm formation (Bitoun et al., 2012a, 2013; Wen and Burne, 2002; Wen et al., 2006). However, different from BrpA, Psr deficiency has no major effect on oxidative stress, cell morphology and cell envelope stress responses, and S. mutans’ infectivity and virulence in the wax worm model. Both BrpA and Psr affect gene expression, including those known to play critical roles in S. mutans biofilm formation, although different sets of genes seem to be targeted. A double deficiency of BrpA and Psr is not viable in S. mutans, which is similar to B. subtilis but different from S. aureus (Bitoun et al., 2013; Kawai et al., 2011; Over et al., 2011). 

Initially identified in B. subtilis, LCP proteins are widely annotated as cell envelope–associated transcriptional regulators (Hubscher et al., 2008; Lazarevic et al., 1992). In Streptococcus agalactiae and Streptococcus iniae, CpsA was shown to be able to bind specifically to the promoter and influence the expression of target genes, including those for capsule biosynthesis (Hanson et al., 2011, 2012). In B. subtilis and S. pneumoniae, there is also evidence that LCP proteins are the long-sought-after enzymes that covalently anchor the anionic cell wall polymers to the cell wall peptidoglycan (Chan et al., 2013; Eberhardt et al., 2012; Kawai et al., 2011). Nevertheless, wide diversity exists in structure and function between members of the LCP family of proteins. It remains unclear how BrpA and Psr modulate the expression of target genes and the pathophysiology of S. mutans.

# Modulators of the bacterial two-component systems involved in envelope stress, transport, and virulence

Rajeev Misra 

School of Life Sciences, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, USA 

## 18.5.1 Introduction

Bacteria are known for their remarkable abilities to adapt to the changing environments in which they live. One of the major ways they achieve this adaptability is through their signal transduction pathways, which allow them to sense and respond appropriately to environmental changes via transcriptional or posttranscriptional regulations (for reviews, see Hoch and Silhavy, 1995; Stock et al., 2000). Signal sensing is achieved directly or indirectly via modulators, by a signal-specific sensor kinase (SK) in which a conserved histidine residue is phosphorylated by adenosine triphosphate (ATP) (Figure 18.5.1). It is for this reason that SKs are also known as histidine kinases (HKs). 

Typically, phosphorylated SKs transfer their high-energy phosphate group directly to the conserved aspartate residue of the cognate response regulator (RR) (Figure 18.5.1). However, this phosphorelay reaction could also involve intermediate steps of intra- and intermolecular phosphorylation. The phosphorylation of the RR results in changes to its DNA- or proteinbinding properties, which in turn changes the gene expression or protein–protein interactions for an appropriate cellular response. Together, SK and RR constitute the two-component systems (TCSs) (see Section 3). 

For over two decades, it has been known that TCSs’ activities are often modulated by additional components referred to as accessory/auxiliary factors or modulators. These additional components primarily target the SK component of a TCS and influence its signal reception and/or various enzymatic activities (for a review, see Buelow and Raivio, 2010). Some of them are also known to connect two different TCSs to widen the cellular responses to different stress signals (for a review, see Mitrophanov and Groisman, 2008). 

The focus of this chapter is the envelope-localized modulators and connectors of TCSs in bacteria (Table 18.5.1). From their outer membrane location, modulators RcsF and NlpE can sense cell surface changes to activate appropriate TCSs. Modulators that are localized in the periplasm (CpxP, LuxP, and TorT) or the inner membrane with a domain exposed to the periplasm (MzrA, SafA, YycH, YycI, and possibly SaeP) can participate in signal recognition or influence the signal-sensing periplasmic loop region of an SK. Finally, modulators that are localized in the inner membrane with no significant surface-exposed loops (UhpC) or a domain exposed to the cytoplasm (SaeQ, LprF, LprJ, and LiaF) can directly influence the transmembrane (TM) or the dimerization and histidine phosphotransfer (DHp) domain of the SK. 

## 18.5.2 RcsF and RcsA, modulators of the RcsCDB TCS

This TCS primarily controls colonic acid capsule synthesis in Escherichia coli K-12 in response to various environmental cues and envelope stress (for a review, see Majdalani and Gottesman, 2005). The RcsCDB TCS is complex because, besides the transmembrane hybrid HK (RcsC) and the cytosolic RR (RcsB), it has another transmembrane component, RcsD, which mediates phosphorelay between RcsC and RcsB. 

The RcsCDB TCS has two modulators: an outer membrane lipoprotein (RcsF) and the cytosolic protein (RcsA) (Figure 18.5.2a). RcsF was first identified among plasmid clones that conferred an RcsB-dependent mucoidy phenotype and allowed growth of an ftsZ mutant on a salt-free medium (Gervais and Drapeau, 1992). The authors postulated that RcsF possibly acted to modulate RcsB phosphorylation directly or indirectly, since overexpression of RcsF did not affect rcsB expression. Castanie-´ Cornet et al. (2006) provided experimental validation of an earlier prediction by Hagiwara et al. (2003) that RcsF is indeed an outer membrane lipoprotein. Given its localization in the outer membrane, RcsF is unlikely to act on the cytosolic RcsB RR directly. Epistasis experiments showed that RcsF acts upstream of RcsC (Majdalani et al., 2005). RcsF was shown to be required for the activation of the Rcs system in response to perturbations in the envelope components, including lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and phospholipids (Majdalani et al., 2005; Shiba et al., 2004, 2012) and other environmental cues such as the presence of zinc (Hagiwara et al., 2003).

Figure 18.5.1 A carton showing the composition of a typical bacterial two-component system (TCS) (see Section 3). In this example, the sensor kinase (SK) is membrane bound, while its cognate response regulator (RR) is cytosolic. Although modulators of a TCS can be found in all bacterial compartments, only the inner membrane-bound modulators are shown here. Modulators can influence a TCS action in signal reception and/or by affecting various activities of SK or RR. H and D, and their phosphorylated forms, represent conserved histidine and aspartate residues, respectively, of SK and RR. A homodimer of the SK is shown. DHp, Dimerization and histidine phosphotransfer; peri, periplasm; IM, inner membrane; cyt, cytoplasm.


These observations suggest that RcsF senses changes in the cell surface structures and then activates the Rcs system by directly or indirectly interacting with the RcsC HK. However, despite the resolution of its three-dimensional structure (Leverrier et al., 2011), it is not well known how the outer membrane– localized lipoprotein RcsF interacts with the inner membrane– localized RcsC to activate the Rcs system. It has been reported that although mislocalization of RcsF to the periplasm or the inner membrane did not activate RcsC in response to changes in the LPS structure, the mislocalized RcsF variants activated the Rcs system either constitutively (Farris et al., 2010) or in response to some envelope perturbations (Hara et al., 2012). These observations suggest that envelope perturbations may enhance accessibility of RcsF to RcsC and that the outer membrane localization of RcsF is not a prerequisite for it to activate RcsC. Clearly, additional work is required to establish the molecular mechanism by which RscF senses envelope stress and activates RcsC. 

The cytosolic modulator RcsA works in concert with phosphorylated RcsB to activate the transcription of a subset of the Rcs-regulated genes (Figure 18.5.2a) (for reviews, see Huang et al., 2006; Majdalani and Gottesman, 2005). Mutations in rcsA along with rcsB and rcsC were obtained in a genetic screen that sought elevated expression of a cps::lacZ fusion (Gottesman et al., 1985). A key feature of RcsA is its short half-life in a background expressing the Lon protease, which limits capsule synthesis (Torres-Cabassa and Gottesman, 1987). Subsequently, it was shown that the ClpYQ protease is also involved in RcsA degradation (Kuo et al., 2004). Initial genetic experiments suggested that RcsA directly interacts with RcsB and that together they activate transcription of genes involved in capsule synthesis (Stout et al., 1991). However, since only a subset of RcsBregulated genes, including those involved in capsule synthesis, requires the presence of RcsA, it appears that promoter composition dictates the requirement for RcsA–RcsB∼P heteromers.

Figure 18.5.2 The outer membrane and periplasmic modulators of TCSs. (a) The RcsCDB TCS has two modulators: RcsF, an outer membrane (OM) lipoprotein, and cytosolic RcsA. RcsC is the histidine sensor kinase that phosphorylates the response regulator, RcsB, via the membrane-bound RcsD protein. RcsF senses perturbation in the OM to stimulate RcsC activity through some unknown mechanism. RcsA, together with phosphorylated RcsB, activates the expression of a subset of Rcs-regulated genes, including that of the cps operon involved in capsule synthesis. The CpxAR TCS also has two modulators: NlpE in the OM and CpxP in the periplasm (peri). Overexpression of NlpE activates CpxAR, while CpxP inhibits this TCS. The physiological and mechanistic aspects of CpxP-mediated CpxAR are better understood than those of NlpE. (b) TorT is the periplasmic modulator of the TorSR TCS that controls the expression of the torCAD operon involved in the anaerobic utilization of trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) as a terminal electron acceptor. TorT bound to TMAO stimulates the TorS hybrid sensor kinase. TorC, a c-type cytochrome, when not bound to heme inhibits TorS. LuxP is the periplasmic modulator of the LuxQUO TCS involved in quorum sensing. Binding of the autoinducer 2 (AI-2) to LuxP changes its conformation and LuxP–LuxQ interactions to activate LuxQ’s phosphatase activity.


In summary, the Rcs system is unique in that two modulators act at different steps of the signaling pathway, with RcsF in the outer membrane receiving environmental and envelope signals and activating RcsC HK, while RcsA in the cytoplasm works with the phosphorylated RcsB RR to influence expression of a subset of Rcs-regulated genes. 

## 18.5.3 NlpE and CpxP, modulators of the CpxAR TCS

CpxA is the transmembrane HK, while CpxR is the cognate RR. Like RcsCDB, the CpxAR TCS is activated in response to envelope perturbations, including changes in the membrane lipid composition and the accumulation of misfolded envelope proteins (for a review, see Raivio, 2014). Once activated, CpxAR can influence expression of several dozen genes whose products affect various envelope functions (Raivio et al., 2013; see Chapters 18.1 and 18.2). Among them, the degP gene encodes a major periplasmic protease whose CpxAR-dependent expression is crucial for reducing the envelope stress stemming from misfolded β-barrel OMPs (Gerken et al., 2010). In 1995, two back-to-back papers from two different laboratories reported the discovery of NlpE (CutF) as an outer membrane lipoprotein that rescued cells from copper sensitivity (Gupta et al., 1995) and the lethal effects of a chimeric protein (Snyder et al., 1995). 

Although it is well documented that NlpE plays a crucial role in positively modulating the CpxA activity, it remains unclear as to the physiological basis for its involvement in activating CpxAR (Figure 18.5.2a; see Chapters 18.2 and 18.3). The resolution of NlpE’s three-dimensional structure shed some light on how NlpE from its outer membrane location can communicate with CpxA (Hirano et al., 2007). The structure shows that NlpE folds into two β-barrels. A possible transient misfolding and unfolding of the N-terminal β-barrel may allow it to assume an extended conformation and move the C-terminal β-barrel away from the outer membrane (Figure 18.5.2a). It is further hypothesized that in its extended conformation, NlpE may come in close proximity to CpxA and may even directly interact with it. NlpE also contains the CXXC motif in the N-terminal domain and two additional cysteine residues in the C-terminal domain. Copperinduced oxidation at the CXXC motif may also influence NlpE folding and thus activation of CpxA (Hirano et al., 2007). All these hypotheses await additional experimental verifications. 

The periplasmic CpxP protein is the second modulator of the CpxAR TCS, which, unlike NlpE, negatively modulates CpxAR activity, presumably by inhibiting CpxA (Raivio et al., 1999). cpxP was identified among genes whose expression was upregulated when NlpE was overexpressed (Danese and Silhavy, 1998). Exactly how CpxP regulates CpxA activity is not clear, but given its location in the periplasm, an attractive model would be that it binds directly to the periplasmic loop region of CpxA (Figure 18.5.2a). It has been shown that CpxP is degraded by the periplasmic protease DegP (Buelow and Raivio, 2005; Isaac et al., 2005), particularly in the presence of misfolded proteins in the periplasm, and that both CpxP and the misfolded substrate are degraded by DegP (Isaac et al., 2005). A rapid degradation of CpxP during envelope stress by DegP would lead to the full activation of the CpxAR TCS. 

In 2007, the Hunke laboratory reported successful in vitro reconstitution of the CpxARP signal transduction cascade (Fleischer et al., 2007; see Chapter 18.2). Their data strongly suggested a direct interaction between CpxP and CpxA, in which the presence of CpxP reduces CpxA autokinase activity without affecting its phosphatase or phosphotransferase activities. Subsequently, by employing in vivo genetic tools, the Hunke laboratory provided more compelling evidence for a direct interaction between CpxP and CpxA, showing that this interaction can be disrupted in the presence of high salt or a misfolded envelope protein (Tschauner et al., 2014). These data are consistent with a model proposed by Isaac et al. (2005), where CpxP in nonstressed cells is thought to bind to CpxA to inhibit its activity; however, under envelope stress conditions, CpxP is displaced from CpxA, leading to its full activation. DegP, whose synthesis is controlled by the CpxAR TCS, also plays a crucial role in modulating CpxA activity since it degrades CpxP along with misfolded substrates. 

## 18.5.4 TorT and TorC, modulators of the TorSR TCS system

The TorSR TCS of E. coli regulates the torCAD operon involved in the utilization of trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) as a terminal electron acceptor during anaerobic respiration (for a review, see Barrett and Kwan, 1985). In addition to anaerobic conditions, the presence of TMAO or related compounds is necessary to stimulate the expression of the torCAD operon. TorS is the hybrid HK (Figure 18.5.2b): Besides the conserved histidine residue for autophosphorylation, it contains two additional sites for intramolecular phosphorelay (Jourlin et al., 1996a). TorR is the cognate RR that positively regulates the expression of the tor-CAD operon (Pascal et al., 1991). torT, sandwiched between torS and torT in the operon, was identified during the DNA sequence analysis of the torR region (Jourlin et al., 1996b). The presence of the periplasmic modulator TorT is mandatory for activation of the torCAD operon (Jourlin et al., 1996b), except in the presence of a constitutive mutation in the torS gene (Jourlin et al., 1996a) or when TorR is overproduced (Jourlin et al., 1996b). Convincing biochemical evidence suggests TorT binds to TMAO in the periplasm and that the binding of this complex to the periplasmic domain of TorS leads to TorS activation (Figure 18.5.2b) (Baraquet et al., 2006). Interestingly, TorS is also under the negative control of TorC, which is the membranebound c-type cytochrome that shuttles electrons to TorA, the TMAO reductase (Gon et al., 2001). When TorC is not in its heme-bound holo form, its apo form negatively regulates TorS by binding to its periplasmic domain (Gon et al., 2001). Thus, TorC autoregulates its own synthesis by controlling TorS HK activity, depending on its maturation (heme-bound) state. 

## 18.5.5 LuxP, a modulator of the LuxQUO TCS

LuxP of Vibrio harveyi works with the membrane-bound hybrid HK, LuxQ (Figure 18.5.2b). Together, they receive the signal to influence the downstream phosphosrelay targets, LuxU and LuxO, and control the production of the master regulator of quorum sensing, LuxR (Bassler et al., 1994; see Section 21). At high cell density, V. harveyi induces three parallel quorum-sensing pathways that act synergistically to influence gene expression (for a review on quorum sensing in Vibrio, see Milton, 2006). LuxP is a part of the signaling pathway involving autoinducer-2 (AI-2) and the LuxQ HK. Interactions between LuxP and the periplasmic domain of LuxQ occur regardless of the presence or absence of AI-2 (Neiditch et al., 2005). However, AI-2-bound LuxP undergoes significant conformational changes that influence ternary complexes formed with LuxP and LuxQ to activate LuxQ’s phosphatase activity and demote its default kinase (without AI-2) activity (Neiditch et al., 2006). 

## 18.5.6 MzrA, a modulator of EnvZ–OmpR and a connector of CpxAR and EnvZ–OmpR

This TCS is classically known for its regulation of the OmpF and OmpC porins in response to medium osmolarity (for a review, see Pratt et al., 1996). EnvZ is the orthodox HK, and OmpR serves as its cognate RR (Figure 18.5.3). MzrA (modulator of the EnvZ–OmpR TCS) was identified among multicopy plasmid clones that improved growth of an E. coli strain simultaneously lacking BamB and DegP proteins (Gerken et al., 2009). BamB is a component of the BAM complex involved in the assembly of the β-barrel OMPs (Charlson et al., 2006; Misra et al., 2015; Vuong et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2005). As stated in this chapter, DegP plays a crucial role in the degradation of envelope proteins, including misfolded β-barrel OMPs (Gerken et al., 2010). 

Overexpression of MzrA produced a phenotype very similar to that of certain pleiotropic envZ alleles, which suggested that MzrA acts to either enhance EnvZ autokinase activity and/or reduce its phosphatase activity (Gerken et al., 2009). By employing a bacterial two-hybrid system, it was determined that MzrA directly interacts with EnvZ (Gerken et al., 2009). Further genetic and molecular analyses revealed that the periplasmicexposed domain of MzrA interacts with EnvZ (Figure 18.5.3)

MzrA is the modulator of the EnvZ sensor kinase of the EnvZ–OmpR TCS involved in controlling the ompF and ompC porin gene expression in response to medium osmolarity. MzrA, through interactions with EnvZ on the periplasmic side of the membrane, either positively activates EnvZ’s kinase activity or demotes its phosphatase activity to cause greater phosphorylation of the OmpR response regulator. The membrane-bound SafA, like MzrA, interacts with the periplasmic-exposed loop of the PhoQ sensor kinase and stimulates its autophosphorylation. The PhoQP TCS is activated in low- $\cdot \mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ medium and positively regulates the expression of genes involved in magnesium transport. UhpC is both a transporter of glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) and a modulator of the UhpBA TCS. Sugar-bound UhpC stimulates the autokinase activity of UhpB. This in turn phosphorylates the UhpA response regulator to stimulate the transcription of uhpT, whose product transports G6P at a rate higher than UhpC.

Prior to the discovery of MzrA’s role in modulating the EnvZ– OmpR TCS, mzrA, along with yqjA, a gene located upstream of it, was identified among genes whose expression went up in response to $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activation (Dartigalongue et al., 2001). Subsequently, it was shown that the yqjA–mzrA operon is under the control of CpxAR (Gerken et al., 2009; Price and Raivio, 2009; Yamamoto and Ishihama, 2006). This and additional experiments allowed Gerken et al. (2009) to conclude that MzrA not only directly modulates the activity of EnvZ–OmpR, but also connects the $\mathsf { C p x A R { - } { \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { E } } }$ and EnvZ–OmpR systems to magnify the cellular response to envelope stress. In the absence of MzrA, EnvZ–OmpR-mediated porin expression resembles that of cells grown in low-osmolarity medium, and the strain still responds to changes in the medium osmolality and other known modulators of EnvZ–OmpR, including pH and procaine. This suggests that MzrA is not the primary receiver of environmental cues that activate EnvZ (Gerken et al., 2009). Interestingly, a fully activated EnvZ–OmpR system downregulates the expression of the yqjA–mzrA operon, indicating the existence of a negative regulatory feedback loop (Gerken et al., 2009). 

## 18.5.7 SafA (B1500), a modulator of the PhoQP TCS that connects EvgSA and PhoQP TCSs

safA (formerly b1500) was discovered by Eguchi et al. (2007) in an attempt to find regulators of the PhoQP TCS that are activated in medium containing low $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } { - } C a ^ { 2 + } }$ (Vescovi´ et al., 1996). Overexpression of SafA (sensor-associated factor A) from a heterologous promoter led to activation of the PhoQP regulon even in the presence of high $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ concentration (Eguchi et al., 2007). The expression of safA, which forms an operon with ydeO, is directly regulated by another TCS, EvgSA, thus allowing the authors to demonstrate that SafA links the EvgSA and PhoQP TCSs (Eguchi et al., 2007). SafA is a small 65-residue protein anchored to the inner membrane, with the C-terminal 41–65-residue region exposed to the periplasmic space where it interacts with the periplasmic loop of the PhoQ HK (Figure 18.5.4a) (Eguchi et al., 2007, 2012). Moreover, this region of SafA has been shown to enhance PhoQ autophosphorylation without affecting PhoQ-mediated dephosphorylation of the PhoP RR (Ishii et al., 2013). 

Previous studies have associated the EvgSA TCS with regulating multidrug resistance (Masuda and Church, 2002; Nishino and Yamaguchi, 2001, 2002) and acid resistance (Masuda and Church, 2002, 2003). A more recent study by Eguchi et al. (2011) showed that SafA plays a pivotal role in EvgSA-initiated, PhoQP-mediated acid resistance. This is because most genes involved either directly or indirectly in acid resistance are regulated by the PhoQP TCS (Eguchi et al., 2011). Thus, by serving as a bridge between EvgSA and PhoPQ, SafA enhances resistance to acid and other stress factors. The activated PhoQP TCS downregulates the expression of the safA–ydeO operon, indicating the existence of a negative feedback loop (Burton et al., 2010). 

## 18.5.8 UhpC, a unique modulator of the UhpBA TCS

The UhpBA TCS (Weston and Kadner, 1988) is involved in activating transcription of the glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) transporter gene, uhpT, in response to the presence of extracellular G6P (Shattuck-Eidens and Kadner, 1981). Once expressed, UhpT can facilitate the transport of many different inorganic phosphate sugars (Dietz et al., 1976). UhpC was initially identified as a G6P transport regulatory mutation, called uhpR (Kadner, 1973). A unique aspect of UhpC is that, besides acting as a modulator of the UhpBA TCS, it shares significant sequence homology with UhpT (Island et al., 1992) and can indeed transport G6P, albeit at a rate lower than that of UhpT (Schwoppe ¨ et al., 2002). Subsequent mutational analysis showed that UhpC’s transport activity can be uncoupled from its ability to sense the presence of extracellular G6P and activate UhpTmediated transport (Schwoppe¨ et al., 2003). An implication of this finding was that transport of G6P through UhpC per se is not required for the activation of UhpBA; rather, binding of external G6P to UhpC changes its conformation that activates the kinase activity of UhpB (Figure 18.5.3). Constitutive UhpC mutants that are presumably locked in the inducing conformation favor this hypothesis (Schwoppe ¨ et al., 2003). An in vitro reconstituted phosphorelay system containing UhpBCenriched membranes showed that G6P influences the rate of UhpB autophosphorylation, but does not affect the rate of phosphor transfer from UhpB∼P to UhpA, nor does it affect UhpBmediated UhpA dephosphorylation (Verhamme et al., 2001). Thus, UhpC functions as both the receptor of the external signal, G6P, of the UhpBA TCS and the modulator (activator) of the UhpB autokinase activity (Figure 18.5.3).

## 18.5.9 YycHI, modulators of the essential YycGF TCS of Firmicutes

YycGF constitutes an essential TCS in many bacteria belonging to the Firmicutes phylum (Fabret and Hoch, 1998), where it plays a central regulatory role in cell wall biogenesis (for a review, see Dubrac et al., 2008). Three earlier observations were key to narrowing down the role of YycGF, and in turn that of the YycHI modulators, in cell physiology: (i) Expression of yycGF, which form an operon with the downstream genes, yycHIJK, is induced during the exponential growth phase and repressed during the stationary growth phase (Fabret and Hoch, 1998); (ii) growth of a strain either bearing a temperature-sensitive yycF allele in the nonpermissive temperature (Fabret and Hoch, 1998) or depleted of YycF (Fukuchi et al., 2000) resulted in the appearance of ghost cells lacking the cytoplasmic content; and (iii) overexpression of YycF led to increased cell division and elevated expression of the ftsAZ operon (Fukuchi et al., 2000). These observations suggested a role of the YycGF TCS in cell envelope and cell wall biogenesis during the exponential phase of growth. 

A clue as to the role of YycH in regulating YycGF came from the discovery that the disruption of yycH overcomes the temperature-sensitive phenotype of an yycF allele and that YycH downregulates yycF-dependent gene expression (Szurmant et al., 2005). Subsequent studies showed both YycH and YycI impose a negative effect on YycGF by interacting with the YycG’s periplasmic loop on the trans side of the membrane (Figure 18.5.4a) (Szurmant et al., 2007). Given that YycGF expression, and presumably their activities, goes up during the exponential growth phase, it stands to reason that YycG must somehow overcome the negative effects of YycHI. Fukushima et al. (2011) provided biochemical and cellular evidence that YycG, through interactions with some unknown cytosolic factors, co-localizes at the septum of dividing cells. Since YycHI do not migrate to the septum, the YycG HK becomes fully activated. During the stationary phase, when cells are not actively dividing, YycHI once again make a ternary complex with YycG, thus inhibiting its activity. The YycHI–YycGF system provides a unique example where altered cellular localization controls the interaction between the modulators and their cognate TCS. 

## 18.5.10 SaePQ, modulators of the SaeQR TCS

The sae (Staphylococcus aureus exoprotein expression) locus was identified among transposon insertional mutants defective in the production of several expoproteins involved in bacterial pathogenesis (Giraudo et al., 1994). Follow-up cloning and complementation experiments led to the identification of an operon coding the SaeR RR and SaeS HK (Giraudo et al., 1999). Subsequent experiments revealed that the sae locus actually contains four genes, with saeP and saeQ located immediately upstream of SaeRS (Novick and Jiang, 2003). The phenotypic data from strains carrying null alleles of saeP or saeQ were complex and hinted at regulatory roles of these two genes in the activity of the SaeQR TCS (Adhikari and Novick, 2008). 

Both SaeP and SaeQ localize to the membrane, with SaeP likely a lipoprotein (Jeong et al., 2012). Employment of a bacterial two-hybrid system and co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that SaePQS form a tri-protein complex (Figure 18.5.4a) (Jeong et al., 2012). They further showed that overexpression of SaePQ inhibited SaeSR-mediated regulation of the downstream target genes (depending on the SaeR-P affinity of their promoters) and that the inhibition was achieved by enhanced dephosphorylation of the SaeR RR. The SaePQ achieved this by inducing the phosphatase activity of the SaeS HK (Jeong et al., 2012). The promoter that transcribes all four sea genes is positively regulated by SaeSR (Adhikari and Novick, 2008). Consequently, increased synthesis of SaePQ will lower SaeSR activity to reset the system to the pre-induced state. Although both SaePQ bind to SaeS HK (Figure 18.5.4a), they apparently are not involved in sensing human neutrophil peptides and polymorphonuclear leucocytes that activate SaeS (Flacka et al., 2014). Whether binding of these activating signals to SaeS influences SaePQ binding to SaeS remains to be investigated. The topology of SaeS suggests the presence of only a small 10-residue extracellular loop where a single mutation, M31A, disrupts SaeS activation, presumably by interfering with the mutant protein’s ability to detect polymorphonuclear leucocytes (Flack et al., 2014). It is not known whether the loop mutation also interferes with SaePQS complex formation. 

## 18.5.11 LprF and LprJ, modulators of the KdpDE TCS in mycobacteria

Most mycobacterial genomes code for low- (TrK) and highaffinity (Kdp) K+ transport systems (for a review, see Cholo et al., 2008). The inducible, high-affinity Kdp system has six protein components, with KdpDE constituting the TCS that controls the expression of kdpFABC. LprF and LprJ lipoproteins were identified as interacting partners of the membranebound KdpD HK by the yeast two-hybrid system and affinity chromatography (Steyn et al., 2003). Additional experimental and computer-assisted analyses indicated that the cytoplasmicexposed regions of LprFJ interact with the cytoplasmic-exposed 

N-terminal domain of KdpD, and that together they interact with the C-terminal kinase domain of KdpD (Figure 18.5.4b) (Steyn et al., 2003). The precise roles of the LprFJ lipoproteins in ligand binding and/or KdpD HK activity modulation remain to be determined. 

## 18.5.12 LiaF, a modulator of the LiaSR TCS of B. subtilis

Mutational analysis identified LiaF as the inhibitor of the LiaSR TCS (Jordan et al., 2006) that responds to envelope stress caused by antibiotics and other envelope-damaging agents (for a review, see Jordan et al., 2008). LiaF is a membrane protein with four predicted TM regions and a large cytosolic domain that, under nonstressed conditions, is assumed to interact with the LiaS HK to inhibit its autokinase activity (Figure 18.5.4b) (Jordan et al., 2006). However, under envelope stress condition, such as that created by a cell wall–damaging antibiotic, the hypothetical LiaF–LiaS complexes are either broken or altered in such a way to allow LiaS to assume its default kinase “on” mode. Genetic studies to determine the stoichiometric relationship between LiaFSR found that they are present at a ratio of 18:4:1 (Schrecke et al., 2013). It is currently not known how, during stress, LiaS overcomes more than four times the amount of LiaF to phosphorylate LiaR. 

## 18.5.13 Concluding remarks

The bacterial TCSs and their modulators play crucial roles in cell physiology. Modulators can influence all aspects of a TCS action, including signal reception, to directly modulate HK and RR activities. Although the focus of this chapter has been the envelope-localized modulators, there are a number of cytosolic modulators that can influence a TCS action (for a review, see Buelow and Raivio, 2010). Therefore, modulators influence TCS action in all cellular compartments. Although we have come a long way in identifying many TCS modulators, much work remains to be done to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of their action.
