## Iron homeostasis

# Iron homeostasis and environmental responses in cyanobacteria: regulatory networks involving Fur

Mar´ıa Luisa Peleato, Mar´ıa Teresa Bes, and Mar´ıa F. Fillat 

Department of Biochemistry and Molecular and Cell Biology and Institute for Biocomputation and Physics of Complex Systems (BIFI), University of Zaragoza, Zaragoza, Spain 

## 19.1.1 Introduction

## 19.1.1.1 Iron is essential in redox biological processes linked to early life steps

Iron metabolism is thought to be related with very early events in the origin of life. Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth’s crust. Several hypotheses place the initial steps of life organization on the surface of iron sulphide minerals, in iron monosulphide bubbles (Wachtershauser, 1988). It has been proposed that iron cofactors arose before the “Great Oxidation Event” (Ilbert and Bonnefoy, 2013). Free oxygen gas was almost non-existent in Earth’s atmosphere more than 3 billion years ago. When free oxygen began entering the environment as a product of cyanobacterial oxygenic photosynthesis, it turned Earth’s iron to rust, forming massive banded iron formations that are still mined today. The free oxygen produced by early cyanobacteria caused iron to be toxic, even though it was, and still is, a requirement for life. In time, the roles of iron were slowly substituted by other metals or other prosthetic groups. It has been proposed that such environmental transition caused a slow shift from the use of iron to magnesium for RNA binding, folding, and catalysis (Athavale et al., 2012). However, the fact that Nature maintains iron in a number of proteins through evolution indicates that it plays a unique and crucial role. As exceptions, some species of Borrelia and Treponema pallidum (obligate intracellular parasites with minimal genomes that rely upon the iron-dependent metabolic processes of their hosts) and Lactobacillus plantarum have been described as organisms that do not require iron (Andrews et al., 2003). On the contrary, the archaeon Ferroplasma acidiphilum, which lives in acidic environments with high concentrations of iron and other metals, has iron in up to 86% of its proteins, including proteins that in other organisms play the same role without containing this metal (Pivovarova et al., 2002). Consequently, according to the authors’ hypothesis, F. acidiphilum, which lives in similar conditions to the ones of the early stages of life, has not lost the original systems based on iron (Pivovarova et al., 2002). 

Iron is particularly important for photosynthetic organisms, such as cyanobacteria, in which it is essential as part of the redox proteins of the photosynthetic electron transfer chain (Shcolnick and Keren, 2006). Cyanobacterial iron requirements exceed non-photosynthetic prokaryotes by 10-fold (Kranzler et al., 2013). Moreover, diazotrophic cyanobacteria exhibit significantly higher iron needs, since nitrogenase and its electron transfer chain contain many atoms of iron (Nicolaisen and Schleiff, 2010; Shcolnick and Keren, 2006). 

## 19.1.1.2 The iron paradox: high demand, low bioavailability, and high toxicity. Evolutionary consequence: fine-tuned homeostasis

Ferrous iron (Fe2+) was very abundant in the Earth’s crust and waters until the oxygenation of the atmosphere by cyanobacterial oxygenic photosynthesis. The increase of oxygen led to iron oxidation and precipitation, drastically reducing its bioavailability and introducing a new factor of selective pressure for life. Cyanobacteria as well as bacteria evolved siderophore and other iron uptake mechanisms, which efficiently acquire this nutrient in unfavourable environments. However, free intracellular iron needs to be kept at permissive levels, as it becomes toxic under aerobic conditions by producing reactive oxygen species via the Fenton reaction (Halliwell and Gutteridge, 1992; see Section 10). 

As mentioned here, iron availability affects almost the entire metabolism. For this reason, complex regulatory networks have evolved to tightly control intracellular iron concentrations, ensuring its essential function yet avoiding cellular damage (Cornelis et al., 2011). Ferritins and other proteins allow iron storage and prevent iron-induced oxidative stress, while transcriptional factors fine-tune iron metabolism. Furthermore, other metal homeostasis networks evolved simultaneously, many times linked to iron metabolism (Nicolaisen and Schleiff, 2010). 

## 19.1.1.3 Cyanobacteria developed very efficient mechanisms for iron acquisition and iron storage

Aquatic organisms able to adapt to iron deficiency have a competitive advantage. The versatility of cyanobacteria to cope with this situation enabled them to dominate the phytoplankton population. Iron deprivation in cyanobacteria induced a variety of responses that range from upregulation of the iron acquisition systems to reduction or substitution of structures or molecules. At the physiological level, Straus (1994) categorizes the iron responses as (i) cell retrenchment (involving loss of phycobilisomes, ultrastructural changes, and pigment changes); (ii) compensation (as induction and synthesis of the flavoprotein flavodoxin): During iron limitation, flavodoxin replaces [2Fe-2S]-ferredoxin as an iron-free electron acceptor for PSI, and in other cases, Ni-SOD or Mn-SOD are synthesized instead of Fe-SOD (Eitinger, 2004); and (iii) acquisition (induction of TonBdependent receptors, synthesis of siderophores, etc.). 

Although many cyanobacteria produce all of the three main types of siderophores, namely catecholates, hydroxamates, or mixed types (Kranzler et al., 2011), reductive iron uptake without the involvement of siderophores has also been reported in Lyngbya majuscule (Rose et al., 2005), Synechococcus spp. (Lis, 2009), and Synechocystis PCC 6803 (Kranzler et al., 2011). The properties and biosynthetic pathways of cyanobacterial siderophores, as well as the alternative iron uptake strategies, have been extensively reviewed in Kranzler et al. (2013). 

Cyanobacteria also exhibit various other physiological and morphological changes in response to iron limitation. For instance, iron deficiency causes a reduction in cell size (Mann and Chisholm, 2000) and induces changes in the photosynthetic apparatus to adapt it to the new conditions. For instance, there is an upregulation of isiA, encoding a chlorophyll-binding protein unique to cyanobacteria (Burnap et al., 1993; Laudenbach and Straus, 1988; Michel and Pistorius, 2004). Under iron deficiency, IsiA accumulates in the thylakoid membrane, where it binds to chlorophyll and forms IsiA–PSI supercomplexes that increase the light capture ability of PSI and protect the iron-limited cells from oxidative damage (Singh and Sherman, 2007). Iron deficiency causes a reduction of linear photosynthetic electron transport and enhances respiratory electron transport (Michel et al., 2003; Pietsch et al., 2007). Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 decreases the acyclic photosynthetic electron transport and increases cyclic photophosphorylation and respiratory activities under iron starvation (Michel and Pistorius, 2004). Photosystem II (PS II) photochemical efficiency decreases in Microcystis spp. under iron starvation (Xing et al., 2007). Moreover, under iron deficiency, several responses to oxidative stress (see Section 10) have been described, evidencing the link between iron starvation and oxidative stress, with photosystems specially affected (Latifi et al., 2005; Shcolnick et al., 2009; Yingping et al., 2014). 

In addition to photoxidation events, physiological responses to changes in light intensity, in relationship to iron acquisition, have also been described. In the potentially toxigenic cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa, iron uptake has been described as light dependent (Utkilen and Gjolme, 1995). 

Iron is also important in cyanobacterial secondary metabolism. Many nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS) are iron regulated. A substantial variety of siderophore structures are produced from similar NRPS assembly lines (Crosa and Walsh, 2002), and a large number of secondary metabolites are also synthesized as response to iron starvation. Among those metabolites, cyanotoxins are of special interest. Iron availability is one of the main environmental conditions that affect the synthesis of microcystins (Sevilla et al., 2008). However, there are no data linking the synthesis of other cyanotoxins such as saxitoxins, anatoxins, lyngbyatoxin, or cylindrospermopsins to iron status (Neilan et al., 2013), though they are also synthesized with involvement of NRPS. 

Microcystins, the most ubiquitous cyanotoxins, have been considered as a response to iron deficiency (Sevilla et al., 2008). Microcystins display structural similarities with bacterial siderophores (Crosa and Walsh, 2002) and have an affinity for iron. Hence, it has been proposed that they could play a role as extracellular iron-scavenging molecules (Utkilen and Gjolme, 1995). However, a possible siderophore activity of microcystins has not yet been clearly demonstrated (Klein et al., 2013). 

Microcystin synthesis has been linked to iron metabolism for many years. Lyck and colleagues (Lyck et al., 1996) showed that during iron depletion, toxic strains of Microcystis maintained cell vitality much longer than the nontoxic strains. Toxic strains also exhibited higher rates of iron uptake than nontoxic strains, suggesting that the microcystin could work as an intracellular chelator of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { + 2 }$ (Utkilen and Gjolme, 1995). Those findings led to the prediction that the synthesis of the toxin would be controlled by the amount of free iron present in the cells, as was shown to occur later (Sevilla et al., 2008). Among many other factors, the ferric uptake regulator protein Fur is a key player in the control of microcystin synthesis (Martin-Luna et al., 2006). Iron deficiency induces the levels of mcyD, which belongs to the mcy operon and is responsible for microcystin synthesis (Kaebernick et al., 2002) as well as microcystin levels in cells (Sevilla et al., 2008). 

## 19.1.1.4 Accommodation to iron deficiency involves a large number of genes from major pathways

The development of “omics”-based technologies has provided much more detailed information about the molecular basis of the pleiotropic changes observed as response to iron deficiency. This plasticity had to be crucial to early organisms at the initial steps of the oxygenation event. A large number of changes in the expression of genes and operons – involved not only in iron metabolism but also in many general cellular pathways, such as respiration, photosynthesis, nitrogen metabolism, glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acids cycle, amino acid synthesis, synthesis of toxins, and antioxidant defences – highlight the responses associated with iron deprivation. Early studies in Synechocystis PCC 6803 (Singh et al., 2003) identified genes known previously to be Fe-regulated, such as isiA, as well as genes of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthetase and phycobilisomes, chlorophyll biosynthesis, energy metabolism, as well as photosystems assembly that were downregulated under iron deficiency. Hierarchical clustering demonstrated that photosynthesis genes, as a class, were repressed under low-iron conditions and induced upon the re-addition of iron. Specific regulatory genes are transcriptionally active in low iron, including two genes that show homology to plant phytochromes (cph1 and cph2) (Singh et al., 2003). 

In Prochlorococcus, about 3.8% to 6.2% of the total genes, depending on the ecotype, respond to iron stress (Thompson et al., 2011). The authors related such variations to the different fitness of these strains at limiting iron concentrations. Also, the close relationship between light availability and iron requirements can be inferred from the differentially expressed genes in Prochlorococcus (Thompson et al., 2011). 

Iron limitation significantly and specifically affects the transcript abundance of a very large number of genes in Synechococcus PCC7002 (Ludwig and Bryant, 2012). Genes whose transcript levels were most affected encoded enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of the siderophore synechobactin (an increase of 55 to 150-fold), TonB-dependent siderophore receptors and TonB family proteins (increased up to 90-fold), and transcripts for iron-related ABC transporters (up to 180-fold). Notably, transcript levels for the isiAB operon increased about 500-fold during Fe limitation, the largest increase observed under this condition. 

Major iron-regulated genes in S. elongatus PCC 7942 have been located in six regions on the chromosome with clusters of genes (Nodop et al., 2008). These gene clusters contain the genes irpA and irpB, the fut genes, the suf genes, the isiABC genes, the idiB operon, and the ackA–pgam genes. Besides, acetate kinase and a phosphoglycerate mutase harbour increased transcript levels under iron limitation, providing additional ATP synthesis by substrate-level phosphorylation (Nodop et al., 2008). In parallel to the reduction of the linear photosynthetic electron transport under Fe starvation, steadystate messenger RNA (mRNA) levels of several genes of the photosynthetic electron transport chain are downregulated (Michel et al., 2003; Pietsch et al., 2007). However, the increase in the respiratory electron transport is in good concordance with the upregulation of three types of cytochrome oxidases (Nodop et al., 2008). Curiously, Synechococcus 7002 transcript levels for universal stress proteins and also for several molecular chaperones (e.g., groEL, groES, dnaK, and dnaJ; see Section 14) and heat shock proteins (e.g., hspA, grpE, and htpG; see Section 13) are not affected under iron (and other nutrient) limitation (Ludwig and Bryant, 2012). On the contrary, transcript levels for nblA, involved in the degradation of phycobiliproteins by the Clp protease, show a 2–3- fold increase upon iron deprivation (Ludwig and Bryant, 2012). 

Proteomic data on the survival strategy of Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 when subjected to long-term iron starvation conditions have revealed significant and reproducible alterations in 10 proteins, of which six are associated with photosynthesis and respiration, three with the antioxidative defence system, and the last, the hypothetical protein all1861, possibly connected with iron homeostasis (Narayan et al., 2011). As in other cyanobacteria, iron-starved Anabaena shows a reduction in growth, photosynthetic pigments, PSI and PSII content, whole-chain electron transport, carbon and nitrogen fixation, and ATP and NADPH content. Interestingly, the upregulated FBP-aldolase, Mn/Fe-SOD, and all1861 all appear to assist the survival of Anabaena subjected to iron starvation conditions (Narayan et al., 2011). In summary, cyanobacterial response to iron starvation exhibits common features, namely a greatly increased expression of the isiAB operon (Ludwig and Bryant, 2012; Nodop et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2003), as well as of genes involved in siderophore biosynthesis and those related to the tonB family. Furthermore, genes encoding the iron-rich PSI complex (i.e., psaA) and other photosynthetic components as petA and petC appear to be downregulated. 

## 19.1.1.5 Central role of ferritin family proteins in iron homeostasis

Ferritins and bacterioferritins, as well as Dps proteins, are ubiquitously present iron storage proteins in cyanobacteria. Ferritins can hold as many as 4500 iron atoms inside its spherical structure formed from subunits, keeping iron in a soluble and nontoxic form. In the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803, bacterioferritins are responsible for the storage of as much as 50% of cellular iron. Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803, as well as many other cyanobacterial species, has two bacterioferritins, BfrA and BfrB, in which either the haem-binding or di-iron centre-ligating residues are absent. Targeted mutagenesis of each of the two bacterioferritin genes resulted in poor growth under iron-deprived conditions. Mutants triggered iron starvation responses even in the presence of normal levels of external iron, thus demonstrating a central role of bacterioferritins in iron homeostasis in these photosynthetic organisms (Keren et al., 2004). Additionally, Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 contains the ferritin-type storage complex MrgA that, together with bacterioferritin, plays a pivotal role in the coordination of iron homeostasis with peroxide and light stress responses (Foster et al., 2009; Shcolnick et al., 2009). The combined action of bacterioferritin and MrgA elicits the safe accumulation and release of iron from the storage complexes, attenuating the damage due to interactions between ferrous iron and the oxygen radicals produced by the photosynthetic apparatus (Shcolnick et al., 2009). 

## 19.1.1.6 A complex network of transcriptional regulators harmonizes cell metabolism as a response to iron availability

Because iron homeostasis is critical for life, a complex network of regulation has been generated during billions of years of evolution. Many of those regulators have dual roles and usually engage in cross-talk with other regulatory pathways, such as nitrogen metabolism, the oxidative stress response, and others. Table 19.1.1 summarizes some of the main cyanobacterial regulators modulated by iron availability. Among them, Fur proteins constitute the main and most ubiquitous iron regulators in prokaryotes. It is assumed that Fur works as a classical repressor using $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ as a cofactor to negatively regulate the expression of its target genes. However, members of the FUR family display a diversity in metal selectivity and biological functions (Lee and Helmann, 2007), including not only sensors of iron (Fur) but also zinc (Zur), manganese (Mur), and nickel (Nur). Also, FUR proteins are involved in sensing peroxide stress (PerR) or the availability of haem (Irr). 

The 39 cyanobacterial genomes available to date (http://genome.kazusa.or.jp/cyanobase) (Nakamura et al., 1998) reveal the presence of several Fur paralogues. Although three Fur-like proteins are commonly found in most cyanobacteria – named FurA (Fur), FurB (Zur), and FurC (PerR in Anabaena PCC 7120) – some Prochlorococcus strains, harbouring the smallest cyanobacterial genomes described so far, contain only two fur genes. This is in contrast with Acaryochloris marina MBIC11017, which exhibits the highest number of Fur and Fur-like paralogues, namely five Fur-like, four PerR-like, and four Zur-like members (Botello-Morte et al., 2013). 

## 19.1.2 FurA: from the control of iron homeostasis to global regulation of cyanobacterial metabolism

The role of FurA in cyanobacterial iron metabolism has been described by Ghassemian and Straus (1996) through the study of a merodiploid mutant of Synechococcus PCC 7942 that produces a reduced amount of the regulator. These cells showed iron deficiency symptoms in iron-repleted medium and constitutively express flavodoxin and hydroxamate siderophores. The relationship between iron status and Fur activity has also been shown in a derivative of Anabaena sp. PCC 7120, where antisense α-furA RNA has been disrupted. This strain shows an increase in FurA content of about 2.5-fold compared to the WT strain Anabaena PCC 7120 and also has a lower iron content than the reference strain (Hernandez et al., 2006a,b). 

Subsequent studies using a FurA-overexpressing strain, where furA has been placed behind a copper-inducible promoter, has allowed the identification of a large set of FurA-dependent genes that belong to different functional categories. In this set of genes, predominant were those involved in iron metabolism, including haem synthesis and degradation pathways (Gonzalez et al., 2010, 2012), photosynthesis (Gonzalez et al., 2010), and the oxidative stress response (Gonzalez et al., 2010, 2011). In particular, the link between FurA and the response to oxidants is of paramount importance for cyanobacteria (see Sections 19.1.2.1 and 19.1.3). 

Furthermore, an in silico genome-wide predictive approach combined with transcriptomic and mobility shift assays increased the knowledge of the FurA regulon in Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 (Gonzalez et al., 2014). Using a stringent selection

Furthermore, those studies evidenced that FurA may act not only as repressor but also by activating gene expression, depending in all cases tested on iron availability and the intracellular iron status (see Chapter 19.2). 

## 19.1.2.1 Cross-talk between FurA and other Fur paralogues

Electrophoretic mobility assays using purified Fur paralogues indicated that FurA interacts specifically with the furB (zur) and furC (perR) promoters, while FurC modulates the ability of FurA and FurB to interact with their own promoters (Hernandez et al., 2004). Further reports based on transcriptomic analyses evidenced that the Zur regulon, in addition to controlling genes involved in zinc homeostasis, includes genes that are involved in iron acquisition systems, such as the TonB-dependent haem transport protein Alr3242 and hemE, involved in haem biosynthesis (Napolitano et al., 2012). Several genes in this pathway are also controlled by FurA, as well as others involved in the oxidative stress defence, which are common targets of FurA and Zur (Table 19.1.2) (Gonzalez et al., 2010, 2011; Sein-Echaluce et al., 2014).

Moreover, the low Zur expression in the AG2770FurAoverexpressing strain is indicative of the cross-talk between FurA and Zur, and suggests that FurA and Zur may work as interactive regulators (Sein-Echaluce et al., 2014). 

PerR (Slr173) has been clearly identified in Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 divergently next to the type 2 peroxiredoxin sll1621 (Kobayashi et al., 2004). Independent transcriptional studies deleting the perR gene disclosed a set of potential targets involved not only in maintenance of redox homeostasis but also in transport across membranes and translocation (sll1450, sll0684, sll0616, sll0681, sll0385, and slr0513), carbon dioxide concentration (sll1030 and sll1031), transposition (sll1397 and sll1780), transcriptional regulation (sigB and sigD), and biosynthetic pathways (sll1688, sll0927, and slr0900), among others (Kobayashi et al., 2004; Li et al., 2004). In Anabaena sp. PCC 7120, it has been proposed that Alr0957 (FurC) works as the peroxide-sensor repressor PerR (Yingping et al., 2014; see Section 10). This was suggested because of (i) the strong induction of alr0957 under oxidative challenge (Lopez-Gomollon et al., 2009; Yingping et al., 2014), (ii) its inactivation in the presence of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ and (iii) the identification of prxA and srxA as Alr0957 targets (Yingping et al., 2014). However, these last two features are also shared with FurA (Gonzalez et al., 2010, 2011; Hernandez´ et al., 2006), which includes in its regulon many genes involved in the oxidative stress response, suggesting that FurA in Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 could perform, shared or not with Alr0957 (FurC), the functions carried out by PerR proteins in other bacteria. 

Furthermore, the tight relationship between iron homeostasis and oxidative stress (see Section 10) is evidenced when transcriptomes of unicellular and filamentous cyanobacteria challenged with iron starvation, deletion of PerR, or oxidative stress induced by chemical or high-light conditions are compared (Foster et al., 2009; Li et al., 2004; Shcolnick et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2003; Yingping et al., 2014). Those studies unveiled a noticeable number of cyanobacterial genes whose transcripts are increased in both oxidative stress and iron starvation conditions. This common response is crucial for the ecological success of cyanobacteria and seems to be modulated by Fur and PerR in a concerted fashion. 

## 19.1.2.2 Role of FurA in coupling iron status to nitrogen-metabolic pathways

Influence of iron status in heterocyst development and functionality: The high demand on iron of nitrogenase reductase and other enzymes involved in nitrogen metabolism makes this micronutrient a limiting element in processes such as nitrogen fixation. In the open ocean, the marine non-heterocystous diazotrophic cyanobacterium Trichodesmium selectively downregulates nitrogen fixation to deal with the limitations imposed by the scarcity of bioavailable iron (Kupper et al., 2008). In addition to cope with the low bioavailability of iron, cyanobacteria have developed different strategies to avoid nitrogenase inactivation by the oxygen evolved during photosynthesis. Filamentous cyanobacteria confine nitrogen fixation to specialized cells called heterocysts (Flores and Herrero, 2010; Kumar et al., 2010). Differentiation of a vegetative cell into a functional heterocyst is a complex process that requires changes in the expression of a plethora of genes, including at least three programmed DNA rearrangements of 10.5, 11, and 55 kb induced by nitrogen deprivation (Carrasco and Golden, 1995; Carrasco et al., 1995; Golden et al., 1985, 1988; Vintila et al., 2011). Unexpectedly, iron deprivation triggers the excision of the 11 kb element, restoring the nifHDK operon even in the presence of combined nitrogen (Razquin et al., 1994). Under those conditions $( - \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } , + \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - } )$ the fdxH and nifH genes are transcriptionally active, though synthesis of nitrogenase is arrested in a later step since nitrogenase activity and the fdxH gene product are not detectable. Moreover, in nitrogen-depleted cultures, nif genes are downregulated by iron stress and nitrogen fixation decreases (Razquin et al., 1994; Sandmann et al., 1990). Those results are in good agreement with the partial suppression of heterocyst differentiation observed in a FurA-overexpressing background (Gonzalez et al., 2013) and indicate that in Anabaena, the synthesis of nitrogenase is limited by the availability of iron. 

Cross-talk between FurA and NtcA: Among the many factors involved in the initiation of heterocyst differentiation and its functionality as nitrogen-fixing cells, NtcA has been identified as a key protein along this process. NtcA is a CRP family transcription factor that recognizes the consensus sequence (GTAN8TAC). Under nitrogen limitation, NtcA activates the expression of not only the main heterocyst-specific genes but also other genes involved in metabolic pathways leading to nitrogen assimilation (Herrero et al., 2004). Likewise, nitrogen control by NtcA has been reported in unicellular, nondiazotrophic cyanobacteria (Muro-Pastor et al., 2005; Ohashi et al., 2011). Interestingly, when Anabaena cells are depleted of combined nitrogen, transcription of furA is enhanced (Lopez-Gomollon et al., 2007b). Analysis of the furA promoter $( \mathrm { P } _ { f u r A } )$ exhibited a canonical NtcA box, and binding of this regulator to it can be assessed by EMSA or footprinting assays. The use of $\mathrm { P } _ { f u r A }$ fused to GFP showed that activation of furA by NtcA took place mainly in the heterocyst. The high level of furA expression in these differentiated cells suggests that this protein might play an additional role in the heterocyst different from transcriptional regulation that could be related to their micro-aerobic environment (Lopez-Gomollon et al., 2007b). 

Unlike in the non-fixer Synechococcus sp. WH7803, where induction of ntcA occurs only when cells were exposed to nitrogen stress but not under phosphorus or iron deprivation (Lindell et al., 1998), modulation of ntcA by FurA has been shown in Anabaena PCC 7120 (Gonzalez et al., 2013). FurA specifically binds in vitro to ntcA and hetR promoters, and, as mentioned previously, its overexpression partially abolishes heterocyst differentiation at an early stage (Gonzalez et al., 2013). In addition to $\mathrm { P } _ { h e t R }$ and $\mathrm { P } _ { n t c A } .$ , FurA recognizes promoters of a source of NtcA-regulated genes playing key roles in nitrogen and central metabolisms, such as glnA, petH, sigC, xisA, and nifH, among others (Lopez-Gomoll´ on´ et al., 2007a). Those data evidence a robust regulatory network involving genes essential for the control of iron homeostasis and nitrogen metabolism whose core is conformed by FurA and NtcA. 

## 19.1.2.3 Interplay of Fur and noncoding RNAs in the iron regulatory networks of cyanobacteria

The participation of an antisense RNA in the regulation of bacterial iron transport genes was first described in Vibrio anguillarum (Salinas et al., 1993; Waldbeser et al., 1993; see also Section 5). This cis-acting α-RNA was mainly expressed under iron-rich conditions and Fur was essential for its synthesis independently of the iron status of the cell (Chen and Crosa, 1996). Unlike the α-RNA from Vibrio, in E. coli the small regulatory trans-acting RNA RhyB is repressed by Fur under ironrich conditions, allowing the expression of iron storage proteins and iron-rich enzymes (Masse and Gottesman, 2002). Although functional analogues of RhyB have been identified in bacteria with different lifestyles (Oglesby-Sherrouse and Murphy, 2013), no RhyB orthologues have been found in cyanobacteria. However, several cis-acting RNAs involved in the control of ironregulated genes have been described. An α-furA RNA was first found in Anabaena PCC 7120 as part of a large dicistronic transcript that also encoded the putative membrane protein Alr1690 (Hernandez ´ et al., 2006). Expression of α-furA was affected by iron and nitrogen availability and contributed to modulate the final concentration of FurA in the cell (Hernandez ´ et al., 2006; Lopez-Gomollon et al., 2007a). Orthologues of α-furA are also present in unicellular cyanobacteria with different genomic contexts, namely M. aeruginosa sp. PCC 7806 and Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 (Sevilla et al., 2011). Furthermore, in M. aeruginosa sp. PCC 7806, furA is part of an operon that also encodes an antisense transcript overlapping the sufE message. The expression of an anti-sufE RNA linked to furA transcription would enable FurA to regulate the assembly of Fe-S clusters in cyanobacteria. 

In addition to α-furA, the cis-encoded regulatory RNA IsiR has been well characterized in Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803. IsiR is expressed specifically during iron-rich conditions and, with FurA, co-represses the synthesis of IsiA under iron-replete conditions (Duhring et al., 2006). More recently, a transcriptomic study of changes in gene expression after iron depletion in Synechocystis unveiled potential novel players of the iron regulatory network in this cyanobacterium that included several noncoding and antisense RNAs, as well as 5′ UTRs and intragenic elements (Hernandez-Prieto et al., 2012). 

## 19.1.3 FurA and cyanobacterial redox homeostasis

## 19.1.3.1 Is FurA a CXXC-based redox regulator?

Cyanobacteria are particularly sensitive to the harmful effect of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by the respiratory machinery and by the photosynthetic electron transport (Blot et al., 2011; Latifi et al., 2009). Therefore, cyanobacteria need dynamic and effective ways to relieve excess electron pressure and maintain redox and iron homeostasis inside the cell. For this purpose, cyanobacteria have developed mechanisms of antioxidant defence and redox buffering consisting of small molecules and protein components (Latifi et al., 2009). At the transcriptional level, Fur-type proteins constitute the main regulatory system that couples in vivo iron homeostasis and oxidative stress response to major physiological processes (Gonzalez et al., 2014; see Section 10). An important issue is to understand how Fur integrates both stimuli to give a concerted response in cyanobacteria. 

The different cyanobacterial Fur homologues contain a varying number of cysteine residues usually located in the Cterminus of the protein. In general, cysteine-containing regulators take advantage of the diverse chemistry of the thiol group to sense ROS, among other oxidants, and directly control the expression of target genes (Antelmann and Helmann, 2011) (see Chapter 17.1). In cyanobacterial Fur homologues at least, a couple of conserved cysteines are arranged in a CXXC motif (Figure 19.1.2). CXXC sequences constitute an essential, canonical signature present in the active site of the most known thiol–disulphide oxidoreductase enzymes (Netto et al., 2007). Recently, it has been demonstrated that FurA from Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 exhibits insulin disulphide reductase activity, according to its ability to reduce insulin with dithiothreitol as an electron donor (Botello-Morte et al., 2014). This activity is absent in other Fur homologues from heterotrophic bacteria (Botello-Morte et al., 2014). FurA from Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 contains two CXXC motifs, namely $\mathrm { C ^ { 1 0 1 } V K C ^ { 1 0 4 } }$ and C141PHC144. The $\mathrm { C ^ { 1 0 1 } V K C ^ { 1 0 4 } }$ motif is the main one responsible for disulphide reductase activity, while $\mathrm { C ^ { 1 4 1 } P H C ^ { 1 4 4 } }$ displays a moderate activity (Botello-Morte et al., 2014). The $\mathrm { C ^ { 1 0 1 } V K C ^ { 1 0 4 } }$ sequence, contained in the HHXHXXCXXC metal-binding signature, is conserved in most cyanobacterial Fur homologues (Figure 19.1.2). It is noteworthy that an identical metal-binding motif (HHX-HXXCXXC) is present in Fur sequences of numerous components of the FUR family in heterotrophic bacteria. However, the crystal structures of some of them reveal that they usually contain two or three metal atoms whose coordination involves amino acids of this motif, particularly both cysteine residues (Butcher et al., 2012; Dian et al., 2011). Interestingly, Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 FurA lacks structural metal atoms according to metal analysis and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry that revealed that neither zinc nor other metals are present in this protein (Hernandez et al., 2002). Instead, biochemical studies on a triple cysteine FurA mutant, containing only both cysteine residues of the $\mathrm { C ^ { 1 0 1 } V K C ^ { 1 0 4 } }$ motif, show that these residues form a disulphide bridge with a redox potential value of −235 mV, which is similar to that of the cytoplasm (Botello-Morte et al., 2014). Although this is an in vitro result, data obtained in vivo indicate that this protein is a monomer in Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 cytoplasm conforming a heterogeneous population with two, one, or none intramolecular disulphide bonds in vivo (Botello-Morte et al., 2014). 

The precise mechanism through which FurA is activated is unknown, although thiol-reducing agents enhance the affinity of FurA for its target DNA in vitro (Hernandez et al., 2006a,b). It is likely that the intramolecular disulphide bridges envisaged in the Anabaena FurA homologue involve neighbouring cysteines in the CXXC motifs, as observed in other proteins with disulphide reductase activity (Quan et al., 2007; Sevier and Kaiser, 2002), suggesting that FurA could function as a CXXC-based redox regulator in Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 and possibly in other cyanobacteria.

## 19.1.3.2 Fur as a haem sensor

FurA from Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 exhibits a CP (cysteine– proline) haem-regulatory motif as part of a second redoxactive motif CXXC $( \mathrm { C ^ { 1 4 1 } P H C ^ { 1 4 4 } } )$ (Botello-Morte et al., 2014). Although this second CXXC motif is not present in around 50% of cyanobacterial Fur homologues, the presence of a CP sequence is highly conserved (see Figure 19.1.2). In fact, it seems to be a hallmark of cyanobacterial Fur sequences since it is absent in most of the iron-responsive Fur homologues from heterotrophic bacteria. A study on the different Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 FurA single cysteine mutants has unveiled that the cysteine of the CP motif serves as an axial ligand of the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ high-spin haem when the protein binds this cofactor. Moreover, reduction of the complex entails a ligand switch. These features, together with the fact that the dissociation constant of the FurA–haem complex is in the micromolar concentration range, have suggested a role of FurA as a haem sensor in this cyanobacterium (Pellicer et al., 2012). 

In photosynthetic organisms, the biosynthesis of bilins, chromophores of the light-harvesting phycobiliproteins and lightsignalling phytochromes, takes place by oxidation of haem. It requires three molecules of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and several reducing equivalents to convert haem to biliverdin IXα, free iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ , and carbon monoxide (CO) (Frankenberg-Dinkel, 2009). Phycobilins in the triplet state can react with oxygen and act as photosensitizers, producing ROS under UV or visible light excess in cyanobacteria (Zolla and Rinalducci, 2002). As a result, elevated ROS levels reduce light-harvesting capabilities, for instance in Synechocystis sp. PCC6803 (Gao et al., 2009). On the other hand, overproduction of haem is toxic to cyanobacteria since it catalyses oxidation, covalent cross-linking, and aggregate formation of protein and its degradation to small peptides. It also catalyses the formation of cytotoxic lipid peroxide via lipid peroxidation and damages DNA through oxidative stress (see Section 10). Therefore, to avoid this toxicity, haem levels must be tightly controlled between haem biosynthesis and catabolism in cyanobacteria. 

Recent studies have demonstrated that, in Anabaena sp. PCC 7120, iron deprivation results in the upregulation of transcription enzymes involved in haem degradation and subsequent release of iron, haem oxygenases I and II. It also triggers transcriptional induction of all haem biosynthesis enzymes (Gonzalez et al., 2012). It appears that the increased degradation of haem as an iron source under iron-limited conditions transcriptionally induces the enzymes involved in its own biosynthesis as homeostatic control to maintain haem and phycobilin levels. Taking into account that $\mathrm { C ^ { 1 4 1 } }$ , the residue that coordinates iron of haem by Anabaena FurA, can eventually form a disulphide bridge as deduced from the moderate disulphide reductase activity shown by the $\mathrm { C ^ { 1 4 1 } P H C ^ { 1 4 4 } }$ motif (Botello-Morte et al., 2014) a relation between FurA redox status and haem sensing by this regulator can be envisaged. Therefore, the possibility arises that cyanobacterial Fur might play a role as a haem sensor that could collaborate in the response to oxidative stress in these phototrophs. 

## 19.1.4 Concluding remarks



Golden JW, Robinson SJ, Haselkorn R. 1985. Rearrangement of nitrogen fixation genes during heterocyst differentiation in the cyanobacterium Anabaena. Nature 314: 419–423. 





Lyck S, Gjolme N, Utkilen H. 1996. Iron starvation increases toxicity of Microcystis aeruginosa CYA 228/1 (Chroococcales, Cyanophyceae). Phycologia 35: 120–124. 





Vintila S, Selao T, Noren A, Bergman B, El-Shehawy R. 2011. Characterization of nifH gene expression, modification and rearrangement in Nodularia spumigena strain AV1. FEMS Microbiology Ecology 77: 449–459. 



Iron is essential in most cyanobacterial metabolic pathways as part of the redox centres in a variety of electron transport proteins. To ensure the precise iron supply and minimize oxidative damage, iron homeostasis is tightly regulated by Fur. Analysis of the FurA regulon in Anabaena unveiled that Fur couples in vivo iron and nitrogen metabolism and the response to oxidative stress to major physiological processes in cyanobacteria. Furthermore, the high percentage of hypothetical proteins exhibiting iron boxes in Anabaena indicates that FurA might control a number of metabolic pathways still unexplored, expanding the functions of FurA-modulated genes in cyanobacteria. In addition to its role as a global regulator, FurA displays disulphide reductase activity associated with its CXXC motifs and also exhibits the features of a sensor of haem. Those findings suggest that FurA plays an active role in the cyanobacterial redoxsignalling pathways beyond the classical working model of transcriptional regulation.

# Interplay between $\mathbf { o } _ { 2 }$ and iron in gene expression: environmental sensing by FNR, ArcA, and Fur in bacteria

Bryan Troxell and Hosni M. Hassan 

Departments of Poultry Science and Microbiology, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA 

## 19.2.1 Introduction

Early Earth was an anaerobic, reducing environment. In this environment, chemical and biological reactions proceeded in the absence of dioxygen $( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } )$ , which can poison many chemical and enzymatic reactions. Following the Great Oxidation Event, which occurred about 2.3 billion years ago, these enzymatic reactions were faced with the problem of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ toxicity. Dioxygen is paramagnetic because it has two unpaired electrons $( \mathrm { e } ^ { - } )$ with parallel spin. This causes spin restriction that favors the univalent reduction of ${ \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } ,$ , which results in the formation of partially reduced $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ intermediates. The single $\mathrm { e ^ { - } }$ reduction of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ forms superoxide anion $( { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } ^ { - } )$ , whereas the $2 \mathrm { e } ^ { - }$ , 2H+ reduction forms hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ , and finally the $3 e ^ { - }$ , 3H+ reduction forms hydroxyl radical (OH∙). These three molecules $\mathrm { ~ - ~ } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ − , $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ , and OH∙ – are examples of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that presented life with a new environmental stress (i.e., oxidative stress; see Section 10). 

Iron (Fe) is an important element in biological systems. In most cells, Fe is considered an essential element. Prior to the Great Oxidation Event, the element Fe was readily accessible because of the solubility of ferrous iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ in anaerobic, reducing environments; however, in the presence of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } , \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ is oxidized to the insoluble form, ferric iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } )$ . The insolubility of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ coupled with the near-universal requirement of Fe by cells presented a hurdle: how to acquire the insoluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } ?$ Bacteria and other organisms have aptly addressed this hurdle through the production of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -binding compounds known as siderophores, which have high affinity for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ . Siderophores are produced within the cell and secreted into the environment, and once they have bound extracellular $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , either the metal is brought into the cell as an $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ –siderophore complex or the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ is solubilized by reduction to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and transported into the cell. Through this process, organisms are capable of acquiring extracellular Fe that is present at very low concentrations. 

During adaptation to changes in the $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentration, cells utilize numerous redox-sensing transcription factors to control gene expression. In general, these transcription factors regulate expression of genes whose protein products participate in a variety of physiological functions related to the influence $\mathrm { { o f O } } _ { 2 }$ upon the cell. For instance, in the facultative anaerobic bacterium Escherichia coli, transcriptional repression of the cytochrome o oxidase complex is controlled by the $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -sensing transcription factor fumarate and nitrate reduction (FNR) (Cotter and Gunsalus, 1992). In addition, FNR activates expression of genes involved in the utilization of alternative $\mathrm { e ^ { - } }$ acceptors (Chippaux et al., 1978; Cotter and Gunsalus, 1989; Lambden and Guest, 1976; Newman and Cole, 1978). Therefore, the FNR protein functions as either a transcriptional repressor or activator of gene expression. FNR contains an $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -labile 4Fe–4S cluster that is required for formation of an active dimer (Lazazzera et al., 1993; Spiro and Guest, 1988; Unden and Trageser, 1991). In this case, the utilization of an iron-dependent cofactor as a sensor exploits the reactivity between $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to control gene expression (Zhang et al., 2012). Thus, FNR is an example of how the oxidation state of Fe is used to respond and adapt to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and its reactive species. In addition to FNR, E. coli expresses a two-component system (TCS) known as the aerobic respiration control (Arc) system, also known as an anoxic redox control system. The Arc system is a signal transduction system that contains the histidine kinase (HK) ArcB and the response regulator (RR) ArcA, which upon phosphorylation becomes an active DNA binding protein that regulates changes in transcription of target genes (Georgellis et al., 1997; Ishige et al., 1994; Iuchi, 1993; Iuchi and Lin, 1988; Iuchi et al., 1989; Tsuzuki et al., 1995; see Section 3). The Arc system becomes active in response to changing $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentrations and is another example of how bacteria adapt to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ fluctuations; however, unlike the FNR protein, the ArcAB proteins do not contain a redox-active Fe cofactor. Similar to the FNR protein, however, the transcription factor ferric uptake regulator (Fur) requires the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ corepressor to regulate transcription. Often, FNR, ArcA, and Fur regulate expression of the same target genes, indicating a regulatory link between $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and Fe via FNR, ArcA, and Fur. In the context of bacterial pathogens, this review focuses on the evidence supporting this link. 

## 19.2.2 FNR, ArcA, and Fur: $\ b _ { 0 } ^ { \phantom { \dagger } } _ { 2 }$ and iron sensors in bacteria

In nature, bacteria transition between conditions of varying $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentrations, which requires rapid and profound changes in the transcriptional architecture in order for the cells to adapt to the new conditions (i.e., the redox state). Upon exposing a culture to a different $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentration, E. coli begins to change transcription of genes within 5–10 min (Partridge et al., 2006; Rolfe et al., 2012; Trotter et al., 2011). As expected, FNR and ArcA are important factors contributing to these transcriptional changes. The shift in $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentration also influences the Fe availability, which impacts Fur regulation. How FNR, ArcA, and Fur are activated under these changing $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { F e }$ conditions has been thoroughly studied (see also Chapter 19.1). 

E. coli mutants that are unable to perform anaerobic respiration with fumarate or nitrate have been isolated in the lab of Dr John R. Guest (Lambden and Guest, 1976). Subsequently, the data suggest that some of these mutants may lack a regulatory gene that activates the ability of E. coli to respire with fumarate or nitrate (Shaw and Guest, 1981). The genetic locus responsible for this phenotype has been known as nirA, nirB, and fnr (Chippaux et al., 1978; Newman and Cole, 1978; Shaw and Guest, 1981). A genetic approach confirmed the FNR protein to have homology to the catabolite activator protein (CAP) or cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) receptor protein (CRP) (Shaw and Guest, 1982; Shaw et al., 1983). Active FNR is a homodimer that possesses a 4Fe–4S cluster and exhibits sitespecific DNA binding. Upon oxidation of the 4Fe–4S cluster, there is a conversion to 2Fe–2S, resulting in dimer-to-monomer formation and loss of DNA binding (Lazazzera et al., 1993, 1996). Damaged 4Fe–4S FNR can be repaired by the iron–sulfur cluster (Isc) pathway (Mettert et al., 2008), which is one of two well-known pathways for the generation of Fe-S clusters. FNR contains four Cys residues (C20, C23, C29, and C122) that are required for redox sensing and gene regulation (Melville and Gunsalus, 1990; Sharrocks et al., 1990). In addition, the isolation and characterization of FNR variants that are resistant to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ inactivation have shown the importance of other amino acid residues in FNR function (Bates et al., 1995, 2000; Kiley and Reznikoff, 1991; Moore et al., 2006). FNR controls activation of numerous genes whose products are important for anaerobic metabolism (Fink et al., 2007; Kang et al., 2005; Myers et al., 2013; Salmon et al., 2003). Also, FNR represses genes whose products are involved in $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and ROS defense. The Mncontaining superoxide dismutase gene, sodA, is repressed by FNR (Compan and Touati, 1993; Hassan and Sun, 1992), and the inactivation of FNR by either $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { o r } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { - }$ is an example of the role of substrate in inducing gene expression (Crack et al., 2007; Sutton et al., 2004). 

Like FNR, ArcA is a global regulator within bacteria. Earlier work identified a mutant with de-repressed anaerobic expression of sdh–lacZ that mapped to the arcA region and was complemented by the arcA gene (Iuchi and Lin, 1988). The phenotypes of the arcA mutation are similar to phenotypes of other mutants that also map to the same loci (Bachmann, 1983), suggesting that ArcA may be a global regulator. Amino acid sequences of ArcA and ArcB suggested the function of these two proteins would be an RR and HK, respectively, comprising a TCS (Iuchi et al., 1990; see Section 3). Following autophosphorylation in response to stimuli, in vitro phosphorylation studies identified residues H292, D576, and H717 within ArcB that were responsible for the phosphorelay to ArcA (Georgellis et al., 1997). During aerobic growth, the membrane-associated quinone pool is oxidized. Seminal work in the study of the ArcAB system showed that the oxidized quinone pool acts to inhibit ArcB kinase activity, which maintains an inactive ArcA (Georgellis et al., 2001; Malpica et al., 2004). Therefore, under anaerobic conditions, the quinone pool becomes reduced, allowing ArcB autophosphorylation and phosphorelay activation of ArcA. However, as is typical with a TCS, the HK, ArcB, also functions as a phosphatase of ArcA to maintain an inactive RR when environmental conditions are not proficient for ArcA activation (Georgellis et al., 1998; Pena-Sandoval et al., 2005). This indicates that ArcA may be phosphorylated even when conditions are not optimal for ArcA-dependent transcriptions. The high-energy donor molecular acetyl phosphate $( \mathrm { A c } \mathrm { \sim } \mathrm { P } )$ has been shown to phosphorylate ArcA in vitro (Drapal and Sawers, 1995; Lynch and Lin, 1996). In vivo data indicate that Ac∼P can phosphorylate RRs, but this is detectable only when the cognate HK is deleted (Dailey and Berg, 1993; Feng et al., 1992; Liu et al., 2009; Wanner and Wilmes-Riesenberg, 1992). Collectively, the phosphatase activity of ArcB provides a significant level of inactivation of ArcA when conditions are not optimal for ArcA regulation. Under low- ${ \bf \nabla } \cdot { \bf O } _ { 2 }$ conditions, the phosphorelay from ArcB to ArcA provides an advantage that allows for adaptation to the changing conditions. 

In most bacteria, expression of Fe acquisition genes is under the negative control by Fur. Fur utilizes $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ as a co-repressor to bind DNA and block transcription of genes whose products are involved in Fe uptake. This negative feedback ensures that intracellular Fe concentrations are optimal. Early studies identified fur mutants in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and E. coli that constitutively expressed Fe acquisition genes regardless of the Fe content (Bagg and Neilands, 1985; Ernst et al., 1978; Hantke, 1981, 1984); these mutants lost the negative feedback control in expression of Fe acquisition genes. In several bacteria, the classical ${ \mathrm { F u r } } { \mathrm { - F } } e ^ { 2 + }$ binding site of GATAAT-GATAATCATTATC has been shown to be Fe responsive (Calderwood and Mekalanos, 1987, 1988; de Lorenzo et al., 1987; Stojiljkovic et al., 1994). Although characterized as an Fe-dependent repressor, recent work demonstrates that Fur can activate gene expression through complex mechanisms (Troxell and Hassan, 2013). In Helicobacter pylori, Neisseria meningi-$t i d i s ,$ and E. coli, Fur is known to exhibit ${ \mathrm { F u r } } { \mathrm { - F } } e ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent activation of gene expression (Carpenter et al., 2009; Delany et al., 2004; Nandal et al., 2010). In addition, apo-Fur has been shown to regulate gene expression in H. pylori, Staphylococcus aureus, and Campylobacter jejuni (Butcher et al., 2012; Deng et al., 2012; Carpenter et al., 2013). In a comprehensive approach to identify mechanisms of Fur regulation in E. coli, Seo and coworkers (Seo et al., 2014) identified apo-Fur and Fur– $\cdot \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activation in addition to the classical ${ \mathrm { F u r } } { \mathrm { - F } } e ^ { 2 + }$ repression. Future studies in pathogenic bacteria, utilizing a similar approach to that reported by Seo and coworkers, may provide new insights into the complex role of Fur. Importantly, the data indicate that Fur regulation in bacteria is complex and involves both Fe-dependent and independent mechanisms of gene regulation that we are just beginning to decipher. Because of the connection between $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentrations and the oxidation state of Fe, it suggests that there may be an interaction (communication) between FNR, ArcA, and Fur. 

## 19.2.3 $\ b _ { 0 } ^ { \phantom { \dagger } } _ { 2 }$ and iron: regulatory signals in biology

Nearly all cells require Fe for survival. However, there are notable exceptions to this Fe requirement in the bacterial world, such as the Lyme disease spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi (Posey and Gherardini, 2000), and some Lactobacillus spp. (Imbert and Blondeau, 1998). Because altered Fe homeostasis leads to conditions of oxidative stress in the presence of $\mathrm { ~ \ O } _ { 2 }$ (see Section 10), the import and export of Fe are often connected with the concentration of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ in the growth environment. Within eukaryotic systems, the iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) control Fe homeostasis through binding iron regulatory elements (IREs) in the $5 ^ { \prime }$ or $3 ^ { \prime }$ untranslated regions of messenger RNAs (mRNAs) (Casey et al., 1988; Rouault et al., 1988). IREs are located in the mRNAs whose gene products control Fe import, export, and storage or require Fe as a cofactor. $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ has been shown to influence the binding of IRPs to IREs (Hanson et al., 1999; Hanson and Leibold, 1998). Moreover, the hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) transcription factors are regulated by IRPs and play a role in the regulation of Fe homeostasis genes (ER Anderson et al., 2013; SA Anderson et al., 2013; Semenza and Wang, 1992; Wang et al., 1995; Wilkinson and Pantopoulos, 2013), which links the importance of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and Fe in these biological systems. In bacteria, $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and Fe regulate the expression of Fe-containing proteins within the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, an important anabolic–catabolic pathway in some bacteria that contains numerous Fe-cofactored enzymes. This pathway is important for the generation of reducing power used in the synthesis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) from the electron transport chain (ETC) through oxidative phosphorylation and in the production of biosynthetic molecules. Several of the proteins in this pathway are posttranscriptionally regulated by the Fe concentration in a mechanism that requires small untranslated RNAs (sRNAs) and the Fur protein (Masse and Gottesman, 2002; Mey et al., 2005b). In addition to Fur, FNR and ArcA also regulate components of the TCA cycle (Evans et al., 2011; Fink et al., 2007). 

## 19.2.4 Regulation of the TCA cycle by FNR, ArcA, and Fur

The TCA cycle provides a significant amount of reducing power that is used in the production of ATP. However, the TCA cycle also provides precursor metabolites that can be used to produce 10 out of the 20 common amino acids. Therefore, the TCA cycle is an important biochemical pathway for both catabolic and anabolic reactions, and increasing evidence demonstrates that the TCA cycle may have a regulatory role within pathogens (Bucker et al., 2014; Dieppedale et al., 2013; Ding et al., 2014; Hartmann et al., 2014; Marrero et al., 2010; Massilamany et al., 2011; Minato et al., 2013a, b). Given the importance of this pathway, it is not surprising that the TCA cycle is also important for virulence in bacteria. As shown in Table 19.2.1, mutants with a disrupted TCA cycle exhibit reduced virulence in infection–virulence models. Aconitase (acn), succinate dehydrogenase (sdh), fumarate reductase (frd), and fumarases (fumAB) contain a Fe cofactor that is required for enzymatic activity. Under certain conditions, expression of these enzymes can sequester a significant fraction of the total intracellular Fe. The human pathogen S. aureus produces a toxin that contains a N-formylated methionine residue (Fitton et al., 1980). Typically, the N-formyl methionine of proteins is enzymatically removed by the Fe-dependent peptide deformylase, but in conditions where aconitase expression is high, this protein sequesters Fe from peptide deformylase, resulting in the secretion of a predominantly N-formylated toxin (Somerville et al., 2003). Fe supplementation or inactivation of the TCA cycle gene acnA reduces the production of the N-formylated toxin (Somerville et al., 2003). Because producing the functional components of the TCA cycle is energetically expensive and sequesters intracellular Fe, this pathway is tightly regulated. 

Regulation of the TCA cycle occurs at multiple levels. In the model organism, E. coli, it has been shown that transcriptional repression of genes within the TCA cycle is accomplished by the $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -sensitive regulators FNR and ArcA (Cunningham et al., 1997; Cunningham and Guest, 1998; Gruer and Guest, 1994;

Levanon et al., 2005; Park and Gunsalus, 1995; Park et al., 1994, 1995a,b, 1997; Perrenoud and Sauer, 2005; Shalel-Levanon et al., 2005). However, posttranscriptional regulation of the mRNAs of these genes is also a significant layer of regulation. Thus, fur mutants are unable to utilize the TCA metabolites, fumarate or succinate, as the sole carbon source, and expression of several genes within the TCA cycle is under positive control by Fur (Hantke, 1987, 2001). It was unclear how Fur could accomplish this type of regulation since its function is characterized as a repressor, not an activator. In the first study to explain this, Masse and Gottesman (2002) demonstrated the posttranscriptional repression by the sRNA ryhB upon genes that are Fur activated. Transcription of ryhB is negatively controlled by Fur, and this explains the mechanism for positive regulation of TCA cycle genes by Fur (Masse and Gottesman, 2002; Vassinova and Kozyrev, 2000). The base-pairing of ryhB with target mRNAs results in their degradation or inhibition of translation (Storz et al., 2004). This regulatory approach is known as the iron-sparing response (Gaballa et al., 2008), because it optimizes the availability of Fe and improves survival. The presence of ryhB-like genes are abundant in the bacterial world and have an important role in the regulation of virulence in pathogenic bacteria (Alice et al., 2008; Broach et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2012; Leclerc et al., 2013; Murphy and Payne, 2007; Oglesby-Sherrouse and Murphy, 2013; Porcheron et al., 2014). These findings suggest that the “iron-sparing response” may be an evolutionarily conserved adaptation to Fe deprivation. With regard to the regulation of the TCA cycle, the roles of FNR and ArcA often act in an opposing manner with Fur regulation. An exception is the control of fumarate reductase, encoded by the frdABCD genes, which is activated by FNR or Fur (Fink et al., 2007; Troxell et al., 2011a,b). The regulation of the TCA cycle and antioxidant Mn–superoxide dismutase (Compan and Touati, 1993; Hassan and Sun, 1992; Tardat and Touati, 1993) are examples of how these three redox-sensing transcription factors, FNR, ArcA, and Fur, can regulate the same target genes. In addition, it supports the connection between $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and Fe sensing to the regulation of biochemical and antioxidative pathways. 

## 19.2.5 Regulation of Fe transport by FNR, ArcA, and Fur in bacterial pathogens

There is a clear link between the concentration of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and the availability of Fe. Since Fe is required by most bacterial pathogens (especially foodborne pathogens) that transit through gradients of ${ \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } ,$ it would be advantageous to acquire Fe under these different conditions. In several pathogenic bacteria, Fur acts as a repressor of both $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ acquisition systems (Cornelis et al., 2009; Genco and Desai, 1996; Pich and Merrell, 2013, Troxell and Hassan, 2013; Wyckoff et al., 2007; Yu and Genco, 2012). As is the case for regulation of the TCA cycle, Fe transport appears to be regulated by FNR, ArcA, and/or Fur in some bacterial pathogens. This has been recently reviewed (Carpenter and Payne, 2014) and is briefly discussed here. In Shigella flexneri, both FNR and ArcA activate expression of the Fur-repressed $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter feoAB (Boulette and Payne, 2007). This is beneficial since, under conditions of low O (FNR– ArcA activation), $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ transitions to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and Fe acquisition mediated through siderophore–Fe3+ would be less optimal. In S. Typhimurium, feoB is important for fitness within a murine host (Boyer et al., 2002; Nagy et al., 2014; Tsolis et al., 1996). However, Fe acquisition through siderophore production appears to be a stronger contributor during infection (Crouch et al., 2008; Nagy et al., 2013), suggesting that $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ acquisition may be the predominant mechanism for Fe acquisition within the host. Indeed, outcompeting S. Typhimurium within the gut by a probiotic E. coli bacterium appears to rely on $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ acquisition systems (Deriu et al., 2013). 

## 19.2.6 Importance of FNR, ArcA, or Fur to bacterial pathogens

Given the importance of an optimal TCA cycle toward virulence in pathogens, it is not surprising that transcription factors regulating this pathway can also regulate, directly or indirectly, pathogenicity in vivo. Because FNR, ArcA, and Fur regulate, at some level, expression and flux through the TCA cycle, it suggests that these global regulators may contribute to virulence. Indeed, mutation of these genes does reduce virulence for several bacterial pathogens (Table 19.2.2). However, it is important to note that deletion of either fnr or arcA does not always result in attenuation. Recent work shows that deletion of fnr within S. Typhimurium results in only a modest fitness defect within the small intestine of mice (Craig et al., 2013). While deletion of arcA results in sensitivity to stresses experienced in vivo (e.g., ROS), virulence of the mutated pathogen is not reduced in murine models (Evans et al., 2011; Flamez et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2002). Data generated using E. coli indicate that a significant overlap exists in regulation of metabolic and biochemical pathways between FNR and ArcA (Federowicz et al., 2014). This indicates that redundancy between FNR and ArcA exists, but whether this overlap exists in other pathogens is currently unknown.

Gallinarum</td><td>fur</td><td>Avian</td><td>(Laniewski et al., 2014)</td></tr><tr><td>Shigella flexneri</td><td>fnr</td><td>Murine</td><td>(Marteyn et al., 2010)</td></tr><tr><td>Staphylococcus aureus</td><td>fur</td><td>Murine</td><td>(Horsburgh et al., 2001; Torres et al., 2010)</td></tr><tr><td>Vibrio cholera</td><td>arcA</td><td>Murine</td><td>(Sengupta et al., 2003)</td></tr><tr><td>Vibrio cholera</td><td>fur</td><td>Murine</td><td>(Mey et al., 2005a,b)</td></tr><tr><td>Yersinia pseudotuberculosis</td><td>fnr/arcA</td><td>Murine</td><td>(Avican et al., 2015)</td></tr></table>

Within bacterial pathogens, FNR, ArcA, and Fur have important roles of gene regulation and contribute to infection models. In Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, both FNR and ArcA contribute to host colonization (Avican et al., 2015), suggesting that anaerobic-like conditions are sensed within the gut. Although still capable of causing disease, deletion of frdA, a key gene in the reductive TCA cycle, reduces persistence (Avican et al., 2015), which supports the contribution of anaerobic metabolism to fitness within the host. Compared to in vitro conditions, Shigella dysenteriae exhibits an increase in the level of proteins important for anaerobic metabolism within infected piglets (Kuntumalla et al., 2011). In addition to the overlap between FNR and ArcA in gene expression, other redox-sensing proteins contribute to activation of virulence genes in response to anaerobic conditions. The redox-sensing regulator, AphB, has been shown to activate expression of virulence genes within Vibrio cholera (Liu et al., 2011). This suggests that there may be significant redundancy within pathogens for controlling gene expression in response to changing $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentrations. Nevertheless, FNR contributes to fitness in animal models for S. Typhimurium, Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis, E. coli (UPEC), N. meningitidis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, S. flexneri, and Y. pseudotuberculosis (Table 19.2.2). The ArcA/B system has been shown to contribute to various animal models for A. pleuropneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and V. cholera (Table 19.2.2). Although data with fnr or arcA mutants show contradictory results (discussed in this chapter) in animal models of infection, data with fur mutants overwhelmingly demonstrate attenuation in vivo (Table 19.2.2). Thus, while FNR–ArcAB may contribute to fitness in vivo depending on the lifestyle of the pathogen and possible redundancy, Fur is a predominant contributor to virulence. 

## 19.2.7 Summary

The ability of bacteria to sense environmental conditions is critical to adaptation and survival. Oxygen and iron are signals that bacterial pathogens utilize to regulate virulence. In order to address the environmental signals of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and iron, bacteria possess redox-sensing transcription factors that control their adaptation to these two signals. Bacterial pathogens also utilize these redox-sensing transcription factors to control their adaptation to the host environment. FNR, ArcA, and Fur are highly conserved transcription factors that have an important role in transcriptional regulation within pathogens. These redoxsensing factors regulate the adaptation to anaerobic and/or lowiron conditions and also regulate metabolic flux through the TCA cycle. Mutations in the TCA cycle or fnr, arcA, or fur often attenuate virulence of bacterial pathogens, suggesting that the ability of metabolic adaptation to the changing environmental $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and iron concentrations is an important step to optimal fitness in the host.

# The iron–sulfur cluster biosynthesis regulator IscR contributes to iron homeostasis and resistance to oxidants in Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Adisak Romsang2,3, James M. Dubbs1, and Skorn Mongkolsuk1–4 

1Laboratory of Biotechnology, Chulabhorn Research Institute, Lak Si, Bangkok, Thailand 

2Center of Emerging Bacterial Infections, Faculty of Science, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand 

3Department of Biotechnology, Faculty of Science, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand 

4Center of Excellence for Environmental Health, Toxicology and Management of Chemicals, Bangkok, Thailand 

## 19.3.1 Introduction

Iron–sulfur (Fe-S) cluster-containing proteins are required for many essential biochemical functions across all domains of life. This is due to their structural versatility and chemical reactivity (Py and Barras, 2010). Fe-S cluster proteins play essential roles in a variety of cellular activities, including respiration, central metabolism, biosynthetic pathways, nitrogen fixation, DNA repair, RNA modification, and gene regulation (Kiley and Beinert, 2003; Lill, 2009; Py et al., 2011). Their ability to undergo redox reactions with gaseous molecules allows them to be used by regulatory proteins to sense the intracellular levels of molecular oxygen (O ) and nitric oxide (NO), which have important biological roles (Crack et al., 2014; Py and Barras, 2010). O serves as a terminal electron acceptor for aerobic respiration and as a precursor of reactive oxygen species (ROS; see Section 10), whereas NO functions as a signaling molecule and as an antimicrobial (see Section 17). Control of gene expression results from conformational changes that affect DNA binding (Crack et al., 2014). 

Fe-S centers come in a variety of forms. The most common is an approximately 90% cubic, 4Fe-4S type. Other examples are rhombic 2Fe-2S, 3Fe-4S, and 8Fe-7S, as well as other types (Fontecave, 2006; Py and Barras, 2010). In most Fe-S cluster proteins, cysteine (Cys) residues coordinate the iron ion, but histidine (His) residues can also be involved (Fleischhacker et al., 2012; Nesbit et al., 2009), as is the case in the Fe-S cluster– containing transcriptional regulator, IscR, found in Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa as well as other bacteria (Py and Barras, 2010). In the case of both E. coli and P. aeruginosa, one histidine and three cysteine residues bind the 2Fe-2S cluster (Fleischhacker et al., 2012; Romsang et al., 2014). 

Fe-S clusters are thought to be one of the most ancient types of protein prosthetic groups, and the basic process by which they are synthesized is conserved among all organisms (Py and Barras, 2010). The Fe-S cluster is first assembled within a protein scaffold before it is inserted into the target protein (Py and Barras, 2010). In bacteria, three independent Fe-S cluster biosynthetic systems have been identified, namely the NIF (nitrogen fixation), ISC (iron–sulfur cluster), and SUF (mobilization of sulfur) systems (Ayala-Castro et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2005; Zheng et al., 1998). The ISC and Suf systems are general Fe-S cluster biosynthetic systems. The NIF system is specific for the assembly and insertion of Fe-S clusters in nitrogenase, the enzyme responsible for nitrogen fixation (Py and Barras, 2010). Some bacteria contain only one system, such as the ISC system in the human pathogen P. aeruginosa (Romsang et al., 2014), and the SUF system in Gram-positive bacilli (Santos et al., 2014) and the Gram-negative plant pathogen Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris (Xcc) (Fuangthong et al., 2015). However, others can contain more than one system, like E. coli and Thermincola potens, which possess both the ISC and SUF systems (see Figure 19.3.1) (Fontecave et al., 2005; Outten et al., 2004; Takahashi and Tokumoto, 2002). 

Regardless of the Fe-S biosynthetic system(s) that an organism contains, the fundamental mechanisms and key proteins necessary for Fe-S cluster biogenesis are similar between them. Sulfur is provided by Cys via a cysteine desulfurase (IscS, NifS, and SufS), which is a phosphate-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the degradation of the L-cysteine to an enzyme-linked S-sulfanyl cysteine (E-S-SH) and L-alanine (Py and Barras, 2010). Apart from their function in Fe-S cluster biogenesis, some cysteine desulfurases are involved in the biosynthesis of numerous sulfurcontaining substances such as thiamine, molybdopterin, and the nucleosides in transfer RNAs (tRNAs) (Kessler, 2006; Shigi et al., 2006).

Figure 19.3.1 Organization of the genes encoding Fe-S biogenesis proteins in several bacterial genomes. The double lines separating the two gene clusters in T. potens indicate that these clusters are encoded at different positions in the genome.


Our understanding of the processes controlling the provision of iron for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis is incomplete. There, are however, a number of proteins that have been proposed as iron donors, including CyaY (a bacterial homolog of eukaryotic frataxin) and iron storage proteins such as ferritins and bacterioferritin (Yao et al., 2011). 

Scaffold proteins, such as IscU, IscA, SufU, SufA, and NifU, form an intermediate assembly site for Fe-S cluster precursor assembly. Other scaffold and electron transfer proteins also play a role in the formation of 4Fe-4S clusters from 2Fe-2S precursors (Giel et al., 2013; Santos et al., 2015). The finished clusters are then transferred to target apo-proteins (Boyd et al., 2014; Roche et al., 2013). 

In E. coli, as well as many other pathogenic bacteria, Fe-S clusters are normally synthesized using the ISC machinery encoded by the isc operon (iscRSUA-hscBA-fdx-iscX), which is expressed constitutively, but upregulated in response to oxidative stress (see Section 10) and iron-limiting conditions (Fleischhacker et al., 2012). As previously mentioned, iscS encodes cysteine desulfurase, while iscU and iscA encode scaffold proteins for 2Fe-2S cluster assembly (Ayala-Castro et al., 2008). Chaperone proteins encoded by hscA and hscB are involved in the formation of 4Fe-4S clusters. They function to destabilize the IscU-Fe-S complex and facilitate cluster delivery to acceptor proteins by regulating cluster release and transfer (Fuz¨ ery´ et al., 2011; Vickery and Cupp-Vickery, 2007). Fdx contains a 2Fe-2S cluster and supplies electrons to reduce sulfane sulfur (S0) produced by IscS to sulfide (S2–), as required for the assembly of Fe– S clusters on the scaffold protein (IscU), and it has been shown that Fdx directly interacts with IscS and competes with IscU and CyaY for binding to IscS (Kim et al., 2013). 

iscR encodes a dimeric transcriptional regulator of the MarA– SoxS–Rob family (Fleischhacker et al., 2012) and contains one 2Fe-2S cluster per subunit (see Figure 19.3.2) (Fleischhacker et al., 2012; Rajagopalan et al., 2013). In E. coli, IscR is capable of binding DNA at two distinct consensus binding sites, denoted type 1 (ATASYYGACTRWWWYAGTCRRSTAT) and type 2 (AWARCCCYTSNGTTTGMNGKKKTKWA) (Giel et al., 2006). The presence or absence of Fe-S clusters in the protein affects the binding site preference of the regulator (Rajagopalan et al., 2013). IscR containing Fe-S clusters binds DNA at both type 1 and type 2 IscR-binding motifs (Crack et al.,

2014; Schwartz et al., 2001). If no Fe-S clusters are present in the dimer, apo-IscR shifts binding site specificity to type 2 IscRbinding motifs exclusively (Nesbit et al., 2009; Rajagopalan et al., 2013). 

The two forms of IscR coordinate the regulation of Fe-S cluster biosynthesis systems. During normal growth, when the Fe-S cluster supply is sufficient, IscR dimers containing Fe-S clusters repress the transcription of the isc operon by binding to two type 1 binding sites present in the promoter–operator region (Schwartz et al., 2001). Under conditions where Fe-S cluster production is insufficient, a buildup of apo-IscR leads to the derepression of isc operon expression and the activation of the suf-operon (sufABCDSE) via specific binding to type 2 IscRbinding motifs within the suf-operon promoter (Nesbit et al., 2009). 

Cellular Fe-S cluster content is the key signal for IscRmediated transcriptional control through these two different types of IscR-binding motifs. It follows that environmental stresses that reduce Fe-S content, such as Fe limitation and Fe-S cluster damage due to oxidative stress (Crack et al., 2012a,b; Imlay, 2006), would affect the expression of the ISC and SUF systems (Fuangthong et al., 2015; Outten et al., 2004; Romsang et al., 2014; Yeo et al., 2006). This occurs through IscR (Fuangthong et al., 2015; Outten et al., 2004; Romsang et al., 2014; Yeo et al., 2006) as well as via direct links with other stress regulators. For example, in the Enterobacteriacea, the control of isc expression is directly linked to Fe starvation through the regulatory RNA, RyhB (Desnoyers et al., 2009; Masse and Gottesman, 2002;´ see Section 5), and to oxidative stress via the oxidant-sensing transcriptional regulator, OxyR (Outten et al., 2004; Yeo et al., 2006). Both iron limitation and oxidative stress are encountered during infection (Atichartpongkul et al., 2010; Cornelis and Dingemans, 2013; Tan et al., 1999), which makes the regulation of Fe-S cluster synthesis a potentially important aspect of the physiological adjustment necessary for the shift to growth within a host organism (Kim et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2014; Runyen-Janecky et al., 2008). 

## 19.3.2 Iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in Pseudomonas aeruginosa

P. aeruginosa is an aerobe with the capacity for facultative anaerobic growth utilizing nitrate as a respiratory electron acceptor (Hunt and Phibbs, 1983). It is of interest mainly because it is a common opportunistic human pathogen infecting burn patients, immunocompromised patients, and people with pneumonias or cystic fibrosis (Lavoie et al., 2011; Lyczak et al., 2000). 

The P. aeruginosa PAO1 genome contains an isc gene cluster consisting of iscRSUA–hscBA–fdx2–iscX (PA3815–PA3808) (Romsang et al., 2014). As shown in Figure 19.3.1, this basic gene organization is conserved among isc operons of the Enterobacteriaceae (E. coli, Shigella flexneri, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, and Klebsiella pneumonia) as well as other Gram-negatives (Azotobacter vinelandii, Erwinia chrysanthemi, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, and Vibrio vulnificus). By contrast, T. potens contains iscR linked to iscS and iscU without other ISC-component genes, while X. campestris carries iscR linked to genes of the suf system (see Figure 19.3.1). 

Comparison of the deduced amino acid sequences indicates that P. aeruginosa IscR shares 77% identity with the IscR from A. vinelandii and approximately 60% identity with the IscR from V. vulnificus, Y. pseudotuberculosis, E. chrysanthemi, and Enterobacteriaceae (Figures 19.3.3 and 19.3.4). P. aeruginosa IscR shares only 39% identity with the IscR from the Grampositive bacterium T. potens and about 20% identity with the IscR from X. campestris. This is reflected in the rooted phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 19.3.3, in which T. potens and X. campestris IscRs do not branch with the others. 

In all cases, Cys92, Cys98, and Cys104 (E. coli numbering), which are known to participate in the coordination of the 2Fe-2S cluster in E. coli IscR, are conserved (Figure 19.3.4). His107 is also involved in coordinating the 2Fe-2S cluster in E. coli IscR (Giel et al., 2013; Rajagopalan et al., 2013), but is absent in IscR from T. potens and X. campestris. It is thought that
