S104 functions as the fourth iron ligand in these organisms (Santos et al., 2015). Figure 19.3.4 shows that residues proposed to constitute the DNA–IscR interface, such as Ser40, Glu43, Gln44, 

Arg59, and Gly60, are also conserved (Santos et al., 2015), with the exceptions of Glu43, which prevents apo-IscR from binding to the type 1 binding sites (Giel et al., 2013; Rajagopalan et al., 2013), as well as Ser40 and Gln44, which are absent in X. campestris IscR. 

The second gene in the operon, iscS, encoding cysteine desulfurase, contains the sequence motif, SSGSAC(T/S)S, spanning the conserved C-terminal catalytic Cys residue characteristic of type 1 enzymes such as NifS and NFS (Liu et al., 2009; Urbina et al., 2001). IscS mobilizes sulfur from L-cysteine for the synthesis of several biomolecules, including Fe-S clusters, molybdopterin, thiamin, lipoic acid, biotin, and the thiolation of tRNAs (Dahl et al., 2013). The sulfur transfer from IscS to various biomolecules is mediated by different interaction partners such as IscU, Fdx, IscX, and CyaY for Fe-S cluster biogenesis; TusA for thiomodification of tRNAs; and ThiI for thiamine biosynthesis and tRNA thiolation (Dahl et al., 2013). 

The third gene in the operon, iscU, encodes a Fe-S scaffold protein (Fontecave and Ollagnier-de-Choudens, 2008; Py and Barras, 2010; Urbina et al., 2001). There are three known types of scaffold proteins: U-type, NFU-type, and A-type (Fontecave and Ollagnier-de-Choudens, 2008; Rouault and Tong, 2008). IscU is a U-type scaffold protein that contains a characteristic sequence motif containing three conserved Cys residues $( \mathrm { C } { \cdot } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 4 \mathrm { t o } 2 6 } { \cdot } \mathrm { C } { \cdot }$ $\mathrm { X } _ { 4 2 \ t o 4 3 } – \mathrm { C } )$ that are required for assembly of the Fe-S cluster (Urbina et al., 2001). There are no other homologs of IscU in the PAO1 genome.

IscA is an iron-binding A-type carrier protein, as are IscA, NfuA, SufA, and ErpA (Py and Barras, 2010; Rouault and Tong, 2008). IscA is thought to be responsible for the transfer of completed Fe-S clusters to target apo-proteins. This is because it has been demonstrated to accept Fe-S clusters from IscU, but transfer in the opposite direction is not possible (Chandramouli et al., 2007). 

Both hscB and hscA encode chaperones that mediate the transfer of finished Fe-S clusters from IscU to target apoproteins. The product of hscB is a J-type co-chaperone protein of approximately 20 kDa that directs IscU to the HscA substrate-binding domain and stimulates the adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis activity of HscA (Fuz¨ ery ´ et al., 2011; Py and Barras, 2010; Vickery and Cupp-Vickery, 2007). HscA, a homolog of the chaperone DnaK, is required for 4Fe-4S formation. It interacts with the IscU–HscB complex, where it facilitates Fe-S cluster transfer at the expense of ATP hydrolysis (Fuz¨ ery ´ et al., 2011). 

fdx2 encodes a ferredoxin that contains a 2Fe-2S cluster and is involved in the formation of 4Fe-4S clusters (Chandramouli et al., 2007; Py and Barras, 2010; Roche et al., 2013). The product of fdx2 is a ferredoxin that contains a 2Fe-2S cluster that is necessary for the reductive coupling of two $2 \mathrm { F e } { - 2 \mathsf { S } ^ { 2 + } }$ clusters to form a single $4 \mathrm { F e } { - } 4 \mathrm { S } ^ { 2 + }$ cluster in homodimeric IscU (Yan et al., 2013). 

The last gene in the isc operon, iscX, is a Fe-S cluster assembly protein composed of only 66 amino acids. IscX has been shown to interact with IscU and IscS both individually and in a ternary complex containing all three (Dahl et al., 2013). IscX inhibits IscS desulfurase activity and functions as an iron donor for Fe-S assembly (Kim et al., 2014). 

The isc operon appears to encode the primary Fe-S cluster biosynthesis system in P. aeruginosa since no homologs of the suf genes are present in the genome (Romsang et al., 2014). However, a number of genes that have Fe-S cluster biogenesis-related function are present. These include nfuA, erpA, cyaY, and yggX (Daung-nkern et al., 2010; A Romsang and S Mongkolsuk, unpublished observations). 

NfuA is a fused protein between an Nfu domain and a degenerate A-type carrier domain, which is thought to be a Fe-S carrier involved in the maturation of certain Fe-S proteins during oxidative stress (Angelini et al., 2008; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2008; Zimbler et al., 2012). In E. coli, NfuA is required for survival under oxidative stress and during iron limitation (Angelini et al., 2008; Zimbler et al., 2012), and it is required for full activity of aconitases in A. vinelandii (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2008). In P. aeruginosa, inactivation of nfuA enhances susceptibility to fluoroquinolone antibiotics, which are known to induce oxidative stress (Daung-nkern et al., 2010). 

The open reading frame (ORF) PA0665 is predicted to encode the Fe-S insertion protein, ErpA. In E. coli, ErpA is an A-type scaffold protein that is essential for both aerobic and anaerobic respiratory growth (Bolstad et al., 2010; Py and Barras, 2010). This may also be the case for P. aeruginosa PAO1 erpA since efforts to inactivate the gene under aerobic conditions have been unsuccessful (A Romsang and J Duang-nkern, unpublished observations). 

Bacterial frataxin (CyaY) is involved in the donation of the iron ions during Fe-S cluster assembly (Py and Barras, 2010; Roche et al., 2013). Finally, YggX, also an iron-binding protein, has been suggested to function in Fe-S cluster repair in E. coli due to the observation that, under exposure to paraquat, a yggXdeletion mutant showed a deficiency in the activity of the Fe-S cluster–containing enzyme, aconitase, compared to the wild type (Gralnick and Downs, 2001; Justino et al., 2007). In E. coli, cyaA and yggX might be functionally redundant since individual mutations in $c y a Y$ or yggX are not associated with phenotypic changes (Justino et al., 2007; Li et al., 1999). However, in S. enteric serovar Typhimurium, CyaY and YggX play distinct supporting roles (Velayudhan et al., 2014). CyaA functions in Fe-S cluster biosynthesis and the repair of labile clusters damaged by oxidants, while YggX functions in Fe-S cluster synthesis, protection, and repair during severe oxidative stress (Velayudhan et al., 2014). 

## 19.3.3 IscR as a transcriptional regulator for Fe-S biogenesis in Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Northern blotting and reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analyses indicate that the P. aeruginosa isc operon (iscRSUA–hscBA–fdx2–iscX) is transcribed as a single polycistronic messenger RNA (mRNA) of approximately 5 kb (Romsang et al., 2014). Unlike E. coli, in which the large polycistronic mRNA is processed to leave a stable mRNA-encoding iscR (Fleischhacker et al., 2012), no stable isc mRNA segments have been detected in P. aeruginosa (Romsang et al., 2014). Transcription of the P. aeruginosa isc operon is constitutive but shows significant induction in the presence of redox-cycling and superoxide-generating agents (menadione, plumbagin, and paraquat) as well as $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and organic peroxides (tert-butyl hydroperoxide and cumene hydroperoxide) (Romsang et al., 2014). 

Initial indications that IscR is a repressor that controls the expression of itself and the isc operon in P. aeruginosa came from the observation that an iscR deletion mutant (ΔiscR) had a 20-fold higher level of isc operon transcription, relative to wildtype PAO1, as measured using real-time RT-PCR that targeted a region $5 ^ { \prime }$ to the deletion cite (Romsang et al., 2014). Expression of plasmid-borne iscR returned transcription to wild-type levels, indicating the direct involvement of IscR (Romsang et al., 2014). 

The sequence upstream of P. aeruginosa iscR contains two putative type 1 IscR-binding motifs denoted site A (5′ AATCCTGAGTAATTTGATCGGTCTT3′ ), between positions −43 and −67, and site B (5′ ATAGTTGACCTAAT TACTCGGATAA3′ ), spanning positions −18 to −42 relative to the iscR transcription start (Romsang et al., 2014). These two motifs share 68% and 76% identity with the consensus sequence for the E. coli type 1 IscR-binding motif (see Figure 19.3.5). The results of gel mobility shift assays confirm that purified His-tagged IscR binds to a DNA fragment spanning both sites. Additionally, the presence of multiple shifted bands suggests the binding of multiple IscR to this isc promoter fragment (A Romsang and S Mongkolsuk, unpublished results). These IscRbinding motifs overlap a putative sigma 70 RNA polymerase consensus promoter sequence. Thus, the binding of IscR to these sites would likely prevent RNA polymerase binding to the promoter and repress the transcription of the isc operon, which is consistent with the observed increased isc transcription in P. aeruginosa ΔiscR that is reversed with the expression of functional iscR (Romsang et al., 2014).

A comparison of the sequences of each of the IscR binding sites is shown along with the consensus sequences for the E. coli IscR type 1 and type 2 binding sites. Consensus sequences are expressed using base notations that are consistent with the rules of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC): A (adenine), C (cytosine), G (guanine), T (thymine), R (A or G), Y (T or C), K (T or G), M (A or C), S (C or G), W (A or T), B (all but A), D (all but C), H (all but G), V (all but T), and N (any).


A recent report in E. coli highlights differences in iscR binding site organization in its isc operon promoter compared to that in P. aeruginosa (Figure 19.3.5). DNase I protection analyses of the E. coli isc promoter revealed that IscR binds to three individual sites within the iscR promoter region (Giel et al., 2006). One region of protection, which encompasses nucleotides −67 to −14 relative to the +1 transcription start site, includes two type 1 IscR binding sites: site A (−65 to −41) and site B (−40 to −16) (Giel et al., 2006). A remaining IscR site, denoted site C, is located from +9 to +26. It does not share sequence similarity with other known IscR-binding sites and has no known function (Giel et al., 2006). The two adjacent type 1 IscR-binding sites, A and B, span the consensus RNA polymerase binding site. Each of these two sites binds the IscR holo-form and is responsible for iscR repression in vivo, where they appear to contribute equally (Giel et al., 2013). Thus, the mechanism of IscR repression in E. coli can be simply explained by promoter occlusion. 

The P. aeruginosa isc promoter is similar to that of E. coli in that it contains two IscR-binding sites at positions corresponding to sites A and B in the E. coli promoter. However, no site corresponding to site C is present (Figure 19.4.5). In P. aeruginosa, site B is primarily responsible for repression. This is based on the observations that site B exhibits higher affinity for IscR binding in vitro and that site-directed mutations in site B increased in vivo promoter activity (approximately fourfold), while mutations in site A had only a small effect on repression (A Romsang and S Mongkolsuk, unpublished results). Moreover, comparison of IscR-binding sites A and B present in the P. aeruginosa iscR promoter with those in E. coli shows that the B site shares 81% DNA sequence identity between the two organisms, while site A shares only 42% identity. The function of site A, if any, in the regulation of the P. aeruginosa isc operon is unclear. Site A in E. coli is clearly a type 1 binding site, while site A in P. aeruginosa shows roughly equal sequence identity to the type 1 (68%) and type 2 (65%) IscR consensus binding motifs (see Figure 19.3.5). Thus, the function of site A likely differs significantly from that in E. coli. 

Recent IscR DNA-binding and target gene expression studies in E. coli have shown that three cysteine residues (Cys92, Cys98, and Cys104) and one histidine residue (His107), which are ligands for 2Fe-2S coordination (Fleischhacker et al., 2012; Santos et al., 2015), are required for repression of target gene transcription (Rajagopalan et al., 2013; Santos et al., 2015). 

Cys92, Cys98, Cys104, and His107 are also conserved in P. aeruginosa IscR, where they perform a similar function. This is based on the results of complementation experiments performed in P. aeruginosa ΔiscR mutant strains expressing IscR mutants carrying single alanine substitutions at Cys92, Cys98, Cys104, or His107 (Romsang et al., 2014). The C92A and H107A iscR mutants failed to repress transcription of the isc operon in the ΔiscR background, while the IscR-C98A and IscR-C104A partially restored repression relative to wild-type IscR. Moreover, oxidant treatment of ΔiscR strains expressing IscR-C98A and IscR-C104A de-repressed isc operon transcription to wildtype levels (Romsang et al., 2014). The inability of IscR-C92A and IscR-H107A to repress isc operon transcription is thought to be due to an inability of these proteins to ligate 2Fe-2S clusters, thus preventing binding of the C92A and H107A mutants to the type 1 binding motifs in the isc-operon promoter and operator (Romsang et al., 2014). By contrast, it is thought that IscR-C98A and IscR-C104A are capable of ligating 2Fe-2S clusters but that the IscR-C98A and C104A holo-forms are present at much lower levels than the wild-type protein. This is supported by spectroscopic analyses of purified His-tagged IscR wild-type and C92A, C98A, C104A, and H107A mutants (Romsang et al., 2014). All of the IscR variant proteins (C98A, C104A, H107A, and C92A) contained a reduced amount of 2Fe-2S clusters relative to wild-type IscR (Romsang et al., 2014). Consistent with the complementation results, the IscR-C92A and H107A contained the lowest levels of 2Fe-2S clusters, while the levels of 2Fe-2S clusters bound by the C98A and C104A mutants were intermediate between those of the C92A and H107A mutants and wild-type IscR (Romsang et al., 2014). The lower levels of the IscR-C92A and IscR-H107A mutant holo-forms could be due to weakened 2Fe-2S cluster attachment, rendering it susceptible to oxidation under aerobic conditions or 2Fe-2S cluster insertion, which may be less efficient. Complementation experiments performed under anaerobic conditions gave results that were similar to those obtained under aerobic conditions (A Romsang and S Mongkolsuk, unpublished observations), perhaps arguing against increased susceptibility of the C98A and C104A mutants to oxidation; however, this particular point has yet to be resolved. 

IscR regulatory targets are not limited to Fe-S cluster biosynthesis genes. Recently, E. coli IscR has been shown to be a global regulator that controls the transcription of at least 50 genes, apart from the well-known isc and suf operons (Giel et al., 2006; Lim et al., 2014; Schwartz et al., 2001; Wu and Outten, 2009). Most of these genes encode Fe-S cluster proteins and include transcriptional regulators such as IscR, SoxR, and Fnr; the Fe-S cluster carriers NfuA and ErpA; TCA cycle enzymes (aconitase and succinate dehydrogenase); and proteins involved in anaerobic respiration (periplasmic nitrate reductase and hydrogenases-1 and −2), among others (Schwartz et al., 2001). IscR also controls some non-Fe-S cluster protein–encoding genes, such as the fim and flu operons (Wu and Outten, 2009), both of which encode cell surface adhesins involved in surface attachment and aggregation that can affect virulence (Schwan, 2011; Wu and Outten, 2009; see Section 22). In P. aeruginosa, IscR is a repressor of tpx encoding a thiol-peroxidase that plays a role in hydrogen peroxide resistance (Somprasong et al., 2012). Moreover, P. aeruginosa IscR indirectly modulates catalase activity at the posttranslational level through its effect on intracellular iron–heme levels (Kim et al., 2009; Romsang et al., 2014). 

## 19.3.4 Involvement of IscR in the oxidative stress response and virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Fe-S clusters are susceptible to damage due to reactive oxygen intermediates (ROS), including hydroxyl radicals, superoxide anion, and hydrogen peroxide, resulting in loss of the functional clusters (Crack et al., 2012a,b; D’Autreaux and Toledano, 2007;´ Imlay, 2006; Py and Barras, 2010; see Section 10). These ROS directly oxidize the Fe-S clusters in proteins, converting the 4Fe-$4 \mathrm { S } ^ { 2 + }$ form to an unstable 4Fe- ${ \cdot } 4 \mathrm { S } ^ { 3 + }$ state, which releases $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ . The resultant $3 \mathrm { F e - 4 S ^ { 1 + } }$ cluster (Djaman et al., 2004; Imlay, 2006) is metastable and rapidly degrades, as shown in Reactions 1 and 2 (Djaman et al., 2004): 

Reaction $\mathrm { 1 { : } O x + 4 F e { - } 4 S ^ { 2 + }  R e d + 4 F e { - } 4 S ^ { 3 + } }$ 

Reaction $2 \colon 4 \mathrm { F e } { - } 4 \mathrm { S } ^ { 3 + }  3 \mathrm { F e } { - } 4 \mathrm { S } ^ { 1 + } + \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ 

Damage to clusters can also occur upon reactions with strongly coordinating species such as sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) and nitrosylating agents such as nitric oxide (NO) (Crack et al., 2012a,b; Zumft, 2002; see Section 17). NO reacts readily with Fe-S proteins, leading to S-nitrosylation of the iron atom in the Fe-S cluster–containing proteins (Imlay, 2006). This sensitivity to certain types of damage allows Fe-S clusters to be used by regulatory proteins as environmental sensors. Examples of this in E. coli can be seen in the aerobic-anaerobic sensing regulator, Fnr, and the oxidative stress sensor, SoxR. Fnr binds a 4Fe-4S cluster under anaerobic conditions that stimulates the formation of an active DNA-binding dimeric form. Exposure to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ oxidizes the cluster to a 2Fe-2S form, leading to protein monomerization and hence loss of DNA-binding ability (Kiley and Beinert, 1998, 2003; Saini et al., 2012). Another example is the transcriptional regulator, SoxR, a 2Fe-2S cluster–containing protein that functions as a sensor of oxidative stress and NO in bacteria (Demple et al., 1999; Kiley and Beinert, 2003; Kobayashi et al., 2014). A reversible one-electron oxidation of the 2Fe-2S cluster converts SoxR to a transcriptional activator of SoxS, which in turn activates stress response genes in the soxRS regulon. NO also activates SoxR by direct nitrosylation of the iron atoms in the 2Fe-2S cluster (Kobayashi et al., 2014; Saini et al., 2012). 

In IscR, the presence or absence of a 2Fe-2S cluster determines target gene promoter specificity as well as whether the protein functions as an activator or repressor (Giel et al., 2006; Nesbit et al., 2009; Otsuka et al., 2010; Yeo et al., 2006). During oxidative stress, damage to the 2Fe-2S cluster leads to a decrease in the level of the IscR holo-form and an increase in IscR apo-form levels. Thus, redox conditions modulate the ligation status of the labile IscR cluster that, in turn, determines a switch in DNA sequence specificity of the regulator. This results in the selective regulation of subsets of genes within the IscR regulon in both E. coli and P. aeruginosa (Giel et al., 2013; Outten et al., 2004; Romsang et al., 2014; Somprasong et al., 2012; Wu and Outten, 2009; Yeo et al., 2006). 

Several studies have shown that inactivation of iscR in P. aeruginosa results in increased sensitivity to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and organic hydroperoxides, as well as to the superoxide generators: plumbagin, menadione, and paraquat (Choi et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2009; Romsang et al., 2014). Similar defects in oxidative stress resistance have also been observed in iscR inactivation mutants of other bacteria (Fuangthong et al., 2015; Jones-Carson et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2014). All of these phenotypes can complement functional iscR, indicating that IscR plays an important role in the oxidative stress response (see Section 10) and suggesting that misregulation of genes in the IscR regulon is responsible for the increased oxidant sensitivity of the ΔiscR mutant (Fuangthong et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2014; Romsang et al., 2014). 

The observed $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ sensitivity of the ΔiscR mutant is due, at least in part, to reductions in the levels and activities of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ detoxification enzymes. In P. aeruginosa PAO1, IscR directly regulates tpx, which plays a role in hydrogen peroxide resistance (Somprasong et al., 2012), whereas iscR inactivation has also been shown to reduce catalase activity in P. aeruginosa (Kim et al., 2009) as well as the plant pathogen Xanthomonas campestris (Fuangthong et al., 2015), Burkholderia mallei (Jones-Carson et al., 2008), and Vibrio vulnificus (Lim et al., 2014). The basis for the iscR mutant’s sensitivity to organic peroxides remains to be determined. 

The basis for the increased sensitivity to the redox-cycling drugs plumbagin, menadione, and paraquat is unknown. There are several possible pathways for toxicity. These drugs generate superoxide anion $( \mathrm O _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - } )$ through a redox-cycling reaction in which single electrons are removed from cellular redox cofactors and transferred to oxygen. Toxicity can result from either the oxidation of cellular components, including Fe-S clusters, or the disruption of normal electron flow via redox-cycling reactions that oxidize the cellular electron carrier pool (Gu and Imlay, 2011; Romsang et al., 2013). These drugs can also irreversibly oxidize NAD cofactors in proteins (Gu and Imlay, 2011; Romsang et al., 2013). 

The sensitivity of the P. aeruginosa ΔiscR mutant to redoxcycling drugs does not appear to be due to ${ \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } } ^ { \bullet - }$ since anaerobic respiratory growth with $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ as an electron acceptor did not affect sensitivity relative to that observed during aerobic growth (Romsang et al., 2013, 2014). The question remains as to how the presence of these redox-cycling drugs is sensed by IscR if superoxide-mediated damage to its Fe-S cluster is not involved. Is the Fe-S cluster in IscR damaged in some other way, or does the disruption of cellular redox status affect Fe-S cluster biogenesis pathways? 

IscR clearly plays a role in virulence. The inactivation of P. aeruginosa iscR attenuates virulence in Drosophila melanogaster and mouse peritonitis models (Kim et al., 2009) and has been shown to reduce virulence in other pathogens such as E. chrysanthemi (Rincon-Enriquez et al., 2008), S. flexneri (Runyen-Janecky et al., 2008), Burkholderia mallei (Jones-Carson et al., 2008), and V. vulnificus (Lim et al., 2014). IscR is also known to be involved in virulence related processes in E. coli where it modulates the formation of biofilms via the regulation of type I fimbria expression (Wu and Outten, 2009). In the foodborne pathogen Y. pseudotuberculosis, IscR is critical for virulence and expression of the type III secretion system through direct regulation of the T3SS master regulator, LcrF (Miller et al., 2014). Recently, it has been shown that IscR senses iron starvation via a shift in the protein to the IscR apo-form, which activates prx3 expression (Lim et al., 2014). Prx3 is a 1-Cys peroxiredoxin that reduces $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ using reducing equivalents supplied via glutaredoxin 3 (Grx3) and glutathione (GSH). This contributes to the survival and virulence of V. vulnificus during pathogenesis (Lim et al., 2014). IscR not only is a key factor for pathogenicity in mammalian pathogens, but also is important for virulence in plant pathogens such as X. campestris (Fuangthong et al., 2015).

Figure 19.3.6 Effect of iscR deletion on P. aeruginosa virulence using a Caenorhabditis elegans host model system. The results of fast- and slow-killing assays are shown between P. aeruginosa wild-type PAO1 and the ΔiscR mutant carrying Tn7 genomic insertions as well as the ΔiscR mutant carrying a Tn7 genomic insertion containing an iscR expression cassette. The worms were scored as live or dead after 3 $^ { 5 , 7 , }$ and 9 h for fast killing and 1, 2, 3, and 4 days for slow killing. The data presented are means and standard deviations of three biologically independent experiments.


The killing of Caenorhabditis elegans by P. aeruginosa is a good example of how iscR can affect virulence in a number of ways. P. aeruginosa can kill C. elegans quickly because of intoxication due to diffusible toxins, such as phenazines, released by the bacteria when grown as a lawn on rich media (Cezairliyan et al., 2013). When grown on minimal media, killing occurs more slowly due to the buildup of cyanide that is generated by the bacteria during growth in the worm gut (Cezairliyan et al., 2013; Glasser et al., 2014; Tan et al., 1999). The results of C. elegans killing assays of worms grown on bacterial lawns of P. aeruginosa strains on rich (panel a) and minimal media (panel b) are shown in Figure 19.3.6. In both cases, worms grown on the P. aeruginosa ΔiscR strain exhibited an increase in mortality in both fast- and slow-killing assays compared to the wild-type PAO1. Wild-type mortality levels were restored by iscR expression from a Tn7 expression construct inserted into the genome in single copy, confirming that the absence of functional iscR was responsible for the phenotype. 

The observed virulence attenuation in the ΔiscR mutant in the slow-killing assays is likely due, at least in part, to reduced oxidative stress defense since inactivation of oxidative stress defense genes has previously been shown to reduce virulence in similar assays (Atichartpongkul et al., 2010; Romsang et al., 2013). Attenuation of virulence in the fast-killing assay may be related to the ΔiscR mutant’s increased sensitivity to redoxcycling agents. Phenazines are a class of toxins that are excreted by P. aeruginosa when grown on rich media (Cezairliyan et al., 2013), and these compounds are thought to act as redox-cycling agents (Cornelis and Dingemans, 2013; Glasser et al., 2014). Moreover, when grown on rich media, the ΔiscR mutant shows an approximately twofold reduction in phenazine production (A Romsang and S Mongkolsuk, unpublished results). While the participation of iscR in oxidant stress resistance and virulence is clear, going forward it will be important to identify exactly which genes in the IscR regulon contribute to virulence and the sensitivities to oxidative stress and redox-cycling agents. 

## 19.3.5 IscR modulates intracellular iron homeostasis in Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Biologically, iron is an essential, albeit potentially toxic, element that is important for bacterial growth and survival owing to its capacity as a cofactor that mediates electron transfer and acid– base reactions (Andrews et al., 2003). However, free iron is dangerous since in the intracellular reducing environment it exists in the ferrous form $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ ), which has the potential to react with $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and catalyze the formation of cell-damaging ROS, particularly the highly reactive hydroxyl radical (OH∙ ) via the Fenton reaction (see Section 10): 

$$
\mathrm{Fe} ^ {2 +} + \mathrm{H} _ {2} \mathrm{O} _ {2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} ^ {3 +} + \cdot \mathrm{OH} + \mathrm{OH} ^ {-} (\text {   Fenton   reaction   })
$$

Since iron-containing proteins are very sensitive to oxidative damage, one of the effects of oxidative stress is an increase in intracellular free iron (D’Autreaux and Toledano, 2007). This is´ reflected by the fact that the expression of genes encoding ironbinding proteins such as dps is commonly induced as part of the bacterial oxidative stress response (Haikarainen and Papageorgiou, 2010). 

Clearly, too much free iron can amplify the effect of oxidative stress, thereby increasing a cell’s sensitivity to oxidants (Troxell and Hassan, 2013), but too little iron can also increase sensitivity since peroxide detoxification enzymes, such as heme-containing catalases and peroxidases, require iron for their activity (Chiancone et al., 2004; Cornelis et al., 2011). It is therefore crucial that cells tightly control the levels of intracellular iron under all growth conditions (Andrews et al., 2003; Chiancone et al., 2004; Cornelis et al., 2011; Troxell and Hassan, 2013). 

Bacteria employ a variety of mechanisms for regulating and maintaining intracellular iron homeostasis. In general, this involves balancing iron import via the excretion and uptake of iron-chelating siderophores with iron storage by proteins like ferritins and general ferric iron-buffering pathways such as heme and Fe-S cluster biosynthesis (Cornelis et al., 2011; Touati, 2000). In order to orchestrate this complex task, a number of regulators have been identified. The most widespread of these is Fur (ferric uptake regulator), a well-characterized iron-dependent transcriptional regulatory protein that is a global regulator of the expression of more than 100 genes involved in functions including iron uptake, metabolism, cofactor assembly, and efflux, as well as many genes encoding iron-containing proteins (Cornelis et al., 2009; Troxell and Hassan, 2013; Vasil, 2007; see Chapter 19.1). Depending on the target, Fur can function as either an activator or repressor by binding to a specific DNA sequence called a Fur-box (Ahmad et al., 2009; Katigbak and Zhang, 2012; Mills and Marletta, 2005). Fur also regulates the expression of certain target genes indirectly via the iron-dependent repression of small noncoding regulatory RNAs (Oglesby-Sherrouse and Vasil, 2010; Vasil, 2007; Wilderman et al., 2004; see Section 5). 

In E. coli, the regulator IscR lies at the core of Fe-S cluster homeostasis regulation, but additional regulators, such as Fur and the peroxide sensing regulator, OxyR, are also involved (Py and Barras, 2010; Roche et al., 2013; Xu and Moller, 2011). E. coli OxyR, in its oxidized form, is known to activate the sufABCDSE (suf) operon in response to peroxide stress. Activation also required integration host factor (IHF) and apo-IscR (Outten et al., 2004). Induction of the suf operon by iron limitation has been proposed to be mediated through the inactivation of Fur (Yeo et al., 2006). 

The specific mechanisms by which IscR affects iron homeostasis in P. aeruginosa are unclear. What is clear is that inactivation of iscR shifts cells into an apparent iron-starved state. For example, a P. aeruginosa ΔiscR mutant shows reduced intracellular iron content as measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) (Romsang et al., 2014). Consistent with this, sensitivity to the intracellular iron chelator, 2,2′ -dipyridyl, was increased (Romsang et al., 2014). Another indication of iron starvation is the fact that siderophore levels also slightly increased relative to wild-type strain PAO1 (Romsang et al., 2014). Siderophores are low-molecular-weight, highaffinity, ferric-iron-specific chelators involved in the binding and uptake of extracellular iron that are produced when iron is limiting for growth (Vasil, 2007). Conversely, iscR overexpression reduced siderophore levels. Complementation experiments using wild-type iscR and the site-directed mutants (C92A, C98A, C104A, or H107A) indicated that Fe-S cluster ligation to IscR was not required for complementation of the increased siderophore phenotype (Romsang et al., 2014), indicating that Apo-IscR is involved. 

The physiological basis for the iron starvation phenotype remains to be elucidated, but one line of evidence suggests that it may be due to a defect in iron uptake. This is because the ΔiscR mutant shows increased resistance to high extracellular iron in the form of either $\mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 }$ or $\mathrm { F e S O _ { 4 } , }$ relative to wild-type PAO1 (Romsang et al., 2014). All of the available evidence seems to indicate that at least one of the roles of IscR may be to upregulate iron acquisition pathways when iron is limiting. It remains to be determined what gene targets are involved, as well as whether the regulation is direct or indirect. 

Alterations in the intracellular iron level have an indirect effect on oxidative stress defenses (see Section 10). A P. aeruginosa ΔiscR mutant exhibits a reduced intracellular iron pool and is more sensitive to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ due to a posttranslational reduction in KatA catalase activity (Kim et al., 2009). Catalase is a heme-containing enzyme that detoxifies $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and is crucial for peroxide resistance (McLeod, 1925). In addition, the activity levels of the heme-containing respiratory electron transport chain enzyme, cytochrome c oxidase, were dramatically reduced in the ΔiscR mutant (Romsang et al., 2014). Evidence clearly indicates that the reduced catalase level is due to heme depletion. The addition of heme to the culture medium restored the wildtype levels of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ sensitivity and increased catalase activity in the ΔiscR mutant (Romsang et al., 2014). Addition of $^ { 2 , 2 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { - } }$ - dipyridyl to the heme-supplemented cultures had no effect on the level of the superoxide dismutase, SodB, a nonheme Fe-S cluster–containing protein, indicating that heme was not acting as a source of free iron and was directly incorporated into catalases and likely other heme-containing enzymes (Romsang et al., 2014). Taken together, the results indicate defects in heme synthesis and the activity of heme-containing enzymes in a ΔiscR mutant. 

In P. aeruginosa, the IscR target genes involved in iron homeostasis are unknown, and it is unclear whether the regulation that occurs is direct. An example of IscR-mediated regulation in response to iron availability is seen in Klebsiella pneumoniae, where IscR directly regulates the expression of genes encoding proteins involved in capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis and iron acquisition in response to environmental iron availability (Wu et al., 2014). Indirect regulation through links with other iron-responsive regulators is also a possibility. In this regard, it is interesting to note that the promoter–operator region of P. aeruginosa IscR contains a sequence similar to a consensus Furbox. Conversely, P. aeruginosa fur contains a putative IscR consensus binding sequence in its promoter–operator region. Furthermore, RT-PCR analyses indicate that inactivation of IscR results in the loss of oxidant-inducible transcription of fur (A Romsang and S Mongkolsuk, unpublished results). In E. coli, one of the regulatory links between fur and the isc operon is through the Fur-regulated regulatory RNA, RhyB (Masse and´ Gottesman, 2002), which directs the processing of the full-length iscRSUA–hscBA–fdx2–iscX mRNA down to a stable segment encoding iscR (Masse and Gottesman, 2002). ´ P. aeruginosa does not possess rhyB, but it does express an iron-inducible regulatory RNA encoded by prrF (Oglesby-Sherrouse and Vasil, 2010; Wilderman et al., 2004). However, at this time, there is no evidence for processing of the iscRSUA–hscBA–fdx2–iscX mRNA.

## 19.3.6 Conclusion



Boyd ES, Thomas KM, Dai Y, Boyd JM, Outten FW. 2014. Interplay between oxygen and Fe-S cluster biogenesis: insights from the Suf pathway. Biochemistry 53(37): 5834–5847. 





Kessler D. 2006. Enzymatic activation of sulfur for incorporation into biomolecules in prokaryotes. FEMS Microbiology Reviews 30(6): 825–840. 





Shigi N, Sakaguchi Y, Suzuki T, Watanabe K. 2006. Identification of two tRNA thiolation genes required for cell growth at extremely high temperatures. The Journal of Biological Chemistry 281(20): 14296– 14306. 



P. aeruginosa IscR directly represses its own transcription along with that of the isc operon in response to the intracellular level of Fe-S clusters. Conditions that result in Fe-S cluster damage, such as exposure to oxidants and redox-cycling drugs (Gu and Imlay, 2011; Imlay, 2006; Romsang et al., 2014), or Fe starvation (Angelini et al., 2008; Outten et al., 2004), which interferes with Fe-S cluster synthesis, cause induction of isc operon transcription. Like the case in E. coli, P. aeruginosa iscR likely also functions as a global regulator. Indications of this are seen in the fact that iscR inactivation affects virulence, expression of extracellular toxins, oxidant sensitivity, and possibly iron uptake (Choi et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2009; Romsang et al., 2014; Somprasong et al., 2012). The effect on virulence is explainable, in part, by a reduction in the expression level of thiol peroxidase and reduced levels of catalase activity since these oxidative stress protective enzymes are known virulence factors (Romsang et al., 2014; Somprasong et al., 2012). The effect on catalase activity is the result of heme depletion probably due to iron starvation. The effect on heme availability extends to other heme-containing enzymes such as cytochrome oxidase (Romsang et al., 2014; Wharton et al., 1976), which would affect the redox state of the cellular electron donor pools. The task now is to determine if the observed phenotypic effects are due to IscR directly or through the action of other regulators. Already, there is evidence that IscR and Fur may regulate one another, potentially shedding light on the effect of IscR on iron homeostasis. Other IscR regulatory targets need to be identified and characterized in order to gain an understanding of the linkages between IscR and other cellular pathways. This will provide insights that may aid drug development and the design of strategies for the control of both human and plant pathogens.

# Transcriptional analysis of iron-responsive regulatory networks in Caulobacter crescentus

Jose F. da Silva Neto ´ 

Departamento de Biologia Celular e Molecular e Bioagentes Patogenicos, Faculdade de Medicina de Ribeir ˆ ao Preto, Universidade de S ˜ ao˜ Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil ˜ 

## 19.4.1 Introduction

Iron is a crucial cofactor of many redox-active enzymes that are involved in fundamental cellular processes, making it an essential micronutrient that is required in micromolar concentrations for most organisms (Andrews et al., 2003). However, bacteria frequently deal with iron scarcity either because the soluble ferrous form $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ is rapidly oxidized to the insoluble ferric form $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } )$ in aerobic environments or because mammalian hosts maintain iron tightly sequestered in storage proteins (Wandersman and Delepelaire, 2004). To solve this problem, many free-living bacteria secrete ferric-chelating molecules termed siderophores, while some pathogens steal iron directly from their hosts (Miethke and Marahiel, 2007; Parrow et al., 2013). Gram-negative bacteria transport these ferrisiderophores by TonB-dependent receptors, which are specific outer membrane transport proteins that are energized by the TonB–ExbB– ExbD inner membrane protein complex (Noinaj et al., 2010). In contrast, iron overload is deleterious for bacterial cells because hydroxyl radical, a harmful reactive oxygen species (ROS), is formed by a reaction between hydrogen peroxide and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Imlay, 2013; see Section 10). To minimize these toxic effects and to ensure the proper iron supply, bacteria have regulatory mechanisms that tightly control iron uptake and its incorporation into heme, iron–sulfur clusters, or storage in ferritins (Andrews et al., 2003). 

The best characterized regulatory mechanism of iron homeostasis in bacteria is mediated by the ferric uptake regulator (Fur; see also Chapter 19.1). Numerous studies in Escherichia coli and in a broad range of bacterial species support a model in which Fur utilizes $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ as a corepressor to bind to DNA promoters of genes encoding iron uptake systems, repressing their expression under iron-replete conditions (Lee and Helmann, 2007). Fur can also mediate positive regulation often indirectly via small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) (Masse´ et al., 2007; Oglesby-Sherrouse and Murphy, 2013; see Section 5) or directly as a transcriptional activator (Delany et al., 2004; da Silva Neto et al., 2009). Recently, novel modes of Fur regulation, including apo-Fur regulation, have been demonstrated (Butcher et al., 2012; Carpenter et al., 2009; Seo et al., 2014). Although the Fur paradigm is prominent, some bacterial lineages harbor other global iron-responsive regulators. In α-proteobacteria, the regulators Irr, found in Rhizobiales and Rhodobacterales, and RirA, restricted to Rhizobiaceae, are the predominant ironresponsive regulators (Rodionov et al., 2006; Rudolph et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2007). While a Fur-like protein is found in all branches of α-proteobacteria, Fur seems to be the master iron regulator only in more basal lineages (Rodionov et al., 2006), as demonstrated in Caulobacter crescentus (da Silva Neto et al., 2009, 2013). Among Rhizobiaceae, these Fur-like proteins are called Mur because they regulate only manganese uptake genes (Johnston et al., 2007; Rudolph et al., 2006). 

In this chapter, I review how C. crescentus maintains iron homeostasis, with a focus on the effect of iron availability on the C. crescentus transcriptome and the role of Fur as a global regulator that controls iron metabolism and oxidative stress defense in this model α-proteobacterium. Despite recent findings concerning the transcriptional response of C. crescentus to iron limitation, little is known regarding the role of these ironregulated genes. Thus, many other aspects related to the acquisition, storage, and utilization of iron still need to be addressed in this bacterium. 

## 19.4.2 The model bacterium Caulobacter crescentus

The Caulobacter species are dimorphic Gram-negative bacteria that are widely spread in aquatic environments and that undergo asymmetric cell division. These species are mesophilic, obligate aerobes that have adapted to live in low-nutrient environments (Abraham et al., 1999). Under these conditions, these bacteria need to acquire scarce iron from their surroundings and deal with the potentially toxic effects of this metal that occur during aerobic metabolism. The freshwater oligotrophic species C. crescentus has become a model system for the study of cell differentiation in bacteria (Laub et al., 2007). Its unusual reproductive cycle is unique among prokaryotes and yields two distinct daughter cells: a motile swarmer cell and a sessile stalked cell. Only the stalked cell is competent to replicate its chromosome and to perform cell division. The complex regulatory network that drives the Caulobacter developmental program is well characterized and this topic has been studied for nearly 40 years (Curtis and Brun, 2010; Kirkpatrick and Viollier, 2012; Laub et al., 2007). More recently, some studies have shown that the Caulobacter developmental program is connected to environmental conditions and to the metabolic state of the cell (Jonas, 2014; Kirkpatrick and Viollier, 2012). Thus, several environmental stressful conditions, such as nitrogen and carbon starvation (England et al., 2010), cellular NADH-level changes (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010), DNA damage (see Sections 8 and 9) (Modell et al., 2011, 2014) and stress-induced protein misfolding (Jonas et al., 2013), activate signaling pathways that alter cell cycle progression. 

Apart from development, numerous studies have focused on understanding how C. crescentus senses and responds to stress conditions and is able to grow in a dilute aquatic environment. An early study of the C. crescentus genome revealed that this species has an overrepresented number of two-component signal transduction systems (TCSs) (see Section 3), extracytoplasmic function (ECF) sigma factors (see Section 4 and Chapter 2.6), and TonB-dependent outer membrane proteins (Nierman et al., 2001). Since then, the role of several regulatory systems in protecting $C .$ crescentus against stress conditions has been experimentally established. The ECF sigma factors ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { E } } , { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { F } } , { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ and their cognate antisigma factors are involved in the transcriptional response to singlet oxygen, ultraviolet-A (UVA), heavy metal, osmotic, and oxidative stress (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2006, 2007; Kohler et al., 2012; Lourenc¸o and Gomes, 2009; Lourenc¸o et al., 2011). The regulatory module PhyK– $\mathrm { P h y R - N e p R - } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ and the TCS LovK–LovR control the general stress response (Foreman et al., 2012; Lourenc¸o et al., 2011). The signaling system FixLJ–FixK–FixT is required for growth under hypoxic conditions (Crosson et al., 2005; see Section 9), while the LexA regulator controls the SOS response to DNA damage (da Rocha et al., 2008; Galhardo et al., 2005), and OxyR contributes to oxidative stress defense via KatG control (Italiani et al., 2011; see Section 10). The RND efflux systems czrCBA and nczCBA are induced by metal stress and contribute to metal detoxification (Braz and Marques, 2005; Hu et al., 2005; Valencia et al., 2013), whereas CztR activates a transporter that is putatively required for zinc uptake (Braz et al., 2010). 

## 19.4.3 Fur is the global iron-dependent regulator of C. crescentus

Two families of global iron-responsive transcriptional regulators have been described in bacteria: the DtxR family, which is found in high-GC-content Gram-positive bacteria, and the Fur family, which is widespread among bacteria (Andrews et al., 2003). Proteins belonging to the Fur family are diverse and include sensors of iron (Fur), zinc (Zur), manganese (Mur), nickel (Nur), heme (Irr), and peroxide (PerR) (Lee and Helmann, 2007; see also Chapter 19.1). The C. crescentus genome encodes two members of the Fur family (Fur and Zur); however, the global ironresponsive regulators Irr and RirA, which are found in other α-proteobacteria, are missing (Nierman et al., 2001; Rodionov et al., 2006). Fur is the master regulator of iron homeostasis in C. crescentus because its regulon contains genes encoding the entire key components of iron metabolism, including uptake, storage, and usage (Figure 19.4.1) (da Silva Neto et al., 2009, 2013). Because of inaccurate control of iron metabolism, a fur mutant is extremely sensitive to oxidative stress in C. crescentus (da Silva Neto et al., 2009). Thus, unlike species from other lineages of α-proteobacteria (Rhizobiales and Rhodobacterales) in which the Fur protein has evolved to sense manganese and is named Mur (Rodionov et al., 2006; Rudolph et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2007), C. crescentus maintains Fur as a usual ironsensing regulator. The Zur regulator contributes to maintaining zinc homeostasis in C. crescentus by regulating transport systems required for both the uptake and extrusion of zinc (Mazzon et al., 2014). Although C. crescentus Fur and Zur coordinate distinct regulons by selectively binding to discrete DNA binding sites (da Silva Neto et al., 2009; Mazzon et al., 2014), some crosstalk has been observed because genes of the Fur regulon were found to be downregulated in a zur mutant (Mazzon et al., 2014). 

## 19.4.4 The C. crescentus Fur regulon

The repertoire of iron-responsive and Fur-regulated genes in C. crescentus has been identified using expression microarray data that were obtained from experiments comparing wild-type cells growing under iron-replete versus iron-limiting conditions or comparing wild-type versus fur-mutant strains (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). C. crescentus genes subjected to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ –Fur-dependent repression include those encoding four TonB-dependent receptors (gene clusters CC0028-27-26, CC0139, CC2194-95-96-97, and CC2928-27-26), the ferrous iron transporter FeoAB (CC0711-12), two predicted ABC transporters (CC3692-93-94-95-96 and CC0683-84), hypothetical membrane-associated proteins that are putative transporters (CC2193-92-91 and CC3059-60-61-62-63), riboflavin biosynthesis enzymes (CC0885-86-87-88-89), and the ferredoxin Bfd (CC3263) (Figure 19.4.1) (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). Such regulation ensures that the Fur-mediated repression of these genes is alleviated only under iron-poor conditions, when C. crescentus must improve its iron uptake capacity. 


Figure 19.4.1 Overview of iron-responsive regulatory networks in Caulobacter crescentus. Genes and biological processes upregulated (red) or downregulated (blue) under iron-limiting conditions are shown. Fur is the master iron-dependent regulator of C. crescentus. Under iron sufficiency, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ –Fur acts as a direct repressor of many genes encoding iron acquisition systems (blunt-headed lines), as well as a direct activator of genes encoding iron-using enzymes (arrow). Other genes could be indirectly activated by Fur via FixK or an unidentified iron-responsive sRNA (traced arrows). See text for details.


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/9474c6763fbe8f1bfcda761c470d6d43f0d5021589ee1d4f06e7826d402ff9d9.jpg)


Although none of these putative iron acquisition systems have yet been characterized, C. crescentus most likely uses them to acquire iron in many different ways, including the uptake of ferrous iron (FeoAB), scavenging from ferrisiderophore complexes (TonB-dependent receptors), mobilization from ferritins (ferredoxin Bfd), and assimilatory ferric reduction (secreted riboflavin) (Figure 19.4.1) (see Chapters 19.1 and 19.2), which are all iron acquisition strategies that have been described previously in other bacteria (Andrews et al., 2003; Crossley et al., 2007; Noinaj et al., 2010; Worst et al., 1998). Whether C. crescentus produces an endogenous siderophore remains an open question because genes encoding enzymes for siderophore synthesis are absent in the C. crescentus genome (Nierman et al., 2001). Additionally, TonB-dependent transducers and FecI-type ECF sigma factors, Fur-downstream signaling pathways that control the synthesis and uptake of siderophores (Braun et al., 2003; Visca et al., 2002), are encoded in the C. crescentus genome, but none of them are regulated by iron or Fur (da Silva Neto et $a l .$ , 2009, 2013). Thus, C. crescentus most likely employs its iron-repressed TonB-dependent receptors to transport siderophores produced by other organisms. Thus far, the roles of only four TonB-dependent receptors of C. crescentus (of 67) in the transport of carbohydrates and zinc have been determined (Eisenbeis et al., 2008; Mazzon et al., 2014; Neugebauer et al., 2005). 

In addition to these $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } .$ –Fur repressed genes, microarray data have allowed the identification of C. crescentus genes that are positively regulated by $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } { - } \mathrm { F u r }$ (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). These genes include many genes encoding ironcontaining enzymes, such as succinate dehydrogenase (sdh operon), NADH ubiquinone oxidoreductase (nuo operon), cytochromes (CC0762, CC1401, and CC2115), the cytochrome P450 enzyme (CC2494), and glutamate synthase (CC3607). In this case, the expression of these enzymes is downregulated under iron scarcity, allowing the relocation of iron to essential enzymes (Figure 19.4.1). This mechanism, which is known as the iron-sparing response, is often mediated by $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } -$ Fur-regulated sRNAs in many bacteria (Masse´ et al., 2007; Oglesby-Sherrouse and Murphy, 2013). Surprisingly, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } { - } \mathrm { F u r }$ also activates many genes encoding transport systems, including porins (CC0925 and CC1409), MFS transporters (CC1628 and CC2485–CC2486), and TonB-dependent receptors (CC0991, CC1099, CC2804, CC3161, and CC3336) (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). Considering that most of these genes are also induced by carbon limitation and activated by the carbon-responsive sRNA CfrA (England et al., 2010; Landt et al., 2010), the substrates these systems transport remain unclear. The $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } { - } \mathrm { F u r - }$ - mediated activation of the transcriptional regulator FixK and of many members of its regulon (Figure 19.4.1) (da Silva Neto et al., 2013) provides a connection between iron homeostasis and the FixK-dependent hypoxia stress response in C. crescentus (Crosson et al., 2005). 

## 19.4.5 The C. crescentus Fur protein as a dual transcriptional regulator

Insights into the Fur binding site sequence and the mechanism of direct regulation mediated by Fur in C. crescentus have been obtained from diverse experimental approaches, including in silico Fur binding site prediction, lacZ–reporter promoter fusions, and in vitro biochemical assays (da Silva Neto et al., 2009, 2013). A similar Fur binding site sequence, which was predicted in silico upstream of many genes regulated mutually by iron and Fur, seems to be implicated in both Fur-mediated repression and activation (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). Accordingly, Fur binds in vitro to at least 11 DNA probes containing these C. crescentus Fur binding sites. These Fur binding sites overlap or are downstream of the –35 and –10 promoter elements of Fur-repressed genes (CC0139, CC0028, CC2928, C2194, and feoA) or are upstream of the –35 promoter element of Fur-activated genes (nuoA, sdhC, and acnA), suggesting a simple mechanism of repression by steric hindrance and activation by direct interaction with RNA polymerase (da Silva Neto et al., 2009). However, the Fur binding sites are more associated with $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ –Fur-repressed genes (16 sites) than with genes positively regulated by $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ –Fur (3 sites), indicating that positive regulation by Fur is also indirect (Figure 19.4.1) (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). Thus, whether some genes could be indirectly activated by Fur via an unidentified iron-responsive sRNA, as verified in other systems, remains unclear (Masse´ et al., 2007; Oglesby-Sherrouse and Murphy, 2013). 

The C. crescentus Fur binding site, which was predicted in silico and validated by electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), site-directed mutagenesis, and DNase I footprinting assay, consists of a 19 bp palindromic sequence (da Silva Neto et al., 2013) that is significantly different from that of E. coli but is highly similar to the $\operatorname { F u r } ^ { \alpha }$ -box predicted for several α- proteobacteria (Rodionov et al., 2006). Moreover, two unknown motifs that were discovered upstream of genes co-expressed during the cell cycle (motif CC 13) and after metal stress (motif M 3) (McGrath et al., 2007) are indeed the C. crescentus Fur binding site, raising the possibility that the expression of the Fur regulon could be connected to cell cycle progression, as has been recently determined for other nutritional and stress conditions (Jonas, 2014; Kirkpatrick and Viollier, 2012). 

## 19.4.6 Fur-independent regulation of iron-responsive regulatory networks in C. crescentus

Microarray data have indicated that iron limitation also affects the C. crescentus transcriptome in a Fur-independent manner (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). Among the genes upregulated exclusively by iron limitation are iscR, one IscR-controlled large operon encoding enzymes of Fe-S cluster biogenesis (see Chapter 19.3), rpoH, and many genes of the heat shock sigma factor RpoH $( \sigma ^ { 3 2 } )$ regulon (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). Many of these genes are also induced by heavy metal stress (Hu et al., 2005; see Section 20). Conversely, iron limitation causes the downregulation of genes encoding proteins involved in amino acid metabolism (mainly methionine biosynthesis), pathways of protein catabolism (peptidases), chemotaxis, and motility (Figure 19.4.1) (da Silva Neto et al., 2013). Although the biological significance of some of these findings remains unclear, iron limitation also causes the upregulation of the heat shock response in Shewanella oneidensis (Yang et al., 2009; see Section 13) and the downregulation of chemotaxis and motility (see Section 22) in Sinorhizobium meliloti and Acinetobacter baumannii (Chao et al., 2005; Eijkelkamp et al., 2011). 

## 19.4.7 Concluding remarks and perspectives

In this chapter, I have provided an overview of the regulatory mechanisms employed by the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus to survive under iron-limiting conditions (Figure 19.4.1). Unlike other α-proteobacterial species, C. crescentus maintains Fur as the global iron-responsive regulator, although many other regulatory pathways are also affected by the change in iron availability. Remarkably, the C. crescentus Fur protein acts as a dual transcriptional regulator, activating few genes directly and many genes indirectly and repressing most genes directly. Despite these advances, we are only beginning to understand the mechanisms whereby C. crescentus responds to iron scarcity. Thus, further work is required to elucidate many other aspects of iron homeostasis in C. crescentus, including: (i) determining whether a putative iron-responsive sRNA can mediate the positive regulation of some Fur-activated genes in addition to the confirmed mechanism of Fur acting as a direct transcriptional activator; (ii) elucidating whether iron limitation is an environmental cue that affects the Caulobacter developmental program via Fur; (iii) discriminating the specific roles of the numerous $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ -Fur-repressed iron acquisition systems in the transport of diverse iron sources, such as ferrous ions and ferrisiderophore complexes; and (iv) defining the role of the TonB-dependent transducers and FecI-type ECF sigma factors predicted in the C. crescentus genome for which regulation appears to be independent of iron and Fur. Future research on these topics will contribute to improving our understanding of the iron-responsive regulatory networks in C. crescentus and to clarifying how iron availability affects its physiology.

# Protein–protein interactions regulate the release of iron stored in bacterioferritin

Huili Yao, Yan Wang, and Mario Rivera 

Ralph N. Adams Institute for Bioanalytical Chemistry and Department of Chemistry, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA 

## 19.5.1 Introduction

Iron is essential for bacteria due to its involvement in multiple metabolic processes, including respiration (heme-containing cytochromes and [Fe-S]-containing ferredoxins) and fundamental enzymatic reactions ([Fe-S]-containing proteins, such as fumarase and aconitase of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle) (Cornelis et al., 2011). Pathogenic bacteria must obtain iron from the host, but humans maintain extremely low $( \approx 1 0 ^ { - 1 8 } \ \mathrm { { M } ) }$ concentrations of free iron, which are further reduced during infections (Bullen et al., 2005; Weinberg, 2009). The strategy of denying essential nutrients to invading pathogens is termed nutritional immunity (Bullen et al., 2005; Hood and Skaar, 2012; Weinberg, 2009), and it has been shown that increasing amounts of available iron during bacterial infection increases virulence (Bullen et al., 1968; Forsberg and Bullen, 1972; Murray et al., 1978; Sazawal et al., 2006; Wright et al., 1981) (see Chapter 19.2). Hence, strategies that interfere with bacterial iron acquisition or homeostasis are regarded as having high potential as therapeutic interventions (Ballouche et al., 2009; Falconer et al., 2014; Foley and Simeonov, 2012; Frederick et al., 2009). 

Despite its essentiality to life, some chemical properties of iron can present challenges to cells: The very low solubility of the ferric ion $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } )$ (about $1 0 ^ { - 1 0 }$ M at pH 7.4) severely limits its bioavailability (Boukhalfa and Crumbliss, 2002), and the soluble ferrous ion $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ ) reacts with hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ to form the highly toxic hydroxyl radical (∙OH) (Touati, 2000; see Section 10). In bacterial cells, iron homeostasis plays a pivotal role due to the propensity of free iron to stimulate the formation of reactive oxygen species such as superoxide $( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { * - } ) , \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , and the highly toxic ∙OH: Hydroxyl radicals are formed when $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ is oxidized by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Figure 19.5.1), while $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet \bullet }$ − and other reducing molecules in the cell reduce $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ back to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (see Section 10). Together, the two processes form the cyclic Haber–Weiss reaction, in which free iron catalyzes the conversion of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - }$ to ∙OH. Consequently, cytosolic levels of free iron are regulated near 5–10 μM, to ensure sufficiency for metabolic needs while preventing iron-induced toxicity (Keyer and Imlay, 1996). 

## 19.5.2 Bacterioferritins are essential to bacterial iron homeostasis

In eukaryotes iron is stored in ferritin (Ftn), while in bacteria iron reserves are stored in Ftn and in bacterioferritin (Bfr), of which the latter is present only in bacteria (Andrews et al., 2003; Rivera, 2014). The subunit fold of eukaryotic Ftns, bacterial Ftns, and Bfrs is conserved and consists of four α-helices (A–D) arranged in a four-helix bundle, and a short helix (E) that is nearly perpendicular to the axis of the bundle (Figure 19.5.2a). Although the overall architecture of Bfrs is similar to that of Ftns in that 24 subunits assemble into a nearly spherical structure with a hollow cavity, their amino acid sequences exhibit little homology (<18%) (Andrews, 2010; Ruvinsky et al., 2014). In addition, Bfrs possess 12 heme groups, which are bound at twofold symmetric intersubunit sites by coordinative interactions with methionine from adjacent subunits (Figure 19.5.2a). Bfr has a spherical and hollow structure with an outer diameter of 120 A and an inner diameter of 80˚ ${ \mathrm { \AA } } ,$ where ≈3500 iron atoms can be stored in the form of a $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral. The heme groups are buried under the external protein surface, with the heme propionates protruding into the interior cavity (Figure 19.5.2b). Bfr functions by (i) utilizing $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ or $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to oxidize $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and store $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ in its internal cavity, and (ii) accepting electrons to reduce $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ in the internal cavity and release $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to the cytosol (Andrews et al., 2003; Liu and Theil, 2005). In bacteria, the concentration of free iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ is maintained by a dynamic equilibrium between $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ stored in ferritin-like molecules and free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Figure 19.5.1). The significance of bacterial Ftn and Bfr in the life cycle and virulence of pathogens is just beginning to emerge, as reflected in recent reports indicating that mutants of Mycobacterium tuberculosis suffer from iron-mediated oxidative stress toxicity, are highly susceptible to killing by antibiotics, and are unable to persist in mice and guinea pig models of infection (Pandey and Rodriguez, 2012; Reddy et al., 2012). A Bfr-deficient mutant of Neisseria gonorrhoeae is growth impaired in iron-limited medium and more sensitive to killing by hydrogen peroxide (Chen and Morse, 1999), and in the plant pathogen Erwinia chrysanthemi mutation of the bfr gene results in impaired iron utilization and growth defects (Expert et al., 2008).

Figure 19.5.1 Schematic representation of bacterial iron homeostasis emphasizing the roles played by bacterioferritin (BfrB) and bacterioferritin-associated ferredoxin (Bfd) in the regulation of cytosolic levels of free iron. Elevated levels are potentially toxic due to the ability of free iron to catalyze the Haber–Weiss reaction, which generates the highly toxic hydroxyl radical.


As indicated here, Ftns and Bfrs function in the dual role of (i) oxidizing $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and compartmentalizing $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , and (ii) mobilizing stored iron when required by metabolism. A significant body of work has been published on the oxidation of $\bar { \mathrm { F e } } ^ { 2 + }$ and storage of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ by Ftns and Bfrs. For recent reviews, the reader is referred to Bradley et al. (2014), Ebrahimi et al. (2015), and Rivera (2014). In comparison, much less is known about the process of iron mobilization. Recent studies carried out with bacterioferritin B from Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa-BfrB) have shed light on the protein–protein interactions that enable electron transfer to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral in the interior cavity of Pa-BfrB and subsequent mobilization of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to the cytosol. The molecular-level understanding that emerged from these investigations, which is thus far unique to Bfr, is reviewed in this chapter. Molecular dynamics simulations carried out with Pa-BfrB have provided additional insights into the paths that may be followed by $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ as it traverses the Pa-BfrB protein coat. This aspect of the work is reviewed in Chapter 19.6.

## 19.5.3 Genomic data suggested a role for protein–protein interactions in bacterial iron homeostasis

In 1989, Andrews et al. reported that in Escherichia coli, the bfr gene is adjacent to a gene coding for a putative ferredoxin (Andrews et al., 1989). Subsequently, this gene was dubbed bfd (bacterioferritin-associated ferredoxin) due to its proximity to the bfr gene and the ability of its product to bind a [2Fe-2S] cluster, which is typical of ferredoxins (Garg et al., 1996; Quail et al., 1996). These authors also reported that the E. coli Bfd protein (Ec-Bfd) binds to E. coli Bfr (Ec-Bfr) and suggested that Ec-Bfd may function either as electron donor to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral in Ec-Bfr for subsequent mobilization of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to the cytosol, or as electron acceptor in the oxidation of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ for subsequent mineralization and storage of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ (Garg et al., 1996; Quail et al., 1996). In 2009, Rivera and coworkers reported that binding of P. aeruginosa Bfd (Pa-Bfd) to Pa-BfrB enables hememediated electron transfer to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ core mineral and the efficient release of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ from the Pa-BfrB cavity (Weeratunga et al., 2009). This study stemmed from mining available information regarding the genetic response of P. aeruginosa to iron starvation and iron-replete conditions (Ochsner et al., 2002): Among the 118 genes upregulated by iron starvation, only bfd and fpr (ferredoxin NADP reductase) encode electron transfer proteins. Under low-iron conditions, the expression levels of bfd and fpr increase about 200-fold and threefold, respectively, while expression of bfrB is downregulated (Ochsner et al., 2002). These observations have been interpreted to suggest a model in which Pa-Bfd and Pa-Fpr participate in the mobilization of iron stored in Pa-BfrB (Figure 19.5.3) (Weeratunga et al., 2009; Yao et al., 2011). In this model, Pa-Bfd transfers electrons from Pa-Fpr to Pa-BfrB to reduce $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ in the core and facilitate the release of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ . 

## 19.5.4 Pa-Bfd is required for efficient reduction of the $\bar { \mathsf { F e } } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral stored in the Pa-BfrB interior cavity

To test the model in Figure 19.5.3, the $f p r ,$ bfd, and bfrB genes from P. aeruginosa were cloned and expressed in E. coli, and the recombinant proteins were characterized biochemically and structurally. Pa-Fpr is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH)-dependent flavin-containing enzyme (Wang et al., 2007, 2008). Pa-Fpr is also thought to transfer the electrons required by Pa-heme oxygenase for the oxidative breakdown of heme into biliverdin and free iron (Wang et al., 2007). Spectroscopic studies showed that Pa-Bfd binds a [2Fe-2S] cluster (Wang et al., 2007). X-ray crystallography, however, revealed that the Pa-Bfd structure is composed of a helix-turn-helix fold, which is different from the canonical ferredoxin fold (Yao et al., 2012). The structure of Pa-BfrB was obtained in iron-free and iron-bound states (Weeratunga et al., 2010).

Adapted with permission from J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2012, 134, 13470–13481. Copyright (2012) American Chemical Society.


An assay was developed to test the model in Figure 19.5.3 (Weeratunga et al., 2009; Yao et al., 2012): $P a \cdot$ BfrB containing 600 $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ ions was prepared and purified. Mobilization of iron from Pa-BfrB was monitored by UV-vis spectroscopy in a cuvette containing an appropriate mixture of proteins and excess bipyridine (bipy), a $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ chelator. Addition of excess NADPH initiates the reactions shown in Figure 19.5.3, and the release of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ from BfrB is determined by $\Delta \mathrm { A } _ { 5 2 3 } .$ the time-dependent formation of the $[ \mathrm { F e } ( \mathrm { b i p y } ) _ { 3 } ] ^ { 2 + }$ complex, which absorbs at 523 nm. The black circles in Figure 19.5.4 track $\Delta \mathrm { A } _ { 5 2 3 }$ normalized to the total absorbance change expected upon removal of all iron ions from $P a \cdot$ -BfrB, following addition of excess NADPH to a solution containing Pa-BfrB, Pa-Fpr, and Pa-Bfd in a 1:15:5 mole ratio. In comparison, the red circles track $\Delta \mathrm { A } _ { 5 2 3 }$ upon addition of NADPH to a mixture of Pa-BfrB and Pa-Fpr in 1:15 mole ratio. Clearly, Pa-Bfd is necessary for the efficient release of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ . 

## 19.5.5 The [2Fe-2S] cluster of Pa-Bfd is required for electron transfer to Pa-BfrB

Early work with Ec-Bfd indicated that the protein is approximately 50 residues shorter than canonical [2Fe-2S] ferredoxins (Grag et al., 1996; Quail et al., 1996), and amino acid sequence alignments showed that the four conserved Cys residues thought to act as ligands for the iron in the [2Fe-2S] cluster are organized in a $\mathrm { C } { \cdot } \mathrm { X } { \cdot } \mathrm { C } { \cdot } \mathrm { X } _ { 3 1 - 3 2 } { \cdot } \mathrm { C } { \cdot } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 } { \cdot } \mathrm { C }$ arrangement, which is distinct from the sequence arrangement of $\mathrm { C y s }$ ligands in canonical [2Fe-2S] ferredoxins. In addition, the Resonance Raman spectra of $E c \cdot$ and Pa-Bfd (Quail et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2007) are nearly identical to those from the [2Fe-2S] cluster in the second domain of NifU, a protein required for the assembly of the metallocluster in nitrogenase. These observations led to the suggestion that Bfd may function as a scaffold for the assembly of [2Fe-2S] clusters for their subsequent transfer into other proteins that utilize iron–sulfur clusters (Quail et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2007). 

To probe the function of the [2Fe-2S] cluster in Pa-Bfd, apo-Bfd was prepared in a cuvette by chelating the iron in the [2Fe-2S] cluster with bipy. Pa-Fpr and Pa-BfrB were then added to the cuvette, and the addition of NADPH resulted in relatively fast growth of $\Delta \mathrm { A } _ { 5 2 3 } $ , which led the authors to suggest that apo-Bfd may be capable of promoting the release of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ from $P a \cdot$ -BfrB; it was speculated that apo-Bfd would help recruit Pa-Fpr to the $P a \mathrm { - }$ BfrB surface in order to facilitate electron transfer (Weeratunga et al., 2009). This notion was investigated further using apo-Bfd that had been prepared, isolated, and characterized prior to its use in iron release assays (Yao et al., 2012): The blue circles in Figure 19.5.5, which track $\Delta \mathrm { A } _ { 5 2 3 }$ upon addition of NADPH to a mixture of Pa-BfrB, $P a { \mathrm { - F p r } } ,$ and apo-Bfd in a 1:15:5 mole ratio, show that iron release from Pa-BfrB does not occur in the presence of apo-Bfd. In contrast, significant acceleration of iron release was observed when NADPH was added to a solution containing Pa-BfrB, Pa-Fpr, apo-Bfd, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { S } ^ { 2 - }$ (black circles in Figure 19.5.5), indicating that $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { S } ^ { 2 - }$ can assemble onto apo-Bfd to form a [2Fe-2S] cluster. In contrast, when apo-Bfd is absent, the rate of iron mobilization is sluggish, even $\mathrm { i f } \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { S } ^ { 2 - }$ are present (red trace). These observations not only provide an explanation for the mobilization of iron from $P a \cdot$ -BfrB in the presence of apo-Bfd prepared in situ, but also demonstrate the requirement of a [2Fe-2S] cluster in Pa-Bfd (Yao et al., 2012).

## 19.5.6 Heme transfers electrons from the [2Fe-2S] cluster in Pa-Bfd to the core mineral iron in Pa-BfrB

The presence of heme in the Bfr structure suggests that the cofactor may function in the transfer of electrons, either from the inner core to the external surface in the process of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ oxidation, or from the external surface to the core in the process of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral reduction and mobilization of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ . To date, there is no evidence that heme participates in electron transfer in the process of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ oxidation (Ebrahimi et al., 2015; Rivera, 2014). The first indication that heme mediates electron transfer from the surface to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral came from stoppedflow studies with Azotobacter vinelandii Bfr (Av-Bfr) (Richards et al., 1996). The $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ core of Av-Bfr was reduced with sodium dithionite, and the release of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ was monitored by measuring the formation of $[ \mathrm { F e ( b i p y ) _ { 3 } } ] ^ { 2 + } ~ ( \Delta \mathrm { A } _ { 5 2 3 } )$ . In similar experiments designed to follow the oxidation state of the heme in $A \nu { \mathrm { - B f r } }$ addition of dithionite resulted in biphasic kinetics, which were interpreted to suggest reduction of heme by dithionite, followed by reoxidation of heme with concomitant reduction of the iron core. 

It was later shown that heme mediates electrons from Pa-Bfd to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ core in Pa-BfrB (Weeratunga et al., 2009). This idea was supported by results obtained from delivering aliquots carrying a fraction of the total equivalents required to reduce all of the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ stored in Pa-BfrB to a mixture of $P a \cdot$ -BfrB, Pa-Bfd, and Pa-Fpr: The blue circles in Figure 19.5.6 show rapid and quantitative release of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ following each aliquot of NADPH, and the red circles show that the Soret band shifts rapidly from 418 nm toward 425 nm and then back to 418 nm, indicating a transient buildup of reduced heme followed by its reoxidation. These observations were interpreted to indicate that heme is reduced by Pa-Bfd faster than it is reoxidized by shuttling electrons to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral. The transient concentration of reduced heme increases with each aliquot of NADPH because as the size of the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral shrinks, electron flux from heme to core mineral decreases. In agreement with the function of heme in transferring electrons from Pa-Bfd bound at the Pa-BfrB surface to the Fe(III) mineral, it was later shown that the rates of iron release from Ec-Bfr are higher when the Bfr contains five hemes/24-mer than when it contains only one heme/24-mer protein (Yasmin et al., 2011). 

In 2012, Rivera and coworkers demonstrated electron transfer between the [2Fe-2S] cluster in Pa-Bfd and the heme in $P a \mathrm { - }$ BfrB (Yao et al., 2012): Reducing Pa-Bfd in a glove box leads to the disappearance of peaks at 334, 424, and 465 nm, which are characteristic of an oxidized [2Fe-2S] center (Figure 19.5.7a). Mixing the reduced Pa-Bfd $( 3 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ with Pa-BfrB (0.08 μM)

## 19.5.7 Structural determination of the Pa-BfrB–Pa-Bfd complex

Crystals of the Pa-BfrB–Pa-Bfd complex were obtained from a solution containing the proteins in a 1:12 Pa-BfrB–Pa-Bfd ratio. The asymmetric unit cell contains three BfrB subunit dimers, each associated with a Bfd molecule (Figure 19.5.8a) (Yao et al., 2012). Consequently, the biological assembly consists of a 24- mer Pa-BfrB and 12 Pa-Bfd molecules (Figure 19.5.8b), each binding at the interface of a subunit dimer above the heme moiety (Figure 19.5.8c). The structure of the complex also revealed for the first time the structure of a Bfd molecule, which consists of a helix-turn-helix fold, and binds a [2Fe-2S] cluster using conserved residues C4, C6, C38, and C41 (Figure 19.5.8d). Each heme in $P a \mathrm { - B f r B }$ is buried deep within the subunit, placing the heme iron approximately 18 A below the external surface, and˚ allowing the heme propionates to protrude into the interior cavity (Weeratunga et al., 2010). As indicated here, heme functions by transferring electrons from the Pa-BfrB surface to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ mineral in the core. The structure of the Pa-BfrB–Pa-Bfd complex showed that the distance between the [2Fe-2S] cluster in Pa-Bfd and the heme in Pa-BfrB is 15.1 A (Figure 19.5.9),˚ and calculations suggest that electron transfer proceeds from the [2Fe-2S] cluster to a vinyl-β carbon in heme via conserved residues Q72 and L71 (Yao et al., 2012). 

## 19.5.8 The Pa-BfrB–Pa-Bfd complex interface

Pa-Bfd binds between two Pa-BfrB subunits, which results in the burial of 607 $\mathrm { \AA } ^ { 2 }$ at the protein complex interface (Yao et al., 2012). The identities of residues from each of the proteins that participate at the complex interface, and their relative contribution to the buried surface, are shown in Figure 19.5.10. Alignment of the Pa-BfrB sequence against Bfr sequences from E. coli 0157, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Yersinia pestis, Shigella dysenteriae, Enterobacter sp., Acinetobacter sp., Vibrio cholera, Salmonella Typhimurium, and Serratia sp. shows 71% average identity and 84% average similarity. A similar alignment of the Bfd sequences shows 42% identity and 69% similarity (Yao et al., 2012). Importantly, the analysis shows that the key residues participating at the $P a { \mathrm { - B f r B - } } P a { \mathrm { - B f d } }$ complex interface are conserved in the sequences of the pathogens listed here, as indicated by the $" * >$ and “:” symbols above the bars in Figure 19.5.10. These observations suggest that the BfrB–Bfd interaction is likely to be of widespread significance. 

A zoomed-in view of the $P a { \mathrm { - B f r B - } } P a { \mathrm { - B f d } }$ interface (Figure 19.5.11) illustrates the proximity of the [2Fe-2S] cluster to the BfrB surface and shows interactions that are likely important to the stability of the complex: (i) Y2 in Bfd anchors to a cleft on the BfrB surface formed by $\mathrm { E _ { A } ^ { 8 1 } }$ and $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { B } } ^ { 6 8 } ; ( \mathrm { i i } )$ ) the side chain of L5 $\mathrm { L } _ { \mathrm { B } } ^ { 6 8 } , \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { B } } ^ { 6 9 } ,$ $\mathrm { N _ { B } ^ { 7 0 } , L _ { B } ^ { 7 1 } , O _ { B } ^ { 7 2 } , L _ { A } ^ { 7 7 } }$ $\mathrm { I _ { A } ^ { 7 9 } } { \mathrm { ; } }$ M1 in Bfd hydrogen bond with the side chains of $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { A } } ^ { 8 5 }$ 5 and E81 , $\mathrm { E _ { A } ^ { 8 1 } }$
