## 19.5.9 Conclusions

The studies summarized in this review show that the BfrB– Bfd interaction enables mobilization of iron stored in BfrB, and that this protein–protein interaction is likely to be of importance in the regulation of iron homeostasis in P. aeruginosa and several other pathogens. The molecular details emerging from the X-ray crystal structure of the Pa-BfrB–Pa-Bfd complex provide valuable insights for future interrogation of the relative role played by key residues at the interface in stabilizing the complex and enabling electron transfer, as well as designing smallmolecule probes to disrupt the BfrB–Bfd interaction in vitro and in bacteria. Results from these studies will likely increase our current understanding of bacterial iron homeostasis and perhaps uncover additional proteins and protein–protein interactions important to bacterial iron metabolism.

# Protein dynamics and ion traffic in bacterioferritin function: a molecular dynamics simulation study on wild-type and mutant Pseudomonas aeruginosa BfrB

Huan Rui1, Mario Rivera2, and Wonpil Im1 

1Department of Molecular Biosciences and Center for Computational Biology, The University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA 2Ralph N. Adams Institute for Bioanalytical Chemistry and Department of Chemistry, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA 

## 19.6.1 Introduction

Iron is required for cells to survive and function properly (Aisen et al., 2001; Andrews et al., 2003). It is usually found at the active sites of enzymes and is an indispensible component of electron transfer chains, as well as oxygen transport proteins (Aisen et al., 2001; Lippard and Berg, 1994). The ability to interconvert between the two principal oxidation states, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and Fe3+, largely determines its importance to cells. In near-neutral solution, iron exists in the form of soluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ . However, this form can be quickly oxidized to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ in a physiological environment due to the presence of oxygen. $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ then forms iron hydroxide and precipitates, limiting its availability to cells. At the same time, the oxidation process that converts $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ produces reactive oxygen species (Aisen et al., 2001), which can damage many crucial cell components like DNA, enzymes, and lipids (see Section 10). Therefore, iron homeostasis in cells has to be tightly regulated. 

Cells use a family of proteins called ferritins to regulate free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration in cytosol (Le Brun et al., 2005). These proteins take soluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , oxidize it to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , and store it as a ferric oxy-hydroxide mineral. This process can be reversed when $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration is low in cells. Under such a circumstance, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ in the minerals can be reduced to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and the minerals dissolve, releasing $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to the cell matrix (Weeratunga et al., 2009; Yasmin et al., 2011). Ferritins are found in all three domains of life. In bacteria alone, there are three types of ferritin-like molecules: bacterioferritin (Bfr), ferritin (Ftn), and DNA-binding proteins from starved cells (Dps) (Andrews et al., 2003). Bfrs and Ftns are spherical proteins composed of 24 subunits with a hollow cavity of approximately 80 A in diameter where the iron mineral is˚ stored. Dps are also spherical proteins, but they are composed of 12 subunits encasing a hollow cavity approximately 45 A in ˚ diameter. 

Several independent groups have already reported the Bfr structures from various organisms (Cobessi et al., 2002; Crow et al., 2009; Frolow et al., 1994; Janowski et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2004; Macedo et al., 2003; Rivera, 2014; Weeratunga et al., 2010) (see Chapter 19.5). The canonical fold of Bfr includes 24 subunits adopting an octahedral 432-symmetry arrangement. Each subunit is composed of a four-helix bundle (helices a–d) with a ferroxidase center in the middle and a short α-helix at the Cterminus nearly perpendicular to the bundle (Figure 19.6.1a). These 24 subunits form 12 subunit dimers, each containing two subunits related by a twofold symmetry and a bound heme at the subunit interface (Figure 19.6.1b). Heme binding distinguishes the Bfr from other ferritin molecules (Andrews, 2010). The 12 subunit dimers assemble to form a nearly spherical protein shell of ∼120 A diameter, enclosing a large central cavity for iron ˚ storage with a diameter of ∼80 A (Figure˚ $1 9 . 6 . 1 \mathrm { e } , \mathrm { f } )$ . The subunit dimers are related to each other by threefold and fourfold rotational symmetry operations. At these symmetry axes on the protein surface, there are two types of openings, termed $3 - f o l d$ pores and 4-fold pores (Figure 19.6.1c,d). There are a total of eight 3-fold pores and six 4-fold pores in a 24-mer Bfr molecule. Two other types of pores are present in the 24-mer shell, but these are not aligned with symmetry axes. The ferroxidase center pores are located in the middle of each subunit (Figure 19.6.1a), and the B-pores (Macedo et al., 2003) are at the intersection of three subunits; four B-pores surround each of the 4-fold pores (Figure 19.6.1d), so that there are 24 ferroxidase center pores and 24 B-pores in a Bfr molecule. 

The pores on ferritin molecules are thought to provide pathways for ions, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ in particular, to enter and exit the ferritin cage. Although ferritin-like molecules exhibit structural similarities, the low sequence conservation among ferritins from different domains of life (Andrews, 2010) imparts the different types of pores with distinct chemical and likely functional roles.

For example, structural studies showed that the 3-fold pores of eukaryotic ferritins are lined with conserved negatively charged residues. Mutating these residues impaired the molecule’s iron uptake efficiency, leading to the suggestions that $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ ions may traffic in and out of eukaryotic ferritins via 3-fold pores (Hempstead et al., 1997; Levi et al., 1996; Tosha et al., 2012; Treffry et al., 1993). A recent molecular dynamics (MD) simulation study on eukaryotic ferritins supports the idea that $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uses 3-fold pores to access the internal cavity (Laghaei et al., 2013). In contrast, the 3-fold pores of Bfrs are lined by layers of alternating positively and negatively charged residues, suggesting that these pores do not support iron traffic across the Bfr shell. Several crystal structures of Bfr have shown that sulfate and phosphate ions bind to several positively charged residues in the 3-fold pores (Macedo et al., 2003; Weeratunga et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2011), suggesting a role of these pores in anion traffic. The 4-fold pores of Bfrs and bacterial Ftns are also structurally distinctive from those of eukaryotic ferritins. The 4-fold pores in eukaryotic ferritins are lined by hydrophobic residues and are narrower than the 3-fold pores. This is buttressed by calculations showing substantial barriers for the entry of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions into eukaryotic ferritin 4-fold pores (Takahashi and Kuyucak, 2003). In contrast, the 4-fold pores in Bfrs typically contain hydrophilic residues, and crystal structures show that in some instances these pores are able to bind monovalent and divalent cations. The presence of these cations in the Bfrs 

4-fold pores has led to the hypothesis that these may serve as portals for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ traffic across the Bfr shell (Liu et al., 2004; Rivera, 2014; Swartz et al., 2006; Weeratunga et al., 2010). The B-pores seem to be unique to Bfrs and bacterial Ftns (Macedo et al., 2003). In all known Bfr structures, the B-pores are lined by hydrophilic and negatively charged residues. The negative electrostatic potential in the B-pores favors the presence of cations in the pore. This point is illustrated in the crystal structures of Azotobacter vinelandii (Av) (Swartz et al., 2006) and Mycobacterium smegmatis (Ms) Bfrs (Janowski et al., 2008), where a $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ ion is coordinated by water molecules within the B-pores. A more recent structure of BfrB from Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa-BfrB) in complex with its cognate electron donor partner, Pa ferredoxin (Bfd), shows $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions in the B-pores, where they are coordinated by three negatively charged residues lining the narrowest section of the pores (Yao et al., 2012). On top of these observations, it has also been noted that B-pores are sufficiently large to accommodate a $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ ion (Macedo et al., 2003; Swartz et al., 2006), thus suggesting that B-pores may function to facilitate iron traffic in and out of Bfrs and bacterial Ftns. 

The functions of the pores are tightly coupled to the dynamics of the molecule. The subunits are not isolated entities; they work concertedly and render the pores functional. This is exemplified in several recent studies concerning ferritin and ferritin-like molecules (Liu et al., 2003; Liu and Theil, 2005). It was observed that fluctuations in the 3-fold pore structure from eukaryotic H-chain ferritin controls the gating of the pore (Liu et al., 2003; Tosha et al., 2012). This type of dynamically controlled gating seems to be present in Bfrs as well. Our MD simulations carried out with Pa-BfrB revealed that regions of the structure surrounding B-pores and 4-fold pores act as sensors of environmental changes (Rui et al., 2012). Specifically, a higher ionic gradient across the BfrB shell produced elevated ion flux across the BfrB shell and a more dynamic BfrB assembly, with most of the fluctuations around hotspots near the B-pores and 4-fold pores. It was later shown that the fluctuations at these hotspots are allosterically linked to the ferroxidase center in each subunit, and therefore could affect the iron oxidation activity of BfrB (Ruvinsky et al., 2014). To further examine the role that protein dynamics play in pore-mediated ion flux in BfrB, we conducted a subsequent MD study of judiciously chosen BfrB mutants (Yao et al., 2015). These two mutations are D34F and N148L, both of which are in regions that show environmentally sensitive fluctuations. D34 is one of the negatively charged residues in the B-pores, which is thought to facilitate cation flux across the BfrB shell, whereas N148 is located in the 4-fold pores, where it coordinates a potassium ion in the structure of wild-type Pa-BfrB (Weeratunga et al., 2010). Although the crystal structures of D34F and N148L are very much like that of the wild-type protein, the mutations drastically affect the behavior of the BfrB molecule. Combining X-ray crystallography, biochemical experiments, and computer simulations, we showed that the mutations not only enhance local packing at the 4-fold and B-pores but also significantly reduce the conformational flexibility of the relatively distant ferroxidase centers, which in turns affects ferroxidase activity (Yao et al., 2015). These findings are comprehensively reviewed in this chapter. 

## 19.6.2 Materials and methods

This section outlines the methodology used in the simulations of Pa-BfrB. For a more detailed description of the building procedure of the Pa-BfrB systems, please refer to our recent publications on Pa-BfrB (Rui et al., 2012; Yao et al., 2015). 

## 19.6.2.1 Construction of a wild-type Pa-BfrB system

The Pa-BfrB structure used in the wild-type simulations (PDB ID: 3isf) (Weeratunga et al., 2010) was retrieved using the PDB Reader module in CHARMM-GUI (www.charmm-gui.org) (Jo et al., 2008, 2014). The ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ solution was used to solvate the Pa-BfrB molecules, and the structure used in the simulations consists of a protein shell made of 24 Pa-BfrB subunits, 12 heme molecules, a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in each of the six 4-fold pores, and a $\mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { 3 - }$ in each of the eight 3-fold pores (Figure 19.6.1a–d). 

## 19.6.2.2 Estimation of initial ion positions in the wild-type Pa-BfrB systems

Having a proper starting system configuration is essential in MD simulations. In the case of Pa-BfrB, the key lies in how to place the ions prior to the MD simulations. Wild-type Pa-BfrB has a net negative charge of −378 e, and an uncorrelated system could take a long time to equilibrate. Under such a scenario, randomly placing the ions throughout Pa-BfrB is not a viable option. Therefore, GCMC/BD (grand canonical Monte Carlo – Brownian dynamics) simulations were employed to generate the initial ion positions, which reflect the electrochemical potential in the system. 

The CHARMM-GUI GCMC/BD ion simulator module (Lee et al., 2012) was employed to calculate the grid-based potential maps for the GCMC/BD simulations (Im et al., 2000). The structure of Pa-BfrB was centered in the origin of a cubic simulation box with 160 A on each side. The grid spacing was set to ˚ 0.5 A. To account for the influence of different protein dielectric ˚ constants $( \varepsilon _ { \mathfrak { p } } )$ on the electrostatic potential, a series of $\begin{array} { r } { \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } } \left( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } } = 2 , \right. } \end{array}$ , 4, 10, 20, and 40) were used in the calculations, resulting in five sets of potential maps. They were denoted by E2, E4, E10, E20, and E40. Five GCMC/BD simulations (GCMC/BD E2-E40) with 30,000 steps each were performed using the last step input file from the GCMC/BD ion simulator module. The positions of the Pa-BfrB atoms, heme molecules, and crystal ions in the pores were fixed. In each simulation, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ were added to the system from the GCMC buffer region equivalent in size to the simulation box and distributed by the subsequent BD simulations. $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ instead of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ was used as the cation species in the GCMC/BD and the following MD simulations because of (i) the accessibility of accurate force field parameters for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ but not for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and (ii) the similarity of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ in that they are both soluble cations. The anion in the GCMC/BD simulations is $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ , which is different from the $\mathrm { H P O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ present in the MD simulations. This is because there are no accurate Lennard–Jones and short-range ion–ion interaction parameters for ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ available in GCMC/BD, but those parameters for KCl are well established and frequently used (Im and Roux, 2002; Lee et $a l .$ , 2012). After 20,000 GCMC/BD cycles, the ion number in any of the given systems becomes stabilized and reaches a plateau value. A snapshot of ion positions was then selected from the stabilized trajectories. To generate the initial ion configuration for the MD simulation systems, half of the $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ were randomly chosen and discarded, and the other half was replaced with $\mathrm { H P O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ − to keep the total negative charge constant. Table 19.6.1 shows the number of ions in each of the five systems with different $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { { p } } }$ . Clearly, there is a negative correlation between the resulting number of ions and $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } }$ . Instead of choosing a particular $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { { p } } } { \mathrm { { } } } ,$ , to reflect the different ionic strengths and their impact on the simulation results, all systems with different $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } } \left( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } } = 2 , 4 , 1 0 , 2 0 \right.$ , and 40) were used in the following wild-type Pa-BfrB MD simulations, and selected systems with $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } } = 2 $ , 10, and 40 were used in the mutant MD simulations.

## 19.6.2.3 MD simulations of the wild-type and mutant Pa-BfrB in ${ \bf K } _ { 2 } { \bf H } { \bf P } { \bf O } _ { 4 }$ solution

In the preparation of the all-atom MD simulations of the wild-type Pa-BfrB, each of the five resulting systems from the GCMC/BD simulations (WT E2-E40) was immersed in a preequilibrated water box of the same size as in the GCMC/BD systems $( 1 6 0 \times 1 6 0 \times 1 6 0 \mathrm { ~ } \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { 3 } )$ . Water molecules within 2.4 A˚ from the ions and the Pa-BfrB heavy atoms were removed. The systems were then subjected to a 210 ps equilibration cycle with decreased positional harmonic restraints on heavy atoms excluding water oxygen. During the equilibration process, some water molecules infiltrated the Pa-BfrB shell, creating vacuum pockets in the ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ solution inside and outside Pa-BfrB. Therefore, the water molecules in the systems were removed after the first cycle of equilibration, followed by addition of water in the manner described in this chapter, except that 2.0 A was˚ used as a distance cutoff instead of 2.4 A, and a second cycle˚ of 780 ps equilibration was conducted. At the end of this cycle, small vacuum regions were still observed, but only in the central cavity. Therefore, a sphere of pre-equilibrated water with a radius of 40 A was appended, and newly added water molecules˚ within 2.4 A of any heavy atoms in the system were deleted. The˚ whole system was then equilibrated without restraints for 20 ps, followed by a 40-ns production. 

The crystal structure coordinates of PDB:4TOD (D34F) and PDB:4TO9 (N148L) (Yao et al., 2015) were used for the mutant MD simulations. We followed the same simulation system setup as in the wild-type BfrB described here and performed a 40-ns production for each system. In each of the D34F mutant systems, 24 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions were randomly chosen and deleted in the bulk solution to neutralize the total system charge (Table 19.6.1). The system names were in the form of ${ \bf \ddot { \Delta } } ^ { \mathrm { a c } } { \bf P } _ { - } { \bf Q } ^ { \mathrm { p } } ,$ where P indicates the nature of the Pa-BfrB structure (i.e., WT, D34F, or N148L) and Q indicates the value of $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } }$ used in the GCMC/BD simulations to generate the initial ion configuration; for example, system WT E20 contains a wild-type Pa-BfrB and the initial ion configuration from the GCMC/BD run with protein dielectric constant $\varepsilon _ { \mathrm { p } }$ set to 20 (i.e., systems with the same Q in their name would have the same number of ions as shown in Table 19.6.1, except in the D34F systems, where 24 K+ in the bulk were removed to neutralize the total system charge). 

## 19.6.2.4 MD simulation protocol

All the simulations were carried out in NPT (constant particle number, pressure, and temperature) ensembles using NAMD2.8 (Phillips et al., 2005) with the CHARMM all-atom parameter set PARAM22 (MacKerell et al., 1998), including the dihedral cross-term corrections (CMAP) (Mackerell et al., 2004) and a modified TIP3P water model (Durell et al., 1994). The van der Waals interactions were smoothly switched off at 10–12 A by ˚ a force-switching function (Steinbach and Brooks, 1994), and the electrostatic interactions were calculated using the particlemesh Ewald method with a mesh size of ∼1 A. The tempera-˚ ture (300 K) and pressure (1 atm) were kept constant during all the simulations by Langevin dynamics and the hybrid Hoover Langevin piston method, respectively. The Langevin damping coefficient was set to 1 $\mathrm { p s ^ { - 1 } } \mathrm { ; }$ ; the decay period and damping timescale were 50 fs and 25 fs, respectively. 

## 19.6.3 Results and discussion

In this section, we review the main findings from the wild-type and mutant Pa-BfrB simulations. 

## 19.6.3.1 Breathing motion in wild-type Pa-BfrB

The overall Pa-BfrB scaffold is stable and exhibits thermal fluctuations. As expected, the N- and C-termini along with loops connecting the helices show the most flexibility. This is seen in the per-residue root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) plot (Figure 19.6.2a, left) for a Pa-BfrB subunit in the wild-type MD systems (WT E2-E40). Interestingly, regions with well-defined secondary structures do not show similar flexibility. In each subunit, specific regions are significantly more dynamic than average. This point is illustrated in Figure 19.6.2b (left column), where the per-residue RMSF is mapped onto a BfrB subunit. In this figure, among all the helical structure elements, the Cterminal half of helix D shows the highest flexibility, followed by the N-terminal half of helix C. These sections in the Pa-BfrB crystal structure also exhibit higher B-factors (black in Figure 19.6.2a, left). Further examination of the RMSF data shows that these regions are not only more flexible than the rest of the protein, but their flexibility is also affected by the local environment (Figure 19.6.2a and 19.6.2b, left). This is especially true for the wild-type BfrB systems, where increasing the ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ concentration results in increased mobility in these regions. The environment sensitivity of parts on eukaryotic ferritin has also been reported (Jin et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2003; Takagi et al., 1998). 

The significance of the flexibility pattern observed in each subunit emerges more clearly when analyzed in the context of the 24-mer assembly. Residues showing a high degree of structural fluctuation cluster around the B-pores and 4-fold pores, as seen in Figure 19.6.2c (left column), which depicts a minimal assembly of six Pa-BfrB subunits containing a 3-fold pore (green star), a 4-fold pore (blue star), and a B-pore (red star). Compared to the highly flexible regions near the B-pores and the 4-fold pores, the 3-fold pores and their surrounding area show much less dynamic activity. The flexibility difference could be related to the functions of these regions. While the less mobile sections of a Pa-BfrB subunit may be important for maintaining the structural integrity of the four-helix bundle and the 24-mer assembly, the more flexible residues impart the dynamic behavior to the pores, which may in turn facilitate iron traffic.

Figure 19.6.2 (a–c) Flexibility in the wild-type and mutant BfrB molecules. The left, middle, and right columns correspond to wild type, N148L, and D34F, respectively. (a) Per-residue backbone RMSF and per-residue crystallographic B-factors in black. (b) Mapping of the per-residue backbone RMSF (from systems WT E2, N148L E2, and D34F E2) onto a BfrB subunit. (c) Mapping of the per-residue backbone RMSF (from systems WT E2, N148L E2, and D34F E2) onto a six-subunit assembly to illustrate relative flexibility at the 4-fold (blue stars), 3-fold (green stars), and B-pores (red stars). Flexibility increases in the color scale from white to red.


Apparently, the breathing motions of the entire Pa-BfrB molecule affect the structure and dynamics of the 3-fold, 4- fold, and B-pores. The pertinent details can be obtained from the simulation trajectories. Figure 19.6.3a shows a snapshot of a 3-fold pore in system WT E2. The pore is formed at the intersection of three subunits. The $\mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { 3 - }$ ion remains bound to the pore at its narrowest section, coordinated by the side chains of R117 and K121 (Figure 19.6.3a). Figure 19.6.3b shows the structure of a 4-fold pore during the simulation. The pore is formed by four E-helices arranged in a way so that their helical axes are roughly parallel to the pore axis. The crystal structure used to start the simulations contains a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ion in each 4- fold pore where it is coordinated by the side chains of N148 and Q151. This $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ion remains inside the 4-fold pore throughout most of the wild-type BfrB simulations, with a coordination pattern similar to that seen in the crystal structure. In a few instances, however, these $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions exit the pore, resulting in new interactions between the side chains of N148 and Q151 located on opposite sides of the pore, causing temporary obstruction of the 4-fold pore. Unlike 3-fold or 4-fold pores, B-pores are not at a crystallographic axis of symmetry. B-pores are lined by a stretch of negatively charged residues. The side chains of D34, E60, E66, D132, and E129 form the most constricted portion of the pore (Figure 19.6.3c). These residues are able to interact with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions and escort them as they pass across the pore, as shown in the snapshot of the Bpore obtained during the wild-type BfrB simulations (Figure 19.6.3c). This pattern is in agreement with recent experimental observations showing that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions are coordinated by D34 from one subunit and by D132 and T136 from another subunit in the B-pores of Pa-BfrB (Yao et al., 2012). In addition, $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ ions have also been observed within the B-pores of Av-BfrB (Swartz et al., 2006) and Ms-BfrB (Janowski et al., 2008). These $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ ions are coordinated by water molecules and are in close proximity to several of the aforementioned acidic residues. In the recently published X-ray structure of an iron-soaked wildtype-like double mutant Pa-BfrB, two iron ions are seen inside the B-pore: one near the interior opening, and the other near the cytosolic surface (Figure 19.6.4) (Yao et al., 2015). These observations have been used to suggest that B-pores may be conduits for ion traffic across the Bfr shell (discussed further).

Figure 19.6.3 (a–c) Architecture and dynamic properties of the pores in BfrB taken from a snapshot in system WT E40: (a) 3-fold, (b) 4-fold, and (c) B-pores. Each pore type is shown viewed from the protein exterior (top) and from a transverse perspective (middle) with the internal cavity at the bottom and with the subunit closer to the viewer removed for clarity. (Bottom) The intrinsic flexibility of each type of pore is highlighted by mapping the per-residue backbone RMSF onto the pore structures (see Figure 19.6.2b,c). Flexibility increases from white to red. The phosphate ions in the 3-fold pores (cyan spheres) are coordinated by the side chains of R117 and K121 from each of the three subunits forming the pore. The $\mathrm { K } ^ { \bar { + } }$ ions (magenta spheres) in the 4-fold pores are coordinated by N148 and N151 from each of the four E-helices forming the pore. B-pores harbor negatively charged residues, including D34, E60, E66, D132, and E129. These residues attract K+ ions and translocate them across the protein shell during the simulations.


The pores have distinctive dynamic behavior as well. The 3-fold pores exhibit only modest dynamic behavior (Figure 19.6.3, bottom). The dynamics around the 4-fold pores and the B-pores are in stark contrast. Residues that show above-average fluctuations are concentrated in the external perimeter of 4-fold pores and along the C-terminal portion of helix D from Q137 to G145. Remarkably, in high-ion-concentration wild-type systems (e.g., WT E2), the flexibility of the C-terminal portion of helix D is increased to a point where repeated folding and unfolding of this part of the helix are observed during the simulation. Figure 19.6.5 depicts three snapshots that characterize these folding and unfolding transitions, highlighting their impact on a 4-fold pore and one of its surrounding B-pores. The unfolding of D helices enhances the lateral mobility of the E helices. This is seen by comparing Figures 19.6.5a and 19.6.5b, where the originally square arrangement of the 4-E-helices is deformed to a rhomboidal arrangement with unequal diagonal lengths. The ratio between the short and long diagonals can register to 0.58 in extreme cases. Because these deformations bring two opposing E-helices in close contact, the 4-fold pores are mostly closed during the simulations. The folding and unfolding events affect the conformation of B-pores as well. Unfolding of the C-terminal half of helix D expands the passageway across the Bpores (Figure 19.6.5b), while refolding either returns the B-pore to its initial closed state (Figure 19.6.5a) or keeps the pore open by stabilizing the deformed nearby 4-fold pore (Figure 19.6.5c).

The dynamic opening and narrowing of B-pores provide the necessary structural perturbations that enable ion traffic across the Pa-BfrB shell (see Section 19.6.3.2). 

## 19.6.3.2 Ion traffic across the wild-type Pa-BfrB shell

Examining the simulation trajectories reveals that $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ use only the B-pores to enter and exit the Pa-BfrB cage. The numbers of incoming and outgoing $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions in each wild-type system are shown in Table 19.6.2. The reasons why B-pores are the preferred entry and exit ports of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ are twofold. First, the B-pores are lined primarily by negatively charged residues: E66 at the outermost layer, D34 and D132 in the middle, and E60 and E129 in the interior opening (Figure 19.6.3c), which provide hydration and favorable electrostatic interactions for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ inside the pore. Second, the dynamic nature of B-pores, which responds to the folding and unfolding transitions at the C-terminus of helix $\mathrm { D } ,$ modulates the B-pores and the local electrostatic and hydration environment of the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions as they traverse the pores. 


Table 19.6.2 Number of K+ ions escaped via the B-pores during the 40-ns simulations.


<table><tr><td></td><td>E2</td><td>E4</td><td>E10</td><td>E20</td><td>E40</td></tr><tr><td>WT</td><td>63</td><td>56</td><td>63</td><td>23</td><td>0</td></tr><tr><td>N148L</td><td>5</td><td>n/a</td><td>14</td><td>n/a</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>D34F</td><td>30</td><td>n/a</td><td>22</td><td>n/a</td><td>8</td></tr></table>

Considering these characteristics of the B-pores along with the observation that iron ions can be present in the B-pores (Yao et al., 2015), it is reasonable to suggest that $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ ions also use them as entry and/or exit portals on the BfrB surface. 

A slight dependence of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux number on the initial $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration $( C _ { K } )$ inside the Pa-BfrB cage was observed in Table 19.6.2. The higher the initial interior $C _ { K } ,$ the more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ are released from the interior cavity. The two main factors accounting for this observation are the concentration gradient of K+ across the Pa-BfrB cage and the flexibility of the Pa-BfrB shell. It is intuitive that $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ flux is proportional to the $C _ { K }$ gradient; the larger the gradient, the larger the observed flux. The second factor contributing to the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux number difference concerns the flexibility of the Pa-BfrB shell because increased fluctuations are observed in $\mathrm { h i g h - } C _ { K }$ systems, such as WT E2 (Figures 19.6.2, left, and 19.6.5). It is highly likely that these concerted motions, which open and close the B-pore, help $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ traffic across the BfrB shell. The significance of the flexibility imparted by wellorchestrated and concerted motions in the 24-mer architecture is illustrated further in Section 19.6.3.3 in the results obtained from the mutant BfrB simulations.

## 19.6.3.3 Reduced flexibility and ion traffic in the mutant Pa-BfrB

To further investigate the function of the pores and the impact of dynamics on BfrB function, we performed the simulations of two Pa-BfrB mutants, D34F in B-pores (Figure 19.6.3c) and N148L in 4-fold pores (Figure 19.6.3b), both of which are known to have impaired iron uptake ability (Yao et al., 2015). The crystal structures of these two mutants are known. Structural comparison between the wild-type and mutant proteins shows that there are no significant global structural differences. When the mutant subunit structures are aligned to that of the wild type, the Cα root-mean-square deviations (RMSDs) are 0.10 A (D34F) and 0.15 ˚ A (N148L). The mutations do not seem ˚ to perturb the structures of the 24-mer assembly either. The Cα RMSDs between the mutants and the wild-type Pa-BfrB 24-mer assembly are 5.5 A and 1.4˚ A for D34F and N148L, respectively.˚ Interestingly, even though the mutations do not cause significant perturbations of the Pa-BfrB structure (Yao et al., 2015), their impact on the dynamic behavior, ion traffic across the shell, and biochemical function of BfrB is striking (Yao et al., 2015). 

The RMSF analysis of the mutant simulations shows that both BfrB mutants are significantly less flexible than the wildtype protein and are far less sensitive to the concentration gradient buildup across the BfrB shell. Figure 19.6.2a compares the per-residue RMSF in the wild-type (left) and the mutant systems (middle and right). In wild-type BfrB (Figure 19.6.2a, left), the flexibility increases with increasing ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ concentration gradient across the BfrB cage (from system WT E40 to WT E2). In contrast, the flexibility of the mutants is significantly dampened and its sensitivity to the concentration gradient of ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ is largely diminished; regions that show higher than average flexibility are now limited to the long loops connecting helices B and C and the N- and C-termini. This is in stark contrast with wild-type BfrB, where in addition to these two structural elements, the C-terminal half of helices D and the Nterminal half of helix C also show a strong tendency to fluctuate (Figure 19.6.2b, left). Mapping the per-residue RMSF onto the minimal assembly of six subunits shows that the B- and 4-fold pore regions, which exhibit the highest fluctuations in wild-type BfrB (Figure 19.6.2c, left), are much less flexible in D34F and N148L BfrB (Figure 19.6.2c, middle and right). 

The reduced flexibility seen in the D34F mutant is likely the result of enhanced packing at the B-pores. In the crystal structure of D34F BfrB (Yao et al., 2015), the F34 side chain forms favorable hydrophobic interactions with the side chain of L63, rendering the B-pores partially occluded. Additional observations from MD simulations of D34F BfrB show that the hydrophobic interactions between F34 and L63 also restrict the conformation freedom of F64, which is one residue downstream of L63 and packs against helix D (Figure 19.6.6b). This favorable hydrophobic interaction network stabilizes the helical structure of helix $\mathrm { D } ,$ therefore limiting the motions of the B-pore. In contrast, helix D in wild-type BfrB is much more dynamic. Its C-terminus (Q137–G145) can sample a wide range of conformational states between a fully folded helix and a coil-like structure (Figures 19.6.5, 19.6.6a, and 19.6.7a). Frequent transitions between these states are seen in the wild-type BfrB simulations, and they facilitate opening and closing of the B-pores (Figure 19.6.5). A comparison between rotameric states of D/F34 in the wild type and D34F mutant is shown in Figure 19.6.6c and 19.6.6d in the form of side chain torsion angle $( \chi _ { 1 } , \chi _ { 2 } )$ distributions. At least two main rotameric states are frequented by D34 in wild-type BfrB, while in D34F only one predominant rotameric state is seen. 

The N148L mutation in the 4-fold pore reduces the flexibility of the B-pores and the entire BfrB via a different mechanism. Leucine at position 148 stabilizes the 4-fold pore as a whole by introducing favorable leucine–leucine interactions within the pore (Figure 19.6.7b). This hydrophobic network restricts the lateral translational motion of helices E, and therefore largely attenuates the breathing motions of the 4-fold pores and residues in the C-terminal portion of helix D (Figure 19.6.7b). As a result, the B-pores in the N148L mutant are much less dynamic than the B-pores in wild-type BfrB and remain mostly closed. 

The lower flexibility of the B-pores in the mutants causes a drop in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport efficiency across the protein shell (Table 19.6.2), even though the initial ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ concentration gradients across the BfrB are the same as the corresponding systems in the wild-type BfrB simulations. These observations strongly suggest that cations like $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ use B-pores as main conduits to enter or exit BfrB, aided by the negatively charged residues in the pores and by the breathing motions of the B-pores. Since these breathing motions are dampened in both the D34F and N148L mutants, the flux of cations across the protein is reduced. These observations underscore the importance of concerted motions in the complex architecture of BfrB on its function (Yao et al., 2015). 

## 19.6.3.4 Ferroxidase center function affected by the 4-fold pore and B-pore dynamics

The simulations show that in the absence of iron, the ferroxidase centers in wild-type and mutant BfrB are occupied by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Figure 19.6.8, top). In wild-type BfrB, these $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions are in dynamic exchange with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the interior cavity. The exchange is promoted by a pedaling motion of the H130 side chain, a ligand to iron inside the ferroxidase center. More specifically, the side chain of H130 in the wild-type BfrB systems is seen to periodically alternate between two conformations. One conformation is similar to the “gate-open” state in the “as-isolated” crystal structure of BfrB, where the ferroxidase center is devoid of iron. The other conformation resembles the “gate-closed” state in the “Fesoaked” crystal structure of BfrB, where two iron ions are bound to the ferroxidase center (Weeratunga et al., 2010). The conformational flexibility of H130 is also evident in the MD simulations, where the average density of H130 side chain conformations sampled (red mesh in the bottom of Figure 19.6.8a) lies halfway between the gate-open (green sticks) and gate-closed (cyan sticks) conformations.

Figure 19.6.6 (a–d) A close-up view of a B-pore taken from the MD simulations of (a) wild-type and (b) D34F BfrB. In wild-type BfrB, the three rotameric states of the F64 side chain are depicted by orange, yellow, and magenta sticks in (a); and the three rotameric states of D34 are indicated in the plot shown in (c). The rotameric exchange of D34 and F64 contributes to the breathing motions of the B-pores as well as ion traffic across B-pores in wild-type BfrB. (b) In the D34F mutant, packing of F34 against L63 (spheres) likely contributes to the lower flexibility of B-pores in the mutant, which is manifested in only one conformational rotamer of the F34 side chain (d), and only one conformation of the F64 side chain, wheat sticks in (b).


In contrast, the conformational flexibility of the H130 side chain in the D34F and N148L mutants is limited. The predominant conformation during the simulations resembles the gate-open state (Figures 19.6.8b–c, bottom). In fact, all the ligands in ferroxidase centers of the mutant experience a drop in flexibility (Figure 19.6.2b). This is likely a consequence of the enhanced hydrophobic packing at the B-pores (between F34 and L63) and 4-fold pores (between L148 side chains within each pore). The reduced flexibility of the ferroxidase centers in the mutants suggests that communication exists between the two types of pores (4-fold and B-) and the relatively distant ferroxidase centers. The dominant mediator of dynamic motions is the C-terminal half of helix D (Q137–G145). This portion of helix D connects the rest of helix D, which encompasses ferroxidase ligand H130 at its N-terminal end, and helix E, which comprises the 4-fold pore. The C-terminus of helix D also contributes to form B-pores. Thus, the N148L and D34F mutations, by stabilizing the C-terminal half of helix D, dampen its folding– unfolding transitions (Figures 19.6.5) and lower the conformational flexibility of the B-pores, 4-fold pores, and ferroxidase center ligands. It is entirely possible that this loss of flexibility in the ferroxidase centers could affect their normal activities, resulting in loss-of-function ferroxidase centers. In fact, this prediction has been recently mirrored in experimental observations indicating that the ferroxidase activity of the D34F and N148L mutants is compromised (Yao et al., 2015). In addition, X-ray crystallographic investigations showed that the conformational flexibility of the ferroxidase center ligands, especially that of H130, is greatly reduced in these mutants (Yao et al., 2015). In this context, it is also interesting that similar allosteric communications between pores and ferroxidase centers have been predicted from coarse-grain calculations involving a recently developed network-weaving algorithm (Ruvinsky et al., 2014).

## 19.6.4 Summary



Jo SW, Cheng X, Islam SM, Huang L, Rui H, et al. 2014. Charmmgui pdb manipulator for advanced modeling and simulations of proteins containing nonstandard residues. Biomolecular Modelling and Simulations 96: 235–265. 



The ferritin and ferritin-like molecules are interesting and challenging systems to study with computer simulations. These are important biological systems. They help regulate iron homeostasis and could have potential pharmaceutical implications. Numerous biochemical and structural studies have been conducted on them and have so far yielded some remarkable findings regarding the iron uptake mechanism of these molecules. Atomistic MD simulations offer a unique means to help interpret some of these findings from a structural and dynamic point of view. In this chapter, we show with all-atom MD simulations of the wild-type and (N148L and D34F) mutant Pa-BfrB that there exists a close interplay of structure, dynamics, and function in the highly complex BfrB. The motions of the 4-fold pores, the B-pores, and the ferroxidase centers are highly correlated, and together these dynamic elements orchestrate iron oxidation activity of BfrB, as well as the permeation of iron ions across the BfrB shell. These findings are supported by recent experimental observations. 



Laghaei R, Evans DG, Coalson RD. 2013. Metal binding sites of human h-chain ferritin and iron transport mechanism to the ferroxidase sites: a molecular dynamics simulation study. Proteins-Structure Function and Genetics 81: 1042–1050. 



The challenges faced when simulating the BfrB systems come mostly from the size of the system and the treatment of ions. The simulations in this chapter are performed on a Linux Cluster with central processing unit (CPU) nodes. We are able to produce a 40-ns trajectory per system with our allocation on the cluster. Still, this is relatively short compared to the physiological time scale, which can be in the micro- or even millisecond range. However, with rapid hardware developments such as graphics processing unit (GPU) computing (Eastman et al., 2013; Salomon-Ferrer et al., 2013) and the availability of supercomputers like Anton (Shaw et al., 2009), the simulation time limits can be pushed up. Microsecond-long simulations of big systems such as potassium channels (Ostmeyer et al., 2013) and G-protein-coupled receptors (Dror et al., 2011) have already been surfacing. Another major hurdle in studying the ferritin molecules is the accurate representation of ions. In the simulations described in this chapter, we used ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { H P O } } _ { 4 }$ as the bathing solution of BfrB. Although ideally we would want to include $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ as one of the cation species to study the interactions between iron and the system, this was not possible because of the lack of an accurate force field for this cation. However, as efforts in improving the current force field and also in developing polarizable force fields grow, we are hopeful that this problem will be solved in the near future. 



Le Brun NE, Lewin A, Moore GR. 2005. Formation of protein-coated iron minerals. Dalton Transactions (22): 3597–3610.
