## Metal resistance

## Lee Macomber and Robert P. Hausinger

Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan, USA 

## 20.1.1 Introduction

Nickel is one of the more abundant elements on the planet and can be found in all biologically relevant environments, ranging from nanomolar levels in some aquatic systems to millimolar levels in serpentine soils (Harrison and Rajakaruna, 2011; He et al., 2005; Kumar and Maiti, 2013; Muyssen et al., 2004; Shaheen et al., 2013). Furthermore, even commensal bacteria are exposed to dietary nickel, with 150–900 μg of nickel ingested per day for humans (Barceloux, 1999; Schaumloffel,¨ 2012). Nickel is an essential cofactor of several enzymes (Boer et al., 2014; Kaluarachchi et al., 2010); however, like other transition metal ions, it is toxic when homeostasis fails (Lemire et al., 2013). The ubiquity of environmental nickel has made it imperative for bacteria to evolve ways to mitigate the stress of nickel exposure. In this chapter, we discuss several common themes surrounding the mechanisms of nickel toxicity in bacteria. While nickel in the environment exists in several forms (Schaumloffel, 2012), we focus on the toxicity of the biologi- ¨ cally relevant, water-soluble Ni(II). We then highlight how the same chemical properties that cause the metal to be toxic are, in fact, used for its sensing and regulation by cells. Furthermore, we describe how bacteria defend against nickel stress by summarizing the known resistance mechanisms. 

## 20.1.2 Nickel toxicity

The mechanisms of nickel toxicity in bacteria have been previously reviewed (Babich and Stotzky, 1983; Macomber and Hausinger, 2011), but interest in this topic continues to grow due to the increasing levels of nickel in industrial pollution (Li et al., 2014; Wuana and Okieimen, 2011) and the recent discovery that nickel defense systems are widespread in nature (Cubillas et al., 2013; Leitenmaier and Kupper, 2013; Nies, 2003). Of¨ note, identifying the specific mechanism of nickel toxicity in any one bacterium is a challenge because the specific target will vary depending on the ecological niche and cellular physiology. 

Here, we summarize several mechanisms in nickel ion toxicity (Figure 20.1.1) and the evidence that supports them. 

## 20.1.2.1 Nickel-dependent inhibition of metalloenzymes and metalloproteins

First-row transition metals share similar atomic radii and biologically relevant charges, making them difficult to differentiate; however, divalent metal cations possess inherent chemical properties that allow each to have a unique impact on life. Hard-soft acid–base theory accounts for the preference of specific organic ligands for particular metals, with nickel classified as a borderline acid that preferentially associates with imidazoles and thiols (Parr and Pearson, 1983; Pearson, 1963). This preference is often seen in the ligands that specifically bind nickel (discussed further in this chapter), and it correlates to the sites of metalloenzymes that are inhibited by this metal. Furthermore, the ligand–metal order of preference for divalent transition metals is described by the Irving–Williams series $\mathrm { ( M n ( I I ) } < \mathrm { F e ( I I ) } <$ < $\mathrm { C o ( I I ) } < \mathrm { N i ( I I ) } < \mathrm { C u ( I I ) } > \mathrm { Z n ( I I ) } )$ , which outlines the general affinity bias of a divalent metal for a ligand donor (Irving and Williams, 1953); thus, nickel will readily compete with the other first-row transition metals other than Cu(II). When homeostasis fails during metal stress, noncognate metals are often inserted into metalloenzymes, thus leading to pathway dysfunctions. 

## 20.1.2.1.1 Inhibition of zinc metalloenzymes

A well-characterized example of nickel toxicity due to the inhibition of a zinc enzyme is that of the class II fructose 1,6- bisphosphate aldolase from Escherichia coli, FbaA, involved in glycolysis (Bock and Neidhardt, 1966; Samland and Sprenger, ¨ 2006; Stribling and Perham, 1973). Physiological studies pointed to the specific inhibition of FbaA by nickel (i.e., low micromolar concentrations of this metal inhibit cell growth on glucose or fructose), but cells have reduced sensitivity to nickel when provided with succinate, lactate, or glycerol that is not metabolized via this enzyme (Macomber et al., 2011). FbaA is inactivated during nickel stress in vivo, and overexpression of fb aA restores growth during nickel challenge. Furthermore, purified FbaA is inhibited by low micromolar concentrations of nickel in vitro. An allosteric zinc atom is displaced in nickel-inhibited FbaA with the consequent incorporation of one nickel atom. Significantly, site-directed variants lacking the allosteric site (D144A, E174A, or E181A) are resistant to nickel inhibition (Macomber et al., 2011). Presumably, the incorporation of a nickel atom at the allosteric site changes the coordination chemistry of the catalytic zinc, thus preventing enzymatic function. These results demonstrate that nickel-dependent inhibition of FbaA is the primary mechanism of nickel toxicity toward E. coli when grown on glucose minimal medium. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/16be44aa823193bf293b9cedb1a77d681d5aff3a483df95b74a2d39f45113fae.jpg)



Figure 20.1.1 Mechanisms of nickel toxicity in bacteria. Nickel may displace metal from the catalytic or allosteric sites of zinc or iron metalloproteins (yellow and blue, respectively), thus leading to enzyme or regulator inactivation. In addition, nickel can bind to enzymes that lack metals (purple), leading to inactivation. While nickel itself is a poor generator of reactive oxygen species (ROS), the displacement of redox-active iron from iron metallocenters can result in ROS production with consequent negative effects involving DNA, protein, and other cellular constituents.


Surprisingly, nickel-dependent inactivation of FbaA also leads to a failure of growth on gluconate minimal medium (Macomber et al., 2011). This result is hypothesized to be due to carbon leakage from the Entner–Doudoroff pathway to glycolysis, subsequently leading to increasing concentrations of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and shutting down metabolism through the buildup of ppGpp (see Chapter 7.1) (Bock and Neidhardt, ¨ 1966; Macomber et al., 2011; Schreyer and Bock, 1973; Schnei-¨ der and Gourse, 2003). Indeed, elimination of this leakage using a gnd (encoding 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase) mutation restores growth on gluconate at previously inhibitory concentrations of nickel (Macomber et al., 2011). These results highlight the interconnectedness of metabolism and the potential difficulties in determining mechanisms of toxicity. 

Additional studies with other purified zinc metalloenzymes reveal sensitivity to micromolar levels of nickel, which is compatible with these enzymes being in vivo sites for toxicity by this metal. For example, the dinuclear zinc-dependent tripeptidase from Pediococcus pentosaceus and aminopeptidases from 

Streptomyces griseus and Streptomyces septatus are inhibited by nickel in vitro (Arima et al., 2004; Ercan et al., 2010; Simitsopoulou et al., 1997). The zinc atoms of this family are coordinated by His, Asp, and Glu, which can all function as nickel ligands (Lowther and Matthews, 2002). The mechanisms of inactivation for these enzymes are not known, but direct competition between nickel and zinc binding is likely to be involved. 

## 20.1.2.1.2 Inhibition of iron metalloenzymes and iron metalloproteins

Nickel toxicity and iron metabolism are clearly linked. In E. coli, iron supplementation leads to the induction of rcnR, encoding a nickel defense regulator, in a Fur-dependent manner (Koch et al., 2007) (see Section 19). Furthermore, strains lacking YqjH (an NADPH-dependent ferric reductase) or SufABCDSE (used for FeS cluster biosynthesis during stress response) are more sensitive to nickel than are wild-type cells (Wang et al., 2011). These results suggest that during nickel stress, cells need to increase iron uptake and induce proteins with tighter iron binding. In fact, the upregulation of genes that increase the concentrations of one metal to compensate for an increased pool of another metal is a common theme in metal homeostasis (Imlay, 2014; see Section 19). While no direct in vivo link has been established between nickel-dependent dysfunction and the inactivation of an iron metalloprotein in bacteria, the in vitro competition for nickel binding to iron-dependent enzymes is well established. 

The Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, a broad family of enzymes with representatives that function in DNA repair, protein modification, nutrient metabolism, and other diverse roles (Hausinger, 2004; Schofield and Hausinger, 2015), nicely illustrate this mechanism of nickel stress. Nickel is proposed to substitute for the reversibly bound catalytic iron in these enzymes according to a leading hypothesis for nickel toxicity in eukaryotes (Chen and Costa, 2009; Chen et al., 2010; Davidson et al., 2005, 2006; Maxwell and Salnikow, 2014). The archetype of this enzyme family in E. coli is taurine:2- oxoglutarate dioxygenase (TauD), responsible for converting 2- aminoethanesulfonate into aminoacetaldehyde and sulfite that is utilized as a sulfur source. TauD holoenzyme is inhibited by nickel with an $\mathrm { I C } _ { 5 0 }$ of 32 μM, while the apoprotein is prevented from undergoing iron metalation by nickel with an $\mathrm { I C } _ { 5 0 }$ of 0.7 μM (Kalliri et al., 2005). As expected, these results suggest that the most likely time for nickel-dependent inhibition of metalloproteins is when it is initially synthesized or during a period of cognate metal deficiency (Imlay, 2014). The iron-binding motif of this family $\left( \mathrm { H i s { - } X { \mathrm { - } } A s p / G l u { \mathrm { - } } X _ { n } { \mathrm { - } } H i s } \right)$ clearly functions as the binding site for nickel, according to crystal structures of several enzyme representatives with nickel at the active site (e.g., PDB ID codes 2xlm and 3dkq along with eukaryotic representatives 2ox0, 2w2i, 2wwu, 2xxz, 3k2o, and 3ms5). 

Several other instances are known for nickel binding to or inhibiting iron metalloproteins. For example, nickel readily binds at the iron site of the hydrogen peroxide sensor PerR (see Section 10), where it is coordinated by four His and one Asn side chains (PDB ID 4i7h) (Makthal et al., 2013). Furthermore, catechol 1,2-dioxygenase of Rhizobium leguminosarum, protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase from the same organism, ATP:cob(I)alamin adenosyltransferase of Salmonella enterica, and atrazine chlorohydrolase from a Pseudomonas species are all sensitive to micromolar levels of nickel in vitro (Buan and Escalante-Semerena, 2006; Chen et al., 1984, 1985; Seffernick et al., 2002). 

The sensitivity of iron-dependent metalloproteins to nickel and the importance of these enzymes in cellular metabolism support the hypothesis that their inhibition accounts in large measure for nickel toxicity; however, direct studies to test this proposal and identify the key target proteins in bacteria are lacking. 

## 20.1.2.2 Nickel-dependent inhibition of non-metalloenzymes

On the basis of hard-soft acid–base theory, one expects nickel to bind to favored residues at selected active sites of nonmetalloenzymes and thus inhibit their activities. For example, nickel binds to an important Cys residue in dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase and prevents the reduction of the adventitious substrate tellurite (Arenas et al., 2014); thus, it is likely that nickel also affects this protein when it is part of enzyme complexes, including pyruvate dehydrogenase and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase. Other proteins with active-site Cys residues that exhibit in vitro susceptibility to nickel inhibition include N-carbamoyl-D-amino acid amidohydrolase from Agrobacterium (Nakai et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2001), pyroglutamyl peptidase I of Leishmania major (Schaeffer et al., 2006), mercury(II) reductase of E. coli and Azotobacter chroococcum (Barkay et al., 2003; Ghosh et al., 1999), cytosine-5 methyltransferase in E. coli, and uracil-5 methyltransferase of E. coli (Hurwitz et al., 1964; Liu and Santi, 2000; Urbonavicius et al., 2007). In addition, uricase from Bacillus fastidiosus (Bongaerts et al., 1978) and arabinose isomerase of E. coli (Meredith and Woodard, 2003) employ or are predicted to employ catalytic His residues that are susceptible to nickel inhibition. 

## 20.1.2.3 Nickel-dependent toxicity involving reactive oxygen species

Under physiological conditions, free nickel ions (defined as the pool of nickel that is weakly and reversibly bound to the cellular milieu) (Imlay, 2014) are in the Ni(II) state and a poor generator of reactive oxygen species when compared with iron and copper (Valko et al., 2005); however, in vivo evidence suggests that nickel toxicosis can lead to oxidative stress. 

While there is no direct link between nickel-dependent cell damage and oxidative stress (see Section 10), several studies have demonstrated a strong correlation between these processes. Proteomic studies in Burkholderia vietnamiensis (van Nostrand et al., 2008) and Pseudomonas putida (Cheng et al., 2009) provide evidence for nickel-dependent increases in superoxide dismutase, thioredoxin, and several other proteins associated with oxidative stress. Furthermore, E. coli sodA sodB mutants are more sensitive to nickel than are wild-type cells (Geslin et al., 2001). Some, but not all, of the nickel toxicity mediated by oxidative stress involves DNA damage. Nickel-stressed S. enterica cells do not increase their mutation rate (Biggart and Costa, 1986), whereas nickel challenge does increase the mutation rate of Corynebacterium (Pikalek and Nec ´ asek, 1983). ´ Mutants of E. coli recA (encoding a vital protein for survival of DNA damage by catalyzing DNA strand exchange and recombination along with protease and nuclease activity) are equally resistant to nickel as wild-type cells (Brandi et al., 1990); however, studies consistent with a DNA damage mechanism show that nickel inhibits the E. coli MutT DNA repair protein, albeit with an $\mathrm { I C } _ { 5 0 }$ of 1.5 mM (Porter et al., 1997). Nickel enhances the mutagenesis rate of alkylating agents by a process that is likely due to repair inhibition (Dubins and LaVelle, 1986; Wozniak´ and Błasiak, 2004; see Section 9). In fact, in eukaryotic systems, nickel-dependent increase in DNA damage is proposed to arise from inhibition of repair processes (Witkiewicz-Kucharczyk and Bal, 2006). Nickel-dependent inhibition of DNA repair may resolve the seeming discrepancy between these DNA damage studies. 

## 20.1.3 Nickel stress regulation

To ensure that nickel does not damage the cell, one could imagine the development of exquisitely sensitive nickel-dependent sensors that bind nickel at low concentrations and upregulate a nickel defense system; however, many organisms utilize nickeldependent enzymes that may be absolutely required for certain environmental conditions (Boer et al., 2014; Kaluarachchi et al., 2010). Therefore, regulatory sensors for nickel must exhibit properties that poise the cellular nickel concentrations appropriately to allow metallation of nickel metalloenzymes while minimizing the toxicity of this metal. This balance has been extensively studied in E. coli (Iwig and Chivers, 2010), as described in Section 20.1.3.1 on the RcnR family. In addition, two other nickel sensor systems associated with nickel defense, NmtR– KmtR and Cnr–Ncc, are briefly summarized. The modes of action and the nickel-binding sites of these sensors are illustrated, with the same types of side chains observed as those associated with binding sites for toxicity (Figure 20.1.2). Although not discussed further, the regulation and defense systems for nickel are nearly inseparable from those for cobalt; we focus on the nickel aspects of these systems, but they often also play a role in cobalt homeostasis. Also not described here are nickel sensors that function to regulate import of this metal ion (Li and Zamble, 2009). 

## 20.1.3.1 RcnR–CsoR family of regulators

The primary regulator of nickel defense in E. coli is RcnR (resistance to cobalt and nickel repressor) (Iwig et al., 2006; Koch et al., 2007). This protein and the copper-responsive CsoR are the two most well-studied members of this regulatory family (Rademacher and Masepohl, 2012). RcnR, an 89-residue protein predicted to contain three alpha-helices and no beta-sheets (Iwig et al., 2008), has a charged N-terminal region followed by a highly conserved nonpolar region and a C-terminal variable region (Iwig et al., 2006). This protein binds to a pair of TACT-$\mathrm { G } _ { 6 } { \mathrm { - N } } { \mathrm { - A G T A } }$ operator sites (Iwig and Chivers, 2009) and regulates both rcnA encoding a nickel efflux system (Section 20.1.4) and rcnR, suggesting that RcnR regulates its own transcription (Iwig and Chivers, 2009; Iwig et al., 2006; Rodrigue et al., 2005). RcnR interacts with an extended region beyond the core binding site, causing the DNA to wrap around the protein, introducing a single negative supercoil (Iwig and Chivers, 2009). Two tetramers bind to the minor groove of the intergenic region with one tetramer per binding motif (Iwig and Chivers, 2009). Transcription of rcnR is induced by nickel challenge (Blaha et al., 2011; Iwig and Chivers, 2009); however, this level of induction is much less than that of an rcnR mutant (Iwig and Chivers, 2009). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/87c4c5f883bf1e7772dfcaa2cea21914eee6771987197443a86bca62b2303b02.jpg)



Figure 20.1.2 Regulation of nickel defense. The presence of nickel leads to release of the repressors (a) RcnR and (b) NmtR from their binding sites on DNA, allowing transcription of their cognate nickel defense systems. In contrast, extracytoplasmic nickel binds to (c) CnrX and, via CnrY, causes the release of ECF CnrH, which stimulates transcription of the associated nickel defense system. Each nickel sensor is proposed to bind the metal ion in octahedral geometry using the ligands illustrated (in panel b, $\mathrm { A s p } _ { 9 1 } \mathrm { \ ' }$ and ${ \mathrm { H i s } _ { 9 3 } } ^ { * }$ ’ are derived from a different protomer than the other ligands, and the protein lacks Met1).


Binding of Ni(II) has little to no effect on secondary structure, but metal binding does stabilize the protein (i.e., increases resistance to urea denaturation) (Iwig et al., 2008). RcnR is a tetramer that binds one nickel $( K _ { \mathrm { d } } < 2 5 ~ \mathrm { n M } )$ per monomer (Blaha et al., 2011; Iwig et al., 2008). Studies identify a 6-coordinate, highspin (S = 1), pseudo-octahedral $\mathrm { M ( C y s ) ( H i s ) _ { 2 } ( O / N ) _ { 3 } }$ coordination environment (Iwig et al., 2008). A thiolate ligand-to-metal charge-transfer transition is observed, with a Cys-Ni(II) distance of 2.54 A (Iwig ˚ et al., 2008). The nickel ligands include the $\mathrm { N H } _ { 2 }$ group of the amino-terminus; the amide of His3; the side chains of His3, Cys35, and His64; and solvent (Higgins et al., 2012, 2013; Iwig et al., 2008). Many RcnR homologs in other bacteria are associated with putative transporters (50%), metalloenzymes (23%), copper chaperones (13%), and cardiolipin synthases or membrane proteins (13%) (Iwig et al., 2006). A search of the E. coli genome reveals no RcnR binding motifs other than those within rcnR and rcnA (Iwig and Chivers, 2009). 

The mechanism by which RcnR regulates RcnAB is well studied (Figure 20.1.2a). Deletion of rcnR causes the constitutive expression of rcnA equivalent to full induction by nickel in wild-type cells (Iwig et al., 2006). Complementation of rcnR on a low-copy-number plasmid restores nickel- and cobaltdependent regulation (Iwig et al., 2006). Alternative divalent cations Cd(II), Cu(II), Fe(II), Mn(II), and Zn(II) have little to no effect on RcnR-dependent expression of rcnA (Blaha et al., 2011; Iwig et al., 2008). In vitro, nickel completely prevents RcnRdependent DNA binding (Iwig et al., 2006). Interestingly, deletion of rcnR leads to a 50% increase in $\mathrm { P } _ { n i k }$ expression $( \mathrm { P } _ { n i k }$ is the promoter for the nickel uptake nik operon) at low concentrations of nickel (<10 nM) due to de-repression of rcnA and corresponding enhancement of nickel export (Iwig et al., 2006). This result demonstrates the necessary balance between nickel import and efflux. 

Consistent with the interplay between nickel and iron metabolism, nickel defense and iron regulation appear to be integrated in E. coli (see Chapter 19.2). Fur binds to the intergenic region between rcnR and rcnA (Koch et al., 2007). Increasing iron concentrations induce rcnR by 2.3-fold, but without affecting rcnAB transcription. Also, in the absence of Fur and the iron-exporter FieF, iron induces rcnA in an RcnRdependent manner (Koch et al., 2007). Deletion of both fieF and fur does not affect the nickel-dependent regulation of rcnA. These results suggest that E. coli experiences conditions where iron may bind to RcnR and lead to inappropriate induction of rcnAB. 

## 20.1.3.2 ArsR family

Found in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, NmtR and KmtR are nickel-sensing members of the ArsR family of metallosensors that use a winged-helix homodimeric fold (Campbell et al., 2007; Cavet et al., 2002; Harami et al., 2013; Osman and Cavet, 2010). Upon binding nickel, NmtR releases from the DNA allowing transcription of nmtA, which encodes a Ni(II) exporter (Figure 20.1.2b). Similar to RcnR, NmtR binds nickel in octahedral geometry, in this case using the alpha-amine of Gly2 (Met1 is removed from the protein) and side chains of His3, Asp91, His93, His104, and His107 (Cavet et al., 2002; Reyes-Caballero et al., 2011). Limited studies on KmtR suggest it functions similarly to NmtR, but with greater nickel affinity (Campbell et al., 2007). 

## 20.1.3.3 ECF family

The regulatory system CnrYXH activates the downstream genes encoding a nickel efflux system, cnrCBAT, in Cupriavidus metallidurans CH34 (Figure 20.1.2c) (Liesegang et al., 1993; Trepreau et al., 2014). CnrY and CnrX are interacting membrane-bound proteins that likely function as an antisigma factor and a sensor of periplasmic nickel, respectively, while CnrH is an extracellular sigma factor (ECF) (Grass et al., 2000, 2005; Ho and Ellermeier, 2012; Mascher, 2013; Nies, 2004; Tibazarwa et al., 2000; Trepreau et al., 2011; see Chapter 2.6; 

Section 4). CnrH is believed to regulate both cnrYXH and cnrCBAT in a nickel-dependent manner (Grass et al., 2000; Tibazarwa et al., 2000). Crystal structures are known for CnrX with bound Ni(II), Co(II), and Zn(II) (PDB IDs 2y39, 2y3b, and 2y3d) (Trepreau et al., 2011). The protein is a dimer (Trepreau et al., 2011) with nickel bound by His42, His46, Glu63 (bidentate), His119, and Met123 in an octahedral configuration (Grass et al., 2005; Trepreau et al., 2011). Furthermore, the CnrX peptide sequence is 76% identical to NccX from Cupriavidus metallidurans 31A (Kim et al., 2008), consistent with an analogous function in nickel sensing for that organism. 

## 20.1.4 Nickel resistance

Bacterial cells can draw upon a range of mechanisms to defend themselves against metal stress (Figure 20.1.3). These diverse approaches include removing excess metal from the cell; decreasing the uptake of metal; compartmentalizing or sequestering the cation, chaperone-based delivery of the appropriate metals to reduce the formation of nickel-substituted enzymes; using alternative enzymes with decreased sensitivity to inhibition; and converting the metal to a less toxic form. We highlight the methods observed for nickel defense; however, it should be kept in mind there is extensive overlap with cobalt resistance. 

## 20.1.4.1 Nickel efflux

Similar to other transition metals, the primary mechanism of nickel resistance in most bacteria is mediated through efflux transporters (Delmar et al., 2014; Nies, 2003; von Rozycki and Nies, 2009). These efflux proteins include a wide variety of transporter families that represent convergent evolution. For each of the efflux systems described, we provide the transporter classification database (TCDB) number (Saier et al., 2014). 

## Ni–Co transporter family (TCDB no. 2.A.113)

RcnA (resistance to cobalt and nickel) was first identified in E. coli (Rodrigue et al., 2005). As mentioned in Section 20.1.3, rcnA is in an operon with rcnB and is regulated by RcnR. The inner membrane transport protein (274 amino acids, 30.4 kDa) (Figure 20.1.3) is membrane bound and predicted to contain six transmembrane domains (Rodrigue et al., 2005) with a His-rich section in the center of the polypeptide (residues 121–146). This domain contains 17 His, 3 Glu, and 3 Asp that are likely to be involved with nickel ion transport (Rodrigue et al., 2005). Deletion of rcnA leads to a two- to threefold sensitization of E. coli cells to nickel (Koch et al., 2007; Rodrigue et al., 2005), while overexpression of rcnA on a high-copy-number plasmid leads to a 100-fold increase in resistance to nickel (Rodrigue et al., 2005). RcnA-dependent efflux is specific to nickel and cobalt as deletion of rcnA does not affect Zn(II) or Cd(II) resistance (Koch et al., 2007). Mutant cells (ΔrcnA) accumulate 1.5-fold more 63Ni(II) than wild-type cells, and the rcnA overexpression strain has one-fifth of the intracellular nickel as control cells (Rodrigue et al., 2005). Furthermore, deletion of rcnA leads to a 60% decrease in intracellular 63Ni(II) concentrations in rcnA non-inducing conditions (LB with 10 nM Ni(II)) (Iwig et al., 2006). Interestingly, deletion of rcnA leads to a 50% decrease in the expression of the nickel import system NikABCDE at low nickel concentrations (<10 nM). These results demonstrate that RcnA is present and functional even at low nickel concentrations and works antagonistically with NikABCDE (Iwig et al., 2006). The regulator of $\mathrm { P } _ { n i k } ,$ , NikR, when bound to nickel represses expression of the importer (Chivers and Sauer, 1999; De Pina et al., 1999). Overexpression of rcnA does not abolish NikR repression of the nik operon, thus RcnA cannot completely eliminate all intracellular nickel (Iwig et al., 2006). Furthermore, an rcnA mutant shows a [NiFe]-hydrogenase-3 deficient phenotype that is restored by deletion of NikR, suggesting that lowlevel rcnA expression is needed to modulate the activity of NikR. These results provide clear evidence that E. coli has fine-tuned its nickel uptake and nickel efflux systems, and it is a likely model for other organisms that utilize nickel metalloenzymes. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/6aceee5f73cc13fca68d5d5773fc6a3c8fc59f4a4d55b68c6246ec417c40371a.jpg)



Figure 20.1.3 Mechanisms of nickel resistance in bacteria. The most commonly observed nickel defense mechanism involves export of the cation (solid black arrows). Examples of exporters representing distinct families include RcnA and its periplasmic modulator RcnB (dark blue), NreB of the MFS family (purple), NccABC of the RND family (green), and the P-type ATPase NmtA (light blue). Some of these transporters are driven by proton motive force, and others by adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis (dashed arrows). Another mechanism involves compartmentation or sequestration of nickel, which can occur outside the cell, in the periplasm, or in the cytoplasm (red arrows). Additional mechanisms (not shown; see text) have been described in a few selected cases.


In E. coli, rcnB (Figure 20.1.3) is encoded immediately downstream of rcnA and makes up the only other member of the RcnR regulon (Bleriot´ et al., 2011; Iwig et al., 2006). More than 150 predicted RcnB homologs are found throughout alpha-, beta-, and gammaproteobacteria according to bioinformatic analysis (Bleriot ´ et al., 2011). The genomic location of the rcnB homologs is highly variable: rcnB is found with rcnA, other efflux pumps, as part of uncharacterized open reading frames or as orphan genes. Sequence alignment of the RcnB enterobacterial homologs suggests a metal-binding motif of His82-Trp83-X-X-Met86. E. coli RcnB is a 112-amino-acid periplasmic protein with a Sec-type signal peptide. The mature protein forms by cleavage of the signal peptide after residue 25, leaving a 9898 Da protein (Bleriot ´ et al., 2011). The nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structure was solved for YohN, an RcnB homolog of Klebsiella pneumonia (PDB code 2l1s) (Wahab et al., unpublished studies). 

As expected for a gene involved in nickel efflux and located in the rcnA operon, transcription of rcnB is induced by nickel and cobalt (Bleriot ´ et al., 2011). Surprisingly, deletion of rcnB does not sensitize cells to nickel or cobalt; rather, it increases the resistance of cells to both of these metals (Bleriot´ et al., 2011; Koch et al., 2007). This result was confirmed by complementing rcnB in trans, which restores wild-type sensitivity (Bleriot´ et al., 2011). Interestingly, anaerobic complementation leads to growth impairment on glucose minimal medium by an unknown mechanism (Bleriot´ et al., 2011). The intracellular nickel content of the rcnB mutant grown in LB medium supplemented with 500 μM Ni(II) is 20% less than in wild-type cells. In minimal glucose medium, wild-type cells demonstrate a 10-fold decrease in growth rate with 50 μM Ni(II) or 15 μM Co(II), whereas the rcnB mutant is insensitive and exhibits an 84% decrease in nickel content compared to wild-type cells. Once again, complementation of rcnB restores the intracellular levels of nickel to concentrations higher than observed in wild-type cells. The use of $^ { \cdot } 6 3 \mathrm { { N i ( I I ) } }$ fails to demonstrate binding to RcnB (Bleriot´ et al., 2011). The presence of copper destabilizes RcnB, with the denaturation $\mathrm { T _ { m } }$ decreasing from $8 6 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for apoprotein to $7 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for the copper-bound protein (Bleriot ´ et al., 2014). On the basis of fluorescence quenching associated with the two Trp residues in RcnB, binding occurs with Cu(II), but not with Ni(II), Co(II), Zn(II), or Mg(II). RcnB binds one copper per monomer with a $K _ { \mathrm { d } }$ of 1.8–6.0 μM, but copper binding disappears in a M86A mutant (see also Chapter 2.12). Interestingly, the M86A mutation also sensitizes cells to nickel challenge despite the lack of evidence for nickel binding (Bleriot´ et al., 2014). The weak binding of copper and the lack of nickel binding to RcnB raise the question of how this protein functions in nickel efflux. 

In contrast with the established connection between RcnB and nickel stress, this protein is unlikely to play a direct role in copper resistance, even though rcnB overexpression confers resistance to copper toxicity and increases cellular copper content as determined by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) (Bleriot ´ et al., 2014). Importantly, rcnB is not induced upon copper supplementation, and an rcnB deletion mutant does not sensitize cells to copper. Using [NiFe]- hydrogenase as a proxy for intracellular nickel concentration, an rcnB deletion shows no effect in a wild-type background; however, the rcnB deletion decreases the activity of hydrogenase in a nickel import mutant (ΔnikABCDE) (Bleriot ´ et al., 2011). Furthermore, overexpression of rcnB in the nik mutant increases the activity of [NiFe]-hydrogenase. These results suggest that RcnB works independently of NikABCDE to modulate intracellular nickel content (Bleriot´ et al., 2011). The authors conclude, however, that RcnB is unlikely to be involved in nickel uptake. In contrast, if cells are preloaded with 63Ni(II), an rcnB mutation leads to an increase in the rate of nickel efflux (Bleriot´ et al., 2011). This finding suggests that RcnB is involved in modulating nickel efflux. 

## RND family (TCDB no. 2.A.6)

The resistance nodulation and cell division (RND) family of transporters encompasses many metal efflux proteins, including those for nickel (Delmar et al., 2014; Nies, 2003). These systems consist of an inner membrane pump, an outer membrane channel, and a periplasmic adaptor protein that utilize the proton motive force to pump molecules into the extracellular space (Haney et al., 2005). These transporters additionally pump periplasmic metals out across the outer membrane, and as such are not found in bacteria lacking outer membranes (Haney et al., 2005). Nickel resistance determinants of the RND family are known in C. metallidurans, Achromobacter xylosoxidans, Bradyrhizobium sp., and Helicobacter pylori (Chaintreuil et al., 2007; Liesegang et al., 1993). For example, the chromosomal cznCBA (cadmium, zinc, and nickel resistance) 

(Stahler ¨ et al., 2006) and the plasmid-borne gene clusters cnr-CBA (cobalt and nickel resistance) (Liesegang et al., 1993) and nccCBA (nickel–cobalt–cadmium resistance) (Figure 20.1.3) (Schmidt and Schlegel, 1994) all contribute to nickel resistance. 

MrdH of P. putida is predicted to be a 41 kDa hybrid transporter protein with an RncA-like domain and an RND-like domain (Haritha et al., 2009). Transcription of mrdH is induced by Cd(II), Ni(II), Zn(II), and Co(II) (Haritha et al., 2009). Deletion of mrdH in P. putida leads to increased sensitivity to and accumulation of Cd(II), Ni(II), and Zn(II) compared to wildtype cells. Surprisingly, the mutant has little effect on Co(II) resistance and no effect on Cu(II) and Pb(II) resistance (Haritha et al., 2009). 

## MFS family (TCDB no. 2.A.1)

The major facilitator superfamily of efflux proteins is defined by 12 transmembrane helices that are divided between two domains (Yan, 2013). Several members of this family (e.g., NreB) have been shown to confer resistance to nickel by pumping cytoplasmic nickel into the periplasm (Chaintreuil et al., 2007; Grass et al., 2001; Marrero et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004, 2008). These nickel-transporting MFS proteins likely utilize the proton gradient to pump nickel against a concentration gradient and are often in an operon with other transporters and/or regulatory proteins. 

## Cdf family (TCDB no. 2.A4)

Cation diffusion facilitators are a ubiquitous family of cation and proton antiporters with six transmembrane domains (Haney et al., 2005). Several members of this family are found to confer nickel resistance, including CzcD of Bacillus subtilis (Moore et al., 2005), DmeF in Cupriavidus metallidurans (Munkelt et al., 2004), and NepA from Rhizobium etli (Cubillas et al., 2013). Phylogenomic analyses of eukarya, bacteria, and archaea identify a Ni(II)/Co(II)-specific clade and reveal several new putative Ni(II) transporters (Cubillas et al., 2013), suggesting a broad utilization of this family for nickel resistance. 

## P-type ATPase efflux systems (TCDB no. 3.A.3)

Initial studies with Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium smegmatis indicated two $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } } – \mathrm { A T P a s e s }$ (CtpD and NmtA–CtpJ) (Figure 20.1.3) that are involved in nickel defense (Cavet et al., 2002; Raimunda et al., 2012); however, subsequent work failed to demonstrate direct cellular export of nickel by these proteins (Raimunda et al., 2012, 2014). Similarly conflicting results showed both nickel-dependent regulation of nmtA (Cavet et al., 2002) and an absence of nickel-dependent induction (Raimunda et al., 2012). Deletion of ctpD in M. smegmatis sensitizes cells to nickel (Raimunda et al., 2012), whereas there is no difference when such mutants are compared with wild-type sensitivity in M. tuberculosis (Raimunda et al., 2014). While more work needs to be done to resolve these issues with CtpJ, it appears that CtpD may have evolved for cobalt, not nickel, efflux. 

## 20.1.4.2 Compartmentalization and sequestration of nickel

Whereas eukaryotic microorganisms are well known to pump nickel into vesicles or synthesize nickel-binding components (Joho et al., 1995; Nishimura et al., 1998), these compartmentalization and sequestration approaches are not widely seen in bacteria for this metal ion; however, a few examples exist. A highly nickel-resistant sulfate reducer, Desulfotomaculum, has been shown to precipitate nickel both as a nickel sulfide and as a nickel–protein complex outside of the cell (Fortin et al., 1994). Streptomyces coelicolor also produces a small protein (SCO4226, 82 residues) that binds to four nickel ions at the surface of the protein dimer (Lu et al., 2014). In vitro binding of nickel causes the aggregation of this protein that likely enhances resistance through sequestration within inclusion bodies (Lu et al., 2014). SCO4226 is induced by nickel, but not Cu(II), Mn(II), or Co(II) (Lu et al., 2014). In a combination of compartmentalization and sequestration, P. putida S4 produces a nickel-inducible protein that binds to and sequesters nickel in the periplasm, thus conferring nickel resistance (Tripathi and Srivastava, 2006). Another H. pylori protein, Hpn, was also found to be a cytoplasmic nickel-binding protein that confers nickel resistance (Ge et al., 2006). Pseudomonas aeruginosa sequesters nickel in its periplasm by creating crystalline nickel phosphides and carbide (Sar et al., 2001). Nickel protein sequestration and periplasmic compartmentalization have also been observed in Cupriavidus pauculus (Pal, 2010). Perhaps related to this mechanism, nickel supplementation leads to production of curli and biofilm formation in E. coli through increased transcription of the positive regulator csgD (Perrin et al., 2009). Whether biofilm formation is a defensive strategy to combat excess nickel remains unknown. 

## 20.1.4.3 Other mechanisms for combatting nickel stress

In theory, proteins that act as nickel chaperones like HypB and UreE could have evolved to ensure nickel is sequestered to protect vulnerable intracellular targets. In fact, this strategy is employed by eukaryotes when handling copper and iron (Palumaa, 2013; Philpott and Ryu, 2014). In the case of HypB and UreE, these proteins clearly are necessary for the metallation of [NiFe]-hydrogenase and urease, respectively (Boer et al., 2014; Farrugia et al., 2013; Kaluarachchi et al., 2010); however, there is currently no evidence to suggest they evolved for defense. In contrast, the cytoplasmic protein HspA, a homolog of GroES (Radford, 2006; Suerbaum et al., 1994; see Section 14), is a nickel chaperone in Helicobacter pylori that is important for full activity of [NiFe]-hydrogenase (but not urease) and for nickel resistance (Schauer et al., 2010). HspA contains a Cterminal domain that contains the nickel-binding domain of the NiCoT transporter family (HX DH) that binds two nickel ions per monomer (Cun et al., 2008; Kansau et al., 1996). Another mechanism appears to be represented by Thiocapsa roseopersicina, which reduces ionic nickel to metallic nickel in a manner that is dependent on $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ metabolism (Zadvornyy et al., 2010). As a final example of a defense mechanism, E. coli and H. pylori undergo a negative chemotactic response to nickel (Borrok et al., 2005; Englert et al., 2010; Sanders et al., 2013; Tso and Adler, 1974). 

## 20.1.5 Conclusions and perspectives

Nickel exhibits toxicity to bacteria by incorrectly substituting into zinc or iron metalloenzymes, binding to the active sites of non-metalloenzymes, and stimulating the production of reactive oxygen species. The inhibitory binding sites closely resemble in structure the nickel-binding sites of regulatory proteins that sense intracellular nickel concentrations and upregulate defense mechanisms. The most widely observed nickel stress response is export of the metal from the cell, with a variety of different export systems being well studied. In addition, alternative defenses against nickel stress are known in selected bacteria, which may fine-tune defenses for a specific niche. 

Future studies to dissect nickel toxicity, regulation, and resistance mechanisms will likely rely heavily on omics techniques. One representative example of this approach involves Pseudomonas putida KT2440. Exposure of this bacterium to 75 μM nickel in succinate minimal medium causes the upregulation of 54 proteins and the downregulation of 46 proteins. Proteins identified as being important for defense against nickel include those acting in antioxidant defense (SodB) and protein synthesis. Interestingly, proteins involved in the synthesis of amino acids derived from 2-oxoglutarate are upregulated (Ray et al., 2013). Valine biosynthesis proteins are upregulated, whereas those involved in leucine biosynthesis are downregulated. The nickel-stressed cells produce a fourfold accumulation of Glu, a twofold accumulation of Ala, and a slight increase in Ile and Leu in the medium. Furthermore, Asp levels are decreased 1.6-fold compared to cells in unchallenged medium. Proteins within the tricarboxylic acid cycle are affected, but some activities increase and others decrease (Ray et al., 2013). Metagenomic libraries of the bacterial rhizosphere of heather were hosted in E. coli and screened for nickel resistance determinants (Mirete et al., 2007). Nickel resistance determinants contained a number of proteins in which the role in nickel resistance is unclear (Mirete et al., 2007). Overall, the combination of transcriptomics, proteomics, metagenomics, and metabolomics has the potential to provide keen insights into the effects of nickel stress in bacteria.

# Metabolic networks to counter Al toxicity in Pseudomonas fluorescens: a holistic view

Christopher Auger, Nishma D. Appanna, and Vasu D. Appanna 

Faculty of Science and Engineering, Laurentian University, Sudbury, Ontario, Canada 

## 20.2.1 Introduction

Metal pollution is an ongoing environmental problem that is known to have adverse health and ecological effects. Although in trace amounts some metals are critical for life, in elevated concentrations all metals exhibit nefarious biochemical activities. Aluminum (Al) is the most abundant metallic element in the Earth’s crust, yet, despite its ubiquity, biological systems have seemingly circumvented the incorporation of this metal in cellular processes (Soni et al., 2001; Verstraeten et al., 2008). The apparent exclusion of Al from all living systems studied thus far certainly raises questions about its toxicological significance. Three key factors are at play to make Al more bioavailable and a menace to biological systems: (i) an increase in anthropogenic acidification of soils, (ii) the increased utilization of the metal for industrial purposes, and (iii) its application as a flocculent in water treatment and utilization in our daily products (Auger et al., 2013; Exley, 2009; Gomez et al., 2008; Kawahara et al., 2007; Yokel et al., 2008). This enhanced bioavailability has resulted in the accumulation of the metal in living organisms such as fish, plants, and humans (Costa et al., 2014; Lemire et al., 2011; Mailloux et al., 2011a; Oberholster et al., 2012; Peto, 2010; Zhang et al., 2014). The skeletal system, the liver, and the brain are some of the primary sites where Al deposits have been observed (Bignucolo et al., 2012; Gomez et al., 2008; Rondeau et al., 2009; Ward et al., 2001). Diseases such as encephalopathy, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and osteomalacia have been associated with the presence of this metal (Bondy 2010; Jaffe et al., 2005; Jeffery et al., 1996). While in fish the gills tend to concentrate Al, in plants the leaves provide an ideal body for the immobilization of this trivalent metal (Grassie et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2002). In spite of an expanding body of literature detailing the harmful consequences of overexposure to Al, there is still substantial debate regarding its safety and usage (Lemire et al., 2009; Tomljenovic, 2011). 

Research dealing with the exposure of Al in microorganisms has further enabled the elucidation of the mechanisms underlying the biochemical interactions of this metal. Concentrations of Al lower than 3 mM have been shown to inhibit the growth of Escherichia coli, with increasing sensitivity to this metal at lower pH (Guida et al., 1991). Furthermore, the uptake of Al is known to utilize Fe transport systems (see Section 19), thus interfering with the ability of microbes to capture this essential micronutrient (Davis et al., 1971; El Hage Chahine et al., 2012). This trivalent metal has also been shown to regulate bacterial motility, disrupt plant nodulation, and perturb photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation in bacteria (Appanna, 1989; Guzzo et al., 1991; Munns, 1986; Pettersson et al., 1985). For an organism to grow and flourish in the presence of a toxicant, adaptation must take place. Pseudomonas fluorescens, the nutritionally versatile soil microbe, accomplishes this task by overcoming the deleterious effects that Al presents. Indeed, this microorganism can tolerate concentrations of Al as high as 50 mM (Appanna et al., 1995a,b; Appanna and St. Pierre, 1996). To understand how such a feat is possible, it is important to elucidate how Al exerts its toxic influence on the molecular systems in the cell. 

## 20.2.2 Biochemical toxicology of aluminum

The molecular targets of Al toxicity are multifaceted and appear to involve the disruption of essential metal homeostasis such as calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), and iron (Fe) (Exley, 2009; Kawahara et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2012; see Section 19). Al has been demonstrated to replace Ca within the bone and interferes with Ca-based signaling events (Nday et al., 2010). Al can also substitute for Mg in the binding to phosphate groups on adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and DNA. However, unlike Mg, Al binds much stronger with the phosphate backbone and disrupts replicative and transcriptional processes, a feature that can be lethal (Exley and Birchall, 1992; Harris et al., 1996; Kawahara and Kato-Negishi, 2011). Membrane lipids are riddled with phosphate groups, which are an attractive target for Al due to the high negative charge. Once bound to the phospholipids of the cell membrane, the membrane becomes rigid and loses its fluidity. Though this binding of Al to the phospholipids interrupts processes relevant to the survival of the cell, it also provides a potential site for the sequestration and detoxification of Al (Jones and Kochian, 1997; Kumar et al., 2009). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/88465bc48d0c40a7733a4f4e4938c751b477f394b5ba38901bb450b30119c665.jpg)



Figure 20.2.1 An overview of the biomolecular targets affected by Al and Al-derived reactive oxygen species.


However, the main target of Al toxicity is Fe-dependent biological processes (see Section 19). As Al and Fe have similar ionic properties, they compete for Fe-binding sites in biomolecules. However, whereas Fe is redox active, Al is redox silent, and the substitution inactivates the target molecule (Exley, 2004; Middaugh et al., 2005). The displacement of Fe by Al leads to a dangerous intracellular event, namely the generation of an oxidative environment. Free Fe can react in the biological milieu via the Fenton reaction to create a variety of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that can indeed unleash numerous cellular dysfunctions (Bondy and Kirstein, 1996; Exley, 2004; see Section 10). The perturbation of Fe homeostasis and the subsequent generation of ROS both contribute to its toxicological effects. Fe is required for many key enzymes that perform oxidation–reduction reactions, and it also allows oxidative energy production to occur (Mailloux et al., 2007a; Mailloux and Appanna, 2007). Many of the enzymes involved in the production of ATP, via the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and subsequently the electron transport chain (ETC), are reliant on Fe-S clusters or heme groups (Hentze et al., 2004; Levi and Rovida, 2009). The disruption of these key prosthetic groups by Al results in a diminished production of energy via oxidative phosphorylation (Han et al., 2013; Lemire et al., 2010; Mailloux et al., 2009). The cumulative effect of the inactivation of these enzymes is an alteration of typical metabolism and, subsequently, ATP production (Figure 20.2.1). Since ATP is the energy currency of the cell, Al toxicity affects all biochemical processes that take place within the bacterium (Chenier et al., 2008). Although a plethora of Al-resistant microorganisms have been uncovered, a detailed analysis of these toxic effects and the subsequent adaptative strategies has eluded researchers (Beris et al., 2011; Martins et al., 2012). Here, we elaborate on how the soil microbe P. fluorescens utilizes its metabolic versatility to survive in Al-rich environments. The biochemical pathways participating in the sequestration of Al and in the adaptation of life in the presence of this trivalent metal are described. A holistic metabolic approach, alluded to in this chapter, not only provides the molecular events responsible for the immobilization of the Al but also expands on how the microbe tailors its processes to accommodate a dearth of Fe induced by the toxicant and the noxious environment triggered by excessive amounts of Al. 

## 20.2.3 P. fluorescens, an Al-resistant microbe

As reported, P. fluorescens can tolerate Al concentrations up to 50 mM in solution (Appanna and St. Pierre, 1994; Appanna et al., 1995a,b). Exposure of the metal to the organism is accomplished by chelating it to citric acid, which translocates across the bacterial membrane as a complex that is then degraded intracellularly. This strategy forces the bacterium to deal with the metal, as its only source of carbon is complexed to Al. After 80 h of growth, 65.1% of the soluble Al is sequestered when P. fluorescens is grown in media containing an Al concentration of 15 mM (Appanna and Pierre, 1996). Analysis of the soluble cell-free extract following 75 h of growth showed that less than 1% of the Al in the media is found in this compartment. The ability of this bacterium to cope with such a high concentration of Al involves a detoxification strategy that primarily consists of excluding it from the cell as an insoluble lipid-containing precipitate tailored to alleviate the toxicity of this metal. The nature of this gelatinous residue harboring Al has been shown to contain oxalate and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), a phospholipid commonly found in biological membranes (Appanna and Pierre, 1996). The immobilization of Al into an insoluble gelatinous precipitate is an extremely effective method for the detoxification of the metal. Not only does it eliminate it from the cell, but also it prevents it from being reabsorbed. However, the expulsion of Al in association with PE necessitates a major reconfiguration of metabolic pathways in order to generate all the ingredients needed for this process to occur efficiently. Furthermore, the organism has to deal with the lack of biavailable Fe promoted by Al (Hamel and Appanna, 2003). 

## 20.2.4 A modified TCA cycle to generate oxalate and ATP

The TCA cycle and the aerobic formation of ATP are heavily reliant upon Fe; aconitase (ACN), succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II), fumarase A (FUM A), Complex I, Complex II, Complex III, and Complex IV all require Fe in order to fulfill their biological functions. In these enzymes, Fe is usually associated as heme or sulfur clusters (see Section 19). ACN has a labile Fe in its Fe-S cluster that is disrupted during oxidative stress (Mailloux et al., 2007b). Upon the loss of the labile Fe, ACN now assumes the role of a signaling molecule termed the iron responsive protein-1 (IRP1). The IRP1 can regulate Fe homeostasis by binding the iron responsive element (IRE) in RNA (Popovic and Templeton, 2007). In this manner, ACN serves as the gatekeeper to oxidative metabolism. If Fe is not present or if the oxidative tension within the cell is too large, oxidative metabolism will be turned off (Heidari et al., 2009). Citrate, the primer for the TCA cycle, will be devoted to alternative pathways that do not require oxidative catabolism. P. fluorescens appears to utilize this strategy to quell the insult imposed by Al. As citrate lyase is not evident in these cultures, the microbe is compelled to utilize the TCA cycle despite a severely diminished ACN. To help solve this dilemma, P. fluorescens drastically upregulates two downstream enzymes, namely isocitrate lyase (ICL) and NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (ICDH–NADP), that act on isocitrate (Middaugh et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2009). While the activity of ICL is increased 6–8-fold, ICDH–NADP is augmented twofold. This arrangement helps facilitate the degradation of citrate, even though ACN is able to only minimally isomerize the citrate (Hamel et al., 2004; Middaugh et al., 2005). 

Complexes I, II, III, and IV require Fe-S and/or heme to safely transfer electrons through the respiratory chain. A perturbation in the availability of Fe is known to severely affect these proteins as well. In order to generate ATP, the microbe employs the enzymes acylating glyoxylate dehydrogenase (AGODH), succinyl-CoA synthetase (SCS), and oxylate-CoA transferase (OCT), which work in tandem with ICL. SCS produces ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation (SLP), thus fulfilling the organism’s energy needs when oxidative phosphorylation is ineffective (Singh et al., 2009). In addition, this metabolic reconfiguration generates oxalate, a dicarboxylic acid and potent chelator of Al that assists in the expulsion of this metal from the cell (Hamel and Appanna, 2001, 2003). Completion of the TCA cycle is rendered possible by the switch from an iron-dependent isoform of fumarase (FUM A) to one that does not require a Fe-S cluster for catalytic activity (FUM C). If not for this metabolic reconfiguration, the TCA cycle would grind to a halt (Chenier et al., 2008). The metabolic network described here allows the bacterium to produce energy, generate critical metabolites, and proliferate when exposed to high concentrations of Al (Figure 20.2.2). Hence, life in an Al environment brings into play a truncated TCA cycle aimed at producing oxalate and ATP, two ingredients that are key for survival (Appanna et al., 2003; Auger et al., 2013; Lemire et al., 2010). 

## 20.2.5 The metabolic switch from NADH to NADPH to counter oxidative stress

Due to defective oxidative phosphorylation under Al stress, NADH cannot be oxidized by the ETC. To prevent NADH from stockpiling, Al-challenged P. fluorescens has been observed to decrease the activity of two key NADH-producing enzymes of the TCA cycle: NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (ICDH-NAD) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGDH) (Lemire et al., 2010). While this strategem limits the further production of ROS via oxidative metabolism, it is important to curtail the accumulation of free radicals, such as the hydroxyl radical generated by Fenton chemistry, which are dangerous owing to their ability to react with and disable crucial biomolecules (Freinbichler et al., 2011; see Chapter 10). Classical enzymatic mechanisms to curb ROS levels, such as catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase–reductase, are at the disposal of the bacterium (Mailloux et al., 2007b, 2011b). However,

Green and red arrows indicate enzymes whose activities are up- and downregulated, respectively.


P. fluorescens invokes several other metabolic reconfigurations to further negate ROS damage. 

As NADPH is required for the regeneration of ROSscavenging molecules such as glutathione, P. fluorescens upregulates enzymes that produce this reducing agent (Figure 20.2.2) (Singh et al., 2005). While the aforementioned ICDH-NADP helps accomplish this, other enzymes that participate in NADPH production, such as malic enzyme (ME) and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH), also show increased activity. A constant supply of NADP for these reactions is assured by increasing the expression of the NAD phosphorylating enzyme, NAD kinase (NADK). Not only does NADK enhance NADPH production, but also it diminishes the level of NAD, a key activator of dehydrogenases (Singh et al., 2005). The latter enzymes produce NADH, which can further exacerbate the intracellular oxidative tension. The activation of NADK switches on the metabolic networks aimed at generating NADPH, a potent reducing agent, and away from the synthesis of NADH, a pro-oxidant (Kussmaul and Hirst, 2006; Singh et al., 2008). Furthermore, the direct utilization of any NADH produced is catalyzed by the H2O-generating NADH oxidase (NOX), an enzyme that is upregulated during Al stress (Chenier et al., 2008). The product of this reaction, NAD, can be utilized to propel redox reactions or for NADP generation by NADK. Not only does the enhanced production of NADPH help fend off Al-induced oxidative stress (see Chapter 10), but also it provides the crucial reducing factor required for lipogenesis, an event that results in the synthesis of PE (Bogdanovic et al., 2014). This interplay involving NADP–NAD and NADPH–NADH is pivotal to avert the dangers posed by Al toxicity (Figure 20.2.3). 

## 20.2.6 Metabolic networks to generate oxaloacetate and citrate, precursors to aluminophore production

While PE and oxalate play key roles in the removal of Al from the organism, they are not the only moities capable of binding this metal and negating its noxious effects. A second metabolic reconfiguration occurs in order to generate another dicarboxylic acid, oxaloacetate, which is used as a precursor to a polycarboxylic aluminophore. This strategy is adopted in media where the phosphate level is 100-fold lower, compared to the environment where PE and oxalate orchestrate the demise of toxic Al (Lemire et al., 2008). The availability of phosphate is a potent modulator of the metabolic pathways that the microbe utlizes to fend off the dangers posed by Al. The homeostasis of oxaloacetate is regulated by numerous enzymes. Malate dehydrogenase (MDH), a critical TCA cycle enzyme, appears to be upregulated by the microbe in order to produce oxaloacetate at a greater rate when Al is present. Pyruvate carboxylase (PC), which carboxylates pyruvate to form oxaloacetate, is also overexpressed by P. fluorescens treated with Al. On the other hand, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), an enzyme that converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, shows lower expression. Furthermore, the activity of nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDPK), a critical enzyme for the generation of the PEPCK cofactor GTP, also shows lowered activity in the Al-treated bacteria (Lemire et al., 2008). PC and PEPCK are normally coupled in the gluconeogenic pathway, allowing the organism to produce intermediates for biosynthetic reactions. However, it appears as though Al toxicity disrupts this process. Thus, this metabolic shift involving the uncoupling of PC and PEPCK enables P. fluorescens to survive Al toxicity via the pooling of oxaloacetate for the generation of aluminophores that help trap and exude this trivalent metal (Figure 20.2.4a). A similar uncoupling of MS and ICL is observed in the modified TCA cycle aimed at the production of oxalate and ATP. In this instance, even though ICL is upregulated sixfold, the glyoxylate generated is funnelled to oxalate synthesis via the enzyme acylating glyoxylate dehydrogenase (Singh et al., 2009).

Green and red indicate enzymes whose activities are up- and downregulated, respectively.


When malate is utilized as a delivery system for Al, P. fluorescens elects to exude the metal utilizing citrate as a chelator, underscoring the importance of the carbon source in the organism’s detoxification strategem (Mailloux et al., 2008). In this instance, the microbe indeed upregulates MDH while lowering the activity of PEPCK, as described in this chapter. However, the organism also increases the expression and activity of PDH and citrate synthase (CS) to further propel the synthesis of citric acid, which can then be used to remediate the intracellular Al problem. While it may seem paradoxical to employ PDH, given the susceptibility of the enzyme to oxidation, it is possible that the lowered concentration of oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA, two feedback inhibitors of PDH, may also contribute to the enhanced activity of the enzyme in the malate media. Oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA are rapidly consumed by the increased expression of CS (Figure 20.2.4) (Mailloux et al., 2008). Therefore, the response of P. fluorescens to Al toxicity appears to be tailored to the environmental conditions and nutrient sources, further validating the metabolic versatility of this organism and the importance of metabolism in these adaptive processes (al-Aoukaty et al., 1992a; Alhasawi et al., 2014; Auger and Appanna, 2015).

## 20.2.7 Al detoxification in a multimetal environment

Although microorganisms are to known to elaborate a specific strategy to counter a given metal, the presence of other metals in the same environment may elicit an entirely disparate detoxification program. P. fluorescens is known to eliminate $\mathrm { C a }$ as calcite and gallium (Ga) sequestered in a hydroxyaspartatederived chelator (al-Aoukaty et al., 1992a,b; Anderson et al., 1992). Fe is immobilized both intracellularly and extracellularly in lipid residue (Appanna and Hamel, 1996). However, when Al is present in media with these metals, the microbe adopts a unified single strategy aimed at all the metals. In this instance, oxalate and PE are the participants involved in rendering these metals biologically inactive (Appanna and St. Pierre, 1996). They are deposited in an insoluble form exocellularly. The metabolic pathways involved in the production of oxalate, NADPH, and ATP in an $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -independent manner are activated. Hence, it appears that this oxalate-based stratagem provides the ideal protection from these metal toxins (Figure 20.2.2) (Singh et al., 2009). 

## 20.2.8 Conclusion and future directions

Although the biotransformation of metals allows an organism to render these toxicants biologically inactive, it is important to appreciate the plethora of processes involved in survival during such environmental challenges. Here, we have described how the dangers posed by Al necessitate a multipronged strategy designed to combat bioavailable Al, a dearth of essential Fe, and an oxidative environment. The enhanced synthesis of oxalate, ATP, and NADPH is critical to this effort. P. fluorescens reengineers its metabolic processes to bioprecipitate $\mathrm { A l } ,$ thus rendering it biologically ineffective (Figure 20.2.5). The metabolic modules that render this decontamination strategy feasible allow for the biotransformation and expulsion of Al without significantly impeding the survival of the organism. Even though ACN, a critical enzyme of the TCA cycle, is severely perturbed, the microbe invokes the participation of ICL and ICDH–NADP, two downstream partners, to facilitate the degradation of citrate. The upregulation of NOX provides an effective route to regenerate NAD, a moiety pivotal to the functioning of the modified TCA cycle. As oxidative phosphorylation is hampered, ATP is synthesized via a substrate-level phosphorylation module orchestrated by SCS and OCT. These metabolic shifts provide ATP, NADPH, and dicarboxylic acids, ingredients that help mediate the survival of P. fluorescens when challenged by Al toxicity. In a multimetal environment, the organism opts for a similar strategy as opposed to a metal-specific detoxification program. This holistic molecular understanding of Al–microbe interactions reveals the pivotal role that metabolism plays in living systems. It is central to devising any biotechnological tools in remediating metal-polluted environments and removing metal contaminants from living systems (Auger et al., 2013; Lemire et al., 2010).

# Genomics of the resistance to metal and oxidative stresses in cyanobacteria

## Corinne Cassier-Chauvat and Franck Chauvat

Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), CEA, CNRS, Univ Paris-Sud, Universite Paris-Saclay, 91198, Gif-sur-Yvette cedex, ´ France 

## 20.3.1 Introduction

The Gram-negative prokaryotic organisms termed cyanobacteria, which perform oxygen-evolving photosynthesis, are viewed as the producers of the Earth’s oxygenic atmosphere (Schopf, 2011), the ancestors of plant chloroplasts (Archibald, 2009), and important contemporary players in biogeochemical cycles of carbon and nitrogen. Indeed, cyanobacteria make up a large part of the biomass for the food chain. Furthermore, they are regarded as a promising “low-cost” microbial factory for $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ capture and storage (25 gigatons per year) (Jansson and Northen, 2010) and the ecologically responsible production of biofuels that save arable soils, clean fresh water, fertilizers, and pesticides for agriculture (Cassier-Chauvat et al., 2014; Rosgaard et al., 2012). This is true for the unicellular model strain Synechocystis PCC6803, which possesses a small genome (Nakamura et al., 1998) that is easily manipulated (Mermet-Bouvier and Chauvat, 1994; Ortega-Ramos et al., 2014; Poncelet et al., 1998). Thanks to its powerful genetics, it is possible to introduce and express in Synechocystis PCC6803 the biofuel production genes that are absent in natural cyanobacteria (Rosgaard et al., 2012). 

Furthermore, because cyanobacteria have colonized most waters (fresh and marine) and soils of our planet, they have evolved as the most diverse groups of bacteria (Hess, 2011; Shih et al., 2013). Thus, cyanobacteria are attractive models to study the influence of the environment on the physiology, metabolism, morphology, division, and differentiation of microbial cells (Cassier-Chauvat and Chauvat, 2014a; Hagemann, 2013; Kirilovsky and Kerfeld, 2013; Maldener et al., 2014; Mejean and Ploux, 2013; Narainsamy et al., 2013). 

Because they invented oxygenic photosynthesis, cyanobacteria were the first organisms exposed to the toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) – singlet oxygen $\big ( \mathrm { ^ 1 O } _ { 2 } \big ) _ { 2 }$ , superoxide anion $( \mathrm O _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - } )$ , hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ , and hydroxyl radical (OH∙) – which are produced by this process (Kirilovsky and Kerfeld, 2013; 

Narainsamy et al., 2011; see Section 10). $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - }$ and/or $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ can oxidize exposed iron–sulfur clusters, or $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ in proteins containing (Fe-S) or Fe mononuclear centers, leading to enzyme inactivation (Dubbs and Mongkolsuk, 2012). The ROS agents can also oxidize the thiol of cysteine residues of proteins (-SH) into sulfenic (-SOH), disulfides (-S-S-), sulfinic $\left( - \mathrm { S O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H } \right)$ , or sulfonic acids $\left( - \mathrm { S O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { H } \right)$ (Imlay, 2013). The disulfide bridges can link two cysteines from the same or different proteins, or from a protein and a molecule of the antioxidant tripeptide glutathione (γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinyl-L-glycine). The formation of such glutathione–protein mix disulfides, also termed glutathionylation, is regarded as a transient protection of cysteine against irreversible oxidation (formation of sulfinic or sulfonic acids) or as a posttranslational regulatory modification (Chardonnet et al., 2014; Marteyn et al., 2013; Sakr et al., 2013). Depending on their nature, these disulfides are repaired by thioredoxins and glutaredoxins enzymes (discussed further in this chapter), while the other ROS are detoxified by various metabolites (ascorbate, carotenoids, glutathione, etc.) and enzymes (superoxide dismutase, catalase, peroxiredoxins, etc.) (Narainsamy et al., 2013; see Section 10). 

Because of their $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ evolving photosynthesis, cyanobacteria were also the first organisms to cope with the oxygenpromoted changes in metal availability: decrease of iron (Fe), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni), and manganese (Mn), and increase of zinc (Zn) and copper (Cu) (Barnett et al., 2012). This constitutes a real challenge because approximately one-quarter to one-third of all cellular proteins require metals (Waldron and Robinson, 2009). Cyanobacteria have a very high requirement for Fe (∼10-fold more than non-photosynthetic prokaryotes) (Kranzler et al., 2013), and they use other metals for various enzymes, such as sulfite oxidases, nitrogenase, and nitrate reductases (molybdenum, Mo); chlorophyll, ATPases, and kinases (Mg); cytochrome oxidase and plastocyanin (Cu); oxygenevolving photosynthetic complex (Mn); hydrogenase and urease (Ni); RNA and DNA polymerases $( Z \mathrm { n } ) ;$ and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ assimilation proteins (Zn) (Blindauer, 2008; Waldron and Robinson, 2009). Consequently, cyanobacteria have evolved elaborate mechanisms to acquire sufficient metal atoms to meet their needs and to adjust them to match supply. 

In addition, cyanobacteria are also frequently challenged by heavy metals, such as aluminum (Al), arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), cesium $( \operatorname { C s } ) ,$ chromate (Cr), mercury (Hg), lead (Pb), and uranium (U), which normally have no beneficial function (Tchounwou et al., 2012). The toxicity of these metals is based on their chemical properties, which allow them to promote the production of ROS; the inactivation of enzymes, basically by reaction with SH groups; and/or the displacement of the normal metal cofactors of numerous metalloproteins (Gregoire and Poulain, 2014; Imlay, 2014; Waldron and Robinson, 2009). The accumulation, in soils and waters, of heavy metals released by natural sources (volcanoes and forest fires) and anthropogenic activities (mining, fossil fuel burning, etc.) is especially problematic because metals are persistent in the environment and accumulate throughout the food chain (Chetelat et al., 2014; Song and Li, 2014; Waldron and Robinson, 2009). 

Cyanobacteria facing metal toxicity trigger various defense mechanisms, such as (i) sequestration (in extracellular exopolysaccharides and/or intracellular polyphosphate granules, or metal-binding proteins metallothioneins or ferritins), (ii) organic or inorganic precipitation, (iii) reduction of metal ions into less bioavailable (less toxic) forms, and (iv) active transport. These mechanisms are important for the biosphere because cyanobacteria constitute the first biological barrier against the entry of toxic compounds into the food chain. 

In prokaryotes, the expression of proteins involved in metal homeostasis and/or responses to oxidative stress and heavy metals is strongly regulated at the level of transcription (Waldron and Robinson, 2009). The underlying transcription factors (TFs) are classified in several families based on at least two domains, which allow them to function as regulatory switches. One domain functions as a signal sensor, which binds the ligand (an oxidant or a metal cofactor) or the protein that conduces the endogenous or environmental information. The other receiver domain is the responsive element, which directly interacts with a regulated target promoter. In the twocomponent systems, the sensor and receiver domains are dispatched in different proteins (see Section 3). The sensor protein (often localized in the cell periplasm) senses the exogenous signal, and subsequently modifies (phosphorylates) itself and its (cytoplasmic) TF partner, to modulate its regulatory activity (Balleza et al., 2009). The sensor proteins need to be very specific in binding mostly (exclusively) their cognate metal, and in responding differently to their own and other metal cofactors (Waldron and Robinson, 2009). Generally, the positively acting TFs (activators) bind ahead of the promoter and facilitate the recruitment of the RNA polymerase that starts transcription. In contrast, the repressors bind mostly to the core promoter, thereby interfering with the binding or activity of 

RNA polymerase. In addition, different TFs can bind on the same promoter, and different promoters can bind the same TF. These complex interactions explain why the same TF can act as a repressor of some target genes and as an activator of other targets (Balleza et al., 2009). 

This review presents the new findings on the responses of cyanobacteria to metal and oxidative stresses, emphasizing on the best characterized unicellular strain Synechocystis PCC6803. 

## 20.3.2 Extracellular defenses against metal stress

The number of metal atoms in a cell is a function of the relative efficiencies of specific metal importers and exporters, and intra- or extracellular sequestration systems. Concerning the latter process, a large number of bacteria synthesize extracellular polysaccharides (exopolysaccharides (EPSs)), which serve as a structural scaffold for the formation of biofilms (see Section 22) and constitute a protective shield against antimicrobial agents (Heindl et al., 2014). In cyanobacteria, the EPSs are involved in the biomineralization of calcium and/or magnesium carbonates, leading to the formation of stromatolites (Jansson and Northen, 2010). The negatively charged EPSs can also operate in the sequestration of metal cations (e.g., Fe), which can be subsequently released and taken up by the cells, thereby protecting them from metal limitation (Jittawuttipoka et al., 2013), which is frequently encountered in nature (Kranzler et al., 2013). EPSs also protect Synechocystis PCC6803 against Cd and Co (Jittawuttipoka et al., 2013) and the nanoparticles ${ \mathrm { C e O } } _ { 2 }$ (Zeyons et al., 2009) and $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ (Planchon et al., 2013), which are intensively used by human industries (Cullen and Maldonado, 2013; von Moos and Slaveykova, 2014). This phenomenon has potential for water treatment (Acharya and Apte, 2013; De Philippis et al., 2011). 

## 20.3.3 Sequestration and export systems for protection against metal stress

Zinc is involved in many essential metabolic processes (zinc finger protein motifs for DNA transcription and detoxification of ROS). However, Zn excess can induce ROS formation, impair photosynthesis, and inhibit the uptake of calcium, an important signal transducer (see Chapter 20.1). In Synechocystis PCC6803, Zn can be exported by an efflux ATPase ZiaA (Slr0798 in cyanobase) (Nakamura et al., 1998), under the control of the Zn-responsive repressor ZiaR (Sll0792). The divergently transcribed ziaA and ziaR genes (Thelwell et al., 1998) belong to a gene cluster involved in sensing and homeostasis of Ni and Co (Garcia-Dominguez et al., 2000). Attesting the importance of ZiaR, we showed that its gene is well conserved in cyanobacteria, with the notable exception of the marine Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus species (Table 20.3.1).
