The presence or absence of the regulatory genes in cyanobacteria is indicated by + or the indicated number (depending on their copy numbers) or − (absence), respectively. The numbers of the regulator genes that are located in well-conserved genomic clusters depicted in Figure 20.3.1 are indicated by the superscript numbers and letters, respectively. For instance, Nostoc PCC7120 and Synechocystis PCC6803, which are highlighted in gray, possess three fur-like genes (fur, zur, and furC in Nostoc PCC7120; and fur, zur, and perR in Synechocystis PCC6803). The Nostoc PCC7120 fur, zur, and furC genes belong to the clusters a, c, and f’, respectively. Nostoc PCC7120 also has one pfsR gene (it belongs to cluster h), one arsR gene (localized in cluster l’), two ziaR genes (one in cluster j’), and 18 pchR genes (14 located in cluster i). 


Furthermore, the ziaR gene is often located in conserved dicistronic gene clusters, which contain either the opposite genes ziaA and ziaR (cluster j’ in Figure 20.3.1) or the ziaR and zntA genes (cluster j; zntA encodes a heavy-metal-translocating Ptype ATPase). 

The ziaA gene (and mntC, sll1598, and Mn transporter) is also regulated by the response regulator Sll0649, which operates in the protection against stress triggered by Cd, Cu, Fe, Mn, or Zn (Chen et al., 2014). Interestingly, Sll0649 interacts with Slr0533, a two-component sensor histidine kinase (Sato et al., 2007; see Section 3). 

Unlike Synechocystis PCC6803, the cyanobacterium Synechococcus PCC7942 has no ZiaA but a metallothionein protein (MT), which binds (stores) metals through the thiol group of its abundant cysteine amino acids (Blindauer, 2011). Elevated concentrations of Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Hg, Ni, Pb, or Zn increase transcription of the MT-encoding gene smtA, which is normally repressed by the product of the divergently transcribed smtB gene, which is homologous to ziaR (Huckle et al., 1993; Morby et al., 1993). 

A large number of cyanobacteria have either an efflux pump, a metallothionein (most marine cyanobacteria, in agreement with the low Zn concentrations of ocean waters), or both (Blindauer, 2011). The intracellular sequestration of metal ions is also facilitated by polyphosphate bodies, which can concentrate Pb, Sr, Mn, Al, Zn, Cu, Cd, and Hg (Acharya and Apte, 2013). 

## 20.3.4 Reduction and export systems for protection against metal stress

Mercury (Hg) and uranium (U) are highly disseminated in natural waters by human activities such as mining and nuclear energy production (Gregoire and Poulain, 2014; Waldron and Robinson, 2009; Wall and Krumholz, 2006). Both Hg and U have no biological function, and they are only known to be toxic. The elemental form of Hg, Hg(0), is volatile and can travel long distances through the atmosphere before settling in terrestrial or aquatic ecosystems (Chetelat et al., 2014). Hg(0) can be oxidized by bacteria to Hg(II), and subsequently detoxified through transformation into insoluble meta-cinnabar (HgS) (Lefebvre et al., 2007), a process resembling the formation of insoluble CdS and ZnS in response to Cd and Zn stresses (Edwards et al., 2013a,b). Furthermore, Hg(II) can be reduced to Hg(0) by the mercuric reductase enzyme MerA (Gregoire and Poulain, 2014; Marteyn et al., 2013). In Synechocystis PCC6803, the widely distributed MerA-like enzyme (Slr1849) operates in the protection against, and the NADPHdriven reduction of, both mercuric and uranyl ions (Marteyn et al., 2013). Similarly, the iron–sulfur (Fe-S) cluster containing protein ferredoxin Fed9 (Slr2059) operates in the tolerance of As and U (and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } )$ (Cassier-Chauvat and Chauvat, 2014b). Such cyanobacterial enzymes with the capacity to reduce several heavy metals are interesting for bioremediation purposes since most polluted sites contain cocktails of toxic metals (De Philippis et al., 2011). 

Cyanobacteria can also be challenged by arsenic (As), which can occur in different redox forms in the environment, such as As(V) in $\mathrm { A s O _ { 4 } }$ (arsenate) or As(III) in $\mathrm { A s O } _ { 3 }$ (arsenite). As an analog of phosphate, arsenate can impair oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis. Arsenite can bind to thiol groups of proteins or the antioxidant glutathione, thereby altering its activity and contributing to ROS generation. Resistance involves the reduction of arsenate to arsenite, and its subsequent export outside the cell. Depending on the organisms, arsenate can be reduced by three unrelated arsenate reductases, using electrons provided by glutaredoxins, mycoredoxins, or thioredoxins. Arsenite can be exported by ArsB proteins (in bacteria) and/or Acr3 proteins (in bacteria, fungi, and plants) (Sanchez-Riego et al., 2014). Arsenite can also be detoxified through conjugation to methyl groups, for instance by the Synechocystis PCC6803 ArsM (Slr0303) enzyme, which uses S-adenosyl methionine and glutathione as methyl donors to form the volatile trimethylarsine product (Sanchez-Riego et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2011).

Synechocystis PCC6803 possesses additional As resistance systems. The main system is encoded by the arsBHC tricistronic operon (slr0944–slr0945–slr0946), under the control of the ArsR repressor produced by the unlinked gene sll1957 (Lopez-Maury et al., 2003). The ArsB protein is an Acr3-like arsenite transporter, while ArsH has a NADPH–quinone reductase activity (Hervas et al., 2012) with no clear function in As resistance (Lopez-Maury et al., 2003; Sanchez-Riego et al., 2014). ArsC is a glutathione–glutaredoxin-dependent arsenate reductase (Kim et al., 2012; Li et al., 2003; Lopez-Maury et al., 2009; Marteyn et al., 2013), which is somehow involved in Cd resistance as well (Houot et al., 2007). The arsR gene is widely conserved in cyanobacteria (Table 20.3.1) and is often localized upstream of arsB (Figure 20.3.1). 

The other, less important Synechocystis PCC6803 arsenate reductase, ArsI, is encoded by two nearly identical genes, arsI1 (sll5104) and arsI2 (sll6037) (Lopez-Maury et al., 2009), which are propagated on the large plasmids pSYSM and pSYSX, respectively. The pSYSM plasmid harbors another arsenic resistance system, encoded by the two divergently transcribed gene clusters suoS (sll5036)–suoR (sll5035 is homologous to arsR) and suoC (slr5037)–suoT (slr5038). The poorly conserved SuoR repressor (Table 20.3.1) controls the common promoter region shared by the two gene clusters suoS–suoR and suoC–suoT. SuoS behaves as a type I sulfide–quinone oxidoreductase, SuoT operates in arsenite transport, and SuoC has no known function (Nagy et al., 2014). 

Recently, it was shown that arsenate and arsenite trigger similar induction of redox-scavenging systems and chaperones, and repression of photosynthesis and growth-related genes (Sanchez-Riego et al., 2014). 

## 20.3.5 The glutathione system plays a pleiotropic role in the defenses against oxidative and metal stresses

The widely conserved tripeptide glutathione (GSH) is essential to the growth and protection of cyanobacteria against oxidative stress (Cameron and Pakrasi, 2011; Narainsamy et al., 2013). The reduced (major) form of glutathione, GSH, maintains the intracellular cell environment in a reduced state. This process generates the oxidized glutathione (its disulfide form, GSSG), which can be regenerated into GSH by, among other factors, the NADPH-using enzyme glutathione reductase, which occurs in many cyanobacteria (Narainsamy et al., 2013) but not Synechocystis PCC6803 (Marteyn et al., 2009). 

GSH can also operate in defense against metals, by chelating them outside the cells in the form of large complexes that cannot penetrate the cells (Thorsen et al., 2012). GSH can also form a Fe(II)GSH complex, which likely supplies Fe for the synthesis of Fe cofactor or (Fe-S) clusters of metalloenzymes (Hider and Kong, 2011), such as glutaredoxins.

These widely conserved enzymes (Grxs) use electrons, provided by either GSH, the thioredoxin reductase enzyme, or other Grxs (Marteyn et al., 2009; Zaffagnini et al., 2012b), to reduce the oxidative-stress-generated disulfides between proteins or between a protein and glutathione (glutathionylation), which otherwise affect protein activity. The dithiol Grxs, which possess a CX2C redox center (C stands for cysteine, and X for any other amino acids), catalyze the reduction of protein disulfides or GSH–protein mixed disulfides (deglutathionylation) (Lillig and Berndt, 2012). The monothiol Grxs, which have a $\mathrm { C X } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ redox center (S stands for serine), operate in Fe sensing, the biogenesis of (Fe-S) clusters of proteins (Rouhier et al., 2010), and, possibly, deglutathionylation (Zaffagnini et al., 2012a). Synechocystis PCC6803 possesses three Grxs, which are dispensable to the standard photoautotrophic growth (Narainsamy et al., 2013; Sanchez-Riego et al., 2013). The dithiol enzymes Grx1 (Slr1562, also known as GrxB) and Grx2 (Ssr2061, also known as GrxA) operate in tolerance to arsenate by providing electrons to the arsenate reductase enzymes (Kim et al., 2012; Lopez-Maury et al., 2009). Grx2-interacting proteins have been identified (Li et al., 2007), such as the antioxidant enzymes catalase– peroxidase and a peroxyredoxin, which interact with a thioredoxin (Trx) protein (Florencio et al., 2006). Emphasizing the crosstalk between the Grx and Trx systems, we found that Grx1 and Grx2 belong to a redox pathway, NAD(P)H-thioredoxin reductase–Grx1–Grx2–ferredoxin 7, which can reduce selenate (Marteyn et al., 2009). The Grx2 enzyme is also involved in tolerance to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Marteyn et al., 2009; Sanchez-Riego et al., 2013; see Section 10) and heat shock (Sanchez-Riego et al., 2013; see Section 13). 

The third Synechocystis PCC6803 glutaredoxin, Grx3 (Slr1846), forms a homodimer bridged by a GSH-ligated (2Fe–2S) cluster, a feature conserved in Grx3 orthologs from cyanobacteria to plants and mammals (Iwema et al., 2009; Picciocchi et al., 2007; Rouhier et al., 2010). 

Concerning the selectivity and redundancy of Grxs, we found that Grx1, but neither Grx2 nor Grx3, physically interacts with the MerA enzyme. Grx1 can reactivate the oxidized (glutathionylated) form of MerA by catalyzing its deglutathionylation. Consistently, Grx1 is crucial for protection against both mercury and uranium, like MerA (Marteyn et al., 2013). 

## 20.3.6 The Fur-like regulators play a crucial role in iron homeostasis and its crosstalk with tolerance to oxidative and metal stresses

Iron, the fourth most plentiful element in the Earth’s crust, is frequently a growth-limiting factor because ancient cyanobacteria raised the oxygen levels that oxidized the soluble ferrous ions $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ to insoluble ferric ions $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } )$ (Behrenfeld and Milligan, 2013; Schopf, 2011). Bacterial cells maintain their iron homeostasis through the (i) synthesis, export, and reimport of powerful ferric ion chelators called siderophores; 

(ii) dedicated uptake systems; (iii) sequestration in intracellular stores (ferritins); and (iv) degradation of iron-containing proteins in response to Fe starvation, and subsequent incorporation of the released Fe atoms into crucial Fe-requiring enzymes (Kranzler et al., 2013; see Chapter 19.1). These processes are controlled by the widespread Fur (ferric uptake regulator) protein. Fe-containing Fur proteins repress the transcription of Feregulated genes through binding to AT-rich DNA elements (Furboxes) present in their core promoters. At low Fe concentrations, Fe-free Fur (apo-Fur) detaches itself from Fur-boxes, thereby allowing transcription of the downstream genes (Kranzler et al., 2013) (see Section 19). 

Together with Fur, Fur-like regulators constitute a superfamily of metal-sensing proteins that control the transcription of genes involved in metal homeostasis and the connected defense against oxidative stress. These metalloregulators comprise Zur (zinc uptake), Mur (manganese uptake), Nur (nickel uptake) (see Chapter 20.1), PerR (response to peroxide stress; see Section 10), and the heme-dependent iron responsive regulator Irr (Fillat, 2014; see Section 19). 

The widely conserved PerR protein regulates its own gene and others involved in the protection against oxidative and metal stresses (Dubbs and Mongkolsuk, 2012). In B. subtilis, each PerR monomer contains a binding site for a structural $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , as well as a regulatory site that binds either $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ or $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ . Repression is achieved when PerR, containing metals bound at both sites, binds DNA at a consensus Per-box, which either overlaps part of the promoter or is immediately downstream from it. PerR senses $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ through the Fe-catalyzed oxidation of some of its histidine amino acid residues, leading to dissociation of the PerR–DNA complex and the subsequent expression of the regulated genes (Dubbs and Mongkolsuk, 2012). 

The other (less) conserved ZUR regulator is mainly involved in repressing the transcription of Zn uptake genes to maintain Zn homeostasis (Fillat, 2014). 

The crosstalk between metal and oxidative stresses (see Section 10) is especially important in cyanobacteria because they perform the two main metal-utilizing oxidant-generating processes, respiration and photosynthesis, and the latter’s iron-rich machinery imposes strong Fe requirements (Fillat, 2014; Kranzler et al., 2013). 

Synechocystis PCC6803 harbors three Fur-like regulators that are widely conserved in cyanobacteria (with the notable exception of the UCYN-A strain) (Table 20.3.1), and belong to gene clusters that are also well conserved (Figure 20.3.1). 

The first Fur-like protein, designated as FurA (Sll0567) because it closely resembles the bacterial Fur regulator, is essential to cell life, like its ortholog in Anabaena (Nostoc) PCC7120 (All1691) (see Chapter 19.1). In this latter host, FurA seems to perform both Fur and PerR functions (Botello-Morte et al., 2013). FurA-binding sites were identified in iron uptake genes (TonB-dependent receptors, an iron(III) dicitrate ABC transporter, and a probable $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } { - } F e ^ { 2 + } }$ permease) and siderophore synthesis. New putative FurA targets involved in zinc uptake (the znuAB operon) and defense against oxidative stress (the 

Flv3 flavodiiron protein or the putative alkylhydroperoxidase) were also identified (Gonzalez et al., 2014). The Synechocystis PCC6803 furA gene is negatively regulated by the PfsR (Sll1392) autoregulator, which is absent in most Synechococcus strains (Table 20.3.1). PfsR also controls several Fe homeostasis genes, such as furA, fut (ferric iron transporter), feoB (ferrous iron transporter), bfr genes (bacterioferritins), ho (heme oxygenases), and isiA (stress-responsive chlorophyll-binding protein) (Cheng and He, 2014). Again, these findings emphasize the connection between metal homeostasis and tolerance to oxidative stress (Cheng and He, 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2014). Furthermore, the abundance of the FurA protein is negatively controlled by the proteolytic FtsH1–FtsH3 heterocomplex located in the cytoplasmic membrane of Synechocystis PCC6803 (Krynicka et al., 2014). 

FurB orthologs are encoded by single copy genes in most cyanobacteria, except in the strains UCYN-A (absence of furB) (Table 20.3.1), Cyanothece (two furB genes), and Acaryochloris marina MBIC11017 (two chromosomal and two plasmidic furB) (Botello-Morte et al., 2013). Unlike FurA, FurB (Sll1937 and All2473) is dispensable to the standard photoautotrophic growth of Synechocystis PCC6803 and Anabaena (Nostoc) PCC7120, respectively (Botello-Morte et al., 2013). The Synechocystis PCC6803 Sll1937 protein has been found to regulate the $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake transporter operon znuCAB, indicating that Sll1937 behaves as the bacterial Zur (Zn uptake) regulator (Botello-Morte et al., 2013). 

The third Synechocystis PCC6803 Fur-like protein, Slr1738, is dispensable to photoautotrophic growth. Slr1738 resembles the bacterial PerR protein in regulating the cell tolerance to oxidative stress (Garcin et al., 2012; Houot et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 2004; Li et al., 2004). Slr1738 also regulates the cell responses to cadmium, which occur in a two-phase temporal process. In the “early” phase, cells regulate a few genes involved in metal uptake and export systems to limit Cd entry. Subsequently, the number of Cd-responsive genes drastically increases. In this “massive-response” phase, Cd downregulates most genes operating in (i) photosynthesis (PS), which normally provides adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and NADPH; and (ii) nutrient (carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur) assimilation and protein synthesis, which normally consume ATP and NAD(P)H. Simultaneously, Cd upregulates numerous genes involved in the degradation of abundant PS proteins, thereby liberating Fe and organic carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur for the synthesis of Cd tolerance proteins. Cd also increases expression of the suf genes involved in the biogenesis and repair (Fe-S) clusters damaged by Cd. Thus, Cd-challenged cells trigger an integrated reprogramming of their whole metabolism, in which the ATP- and nutrients-sparing downregulation of anabolism limits the poisoning incorporation of Cd into metalloenzymes, while the PS breakdown liberates nutrient assimilates for the synthesis of Cd tolerance proteins (Houot et al., 2007). In contrast, cells challenged with $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ preferentially accelerate the intake of iron from the medium, to supply Fe atoms for the synthesis and repair of Fe and (Fe-S) requiring metalloenzymes (Houot et al., 2007). 

These data emphasize that Fe homeostasis plays a crucial role in cyanobacterial defenses against oxidative and heavy metal stresses (see also Chapter 19.1). 

Unlike Synechocystis PCC6803, Anabaena (Nostoc) PCC7120 has no PerR (Table 20.3.1), the functions of which are likely carried out by FurA. Anabaena (Nostoc) PCC7120 possesses a FurC regulator (Alr0957), which exhibits a significant gap in homology with the more abundant FurA and FurB proteins (Botello-Morte et al., 2013; Kranzler et al., 2013). The FurC regulator is well conserved in cyanobacteria, and it is expected to be present in a few species including Synechocystis PCC6803 (Table 20.3.1). Both the Anabaena (Nostoc) PCC7120 FurB and FurC proteins seem to control the expression of the autoregulator FurA (Kranzler et al., 2013). 

## 20.3.7 The PchR-like regulators operate in the tolerance to oxidative stress and heavy metals

In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the synthesis of the Fe-chelating siderophore pyochelin (Pch) is controlled by the Fur regulator and by the Fur-controlled transcription activator PchR (Youard et al., 2011; see Chapter 19.3). The Pch biosynthesis genes of P. aeruginosa are organized in two divergent operons, pchDCBA and pchEFGHI, which are clustered with the pyochelin uptake operon fptABCX and the regulatory gene pchR. Under ironreplete conditions, the biosynthesis of Pch and the uptake system for ferriPch are repressed by Fe-Fur, which also represses the expression of the pchDCBA, pchEFGHI, pchR, and fptABCX genes. When iron becomes limiting, Fur dissociates from the Fur-boxes of these genes, restoring a basal level of gene expression. Full expression of the piochelin synthesis and transport operons pchDCBA, pchEFGHI, and fptABCX requires the transcriptional activator PchR. Pch (probably in its iron-loaded form) acts as an effector molecule of PchR and allows this regulator to bind the PchR-box in the promoter regions of these genes. Binding of PchR ∼ Pch to the PchR-box in the pchD promoter also represses transcription of pchR itself, as this PchR binding site is located downstream of the pchR transcription start. 

Though Synechocystis PCC6803 does not produce piochelin, it possesses three pchR-like genes pchR1 (sll1205), pchR2 (sll1408), and pchR3 (slr1489), which are regulated positively by Fe limitation, and negatively by Fe excess (Houot et al., 2007). The pchR1 and pchR3 genes are highly expressed (Das et al., 2012). They are upregulated by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and downregulated by Cd, unlike pchR2 that is almost unaffected (Houot et al., 2007). Both pchR2 and pchR3 are also regulated by Zn excess, negatively (pchR2) and positively (pchR3). The three pchR genes, which are dispensable to the standard photoautotrophic growth, operate in the tolerance to oxidative and metal stresses (Soni et al., 2012). The three ΔpchR mutants are more tolerant to iron excess, and slightly more sensitive to iron limitation, than the WT strain. The ΔpchR1 and ΔpchR3 mutants are more resistant to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ than the WT and ΔpchR2 strains in that order. Hence, PchR1 and PchR3 behave similarly as the PerR regulator of B. subtilis (Bsat et al., 1998) and Synechocystis PCC6803 (Houot et al., 2007), in being induced by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and negatively involved in the protection against this toxic agent. The ΔpchR1 and ΔpchR3 mutants are also more tolerant than the WT and ΔpchR2 strains (Soni et al., 2012) to Cd and Co, which impair iron homeostasis and generate oxidative stress (Barras and Fontecave, 2011; Houot et al., 2007). That the pchR genes are well conserved in the wealth of fresh water or coastal cyanobacteria, which are often challenged by metal stress, is consistent with the absence of pchR in the Prochlorococcus species (Table 20.3.1), which live in open ocean where metal availability is rather constant. Also interestingly, PchR2 and PchR3 have been found to interact with the two-component response regulators Sll0789 and Slr1037, respectively (Sato et al., 2007). 

## 20.3.8 Conclusion



Edwards CD, Beatty JC, Loiselle JBR, Vlassov KA, Lefebvre DD. 2013b. Aerobic transformation of zinc into metal sulfide by photosynthetic microorganisms. Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology 97: 3613–3623.

As they have invented oxygen-evolving photosynthesis, which requires metals and often produces oxidants, cyanobacteria have developed most of the mechanisms to protect themselves against oxidative and metal stresses. These processes are important because cyanobacteria play a crucial role for the biosphere and have valuable biotechnological interests. Furthermore, many of the stress tolerance players, such as the glutathione system, have been conserved in higher eukaryotes, which are more complex to study than cyanobacteria. In the past few years, significant progress has been made in our understanding of ROSscavenging and detoxification processes in cyanobacteria. In addition, metal sensors, transporters, and stores have been characterized. Collectively, these findings pinpoint the crucial connection between glutathione, iron homeostasis, and the defenses against oxidative and (heavy) metal stresses.

# Cross-species transcriptional network analysis reveals conservation and variation in response to metal stress in cyanobacteria

Jiangxin Wang1,2, Gang Wu3, Lei Chen1,2, and Weiwen Zhang1,2 

1School of Chemical Engineering & Technology, Tianjin University, Tianjin, PR China 

2Key Laboratory of Systems Bioengineering, Ministry of Education, Tianjin, PR China 

3Department of Biological Sciences, University of Maryland at Baltimore County, Baltimore, Maryland, USA 

## 20.4.1 Introduction

The recent exponential growth in transcriptomics datasets allows researchers to combine expression experiments from multiple species to identify genes that are not only conserved in sequence but also regulated in a similar way (Cai et al., 2010). Comparative transcriptomic analysis has led to improving functional gene annotation and inferring the evolution of gene interaction and regulatory networks (Cai et al., 2010) as well as analysis of brain-imaging data (Chen et al., 2008; Emilsson et al., 2008; Oldham et al., 2006; Miller et al., 2010; Voineagu et al., 2011; Winden et al., 2009). 

As important primary producers and significant contributors of the fixed carbon budget in many terrestrial and marine environments, cyanobacteria have been present for ∼2.5 billion years in many different environments, ranging from coast to open sea (Giordano et al., 2005). Currently, the marine cyanobacteria Synechococcus and Prochlorococcus species are together responsible for at least 20% of global carbon fixation (Li, 1994). They play such significant roles in the carbon cycle that it is essential to understand to what environmental stresses they are susceptible and how they respond. 

Metals are important environmental factors for cyanobacteria. Iron is required for photosynthesis, its limitation and restriction of primary productivity have been reported for some oceanic regions (Boyd et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2004), and it has been considered as one important factor in the ecology of cyanobacteria. Early studies have found the limitation of Prochlorococcus cell division rates by iron in the equatorial Pacific (Mann and Chisholm, 2000; Rusch et al., 2010; Stuart et al., 2009). The physiology and biochemistry associated with the iron-limited continuous culture of Synechococcus PCC 

7002 (Wilhelm and Trick, 1995) and S. elongatus PCC 7942 (Nodop et al., 2008) have also been examined. 

Copper is another metal commonly present in natural environments (see Chapter 2.12). It has been reported that different cyanobacteria species have various levels of copper tolerance, with Prochlorococcus species thought to be more sensitive to copper than Synechococcus species (Mann et al., 2002). Within Synechococcus species, copper tolerance has also been shown to vary significantly (Brand et al., 1986), with coastal species of Synechococcus species exhibiting increased tolerance to copper shock and distinctive transcriptional responses relative to those of open-ocean species (Thompson et al., 2011). 

To obtain a better understanding of the metabolic response of cyanobacteria to metals, in this study we applied a cross-species transcriptional network analysis to four cyanobacteria species under two conditions of metal stress. 

## 20.4.2 Materials and methods

## 20.4.2.1 Dataset acquisition

Microarray datasets of four cyanobacteria species – Prochlorococcus MED4 (PMM), Prochlorococcus MIT9313 (PMT), Synechococcus 9311 (SYG), and Synechococcus WH 8102 (SYW) (Stuart et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2011) – were downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (Table 20.4.1). 

The experimental details can be found in the original publications (Stuart et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2011). The updated genome annotation for all four species was downloaded from the US National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). KEGG pathway and COGs (clusters of orthologous groups of proteins) information was obtained from the KEGG Pathway Databases (http://www.genome.jp/kegg/pathway.html) and the COG Database of NCBI (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih .gov/books/NBK21090/).

## 20.4.2.2 Network construction

For each cyanobacteria species, we created a transcriptional network from the microarray data, first by calculating weighted Pearson correlation matrices corresponding to gene expression, and then by following the standard procedure of weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to create the networks (Zhang and Horvath, 2005). The network for each module was generated with the minimum spanning tree with a dissimilarity matrix from WGCNA. The modules with $r > 0 . 6$ or $r < - 0 . 6 ,$ and p-value less than 0.05, were extracted for further investigation. KEGG pathway analysis was applied to detect the common pathways involved among different modules. 

To establish cross-species signature genes in this analysis, and to define conservation in terms of stress response across cyanobacterial species, phenotype-correlated modules and the associated genes in each species were extracted. To assess coexpression perseveration between the species on a module-bymodule basis, we first calculated a value of the module membership (MM) – a measure of how well each gene correlates with the first principal component of gene expression within a module, termed the module eigengene. We then imposed a threshold based on MM values (r, p) to make the final module assignments. 

## 20.4.3 Results and discussion

## 20.4.3.1 Construction of cyanobacteria metal response networks

The final datasets used in our analysis included transcriptional measurements of a total of 50 samples from four cyanobacteria species (PMM, PMT, SYG, and SYW), representing iron depletion (PMT and PMM; see Section 19) and high copper toxicity (SYG and SYW; see Chapter 2.12) treatments (Table. 20.4.1) (Stuart et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2011). The results showed that all stress-treated datasets tended to be grouped together and can be visibly separated from the controls, suggesting the stresses of iron depletion and copper toxicity cause significant changes at the transcriptional level. Next, analysis of the transcriptional networks showed that a total of 17, 21, 32, and 28 distinct transcriptional modules could be detected within the transcriptional networks of PMT, PMM, SYG, and SYW, respectively. More transcriptional modules were detected in SYG and SYW than in PMT and PMM, probably due to the relatively large genome sizes of Synechococcus (Palenik et al., 2003, 2006; Rocap et al., 2003). 

Among all active transcriptional modules detected in each of the species, we found that 5 of 17 and 6 of 21 detected modules significantly correlated with iron depletion condition in PMT and PMM, respectively (Table 20.4.2); and 12 of 32 and 11 of 28 detected modules significantly correlated with high copper toxicity in SYG and SYW, respectively (Table 20.4.2). As a result, we obtained a total of 5–12 phenotype-correlated modules in different species, and the KEGG pathway analysis showed that a total of 62–79 KEGG pathways were involved in these modules (Table 20.4.2). Interestingly, 69 and 49 KEGG shared pathways were detected in PMT–PMM to iron depletion and SYG–SYW to high copper toxicity, respectively (Table 20.4.2). 

The iron-responsive PMT greenyellow module contained genes known to be involved in biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, other metabolites such as different amino acids, and microbial metabolism in diverse environments. In addition, the eigengenes of the PMT greenyellow module were significantly correlated with DNA mismatch repair and homologous recombination. Several species of cyanobacteria produce secondary metabolites such as xanthophyll carotenoids, and their synthesis is often upregulated in response to high light intensity, ultraviolet radiation (see Section 8), and desiccation (Zhu et al., 2010; see Section 12). The ability to exist in two redox states makes iron an essential cofactor for proteins involved in numerous major cellular processes, including respiration, amino acid metabolism, and DNA metabolism. For instance, iron starvation reduced most amino-acid-related genes since many enzymes involved in this biosynthesis are iron dependent (Ihrig et al., 2010; Ledala et al., 2010) (see Section 19). It has been reported that iron starvation also induced DNA recombination and DNA repair processes in a Gram-negative diplococci bacteria (Bakker, 2002; Serkin and Seifert, 2000). 


Table 20.4.2 Modules and KEGG pathways significantly responsive to the metal treatments.


<table><tr><td>Metal stress</td><td>Species</td><td>Modules related to phenotype</td><td>KEGG pathways</td><td>Common pathways</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="2">Iron</td><td>PMT</td><td>5</td><td>79</td><td>65</td></tr><tr><td>PMM</td><td>6</td><td>68</td><td></td></tr><tr><td rowspan="2">Copper</td><td>SYW</td><td>12</td><td>63</td><td>49</td></tr><tr><td>SYG</td><td>11</td><td>62</td><td></td></tr></table>

The copper-responsive SYW yellow module showed a significantly high correlation between ribosome biosynthesis and assembly (syw03010, total 20 related genes enriched) and the copper toxicity treatments $( p = 6 . 7 8 \mathrm { E } . 1 5 )$ , suggesting an involvement of a protein synthesis program in copper resistance (see Chapter 2.12). The module was enriched with the KEGG pathways of carbon fixation in photosynthetic organisms and protein export, and it also included many genes related to photosynthesis, the pentose phosphate pathway, nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism, and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism. 

The genes involved in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon degradation were identified in the copper-responsive SYG darkgreen module. The module also showed a significant relationship with amino acid metabolism (histidine, tyrosine, cysteine and methionine, arginine, and proline), except that the genes in this module were all upregulated. KEGG pathway analysis indicated that the SYG darkgreen module was enriched with genes encoding photosynthesis antenna proteins, and genes related to microbial metabolism in diverse environments and oxidative phosphorylation. Besides, the pathway analysis indicated that the SYG brown module was overrepresented with genes participating in signal transduction activity, including response regulators, two-component systems, and histidine kinases (see Section 3). In addition, the other correlated genes included ATPbinding component (ABC) transporters, starch and sucrose metabolism, and arginine and proline metabolism. 

The WGCNA results showed a high degree of cross-species module conservation between PMM and PMT under iron depletion condition, and between SYW and SYG under high copper condition, suggesting possible core response to each of the stress treatments. In addition, the overlaps between iron depletion and copper toxicity responsive modules were also observed, suggesting the possible core and general responses to metals or possible crosstalk between two different response networks. 

Based on the WGCNA analysis, a total of 27 shared metalresponsive KEGG pathways between two metal stresses were determined, which included 20 pathways of amino acid and starch, nitrogen, and sulfur metabolism; two pathways of photosynthesis and porphyrin and chlorophyll metabolism; and one pathway each for ABC transporters, oxidative phosphorylation, mismatch repair, and biosynthesis of secondary metabolites. Based on the fact that they responded to both iron depletion and high copper toxicity in multiple cyanobacteria species, we proposed that these pathways might represent the core metalresponsive pathways. Several pathways were also found shared in both PMM and PMT to iron depletion, but they were only detected in either SYG or SFW. For example, ribosome, fatty acid biosynthesis, citrate cycle, DNA replication and homologous recombination, and some metabolism pathways were shared under iron depletion. In contrast, there were several pathways shared in SYG and SYW to copper toxicity, but these did not appear in both PMM and PMT, such as glycerophospholipid metabolism and photosynthesis antenna proteins, which may be copper-specific responsive pathways in cyanobacteria. By considering those pathways, we further defined that the possible iron-specific pathways involved in iron depletion in cyanobacteria included thiamine metabolism, riboflavin metabolism, and RNA polymerase. 

We then further identified the shared genes between responsive modules in different cyanobacteria species based on the significance of MM values. The results showed that a total of 440 and 430 genes were found correlated with iron depletion in PMM and PMT, respectively, with only 34 of them shared between PMM and PMT with confident low p-values. Similarly, the numbers of the copper-correlated genes were 736 and 580 in SYG and SYW under copper toxicity, respectively, with only 70 of them shared between SYG and SYW. 

Under condition of iron depletion, the shared genes with functional annotation information in PMT and PMM were narrowly distributed in several major modules, such as turquoise (23 shared genes), red (8), and royal blue (3) in PMT, and greenyellow (12), green (5), magenta (5), pink (5), purple (4), and cyan (2) in PMM. Most of the genes enriched in PMM green and greenyellow modules are involved in metabolism; the PMM magenta module included cell division and transcriptional regulation; the PMM pink module included prophyrin and chlorophyll metabolism; and PMM purple modules contained RNA and protein degradation proteins. The module with the largest shared gene number was the turquoise module in PMT, which included genes related to oxidative phosphorylation, electron carrier activity, cell division, transcriptional regulation, prophyrin and chlorophyll metabolism, and other metabolic enzymes and proteins. 

A high concentration of copper regulated 69 shared genes in SYW and SYG, most of which were grouped into a limited number of modules. For example, 20 shared genes were found in the SYG turquoise module, 14 genes in the SYG brown module, 12 in the SYG purple module (see Chapter 2.12), 10 in the SYG darkturquoise module, 6 in the SYG midnightblue module, 5 in the SYG darkgreen module, 4 in each of the SYG pink and white modules, and 3 in the SYG paleturquois module. Base on their functional classification, 38 genes were involved in metabolism, 7 genes were related to photosynthesis and porphyrin and chlorophyll metabolism, 4 genes were related to oxidative phosphorylation, 4 genes were related to two-component systems, 2 genes were related to ferredoxins, and 1 gene was related to cell division checkpoint, circadian clock, and potassium and sodium ion uptake. 

Interestingly, our cross-species analysis revealed nine common shared genes among these four cyanobacteria species under two different metal stress conditions. They were ABC transporter, carboxypeptidase Taq metallopeptidase, cell division protein (ftsW), ferredixin, isocitrate dehydrogenase (NAD+) (idh3), LysM domain, phosphoribosylaminoimid-azolecarboxamide formyltransferase–IMP cyclohydrolase (purH), phycocyanobilin:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (pcyA), and 6-pyruvoyl tetrahydrobiopterin synthase (pts). However, not all of these genes shared the same expression patterns cross-species, except for one gene, ftsW, which was downregulated in all four species under either iron starvation or copper addition. 

For high copper toxicity, a recent study showed that coastal strains of marine Synechococcus species (SYG in this study) exhibited increased tolerance to copper shock and a distinctive transcriptional response relative to open-ocean strains (SYW) (Stuart et al., 2009). SYG was predicated to be more metal tolerant and may in general be better in adapting to fastchanging environments, including biotic and abiotic environmental stresses other than copper. Early studies showed that toxicity of excess copper may arise through several mechanisms: production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), metal competitive binding, and photosynthesis inhibition (Garcia-Villada et al., 2004; Michel and Pistorius, 2004; Stuart et al., 2009; see Chapter 2.12; Thompson et al., 2011). In this study, we found that significant copper-responsive modules existed in both species of SYG and SYW. Modules of SYW greenyellow and SYG darkgreen both contained genes related to amino acid metabolism and microbial metabolism in diverse environments, representing a general stress response. Meanwhile, more specific responses were also found in the SYW yellow module that contained a downregulated cluster of ribosomal genes, and in the SYG brown module that had upregulated signal transduction and response such as curated two-component systems, RRs, and HK systems (see Section 3). The overlap of orthologous genes between SYW– SYG was modest, with only 46 orthologous genes being significantly regulated by high copper (see Chapter 2.12). 

The only gene downregulated in all four cyanobacteria species is ftsW, which encodes a cell-division integral membrane protein. The gene has been found essential in Escherichia coli (Boyle et al., 1997) and was required for Z-ring stabilization during sporulation septation in Streptomyces coelicolor (Mistry et al., 2008). Both FtsQ (another cell division protein) and FtsW are indispensable to Synechocystis, and their depletion led to slow growth and giant cells (Marbouty et al., 2009). A recent study indicates that FtsW is also directly involved in DNA damage checkpoints coordinately interacting with an SOS regulon in Caulobacter crescentus (Fraipont et al., 2011), and the downregulation of this gene might inhibit cell division (Modell et al., 2011). Because both iron depletion (see Section 19) and high copper can cause oxidative stress (see Section 10) and DNA damage (Stuart et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2011), it is speculative that the ftzW gene may play an important role in cellular defense to environmental disturbance. 

Several other stress-regulated genes were also detected in all four selected cyanobacteria species; however, they did not show the regulation in the same direction (i.e., upregulation or downregulation) uniformly in all species. For instance, the ABC transporter (Bliss et al., 1996) was upregulated in PMM and SYW but downregulated in PMT and SYG; carboxypeptidase Taq metallopeptidase was upregulated in SYW but downregulated in the other three species. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (NAD+) (idh3), involved in several metabolism pathways like the citrate cycle and the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, was upregulated in PMM and downregulated in PMT, SYG, and SYW. Similar to idh3, a LysM domain protein, a LysM-containing protein that was first shown to be involved in bacterial cell wall degradation (Zhang et al., 2009) was also upregulated in PMM but downregulated in PMT, SYG, and SYW. Interestingly, PurH, catalyzing the last two steps of de novo purine biosynthesis in bacteria and eukaryotes (Qiu et al., 2011), was upregulated in iron depletion but downregulated in copper toxicity treatments. 

It would be interesting to compare strategies of cyanobacteria responding to different environmental perturbations, in this case iron depletion and copper toxicity. Based on the shared genes identified, we have found some similar strategies adopted by the cyanobacteria to deal with different stresses, such as reducing FtsW to block the cell division preventing DNA mismatch under oxidative stress caused by metal stress (Shcolnick and Keren, 2006). The common gene shared in both treatments, pts, was interesting, although the possible function of this gene in both metal stresses is still unknown. Further investigation of these shared genes showing differential expression in different species may shed light on their adaptation to a unique environment. Based on our WGCNA analysis results and previous studies (Castielli et al., 2009), the responses regulated by metals in cyanobacteria were schematically shown in Figure 20.4.1. 

Interestingly, only one pair (petF, ferredoxin, PMM0898/ PMT1429) of four iron-responsive genes reported previously (the others are isiB PMM1771/PMT0801, hli05/08 PMM1404/ PMT1154, and idiA PMM1164/PMT0287) (Thompson et al., 2011; see Section 19) appeared in our shared gene list, whereas the other three genes have a low correlation with the modules (with r ranging from 0.001 to 0.42). It could be speculated that these highly regulated genes reported previously could be the secondary response of the stress. 

In summary, with the help of the WCGNA network analysis, we can obtain novel insights into the molecular response to environmental changes that will otherwise not be achieved by analyzing data from a single species. In addition, our cross-species analysis has found some obvious differences between two metal treatments – for example, genes of two-component systems, phosphate regulon response, and osmolarity sensors were differentially expressed only by copper addition – while urea ABC transporters and DNA replication and cell cycle genes were differentially regulated only under iron depletion. These features were not observed in any single-species analysis before, which provided evidence that cross-species WGCNA analysis could be a powerful tool to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the interaction of microorganisms with their environment. The extraction of hub genes highly connected with other genes (connection number > 8) in cyanobacteria genomes may be valuable in determining essential genes for cyanobacteria. Finally, in our WGCNA analysis, we found that many hypothetical genes with unknown function were grouped with important genes in some stress-correlated modules. Although they were not discussed in detail in this chapter due to the fact that not much functional information is available for them, we believe that further deciphering their functions will provide new insights into the stress responses in cyanobacteria.

# The extracytoplasmic function sigma factor–mediated response to heavy metal stress in Caulobacter crescentus

Rogerio F. Lourenc ´ ¸o and Suely L. Gomes 

Departamento de Bioqu´ımica, Instituto de Qu´ımica, Universidade de Sao Paulo, S ˜ ao Paulo, Brazil ˜ 

## 20.5.1 Introduction

In addition to carbon and nitrogen sources, all bacteria must acquire small amounts of some heavy metals from their surroundings in order to keep essential biochemical functions and ensure cellular survival and propagation. If chemiosmotic gradients exist, metals commonly enter the cytoplasm through constitutive uptake systems, which quickly satisfies bacterial requirements (Nies, 1999). However, in polluted environments, metals can accumulate at high levels inside the cell, triggering toxic effects that surpass their beneficial roles. In addition, the nonspecific nature of metal uptake systems allows the inappropriate entrance of structurally similar metal ions that have no importance in microbial systems, but instead cause death by disturbing bacterial physiology (Burke and Pfister, 1986; Nies and Silver, 1989; Tynecka and Malm, 1995). 

By undergoing redox reaction, several metal ions are able to directly oxidize biomolecules and participate in the generation of reactive oxygen species (Stohs and Bagchi, 1995; see Section 10). In contrast, other metals occur exclusively in one characteristic oxidation state, but are harmful due to their high affinities for the sulfhydryl group (Cuypers et al., 2010; Quig, 1998; Valko et al., 2005). When this functional group is part of a protein, metal binding can affect the function of the macromolecule by either causing a conformational change or blocking the specific role played by the cysteine residue. The high abundance of glutathione makes this sulfhydryl-containing tripeptide the main target of heavy metal ions acting through this mechanism. Association of the metal with glutathione results in a complex sequence of reactions yielding oxidized glutathione and oxygen peroxide (Cuypers et al., 2010; Kachur et al., 1998). As the metal is released at the end of the sequence, successive cycles of metal association and dissociation lead to glutathione depletion and reactive oxygen species accumulation (Lopez et al., 2006). Therefore, both classes of heavy metals (redox-active and redox-inactive) are able to cause oxidative stress in the cells, which accounts at least in part for the decreased growth and viability under metal stress. Additionally, a third potential harmful effect is related to the capability of some metals to prevent other ions to execute their function. This interference can occur by reducing the uptake of the ion or dialyzing it from the correspondent metalloprotein (Nies, 1999). 

To decrease the toxic effects of metal ions, bacteria have evolved several mechanisms, such as active metal extrusion from cells, binding to specific molecules, and reduction to a less toxic oxidation state (Nies, 1999). As oxidative stress is an inadvertent consequence of metal exposure (Stohs and Bagchi, 1995), elimination of reactive oxygen species and repair of oxidized macromolecules also contribute to proper cellular protection (see Section 10). However, it must be considered that the last two defense mechanisms are nonspecific to metal stress, as other environmental conditions are known to cause a disturbance in the normal redox state of cells, such as exposure to high light intensity or xenobiotic compounds. 

As protein synthesis has an energetic cost, expression of defense systems conferring resistance to cells under heavy metal stress occurs uniquely or at a greater extent when the metal concentration rises beyond a critical limit. In general, this increase in expression is a consequence at least in part of a transcriptional control, in which one or more regulatory proteins affect the rate of transcription initiation from promoters corresponding to heavy metal–responsive genes. Besides the regulatory component, a molecular system enabling cells to respond and adapt to a stress condition also requires a sensorial counterpart. Therefore, parallel to defense mechanisms, proteins involved in sensing and responding to an increase in the concentration of heavy metals have also evolved in bacteria. 

Owing to a progressive contamination of soil and aquatic environments associated with anthropogenic activities, the presence of molecular systems involved in signal transduction and defense to heavy metal stress has become even more critical to ensure the integrity of microbial communities. As judged by the higher potential to pose a threat to ecosystems (Chowdhury and Chandra, 1987), adaptive responses are particularly important to those heavy metals that have harmful but not beneficial effects to bacterial species, including the divalent cations cadmium $( \mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } )$ and mercury $( \mathrm { H g } ^ { 2 + } )$ and the hexavalent chromium existing as the oxyanions chromate $\left( \mathrm { C r O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - } \right)$ and dichromate $\displaystyle { \left( \mathrm { C r } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 7 } { } ^ { 2 - } \right) }$ . 

As other aquatic species, the free-living alphaproteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus must deal with an accumulation of these very toxic heavy metals. So far, four alternative sigma factors, all from the extracytoplasmic function (ECF) subfamily (see Chapter 2.6), have been associated with the bacterial response to heavy metal stress. Here, the role and regulation of these ECF sigma factors are discussed in light of recent studies in $C .$ crescentus. Important contributions arising from studies in the corresponding systems of other species are presented as well. It is worth mentioning that the aspects of the orthologous systems highlighted in this chapter are those adding information about the heavy metal stress response, and therefore this chapter does not cover all the progress concerning these molecular systems. 

## 20.5.2 $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { F } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { E } }$ , two unrelated ECF sigma factors involved in heavy metal and oxidative stress

C. crescentus $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ is one of the ECF sigma factors contributing to the transcriptional response to heavy metal stress, as activation of this protein is triggered by the presence of cadmium and the chromium oxyanions chromate and dichromate (Kohler et al., 2012). Although an imbalance in the redox state of the cell is expected in the presence of cadmium and chromium, activation of $\bar { \mathsf { \Phi } } _ { \mathfrak { O } } \mathbb { F }$ occurs in an oxidative stress–independent manner. This conclusion is based on the observation that neither an increase in the concentrations of superoxide radical and hydrogen peroxide nor treatment with a thiol-specific oxidant is sufficient to activate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ (Kohler et al., 2012). 

Control of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ activity is achieved by NrsF (negative regulator of sigma F), a protein recognized as a second component in this molecular system (Figure 20.5.1). Owing to its ability to keep expression of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ -dependent genes at basal levels in the absence of cadmium and chromium (Kohler et al., 2012), NrsF fulfills a clear role as a negative regulator of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ activity. Predicted to have six transmembrane helices, NrsF is expected to reside in the bacterial inner membrane (Figure 20.5.1). The portion of the protein probably exposed to the cytoplasm comprises 25 residues at the N-terminus and two linkers with around 10 amino acid residues each. In contrast to the situation of other well-characterized sigma–antisigma pairs (Campbell et al., 2003, 2007; see Section 4 and Chapter 2.6), neither cytoplasmic segment is long enough to be folded in a protein domain able to contact $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ by binding between its $\sigma _ { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { 4 }$ regions. Independently of the mode by which NrsF contacts $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } } ,$ , interaction of the proteins keeps the sigma factor away from the RNA polymerase core enzyme (Figure 20.5.1). 

C. crescentus NrsF has three cysteine residues (Cys102, Cys131, and Cys181). While one residue seems to be located in the middle of a transmembrane helix (Cys102), the other two are in the termini of successive helices (Cys131 and Cys181), positioning them in contact with the periplasm (Figure 20.5.1). Both periplasmic cysteine residues seem to play a role in NrsF– $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ interaction, as a partial activation of the sigma factor occurs when either of these residues is individually replaced by alanine (Kohler et al., 2012). However, the responsiveness of the system is still preserved in the absence of one cysteine residue, as the maximum activity of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ is achieved following heavy metal stress. The effect of double substitution is even more pronounced with respect to substitution of only one residue, with maximum $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ activity even in the absence of metal ions. This discrepancy concerning the effects of single and double substitutions is consistent with the presence of the cysteine residues in the reduced state. 

A striking possibility for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ activation is that the sulfhydryl groups of both Cys131 and Cys181 participate in essential amino acid interactions with other residues, which, when blocked, could cause a conformational change in NrsF and the release of the sigma factor. In this scenario, disruption of amino acid interactions is thought to be triggered by association of cadmium and chromium oxyanions to Cys131 and Cys181. Regardless of the fact that the tridimensional arrangement of the transmembrane helices for NrsF is presently unavailable, it is possible that both essential cysteine residues are located in close vicinity to each other in the periplasm. If true, a metal ion could contact both residues simultaneously, a feature with precedence in the literature (Klaassen et al., 1999; Presta et al., 1995). 

Once released into the cytoplasm, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ is able to direct transcription of a small regulon. As a conserved promoter sequence is found in the upstream regions of all $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ -dependent genes and no additional putative transcriptional regulator is under control of this sigma factor even after a half-hour of metal stress (Kohler et al., 2012), $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ seems to be the single regulatory protein in this molecular system. 

Genes potentially involved in the oxidative stress response (repair of oxidized methionine and elimination of superoxide radical) (see Section 10) and in sulfur metabolism are in the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ regulon (Alvarez-Martinez et $a l .$ , 2006; Kohler et $a l .$ , 2012). While oxidative stress genes confer bacterial protection to the increased concentration of reactive oxygen species, genes related to sulfur metabolism could provide cells with sulfate by an alternative route. The latter category is particularly important under chromium stress, as sulfate uptake becomes compromised because the downregulation of a sulfate transporter gene is a defense strategy to avoid intracellular accumulation of chromium (Henne et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2005; Thompson et al., 2010). Curiously, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ controls two homologous loci, each encompassing three genes (Kohler et al., 2012). One of these duplicated loci is adjacent to sigF–nrsF and forms a tetracistronic transcriptional unit with an additional gene. No biological significance for the presence of three pairs of paralogous proteins is apparent, mainly because no function has been assigned to these proteins yet. 


Figure 20.5.1 Activation of ECF sigma factors under heavy metal stress in Caulobacter crescentus. (a) Under unstressed condition, the ECF sigma factors σF, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ , and σT are bound to the cognate antisigma factors NrsF, ChrR, and NepR, respectively. (b) When C. crescentus experiences habitats contaminated with cadmium $( \mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } )$ , all sigma factors are released from inhibition to form RNA polymerase holoenzymes competent for transcription of specific genes. In the presence of chromium $\mathrm { ( C r O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ and $\mathrm { C r } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 7 } { } ^ { 2 - } ) , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ are also activated. While a single protein, the cognate antisigma factor, has been implicated in the control o $\mathrm { \hbar } _ { \mathrm { v } } \mathrm { F }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } , \mathsf { a }$ complex network is involved in regulation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ activity. In the latter case, the signaling is initiated by a phosphorylation flow involving the sensor histidine kinase PhyK and the response regulator PhyR. Upon phosphorylation, PhyR undergoes a conformational change, exposing its N-terminal domain that mimics $\overline { { \sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } } } }$ itself. As a consequence, NepR is tethered from the sigma factor, releasing σT. The proteins in the sigma factor signaling cascade are represented according to the domain architecture as follows: $\sigma _ { 2 } ,$ sigma factor region 2; $\sigma _ { 4 } ,$ sigma factor region 4; ${ \sigma } _ { 2 } \mathrm { L }$ , sigma factor region 2-like; ${ \sigma } _ { 4 } \mathrm { L }$ , sigma factor region 4-like; ASD, antisigma domain; CLD, cupin-like domain; REC, response regulator; double-PDC, putative sensor domain; HAMP, helical linker domain, HisKA 2, dimerization and phosphoacceptor domain; HATPase c, ATPase domain. Numbers denote the successive transmembrane regions, and cysteine residues with expected roles in signal transduction are displayed as red circles. Core RNA polymerase is presented according to its protein subunits α, β, and β’. N and C are the amino- and carboxy-terminus, respectively, of transmembrane proteins. All domains were predicted according to the Pfam protein families database.

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/922f4308889cf04239904760646726fdaa16c5cea20376da2978daccebacf3df.jpg)


As judged by the distribution of its component proteins, the $\mathrm { N r s F - } \mathrm { \overline { { o } } ^ { F } }$ system is present in a limited number of bacteria. Instead of being a characteristic marker of a monophyletic group, NrsF and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ are present in species belonging to a few phylogenetically unrelated families of alpha-, beta-, gamma-, and deltaproteobacteria (Figure 20.5.2). Nearly half of these bacteria also possess at least one chromosomal locus homologous to the tetracistronic operon found to be dependent on $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ in C. crescentus, generally in close proximity to the sigma–antisigma factor genes (Figure 20.5.2). In a similar manner, genes related to repair of oxidized methionine (msrA) and sulfur metabolism (yedY) are located near the corresponding sigF–nrsF operon in some bacteria (Figure 20.5.2). Therefore, the genomic organization provides evidence that similar functions are dependent on $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ orthologs. 

Besides the functional characterization in C. crescentus, the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ mediated stress response has been investigated in an additional alphaproteobacterium, the soybean nitrogen-fixing endosymbiont Bradyrhizobium japonicum. Change in the activity of B. japonicum $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ was demonstrated in the presence of the reactive oxygen species hydrogen peroxide and singlet oxygen (Masloboeva et al., 2012), leaving the possible involvement of this system with heavy metal stress response to be investigated. The finding that the fold change in expression of B. japonicum $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ by hydrogen peroxide exposure increases with reduction in the oxygen pressure is consistent with a possible activation of the sigma factor by the cellular aerobic metabolism (Masloboeva et $a l . ,$ , 2012). As judged by the basal $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ activity in C. crescentus grown in the absolute absence of cadmium and chromium (Kohler et al., 2012), an oxidative stress elicited by the intrinsic bacterial aerobic metabolism also seems to modulate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ activity in C. crescentus. Therefore, an emerging picture is that the $\mathrm { N r s F - } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ system responds to both heavy metal and oxidative stresses. 

Another important contribution of the study in B. japonicum is the clear demonstration that the negative regulation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ by NrsF is dependent on the direct binding of the proteins (Masloboeva et al., 2012), confirming the role of NrsF as an antisigma factor. B. japonicum NrsF possesses two cysteine residues at positions equivalent to the periplasmic cysteines of the $C .$ crescentus protein. While both C. crescentus residues are probably required for NrsF structure (Kohler et al., 2012), only one (Cys129) seems to play the same function in the B. japonicum protein (Masloboeva et al., 2012). The second residue in the latter bacterium (Cys179) has been found to be essential for releasing the sigma factor under hydrogen peroxide stress. Although an overall structure conservation is expected among the orthologous antisigma factors, differences in specific amino acid interactions could be responsible for the disparities in the exact molecular mechanism by which an NrsF ortholog integrates a stress condition into a transcriptional response. It should be noted that NrsF is responding to different signals in C. crescentus and B. japonicum. Therefore, the possibility that the B. japonicum protein is affected by heavy metal even in the absence of Cys179 (equivalent to $C .$ crescentus Cys181) cannot be ruled out. 

In Azospira suillum, several genes in close vicinity to the orthologous pair sigF–nrsF have been found to be required for perchlorate reduction, enabling the bacterium to grow in the presence of this compound as the sole electron acceptor for anaerobic respiration (Melnyk et al., 2014). $s i g F$ and nrsF are not themselves needed for A. suillum growth under this condition; however, the genomic organization is indicative of the possible role for these genes in the presence of perchlorate. More specifically, sigF could play a role in protecting cells from oxidative damages caused by the powerful oxidant chlorite, which arises as an inadvertent consequence of perchlorate reduction (Coates and Achenbach, 2004; Kwolek-Mirek et al., 2011; see Section 10). 

In accordance to a possible function of A. suillum sigF in oxidative stress response, genes preventing or counteracting oxidative damages are upregulated in Shewanella algae when the bacterium grows by chlorate respiration (Clark et al., 2014), another condition leading to chlorite generation (Bender et al., 2004). Orthologs of genes that in C. crescentus belong to the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } . }$ dependent tetracistronic transcriptional unit are also induced in the presence of chlorate (Clark et al., 2014). Interestingly, the control of these genes in S. algae is accomplished by an unrelated sigma factor, as genes corresponding to sigF and nrsF are not found in the genome of S. algae. A clue about regulation of the oxidative stress response genes in S. algae is provided by the observation of genes encoding a sigma factor and its possible cognate antisigma factor among the chlorate stimulon. In summary, the reports on chlorate and perchlorate reduction reaffirm the engagement of sigF with oxidative stress caused by a multitude of unfavorable environmental conditions, in addition to heavy metal stress. 

When C. crescentus NrsF and its orthologs in B. japonicum and A. suillum are compared to the antisigma factor CarR of Myxococcus xanthus, virtually no similarity at the level of their primary structure is found. However, a striking identical membrane topology is observed, regarding the number of transmembrane regions, length of cytoplasmic and periplasmic segments, and occurrence of cysteine residues at the terminus of each successive transmembrane helix (Galbis-Martinez et al., 2012). Interestingly, the sigma factor regulated by CarR is also activated under oxidative (singlet oxygen) and metal (copper) stresses (Browning et al., 2003; Moraleda-Munoz et al., 2005). Therefore, CarR and NrsF could use a similar mechanism to sequester the corresponding sigma factor and perhaps to perceive the environmental signals. 

A second ECF sigma factor recognized by its ability to mount a transcriptional response to heavy metal stress in C. crescentus is $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ (Lourenco and Gomes, 2009; see Chapter 2.6). Regarding the repertoire of heavy metals that the bacterium may encounter in its natural habitat, only cadmium has been shown to trigger $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activation. Again, the increase in activity of the sigma factor is not associated with elevated production of superoxide radical and hydrogen peroxide, nor caused by glutathione depletion. Singlet oxygen and organic peroxide are able to activate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ , but even these reactive oxygen species do not mediate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activation in the presence of cadmium. This statement agrees with the observation that the release of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ from inhibition exerted by the cognate negative regulator ChrR under cadmium stress is affected by the replacement of cysteine residues in the latter protein (Cys186 and Cys188) (Lourenco and Gomes, 2009). However, activation of the sigma factor in the presence of singlet oxygen or organic peroxide is not perturbed by the amino acid substitutions.
