Residue Cys188 plays no role in ChrR structure but is absolutely required for dissociation of the sigma–antisigma complex in the presence of cadmium (Lourenco and Gomes, 2009). Thus, the sulfhydryl group of Cys188 seems to make no essential contacts with other amino acids within the protein. Nonetheless, this functional group could be required for cadmium binding and for the subsequent effects that would ultimately lead to a structural change in ChrR. In contrast, Cys186 probably participates in amino acid contacts crucial to keep the protein structure required to properly bind and sequester $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } { } _ { ; }$ , a hypothesis based on the partial increase in $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activity associated with the replacement of this residue (Lourenco and Gomes, 2009). Because this functional group still allows a further activation of ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { E } } { } _ { ; }$ , but without reaching the maximum level, it is reasonable to suppose that the position of the primary cadmium-sensing residue Cys188 is altered in the protein with Cys186 replaced, affecting the capability to fully sense the metal and release $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ . 

Instead of participating in $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activation under cadmium exposure, singlet oxygen and/or organic peroxide are thought to mediate the release of the sigma factor from inhibition when cells experience ultraviolet-A (UVA) irradiation, a stress condition known to stimulate the generation of both reactive oxygen species (Baier et al., 2006; Wondrak et $a l .$ , 2006; see Section 8). Interestingly, in the absence of cadmium and UVA irradiation, the pool of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is kept in a completely inactive state, indicating that the bacterial aerobic metabolism is not sufficient to release this sigma factor from inhibition. Therefore, although two unrelated sigma–antisigma systems are involved in the C. crescentus response to heavy metal and oxidative stress, the collection of signals directly perceived and the mechanisms responsible for sensing and transducing these signals to activate each sigma factor are remarkably different. 

The main role of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is to control the expression of genes involved in the repair of biological molecules that are damaged under oxidative stress (Lourenco and Gomes, 2009; see Section 10), which is a feature of both cadmium stress and UVA irradiation (Lopez et al., 2006; Wondrak et al., 2006). This includes genes potentially involved in repair of oxidized methionine, folding of denatured protein, and synthesis of a nucleotide. Together, these genes contribute to avoid accumulation of denatured protein and incorporation of oxidized nucleotides in nucleic acids. In addition, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ controls the expression of a gene responsible for cyclopropanation of unsaturated fatty acid. By eliminating double bounds without changing physical and chemical properties, fatty acids become less susceptible to reactive oxygen species (Cronan, 2002). Thus, this function can protect unsaturated lipids from peroxidation. Both C. crescentus genes from the photolyase–cryptochrome family are also dependent on C. crescentus $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ . Regardless of their exact function, acting either in DNA repair or in blue light sensing, both genes seem to be related specifically to protection against UVA irradiation, which is in contrast with the expected contribution of the other $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } .$ -dependent genes. 

Orthologs of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ and ChrR are present mostly in representatives of alpha- and gammaproteobacteria and are a feature of a minority of species in each group (Figure 20.5.2). Remarkably, a set of genes is of interest due to its conserved location in the vicinity of the rpoE–chrR operon. Among these genes are those functioning in cyclopropanation of unsaturated fatty acid $( c f a S )$ and absorption of light for DNA repair or sensing environment (phr), as well as two genes whose exact functions are still unknown (RSP 1090 and RSP 1091 in R. sphaeroides). As a $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ -dependent sequence is located upstream of transcriptional units encompassing these genes, it has been proposed that they represent the ${ \mathrm { C h r R - } } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ regulon core (Dufour et al., 2008). 

As demonstrated by a study of the same molecular system in R. sphaeroides (Campbell et al., 2007), ChrR is a soluble cytoplasmic protein that makes an extensive contact with $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ under unstressed condition (Figure 20.5.1). ChrR in this bacterium possesses a zinc-binding motif (HxxxCxxC) in its Nterminal $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } .$ -interacting domain, which is responsible to coordinate a zinc ion along with an additional histidine residue near the N-terminus of the protein (Campbell et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2001). Except for the histidine in this motif, all other three residues are essential for zinc binding and protein structure. While conserved in almost all ChrR orthologs, only the non-essential histidine is present in C. crescentus, despite the overall conservation of the protein. Thus, C. crescentus ChrR must acquire the functional fold even in the absence of a zincbinding motif, although it remains unclear if this protein can coordinate zinc using different residues. 

The structural model of the R. sphaeroides complex ChrR– $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ implies that the corresponding Cys186 and Cys188 are not participating in a disulfide bond (Campbell et al., 2007), which is in perfect agreement with the different contributions of each residue for ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { { \breve { \mathrm { E } } } }$ activation in C. crescentus. The presumption from the work with the R. sphaeroides system that only Cys188 is exposed to solvent also corroborates the nature of this residue as the primary target of cadmium in the C. crescentus protein. Curiously, R. sphaeroides $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is not activated by cadmium at concentrations sufficient to induce the C. crescentus sigma factor (Newman et al., 2001). Once more, this disparity shows that particular structural features of an antisigma factor can result in differences in its ability to dissociate from the cognate sigma factor in the presence of specific signals. In this context, a striking possibility is that the response to cadmium is a feature of the presence of the cysteine residues and the absence of the N-terminal zinc-binding motif. 

The participation of orthologs of ChrR and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in response to oxidative stress caused by singlet oxygen has been investigated in two additional alphaproteobacteria, the non-phototrophic species Azospirillum brasilense (Gupta et al., 2013; Mishra et al., 2011), and the aerobic anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria Roseobacter denitrificans (Berghoff et al., 2011). Curiously, A. brasilense possesses a pair of each protein composing the ChrR– $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ system, one constitutively expressed and another under the control of singlet oxygen (Gupta et al., 2013). Both A. brasilense antisigma factors and R. denitrificans ChrR have a zinc-binding motif in the N-terminal domain along with the conserved cysteine residues at the C-terminus. Therefore, these bacteria represent interesting systems in which the possible involvement of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in response to cadmium could be tested. 

## 20.5.3 $\mathbf { \sigma } ^ { \mathsf { T } }$ and $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { \mathbf { 0 } } \mathbf { 0 } _ { }$ , two paralogous ECF sigma factors mediating general stress response

Unlike the situations discussed for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } { } _ { ; }$ , a multitude of unrelated stress conditions has been described as causing activation of the paralogous ECF sigma factors $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ , including the heavy metals cadmium and chromium (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2007; Britos et al., 2011; Hottes et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2005; Lourenco et al., 2011). Due to these observations, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ are regarded as the sigma factors involved in the control of the general stress response in C. crescentus (see Chapter 2.6). Despite their overall conservation, these proteins do not make equivalent contributions to the transcriptional response. $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ is the master regulator and the principal, if not the single, sigma factor responsible for expression of $\propto ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2007). On the other hand, at least under sucrose stress and carbon starvation, two other conditions leading to activation of these paralogous sigma factors, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ makes little contribution to the stress response (Britos et al., 2011; Lourenco et al., 2011). 

A significant effect on the bacterial transcriptome was demonstrated so far only after $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ overexpression in a $s i g T$ -null mutant background (Lourenco et al., 2011). Remarkably, the upregulated genes corresponded to a subset of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ regulon. As the promoter region of all $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ -dependent genes possesses a sequence recognized by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ , and these genes are those induced to greater extents under stress condition, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ presumably binds $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } } .$ - dependent promoter elements with lower affinity. Therefore, it is reasonable to suppose that sigU is reminiscent of a gene duplication event and currently plays just a modest function during stress response in $C .$ crescentus by amplifying the fold change in the expression of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { \mathbf { { \sigma } } } ^ { \prime }$ target genes (Figure 20.5.3). 

Interestingly, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ is under both transcriptional and posttranslational control. Regulation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ at the transcriptional level occurs as a consequence of its ability to drive the RNA polymerase to direct transcription of the corresponding gene $s i g T$ (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2007). Unlike this transcriptional control, which depends uniquely on $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ itself, posttranslational control o $\mathsf { f o } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ is mediated by a set of proteins acting in concert to ultimately determine sigma factor activity and the expression levels of its target genes (Figure 20.5.1). One of these regulatory components, the NepR protein, acts as an antisigma factor based on its ability to directly bind $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ and negatively control the expression of both $s i g T$ and sigU (Herrou et al., 2010; Lourenco et al., 2011). 

Despite the notable sequence similarity between these sigma factors, NepR proved to be specific for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ . Additionally, neither an open reading frame coding for a putative antisigma factor exists immediately upstream of $s i g U ,$ , nor a NepR paralog is present in C. crescentus. If it is really true that ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { { U } } }$ regulation lies absolutely at the transcriptional level, an interesting conclusion emerges: $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ also functions to prolong the stress response even after the inducing signals disappear and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ is sequestered by NepR, or $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ is under a proteolytic control to ensure rapid shutdown of both sigma factors. 

The second C. crescentus protein participating in the transcriptional response mediated by the paralogous sigma factors is the response regulator named PhyR. This protein is considered atypical because of the presence of an N-terminal domain with a sigma factor–like fold (regions similar to $\sigma _ { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { 4 }$ associated with a flexible linker) in addition to the C-terminal receiver domain (Figure 20.5.1). Despite this characteristic fold, PhyR lacks residues in both regions $\sigma _ { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { 4 }$ known to be essential for association with RNA polymerase core enzyme and −35 and −10 promoter elements, ruling out its action as a bonafide sigma factor (Staron et al., 2009). Actually, PhyR has been demonstrated to function as an antisigma factor antagonist, directly binding NepR through its N-terminal sigma factor–like domain (Herrou et al., 2010, 2012; Lourenco et al., 2011). Curiously, although regions $\sigma _ { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { 4 }$ of PhyR can move against each other, NepR associates with this protein domain by wrapping the regions in a closed conformation (Herrou et al., 2012). Considering that the sigma factor–like domain of PhyR and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ compete for NepR, the same interaction pattern is expected in the sigma– antisigma complex. This represents a situation at odds with the association between ChrR and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ (Campbell et al., 2007). 

This partner-switching mechanism determining $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ activity is controlled by an elaborated flow of a phosphoryl group (Figure 20.5.1). PhyR is in either an unphosphorylated or phosphorylated state, and its ability to contact NepR absolutely depends on the presence of a phosphoryl group at the receiver domain (Herrou et al., 2010, 2012; Lourenco et al., 2011). Upon phosphorylation, PhyR undergoes a conformational change in which the receiver domain moves apart from the sigma factor–like domain, exposing the surface in the latter domain required for NepR binding (Herrou et al., 2010, 2012). Phosphorylation and activation of PhyR are dependent on the histidine kinase protein PhyK (Foreman et al., 2012; Lourenco et al., 2011), suggesting the involvement of a two-component system in the control of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ . 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/3c79d18a-f6b7-4ad4-9deb-d4b8b2934fe8/438160a9dc87838104ccfe698b0951c4f3f950c8970a2181f5b8082c0e287e6f.jpg)



Figure 20.5.3 Modulation of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } } .$ -mediated heavy metal stress response in Caulobacter crescentus. The ECF sigma $\mathrm { f a c t o r } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ is controlled at the transcriptional level by its paralog $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ and is able to positively modulate the stress response by directing expression of a subset of the σT regulon. The two-component system consisting of the histidine kinase protein LovK and the cognate response regulator LovR is also under the transcriptional control of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ . While acting as a typical kinase of LovR, the protein LovK seems to present a phosphatase activity toward the response regulator PhyR, therefore contributing to negatively modulating the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ -mediated heavy metal stress response. By decreasing the whole transcriptional response and stimulating the expression of selected target genes, the combination of the two opposing effects is thought to make the stress response even more specific. The proteins participating in modulation of $\infty ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ activity are represented according to the domain architecture as follows: $\sigma _ { 2 } ,$ sigma factor region $2 ; \sigma _ { 4 } ,$ sigma factor region 4; $; \sigma _ { 2 } \mathrm { L }$ , sigma factor region 2-like; ${ \sigma } _ { 4 } \mathrm { L } ,$ sigma factor region 4-like; REC, response regulator; PAS–Lov, putative sensor domain; HisKA 2, dimerization and phosphoacceptor domain; HATPase c, ATPase domain. Core RNA polymerase is presented according to its protein subunits α, β, and β’. All domains were predicted according to the Pfam protein families database.


A second pair of proteins consisting of the histidine kinase LovK and the cognate response regulator LovR was found to modulate the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ -mediated response (Figure 20.5.3). In contrast to PhyK–PhyR, the pair LovK–LovR functions to decrease the activity of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { \infty } \mathrm { T }$ (Foreman et al., 2012). As the corresponding genes lovK and lovR are under the direct control of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } } { } _ { ; }$ , LovK–LovR are presumed to exert a negative feedback, downregulating the expression of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } } .$ -dependent genes. Although this still remains to be investigated, it has been hypothesized that this effect could be a consequence of a cross-regulation between PhyK–PhyR and LovK–LovR. Whereas a kinase activity is evident upon its primary target LovR, a phosphatase activity is proposed as the main function of LovK over PhyR (Figure 20.5.3). Thus, by decreasing the concentration of phosphorylated PhyR, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ activity is reduced. Surprisingly, LovK is able to indirectly activate the sigma factor in a phyK mutant background, especially if LovR expression is abolished in the cell (Foreman et al., 2012). A possible explanation for this finding is that LovK has the ability to transfer a phosphoryl group to PhyR in the absence of PhyK. In short, LovK seems to both phosphorylate and dephosphorylate PhyR, with a remarkable preference for the last activity. 

PhyK can be considered a prototypical histidine kinase protein by presenting an N-terminal sensor periplasmic domain between two transmembrane segments and a C-terminal cytoplasmic portion responsible for the kinase activity (Figure 20.5.1; see Section 3). Although no significant similarity is evident over the primary structure of the N-terminal region, the predicted tridimensional fold resembles a double-PDC domain, which is responsible for binding ions or small molecules in characterized proteins (Cheung and Hendrickson, 2010). 

Interestingly, a cysteine residue (Cys95) expected to lie in the corresponding ligand-binding region of PhyK is required for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ activity (Lourenco et $a l .$ , 2011). Therefore, it is probable that PhyK senses at least part of the periplasmic signals through this cysteine residue. In the case of heavy metal stress, for instance, activation of PhyK could be triggered by the association of the metal ion with Cys95, in a manner similar to that proposed for cadmium sensing by ChrR. The putative double-PDC domain of PhyK also possesses an additional cysteine residue (Cys67). Nonetheless, no contribution to activation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ has been attributed to this residue, as the capability of the molecular system to respond to stress is still evident in the absence of the corresponding sulfhydryl group (Lourenco et al., 2011). 

Differently from PhyK, LovK is a cytoplasmic protein with a PAS–LOV domain located in its N-terminus (Figure 20.5.3). The presence of a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) molecule bound to the PAS–LOV domain enables the protein LovK to act as a blue light sensor, but this biochemical property proved to be absolutely dependent on the oxidized state of the cofactor (Purcell et al., 2007, 2010). Therefore, LovK has been referred to as a conditional photosensor regulated by the oxidative state of the cytoplasm. Also for LovK, the single cysteine residue in the sensing region of the protein (Cys70) has been revealed as crucial for both photochemical reaction in the LOV domain and autophosphorylation of the histidine kinase domain (Purcell et al., 2007). Therefore, both the kinase and phosphatase involved in the control of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ seem to perceive molecular cues through a cysteine residue in the sensing domain. 

In principle, PhyK and LovK could integrate different signals in a final response, with PhyK activation leading to increased $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ activity and LovK stimulation contributing to reduce the activity of the sigma factor. However, this situation does not necessarily occur, as an enhanced cell–cell attachment triggered by LovK is not observed by disrupting $s i g T$ (Foreman et al., 2012). Therefore, the two-component system LovK–LovR plays other biological functions in addition to decreasing $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ activity. 

Activities required for the proper physiology of the cell envelope under stress condition are controlled by ${ \bar { \mathbf { o } } } ^ { \mathrm { { T } } }$ , including peptidoglycan recycling, maintenance of outer membrane integrity, and lipid modification (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2007; Foreman et al., 2012; Lourenco et al., 2011). Although the exact functions of several other $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ -dependent genes are completely unknown, their association with stress response is reasonable judging by the fact that orthologs are upregulated in the presence of unfavorable growth conditions. As nearly all $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ -dependent genes identified by now are downstream of a sequence proposed to be recognized by the sigma factor (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2007; Lourenco et al., 2011), the functions upregulated comprise the primary response of $C .$ crescentus to an adverse situation. In addition, a considerable set of other genes is also expected to be secondarily activated as part of the C. crescentus general stress response, as several regulatory genes are in the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ regulon. 

Contrary to the situation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } { } _ { ; }$ , which are restricted to some species belonging to more than one proteobacterial group, orthologs of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ have been considered molecular markers of alphaproteobacteria, with exception of obligate intracellular species belonging to the Rickettsiales branch (Staron and Mascher, 2010; Staron et al., 2009). This distribution is in agreement with the observation that an ortholog of the general stress response sigma factor RpoS is missing in alphaproteobacteria. PhyR and NepR are also widespread among species belonging to this phylogenetic group (Staron and Mascher, 2010; Staron et al., 2009), and together with $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ , these proteins comprise the conserved regulatory core of the general stress response. 

In several species, a histidine kinase gene is also located in the same locus of sigT orthologs (Figure 20.5.2). Nonetheless, the corresponding proteins functionally characterized by now have proved to be heterogeneous regarding to the effect upon PhyR phosphorylation and activity: acting as a typical kinase (Foreman et al., 2012; Lourenco et al., 2011), acting as a phosphatase (Kaczmarczyk et al., 2011), or still playing both activities (Sauviac and Bruand, 2014). Interestingly, control of PhyR is not a particularity of genes in the vicinity of sigT orthologs, as a kinase activity was also demonstrated for products of genes located elsewhere in the genome (Kaczmarczyk et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014). Different among the species is also the spectra of unfavorable conditions activating orthologs of PhyR and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ (Francez-Charlot et al., 2009; Gourion et al., 2009; Gourley et al., 2014; Iguchi et al., 2013; Kulkarni et al., 2013; Lourenco et al., 2011; Martinez-Salazar et al., 2009; Sauviac et al., 2007). With respect to heavy metal stress, only activation of the C. crescentus system is currently documented, presumably because the inducing effect of this stress condition upon PhyR and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ has not been investigated in other bacteria. 

Interestingly, the existence of the sigma factor gene in duplicated or even higher numbers of copies is a feature of other species. The relative contribution of paralogous sigma factors has been investigated in the nitrogen-fixing alphaproteobacterium Rhizobium etli as well. According to this study, the sigma factors act in a nonlinear pathway, in that each protein controls a specific set of genes, with limited overlap between the regulons (Jans et al., 2013). Therefore, although the function of paralogous sigma factors has been dissected in only two bacteria by now, the data are sufficient to conclude that the relative contribution of each protein can vary drastically among species. 

## 20.5.4 Contribution of the sigma factors to global response to heavy metal stress

Remarkable changes in the transcriptional and translational profiles are evident when C. crescentus experiences stress caused by cadmium or chromium (Hu et al., 2005; Yung et al., 2014). By considering the cellular effects of these heavy metals, the enrichment of cells with transcripts and proteins involved in elimination of reactive oxygen species and repair of oxidative damage in biological molecules is not surprising. With respect to heavy metal detoxification, this strategy seems to be employed by C. crescentus in response to cadmium, as genes presumably involved in active efflux of this metal are present in the genome of the bacterium and are upregulated. Curiously, cadmium leads to increased expression of an arsenic resistance system. Although its relevance for bacterial response to cadmium is currently unknown, upregulation of this defense system is thought to occur as a consequence of metal binding to the repressor ArsR (Hu et al., 2005; Yung et al., 2014). This assumption is in agreement with the consideration that cadmium activates the C. crescentus sigma factors by binding to cysteine residues in the cognate sensor proteins (antisigma factor or histidine kinase). 

In contrast to cadmium response, protection against chromium does not rely on metal detoxification, as genes playing possible roles in chromate efflux or reduction are missing in C. crescentus (Nierman et al., 2001). Besides counteracting oxidative damage, cells undergo a substantial change in the proteome of the outer membrane and activate a response focused on denatured and misfolded proteins (Hu et al., 2005; Yung et al., 2014). Therefore, the responses of C. crescentus to cadmium and chromium are strikingly different with respect to the functional categories activated. In addition, even the defense against oxidative stress, which is a common trait of heavy metal response, exerts different relative contributions to the global response to each metal, with cadmium eliciting upregulation of more transcripts and proteins related to this cellular process (Hu et al., 2005; Yung et al., 2014). 

Besides the difference in the functions required, the behavior of the sigma factors in the presence of either heavy metal is also distinct. Each sigma factor controls a specific regulon, with virtually no overlap (Table 20.5.1), therefore exerting a particular contribution to heavy metal response. Genes regulated exclusively by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ , including sigE itself, were found induced just under cadmium exposure, an observation in accordance with the fact that this sigma factor is not activated in the presence of chromium. Similarly, the finding that almost all genes under the control of either ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { { F } } }$ or σT are upregulated following bacterial exposure to cadmium and chromium is also expected when one considers that these sigma factors respond to both heavy metals. Interestingly, the discrepancy between the behavior of σF and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ relies on their control, because whereas activity and expression of $\mathbf { \sigma } _ { \mathbf { { 0 } } } \mathrm { { T } }$ increase under metal stress, only σF activity is stimulated, suggesting lack of autoregulation in the latter case. 

Even controlling specific regulons, σF, σE, and σT account for just a subset of genes that are upregulated in the presence of cadmium and chromium. This observation provides evidence for the participation of other molecular systems in the bacterial response to cadmium and chromium, which might account for upregulation of essential genes that are not under the control of the sigma factors (Braz and Marques, 2005; Valencia et al., 2013). In fact, several proteins from distinct families of transcriptional regulators are upregulated in the presence of cadmium, chromium, or both (Hu et al., 2005; Yung et al., 2014). 

The somewhat discrete contribution of each sigma factor to cadmium and chromium responses provides a reason for the absolute lack of phenotype of mutant backgrounds in either sigF or sigE following exposure to cadmium and chromium stresses (Kohler et al., 2012; Lourenco and Gomes, 2009) and perhaps for cells with $s i g T$ disrupted. If the involvement of A. suillum $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ in oxidative stress response is really true, then the observation that this sigma factor is not essential for bacterial growth under perchlorate respiration seems reasonable (Melnyk et al., 2014). In this scenario, other molecular systems could compensate for the absence of $s i g F$ in both C. crescentus and A. suillum. The presence of multiple systems involved in the same response is particularly advantageous in environments with constant fluctuations in physical and chemical parameters, as spontaneous lack of one molecular system does not drastically affect the bacterial ability to persist in such environments. Nonetheless, the requirement of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } } ,$ , $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } ,$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ for C. crescentus resistance to oxidative stress has been demonstrated (Alvarez-Martinez et al., 2006; Lourenco and Gomes, 2009; Lourenco et al., 2011), reinforcing the involvement of these ECF sigma factors in protection against oxidative damage related to heavy metal stress. 

## 20.5.5 Outlook

All C. crescentus sigma factors from the ECF subfamily addressed in this chapter participate in the bacterial response to cadmium and chromium. The maintenance of these sigma factors highlights that C. crescentus frequently experiences sites contaminated with cadmium and/or chromium and that the concerted action of these sigma factors allows the bacterium to respond and adapt to the stress condition. Although orthologs of these sigma factors have been characterized in a number of bacteria susceptible to heavy metal stress in their natural habitats, their involvement in this response remains virtually unknown. These orthologs and, more importantly, their cognate sensor components represent a set of natural proteins with both conserved and variable amino acid residues. By comparing the ability of these proteins to sense heavy metals and transduce the signal to the sigma factors, the role of individual residues can be uncovered. 

Very striking is the finding that conserved cysteine residues are required for the proper activities of the possible sensor components of the molecular systems considered. Nevertheless, the exact nature of the activating signals and the mechanisms responsible for inactivation of these sensor proteins are completely unresolved questions that deserve future consideration. Particularly, it is important to address whether cadmium and chromium mediate their action by directly binding to the cysteine residues of the sensor component, to other residues of the same proteins, or to accessory proteins that transduce the signal to the antisigma factors. In addition to the mechanisms leading to inactivation of the sensor component, elucidation of the complete array of functions under the control of the sigma factors, focusing mainly on the hypothetical proteins, is another interesting question. By responding to all these questions properly, insights and knowledge about the strategies used for bacteria to respond and adapt to heavy metal stress could be applied to design more effective species for bioremediation of environments contaminated with cadmium and chromium.

# Metal ion toxicity and oxidative stress in Streptococcus pneumoniae

Christopher A. McDevitt, Stephanie L. Begg, and James C. Paton 

Research Centre for Infectious Diseases, School of Biological Sciences, University of Adelaide, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia 

## 20.6.1 Introduction

Streptococcus pneumoniae (also known as pneumococcus) was first isolated by Pasteur in 1881 and is a Gram-positive, catalase-negative, aerotolerant, anaerobic bacterium and a common component of the human nasopharyngeal microbial flora. Pneumococcal carriage is predominantly asymptomatic, but a small percentage of carriers develop serious and potentially fatal invasive diseases such as pneumonia, meningitis, and bacteraemia, or less serious but highly prevalent diseases such as otitis media and sinusitis. Globally, S. pneumoniae causes more than 1 million deaths annually, mostly in children under 5 years of age in developing countries, but the pneumococcus also afflicts the elderly and immunocompromised (World Health Organization, 1997). Management of pneumococcal disease is being complicated by steadily increasing rates of resistance to existing antimicrobial drugs. Deployment of pneumococcal polysaccharide–protein conjugate vaccines has reduced the incidence of invasive disease in regions where these expensive vaccines have been deployed, but significant challenges remain. Most notably, the conjugate vaccines have limited serotype coverage (currently up to 13 of the 93 known serotypes), and the complexity and costs associated with manufacture restrict their availability in developing countries, where the burden of pneumococcal disease is greatest (Bogaert et al., 2004; Rajam et al., 2008). Furthermore, increasing reports are emerging that the widespread use of (limited serotype coverage) conjugate vaccines has resulted in replacement carriage and disease caused by non-vaccine serotypes (Cohen et al., 2010; Croucher et al., 2011). This has been attributed to unmasking of pre-existing non-vaccine type strains resident in the population, as well as by genetic recombination, resulting in capsular serotype switching between included and non-included serotypes. As a consequence, new strategies are required to manage the continuing threat that S. pneumoniae presents to global human health. Recent studies have suggested that an understanding of the role of essential micronutrients, such as metal ions, and their role in microbial physiology may provide new therapeutic avenues or vaccine targets. This chapter will summarize our current understanding of metal ion homeostasis in S. pneumoniae, as well as the implications for metal ion toxicity and mechanisms for oxidative stress management. 

## 20.6.2 Metal ions and S. pneumoniae

Metal ions are essential for all forms of life. In biological systems, metal ions fulfil both structural and functional roles within the cell, and thereby facilitate vital biochemical processes. S. pneumoniae acquires metal ions from the host environment by use of specific import pathways, predominantly primary and secondary active transporters (Brown et al., 2001, 2002; Dintilhac et al., 1997; McAllister et al., 2004; Neef et al., 2011; Plumptre et al., 2014a). The first-row transition metal ions (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) have particularly prominent roles in cellular functions, where they act as essential cofactors for up to half of all known metalloproteins (Waldron and Robinson, 2009). Thus, the acquisition of transition metal ions is crucial for host colonization, and consistent with this inference, the transporters associated with their uptake across the cell membrane have been shown to be key virulence factors (Lewis et al., 2012). However, host niches also show considerable variation in metal ion abundance during the course of bacterial infection and the associated inflammatory response (Hood and Skaar, 2012). This can occur via host-mediated sequestration of nutrients by proteins such as calprotectin, which chelates manganese and zinc ions, or transferrin, which sequesters iron, and thereby limit bacterial propagation by restricting access to essential nutrients (Corbin et al., 2008; Kehl-Fie and Skaar, 2010; Weinberg, 2009; White et al., 2009). In addition to sequestration of nutrients, modulation of specific ions, such as zinc, has been reported in tissues during infection in order to prosecute metal overload against the bacterium. The phagolysosome of innate immune cells has been shown to actively modulate phagolysosomal metal ion concentrations to employ copper and/or zinc ions to kill pathogenic bacteria (Botella et al., 2011; Jabado et al., 2000; White et al., 2009). Hence, invasive pathogens such as the pneumococcus must be able to adapt to significant variations in extracellular metal ion abundances while acquiring essential transition metal ions. S. pneumoniae, like many bacterial organisms, employs a range of specific transporters for the uptake of each metal ion. 

However, transition metal ions in excess are also known to mediate significant cellular toxicity. As a consequence, the intracellular accumulation of metal ions must be tightly regulated so as to balance the needs of having a sufficient abundance, to facilitate the fidelity of biological processes, without accumulating excess, which would result in metal intoxication and perturbation of cellular function (Lemire et al., 2013; Waldron and Robinson, 2009). The antimicrobial properties of metals were recognized early in human history, with the historical use of copper and silver vessels for water disinfection and food preservation dating back to the ancient Persians, Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians (McKhann et al., 1948). Although their use as antimicrobial agents waned with the discovery of antibiotics in the 20th century, the rapid acquisition of drug resistance in many bacterial species has led to a renewed interest in these properties. However, although metal ions are known to mediate toxicity in biological systems, the molecular basis or bases for how this arises remain unclear. Current studies of metal toxicity have examined the roles and relative contributions of the cellular metal ion homeostatic pathways. Metal ion homeostasis involves a complex interplay of protein and small-molecule systems that comprise metalloregulatory networks, uptake and efflux transporters, metallochaperones, and buffering molecules. As a consequence, elucidation of the bioinorganic chemical basis for metal ion toxicity in a cellular context has not been directly addressed due to the inability to remove the metal ion homeostatic components without impairing cell viability. However, in spite of these limitations, indirect studies have indicated that there are five general phenomena associated with metal ion toxicity (Lemire et al., 2013). These are the generation of intracellular oxidative stress (see Section 10), genotoxicity, the impairment of protein function (mismetallation), membrane perturbation (see Section 18), and nutrient starvation. Here, we will review the known roles and homeostatic mechanisms of the first-row transition metal ions employed by the pneumococcus. We will then examine their potential toxic mechanisms with a particular focus on oxidative stress in S. pneumoniae. 

## 20.6.2.1 Manganese

Manganese, which predominantly occurs as the divalent cation $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ in biological systems, is an essential trace element for all known forms of life (Papp-Wallace and Maguire, 2006). S. pneumoniae utilizes $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ in many cellular processes both as a metal cofactor for enzymes, such as those involved in capsule production (Morona et al., 2002), aerobic tolerance (Spellerberg et al., 1996), phosphorylation, hydrolysis, carbon metabolism, and decarboxylation (Papp-Wallace and Maguire, 2006), and in regulation of gene expression (Honsa et al., 2013). Although iron is typically the most common transition metal ion in biological systems, the pneumococcus shows significantly higher accumulation of cellular $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ than $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + / 3 + }$ (Jacobsen et al., 2011; McDevitt et al., 2011; see Section 19). The lower utilization of iron, relative to $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , has been attributed to the smaller number of iron–sulphur cluster-containing proteins within the pneumococcus and its lack of a complete respiratory chain (Hoskins et al., 2001; Lanie et al., 2007; Lisher and Giedroc, 2013; Tettelin et al., 2001; Yesilkaya et al., 2013). These physiological adaptations may provide a selective advantage for the pneumococcus, a host-adapted pathogen, enabling it to propagate in the iron-restricted niches that it colonizes (Jakubovics and Jenkinson, 2001). Manganese acquisition in S. pneumoniae is facilitated by pneumococcal surface antigen A (PsaA), a cell-surface lipoprotein metal receptor. Recruitment of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions by PsaA is essential for host colonization and virulence, as loss of any gene in the psa operon abrogates $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake and attenuates virulence in both intranasal and intraperitoneal murine challenge models (Dintilhac et al., 1997; Johnston et al., 2006; McAllister et al., 2004). However, while loss of psaA is not lethal, it does result in an absolute dependency on $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ supplementation into the growth medium (Dintilhac et al., 1997; Johnston et al., 2006; McAllister et al., 2004). As the pneumococcal genome does not encode any homologues of any known alternate $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters, such as a $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ -specific NRAMP or Ptype ATPase (Papp-Wallace and Maguire, 2006), extracellular $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ is most likely acquired, albeit with significantly less efficiency, by alternate nonspecific uptake pathways. 

PsaA belongs to the Cluster A-I subgroup of solute-binding proteins (SBPs) and interacts with an adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding cassette (ABC) transporter. The ABC transporter comprises PsaB, the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) that hydrolyses ATP to provide energy for uphill transport of the ions via PsaC, the transmembrane domain (TMD), into the bacterial cell. Intriguingly, metal ion ABC transporters, such as PsaBC, that employ SBPs lack discrete binding sites for the ion within the transporter and, as such, are entirely dependent on the SBP for recruiting the cognate metal ion cargo (Counago ˜ et al., 2012; Davidson et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 2012). PsaA was the first Cluster A-I SBP for which high-resolution structural data were obtained (Lawrence et al., 1998; Pilling et al., 1998). Although $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ rather than $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ was observed at the metalbinding site in the protein, recent studies have provided significant advances in our understanding of how PsaA achieves selectivity for metal ions. Notably, although the physiological role of PsaA is to recruit $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions in vivo, in vitro the protein has been shown to be able to interact with any divalent first-row transition metal ion. Indeed, the ability of PsaA to interact with $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ is consistent with studies of PsaA homologues in other streptococcal species, such as S. gordonii and S. sanguinis, that show similar interactions for both $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Crump et al., 2014; 

Jakubovics et al., 2000). Although in vitro experiments have suggested that iron acquisition is at least partially dependent on the PsaA homologues, ScaA and SsaB, respectively, the in vivo relevance of this interaction (if any) remains to be ascertained, given that $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ would not exist as a freely soluble divalent cation in aerobic biological systems. High-resolution structural studies combined with mutagenesis revealed that PsaA employed a “spring-hammer” binding modality, in contrast to the Venus flytrap mechanism observed for other ABC transporter–associated SBPs (Counago ˜ et al., 2014). In essence, the spring-hammer mechanism showed that metal ions that prefer four-coordinate binding (i.e., ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + } )$ induce a more stable conformation of PsaA, thus resulting in “jamming” of the SBP due to the metal ions being bound in an essentially irreversible manner. By contrast, those divalent transition metal ions that prefer six-coordinate binding $( \mathrm { e . g . , M n ^ { 2 + } } )$ result in a less stable conformation of the protein, thereby permitting reversible metal ion binding. As a consequence, although the metal ion–binding site of PsaA is incapable of providing absolute selectivity for $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions, functional selectivity is achieved by virtue of its inability to release metal ions such as ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Counago ˜ et al., 2014). In the context of the physiological niches colonized by S. pneumoniae, the spring-hammer mechanism enables acquisition of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions over more prevalent $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ ions. 

Transcriptional regulation of the psaBCA operon is controlled by PsaR. The PsaR repressor protein negatively regulates the Psa import machinery in response to $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ abundance (Kloosterman et al., 2008; Lisher et al., 2013). High-resolution structural studies of S. pneumoniae PsaR revealed a homodimeric DNA-binding protein with two distinct metal-binding sites (Lisher et al., 2013). Although one site appears to be primarily structural and coordinates $\bar { Z } \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions with extremely high affinity $( K _ { \mathrm { D } } \geq 1 0 ^ { 1 3 } ~ \mathrm { M } ^ { - 1 } )$ , the second site mediates metal selectivity and, in turn, modulates the role of PsaR in DNA binding. Intriguingly, despite the higher apparent affinity of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , relative to $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , for the second site, $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ binding was essential for the activation of DNA binding. This appears to arise from the higher allosteric coupling free energy released when $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions bind to the second site, by comparison with $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions. Therefore, PsaR is regulated by the cellular abundance of both $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions, but with only the Mn-bound form of PsaR acting as a negative repressor for the psaBCA operon. This competitive allosteric regulation of PsaR also has physiological implications, as extracellular $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions are capable of competitively inhibiting $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake. The consequence of this would be to shift the intracellular equilibrium to the de-repressing Zn-bound form of PsaR and thereby enable transcription of the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ -uptake machinery (Kloosterman et al., 2008; Lisher and Giedroc, 2013). 

## 20.6.2.2 Iron

Iron acquisition is a major challenge for invasive pathogens as Fe bioavailability is tightly regulated in the host environment. 

The majority of Fe is sequestered within the tetrapyrrole ring of heme, which is in turn bound to hemoglobin in erythrocytes (De Domenico et al., 2008; Heinemann et al., 2008). The role of Fe in pneumococcal pathogenesis has been studied since the early 1990s, but it was the work of Brown et al. that first identified the cellular machinery responsible for scavenging Fe from the host environment (Brown et al., 2001; Tai et al., 1993, 1997; see also Section 19). A study of virulence determinants in pneumococcal pathogenicity-associated islands revealed two Fe acquisition pathways, initially described as the pit1BCDA and pit2ABCD (pneumococcal iron transporter 1 and 2) operons, but now referred to as piuBCDA and piaABCD. More recently, a third Fe uptake operon was described, the pitADBC operon, which reclaimed the earlier nomenclature (Brown et al., 2002; Hoskins et al., 2001). All three Fe uptake operons encode ABC permeases, with the genes, piuA, piaA, and pitA encoding the lipoprotein SBP components. Although the ligand specificities of the three SBPs have not been unequivocally defined, there are sufficient data to suggest that these distinct Fe-specific ABC permeases interact with different forms of bioavailable Fe. PiuA has been shown to be involved in $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -dicitrate uptake and sequestering hemin and hemoglobin from the host as a source of Fe (Tai et al., 2003). High-resolution structural analysis of PiaA showed that it bound ferrichrome, a hydroxamate siderophore (Cheng et al., 2013). Although the pneumococcus does not produce siderophores, these data suggest that S. pneumoniae may employ PiaA to steal those produced by other bacteria in the human host. This type of bacterial hijacking or competition for non-native siderophores is a common Fe acquisition mechanism observed in other pathogenic bacteria (Hibbing et al., 2010). PitA appears to interact with $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , as mutagenesis studies showed that growth medium supplementation with $\mathrm { F e C l } _ { 3 }$ could partially restore the growth defect of a ΔpitA mutant strain (Brown et al., 2002). Further studies in this area to definitively map the ligand specificities of the SBPs, and by extension the ABC permeases, are required. 

Intriguingly, while three Fe uptake pathways have been described in the pneumococcus, to date no Fe efflux pathway has been identified. Intracellular Fe homeostasis appears to be primarily regulated via the non-haem ferritin-binding protein, Dpr, which acts as an intracellular store for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hua et al., 2014). The response regulator that controls expression of Dpr is RitR (repressor of iron transport), an orphan response regulator (see Section 3) that is directly associated with maintenance of Fe homeostasis in the pneumococcus (Ulijasz et al., 2004). In addition to Dpr, RitR is also able to regulate the transcription of multiple genes involved in Fe homeostasis, such as those from the piu operon (Ulijasz et al., 2004). Under conditions of Fe excess, RitR will repress the transcription of the Fe uptake pathways. The innate difficulties of utilizing Fe in an intracellular environment have resulted in the evolution of alternative metal ion requirements. It has been speculated that, for this reason, S. pneumoniae utilizes manganese in place of iron for many cellular processes. 

## 20.6.2.3 Cobalt and nickel

Cobalt and nickel (see Chapter 20.1) are the two biologically significant metal ions for which the least amount of data is available, with respect to pneumococcal physiology. Studies of pneumococcal metal ion accumulation have shown that cellular abundance of $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ is typically two orders of magnitude less than that of Mn2+, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 / 3 + }$ , or $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ when analysed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) (Counago ˜ et al., 2014; Eijkelkamp et al., 2014; McDevitt et al., 2011). Although high-affinity uptake systems for $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ have not yet been found in the pneumococcus, and seem unlikely given their low cellular abundance, their presence cannot be excluded. Bioinformatics has identified several uncharacterized putative E1– E2 P-type ATPases in the S. pneumoniae genome, and one or more of these may facilitate import, or export, of $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ and/or $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ . In other bacteria, cobalt is typically associated with cobalamin (vitamin $\mathrm { B } _ { 1 2 } )$ and acquired via the Btu permease (DeVeaux and Kadner, 1985; Giannella et al., 1971). However, S. pneumoniae lacks the Btu permease, and there is no direct evidence that it uses vitamin $\mathrm { B } _ { 1 2 } .$ Thus, while the acquisition pathways of these transition metal ions remain to be elucidated, several studies have examined potential efflux routes. Increased cellular accumulation of $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ has been associated with upregulation of the cation diffusion facilitator (CDF) family transporter CzcD (Kloosterman et al., 2007). The czc locus has been shown to mediate $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + } , \mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and cadmium resistance in several organisms, most notably Cupriavidus metallidurans (Anton et al., 1999; Nies, 1992a,b). By contrast, recent studies have shown that the czcD homolog in S. pyogenes is associated only with protection against $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions (Ong et al., 2014). As a consequence, although transcriptional analyses have shown that czcD expression levels are upregulated in the presence of either cobalt or nickel (Kloosterman et al., 2007), there remains a paucity of direct evidence for a role in polyspecific cation protection in S. pneumoniae. Despite the minimal research into ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ in S. pneumoniae, a recent study has found numerous pneumococcal proteins that contain putative $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ - and Ni2+-binding sites (Sun et al., 2013). In this study, $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ was predicted to provide a largely structural role in ribosomes, while $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ appeared to fulfil functional roles in proteins such as transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetases. 

## 20.6.2.4 Copper

Studies of pneumococcal metal accumulation have shown significant levels of cellular Cu (see Chapter 2.12) despite the fact that no ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake pathway or $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent cellular processes have been identified to date (Counago˜ et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2013; McDevitt et al., 2011). This implies that either the pneumococcal cupro-proteome has not yet been identified, or that Cu is nonspecifically transported via divalent metal ion transporters. Although the ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake mechanism(s) and a cellular role for the accumulated Cu ions are lacking, the pneumococcus has evolved a complex set of mechanisms to regulate the levels of cellular Cu. Copper regulation is crucial as the reducing intracellular environment results in the reduction of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ to $\mathrm { { C u ^ { + } } }$ . The potential for cellular damage from $\mathrm { { C u ^ { + } } }$ is mitigated by the cop operon, which comprises three genes: copY, the operon regulator; cupA, a copper transport protein with homology to a cupredoxin; and copA, a P-type ATPase responsible for $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ efflux (Fu et al., 2013; Shafeeq et al., 2011b). In the absence of a functional cop operon, the pneumococcus becomes highly susceptible to $\mathrm { { C u ^ { + } } }$ toxicity. This becomes particularly dramatic in murine models of lung infection where ΔcopA and ΔcupA strains of S. pneumoniae are attenuated for colonization and virulence (Fu et al., 2013; Shafeeq et al., 2011b). Highresolution structural studies have shown that CupA facilitates Cu export by an elegant transfer mechanism, in which $\mathrm { { C u ^ { + } } }$ is transferred from a low-affinity site of CupA to a high-affinity site of CopA (Fu et al., 2013). Although questions remain regarding how $\mathrm { { C u } ^ { + } }$ is recruited to these two integral membrane proteins, and whether CupA binds $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ or $\mathrm { { C u ^ { + } } }$ , the work of Fu et al. already provides a significant advance in our understanding on pneumococcal Cu homeostasis. Additional genes have also been suggested to be involved in Cu homeostasis – notably, cutC, ctpC, and $c t p E -$ based on their homology to known Cubinding proteins (Shafeeq et al., 2011b). However, they have not been observed to be regulated by Cu abundance in S. pneumoniae, so their involvement, if any, in Cu homeostasis remains to be ascertained. 

## 20.6.2.5 Zinc

Zinc is the second most prevalent transition element commonly found in biological organisms (Andreini et al., 2006a,b). In prokaryotes, $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ has been predicted to interact with approximately 5% of all proteins (Andreini et al., 2006b), while a recent study suggested that in S. pneumoniae, $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ could interact with nearly 8% of the entire proteome (Sun et al., 2011). Metal accumulation studies of S. pneumoniae have shown that cellular accumulation of $\mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ significantly exceeds that of Fe and is comparable to that of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , the most abundant transition element in S. pneumoniae (Counago˜ et al., 2014; Jacobsen et al., 2011; McDevitt et al., 2011). The prevalence of $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ has been presumed to arise from it being redox inert, and therefore stable in a +2 oxidation state (Giedroc and Arunkumar, 2007), making it ideal for the stabilization of protein structural folds. In addition, its Lewis acid properties also allow it to accept electrons from other molecules, thereby providing a catalytic functionality for $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions in enzymes such as proteases (Panina et al., 2003). 

The pneumococcus has an absolute requirement for $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , as perturbation of zinc homeostasis results in the attenuation of virulence in murine infection models (Bayle et al., 2011; Plumptre et al., 2014a). S. pneumoniae acquires $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ by use of an ABC permease that interacts with two $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ -specific SBPs, AdcA and AdcAII (Bayle et al., 2011; Dintilhac et al., 1997; Dintilhac and Claverys, 1997; Plumptre et al., 2014a). The adc operon encodes for the ABC transporter, adcC (NBD) and adcB (TMD); the SBP, adcA; and a MarR family transcriptional regulator, adcR. By contrast with adcA, adcAII is an “orphan” SBP and is transcriptionally clustered outside of the adc operon, located upstream of the pneumococcal polyhistidine triad (Pht) phtE and phtD genes, another gene family associated with $\bar { Z } \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ homeostasis (Loisel et al., 2008; Ogunniyi et al., 2009; Reyes-Caballero et al., 2010; Shafeeq et al., 2011a). The Pht proteins are a group of pneumococcal cell surface–associated proteins that includes four members, PhtA, PhtB, PhtD, and PhtE. The Pht proteins contain multiple His triad motifs (HxxHxH) and have been subdivided into three broad groups on the basis of primary structure comparisons (Adamou et al., 2001; Loisel et al., 2011; Plumptre et al., 2012). Consistent with the transcriptional clustering of the pht genes with adcAII, the Pht proteins have been shown to interact with $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and directly contribute to the efficiency of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake by AdcAII (Loisel et al., 2011; Ogunniyi et al., 2009; Plumptre et al., 2012, 2014a,b; Rioux et al., 2011). 

The cellular abundance of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ is sensed by the transcriptional regulator AdcR. However, despite being upstream of the Adc permease machinery, AdcR appears to only exert relatively weak transcriptional control over the transcription of these genes (Plumptre et al., 2014a). An examination of the protein abundance of AdcA showed only minor changes in the abundance of the Adc permease in response to $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , suggesting that the permease is more or less constitutively expressed. By contrast, the adcAII and the pht genes show significant transcriptional plasticity in response to $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ abundance, modulated via AdcR. Collectively, these findings suggest that the pneumococcus has an unusual, but coordinated response to management of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake, wherein the primary ABC permease has limited transcriptional responsiveness, but its efficiency can be supplemented by AdcAII and the Pht proteins. In addition to AdcR, the $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ -responsive TetR family regulator SczA also senses intracellular $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and controls the transcription of czcD (Kloosterman et al., 2007). CzcD is presumed to be the primary $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ efflux pathway based on transcriptional responsiveness to increased $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ abundance and the similarity to other characterized $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters. However, definitive studies in the pneumococcus remain lacking. Overall, the coordinated response of AdcR and SczA to low and high intracellular $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations, respectively, allows the maintenance of a finely tuned homeostatic environment that is crucial for the survival and virulence of S. pneumoniae. 

## 20.6.3 Transition metal ion toxicity and mismetallation

The metal ion homeostatic mechanisms that regulate pneumococcal metal ion concentrations ensure sufficient cellular abundance for fidelity of cellular processes, while concomitantly preventing metal intoxication and damage to cellular processes. The arbiters of cellular metal ion abundance are the transcriptional metalloregulatory proteins. The prevailing hypothesis is that the metal-dependent regulators employ simple thermodynamic control, wherein the corresponding affinities of the uptake and efflux regulators compete for the metal ions, and thereby define the intracellular set points for metal ion bioavailability and control the “buffering” concentration range (Guerra and Giedroc, 2012). This scenario has been elegantly demonstrated for the regulation of the $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake and efflux pathways in E. coli (Outten and O’Halloran, 2001). Dysregulation of cellular metal accumulation results in either metal ion deficiency or intoxication. 

Over-accumulation of transition metal ions can result in toxicity via a number of mechanisms. Impairment of protein function via the acquisition of a non-facile metal ion cofactor highlights the fundamental challenge that metalloproteins encounter when attempting to bind the correct metal ion. This process, also referred to as mismetallation, appears to principally arise from the conformational and dynamic flexibility that occurs within proteins and, as a consequence, results in imperfect steric selection between metal ions. This is especially true of nascent polypeptides that have yet to adopt their final tertiary conformation. As a consequence, the affinities of metal ions for proteins are primarily governed by the ligand field stabilization energies of the metal ions. This creates the universal order of preference that, for divalent metals, is the Irving–Williams series (Irving and Williams, 1953). This is also referred to as the order of stability for divalent transition metals, where affinity in order of increasing atomic number can be represented as $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } / C a ^ { 2 + } < }$ $\mathrm { M n ^ { 2 + } < \bar { F } e ^ { 2 + } < C o ^ { 2 + } < N i ^ { 2 + } < C u ^ { 2 + } > Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ . It has been proposed, on the basis of cellular analyses of metal ion abundances, that the Irving–Williams series underpins the biological abundance of each metal, such that selective metal binding by nascent protein chains can be achieved (Tottey et al., 2008). From the perspective of metal toxicity, the functions of metal-dependent proteins and enzymes are likely to be disrupted if the ability to acquire the correct metal is abrogated due to competition from over-accumulated, non-facile metal ions. Thus, by regulating the cellular metal ion abundance, metalloregulatory proteins play a major role in indirectly controlling the metallation state of intracellular metalloproteins and preventing mismetallation. 

However, in contrast to the carefully poised intracellular concentration of metal ions, bacteria are unable to exert control over the extracellular environment, and, as such, the prevailing ion abundances can result in mismetallation of extracellular metalloproteins and metal ion receptors. Recent studies have shown how host nutritional immunity can exploit impaired metallation or mismetallation during host bacterial invasion (Corbin et al., 2008; Damo et al., 2012; Hood and Skaar, 2012). This mismetallation of cell-surface metal ion receptors has been shown to result in impaired or abrogated metal ion acquisition, resulting in growth arrest or cell death. In the pneumococcus, this has been shown for the Psa permease, where extracellular $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ binds irreversibly to the SBP, PsaA, and results in impaired $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake (Counago ˜ et al., 2014; Eijkelkamp et al., 2014; McDevitt et al., 2011). The resultant depletion of cellular $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ in S. pneumoniae has a strong association with the susceptibility to oxygen and reactive oxygen species (ROS). 

## 20.6.4 Transition metal ions and oxidative stress

Although the pneumococcus is an anaerobic organism and does not directly use molecular oxygen for growth, it can consume it via the concerted reduction by cytoplasmic NADH oxidase (Nox) and pyruvate oxidase (SpxB) (Auzat et al., 1999; Pericone et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2001), to increase the yield of ATP per mole of glucose. As a consequence, management of oxygen and oxidative stress comprises crucial aspects of its lifestyle in aerobic environments. In many organisms, including S. pneumoniae, oxidative stress (see Chapter 10) can arise from the perturbation of Fe homeostasis (see Section 19). The autocatalytic interaction of soluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ with partially reduced forms of oxygen ${ { ( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } } ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } )$ is referred to as Fenton chemistry, and it generates highly damaging hydroxyl radicals (OH∙). In a cellular context, the Fenton reaction can occur via ROS-mediated oxidative attack on solvent-exposed $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ atoms from mononuclear Fe or 4Fe-4S cluster containing enzymes. This results in protein oxidation, the generation of OH∙, and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ dissociation. Therefore, the accumulation of Fe and its survival in aerobic environments necessitate that the pneumococcus utilizes a number of mechanisms to limit the capacity by which transition metal ions can mediate oxidative stress. 

Studies of the metal ion abundances in S. pneumoniae show reduced $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + / 3 + }$ and increased $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , relative to other bacteria. The lower Fe abundance in the pneumococcus would be consistent with a reduction of Fe incorporation into the metalloproteome, thereby reducing the possibility that Fenton chemistry could occur. The concomitant increase in $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ abundance would also assist the pneumococcus to harness the intrinsic antioxidant properties of this metal ion. Manganese in many organisms has a prominent role as an essential cofactor of the superoxide dismutase, where it catalyses the one-electron dismutation of superoxide $( { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } ^ { - } )$ to oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (Eijkelkamp et al., 2014; Papp-Wallace and Maguire, 2006; Yesilkaya et al., 2000). In S. pneumoniae, transcription of the gene encoding superoxide dismutase, sodA, has been shown to be directly influenced by $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ abundance, although the precise regulatory mechanism remains unclear (Eijkelkamp et al., 2014). Studies have shown that decreased $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulation results in reduced SodA activity (Eijkelkamp et al., 2014; Tseng et al., 2002; Yesilkaya et al., 2000), while also impacting pnuemococcal virulence in murine intranasal infection models (Tseng et al., 2002). Intriguingly, recent studies have suggested that pneumococcal SodA may contain a cambialistic metal cofactor (Eijkelkamp et al., 2014), similar to other streptococcal species (De Vendittis et al., 2010; Jakubovics et al., 2002; Niven et al., 1999), but direct in vivo evidence has proven elusive. In addition to contributing to enzymatic protection against oxidative stress, $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ has also been shown to protect by potentially substituting for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ in non-redox metabolic enzymes (Sobota and Imlay, 2011), and by direct protection against oxidative stress as a low-weight molecular pool of Mn– phosphate and Mn–carbonate complexes to catalyse superoxide disproportionation (Archibald and Fridovich, 1981; Daly et al., 2004, 2010; Eijkelkamp et al., 2014; Tseng et al., 2001). However, direct evidence for these mechanisms in S. pneumoniae remains lacking. Further support for the crucial role of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ in protection against oxidative stress has been shown in a study of the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ efflux pathway and the CDF protein MntE. Analysis of a ΔmntE strain showed increased levels of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulation, relative to the wild type, which resulted in greater tolerance to oxidative stress and increased $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ production (Rosch et al., 2009). In addition, adjacent to the psa operon is the gene tpxD, formerly known as psaD, which encodes a thiol peroxidase, which catalyses the detoxification of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Hajaj et al., 2012). Transcription of tpxD is co-regulated with the psa operon, but it is also influenced by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ levels by virtue of transcriptional activation from its own promoter. However, while tpxD is induced by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } .$ , the psa operon is repressed. Thus, the cellular abundance of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ has the potential to also regulate $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ acquisition by influencing transcription of the psa permease. 

Intracellular metal ion buffering has been suggested to be associated with the abundance of the thiol-containing tripeptide glutathione (γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinyl-glycine). Glutathione is the most common intracellular thiol found in most prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Masip et al., 2006). In addition to its disulphide reductase activity, glutathione is known to protect cells from many forms of physiological stress. The pneumococcus is incapable of de novo glutathione biosynthesis, but instead is reliant upon glutathione uptake via the Gsh permease (Potter et al., 2012). The oxidized disulphide-bonded, dimeric form of glutathione (GSSG) is then reduced by the glutathione oxidoreductase (Gor) to the reduced form GSH. The ratio of GSH to GSSG in the cytoplasm is tightly controlled by Gor, which uses reducing equivalents from NADPH. However, the disulphidereducing activity of GSH is not essential in some organisms due to compensation by the thioredoxin–thioredoxin reductase system (Fernandes et al., 2005). Glutathione is associated with a multitude of protective roles in addition to metal ion buffering, including resisting reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (see Sections 10 and 17), and ameliorating osmotic and acid stress (Masip et al., 2006; see Sections 11 and 16). A recent study shows that S. pneumoniae resistance to metal ion intoxication is directly affected by the loss of the Gsh permease and, to a lesser extent, by loss of Gor (Potter et al., 2012). The disruption of the Gsh permease also significantly reduces pneumococcal virulence, whereas the Δgor strain remains as virulent as the wild type (Potter et al., 2012). Treatment with paraquat, which generates superoxide in the bacterial cytoplasm, negatively affects the growth of both mutant strains, although their resistance to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ is unaffected (Potter et al., 2012). Taken together, the balance of evidence implicates glutathione as having a key role in pneumococcal metal ion buffering, but it is unclear whether its contribution to oxidative stress management is direct or indirect. Polyamines have also been associated with protection against oxidative stress in other organisms (Chattopadhyay et al., 2003). However, a recent study of the pneumococcus showed that they do not have an apparent role in protection against metal ion toxicity or endogenous oxidative stress (Potter and Paton, 2014). 

Additional metal ion toxicities related to oxidative stress include the genotoxic impact of certain metal ions and disruption of cell membrane integrity (see Section 18). In addition to oxidative protein damage, $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } .$ -mediated Fenton chemistry has been linked to increased DNA damage and cell death. Other transition metal ions, such as $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ , have also been implicated in genotoxicity to bacteria, but whether this occurs directly or indirectly has not been definitively established. Genotoxic impacts have not been associated with all transition metal ions, as studies of E. coli have shown that $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ and ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ do not increase mutation rates. Thus, the precise mechanisms of DNA damage due to metal ion toxicity remain unclear. Perturbation of cell membrane stability and/or integrity has been proposed as another mechanism of metal toxicity. Metal ions, including $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { { C u ^ { + } } }$ , have been implicated in disrupting bacterial membrane integrity. Lipid peroxidation has been suggested as a mechanism by which cell membrane integrity could be disrupted. However, the monounsaturated fatty acid content of bacterial membranes makes them significantly less reactive to in vitro lipid peroxide chain reactions, and hence it remains unclear whether metal ions induce lipid peroxidation in vivo. Overall, detailed studies of the genotoxicities and membrane integrity metal toxicities in S. pneumoniae remain to be performed.

## 20.6.5 Concluding remarks

Understanding the molecular bases of bacterial metal ion homeostasis has been the focus of many recent studies. Collectively, these works have revealed the complexities of bacterial regulation of cellular metal ion abundances and, with respect to S. pneumoniae, provided a foundation by which the dynamic, competitive interaction between host and pathogen for metal ions at the host–pathogen interface can be deciphered. The bioavailability of transition metal ions in the host environment clearly exerts profound effects on invasive bacterial pathogens. Recent studies have shown how host manipulation of transition metal ion abundances can be exploited to impair bacterial colonization, by either depriving the pathogen of essential ions for growth or prosecuting metal ion intoxication. However, pathogens such as S. pneumoniae have evolved sophisticated and intricate metal ion homeostatic mechanisms to limit the impact of extracellular metal fluxes on essential cellular processes. Studies into the complexities of the host–pathogen interaction are now focussing on addressing the molecular mechanisms by which S. pneumoniae regulates intracellular metal ion concentrations and prevents dysregulation of metal homeostasis by extracellular stresses. This knowledge is crucial for revealing the processes that underlie the origins of intracellular oxidative stress, the current mechanisms of which have largely been revealed through indirect experiments. Together, these insights will aid in understanding how host immune effector cells leverage higher order transition-row metal ions, such as Cu and $Z \mathbf { n } ,$ to aid in clearing invading pneumococci. Collectively, by providing an understanding of how both host and pathogen compete for and manipulate metal ion abundances during infection, this knowledge may aid in identifying new routes for the development of novel therapeutic or preventative strategies.
