## Quorum sensing

## C H A P T E R 21.1

# Quorum sensing and bacterial social interactions in biofilms: bacterial cooperation and competition

Yung-Hua Li1,2 and Xiao-Lin Tian1 

1Department of Applied Oral Sciences, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada 

2Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada 

## 21.1.1 Introduction

Microbes in nature are predominantly associated with surfaces and live in multispecies biofilms, which account for over 99% of microbial life on Earth (Costerton et al., 1999; Davey and O’Toole, 2000). Biofilms are spatially structured communities whose functions depend on complex webs of symbiotic interactions (Burmolle et al., 2014). High cell density and close proximity of diverse species of microbes are typical of life in natural biofilms, where organisms physically interact with each other and develop complex social interactions that occur both within and among species (Webb et al., 2003; see Section 22). Even without physical contact, microbes living in the same community may secrete small diffusible molecules to interact with each other (Keller and Surette, 2006). Structural and physiological complexities of biofilms have led to the idea that microbes in biofilms frequently cooperate for social activities as groups, which are analogous to multicellular organisms (Parsek and Greenberg, 2005). Indeed, microbiologists have discovered an unexpectedly high degree of multicellular behaviors that have led to the perception of biofilms as “cities” of microbes (Watnick and Kolter, 2000; see Section 22). Particularly, many bacteria are found to regulate diverse physiological processes through a mechanism called quorum sensing (QS), in which bacterial cells produce, detect, and respond to small diffusible signal molecules to communicate for coordinated activities in a cell density–dependent manner (Miller and Bassler, 2001; see Chapter 2.18). During quorum sensing, bacterial cells cooperate to obtain group-specific benefits or “public goods,” such as signal molecules, extracellular polymers, exoenzymes, antibiotics, or virulence factors (Celiker and Gore, 2012). Bacteria achieve strength by increasing cell density or by collectively producing virulence factors required for pathogenesis (Antunes et al., 2010). Through population cooperation, bacteria can impact their environments in many ways that are simply impossible for individual cells (Nadell et al., 2009). 

Increasing evidence suggests that quorum-sensing-mediated cooperative activities are widespread in bacteria, which have important implications in bacterial ecology and pathogenesis (Li and Tian, 2012). From an evolutionary point of view, however, such cooperative activities may create conflicts or even potential risks to the populations, because evolutionary theory predicts that individual cells that cooperate can be exploited by selfish individuals or “cheaters” that do not cooperate but reap the benefits from cooperators (West et al., 2006). The question then arises as to why individual cells cooperate at their own cost to increase the fitness of non-cooperative cells, which appears to be totally against Darwin’s theory of natural selection. Natural biofilms are characterized by species diversity and high cell density, and, when coupled with environmental fluctuations, they often create an environment that is conducive to fierce competition among bacteria (Czaran et al., 2002; Foster and Bell, 2012). Thus, it remains unclear how and when quorumsensing-mediated cooperation takes place in biofilms and how such cooperative activities can be maintained in nature. In this chapter, we review some examples of bacterial social interactions with a focus on bacterial cooperation, conflict, and competition and implications in microbial ecology and evolution. 

## 21.1.2 Bacterial social interactions in biofilms

Natural biofilms are characterized by species diversity and high cell density (Davey and O’Toole, 2000). This suggests that microbes in biofilms should display intermicrobial interactions that enhance the overall function of biofilms while forming biofilm structure, carrying out metabolic activities, and expressing pathogenesis. It is widely accepted that biofilm formation is a dynamic, developmental program that often results in a predictable biofilm life cycle (Watnick and Kolter, 2000; see Section 22). During biofilm formation, microbes likely cooperate to form multicellular communities by sophisticated mechanisms (Nadell et al., 2009; Parsek and Greenberg, 2005). In particular, increased cell density and the proximity of cells in biofilms may facilitate chemical signals to cross strains and species, promoting cell–cell communication and social interactions. Many bacteria regulate their physiological processes and social activities through a quorum-sensing mechanism, including biofilm formation (Cvitkovitch et al., 2003; see Section 22), bacteriocin production (van der Ploeg, 2005), spore and fruiting-body formation (Celiker and Gore, 2013), genetic competence (Claverys et al., 2006; Li et al., 2001), programmed cell death (Lewis, 2000; Rice and Bayles, 2008), and virulence factors (Antunes et al., 2010). The processes controlled by quorum sensing are diverse and reflect the specific needs of particular communities. In many bacteria, quorum sensing represents a central mechanism to regulate social activities, allowing bacteria to reap benefits that would be unattainable to them as individual cells (Federle and Bassler, 2003; Li and Tian, 2012; Xavier, 2011). 

The significance of interbacterial interactions was first realized and thoroughly described for bacteria residing in the oral cavity (Kolenbrander et al., 2010; Kuramitsu et al., 2007). Dental plaque is a well-recognized biofilm community characterized by its vast biodiversity (>700 species) and high cell density $( \dot { 1 } 0 ^ { 1 1 }$ cells/g wet wt.), which allow microbes to develop complex interactions (Kuramitsu et al., 2007). Cooperative interactions among bacteria in dental biofilms have been well studied, including bacterial co-aggregation and co-adhesion that facilitate bacterial colonization on the tooth surfaces, nutritional synergy or complementation enabling bacterial growth in saliva, and formation of food chains through metabolic cooperation among species (Kuramitsu et al., 2007; Marsh et al., 2011). Many bacteria also use a quorum-sensing mechanism to coordinate their group activities in dental biofilms (Kolenbrander et al., 2010; Li et al., 2001, 2002). These cooperative interactions probably play important roles in the development of dental biofilms (see Section 22). However, competition or antagonistic interactions among different species or strains may be equally important for the maintenance of a balanced relationship between microbes in dental biofilms. For example, many bacteria in dental biofilms are able to generate toxic products, such as lactic acid, $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ , bacteriocins, or proteases, which exert antagonistic effects and are important strategies for bacterial competition (Figure 21.1.1). Among these products, bacteriocins produced by many species play major roles in interspecies competition in dental biofilms (Kreth et al., 2005a,b; Merritt and Qi, 2011). Importantly, production of bacteriocins by these bacteria is finely regulated by quorum sensing that also regulates genetic competence, stress response, and biofilm formation (Kreth et al., 2005a; Li et al., 2001; van der Ploeg, 2005; Wescombe et al., 2009). This suggests that bacteria require quorum-sensing-mediated cooperation to produce effective doses of bacteriocins for competition. Interestingly, despite competition, all of these species are found to coexist and persist in dental biofilms (Kreth et al., 2005a; Kuramistu et al., 2007), indicating that some regulatory mechanisms play critical roles in balancing bacterial cooperation and competition in dental biofilms.

## 21.1.3 Bacterial competition in biofilms: does it involve cooperation?

In most ecosystems, bacteria often face a major challenge of resource limitation, which inevitably results in competition among species or strains. To survive and pass their genes to the next generation, bacteria have to cope with a constant battle of competition (Amarasekare, 2002). The potential pool of bacterial competitors is vast, and a wide range of mechanisms can be responsible for the emergence and radiation of dominant bacterial populations. Microbial ecologists have long recognized two types of competition: exploitation competition that occurs indirectly through resource consumption, and interference competition that causes a direct, antagonistic effect on competitors (Foster and Bell, 2012; Griffin et al., 2004; Hibbing et al., 2010). There is good evidence that both exploitative and interference competition are prevalent in biofilms, strongly influencing the outcome of natural selection of bacteria (Hibbing et al. 2010). However, most research into interbacterial competition has focused on elucidating biochemical mechanisms underlying different interactions, and it generally assumes that competition occurs among individual cells. Although individual cells can clearly compete with each other, competition mechanisms in individual cells may differ from those available to entire populations. There is growing appreciation that bacteria often engage their competition strategies that require cooperative behaviors (Celiker and Gore, 2012; Freilich et al., 2011). Quorum-sensingmediated production of antimicrobial molecules or bacteriocins in bacteria has provided an excellent example of such cooperation against competitors (Merritt and Qi, 2011; Riley and Wertz, 2002; see Chapters 21.3, 21.4 and 21.5). Recent studies show that bacterial cooperation to resist competition may be a widespread phenomenon in nature (Cordero et al., 2012; Morlon, 2012). 

## 21.1.3.1 Resource competition

Bacteria depend on metabolic pathways to convert resources, such as sugars, into energy for growth and reproduction. Therefore, bacteria in nature often face the dilemma of how to allocate limited resources to increase their growth and reproduction. Bacterial competition for common resources is a typical exploitative competition and can be strong in many natural ecosystems (Foster and Bell, 2012). Efficient use of common resources conforms to the classical definition of a cooperative trait: It is beneficial to the group because more biomass is produced per unit resource, but costly to individuals because each cell produces energy and divides at a slow rate (MacLean and Gudelj, 2006). Bacterial competition for nutritional resources between and within species used to be a major focus of microbiological studies. Jacques Monod, a pioneer in the studies of bacterial growth kinetics, first demonstrated the relationship between growth-limiting substrates and growth rates, leading to the equation that well predicts bacterial growth kinetics in defined liquid cultures (Monod, 1949). Based on the prediction using Monod’s equation, one can determine the outcomes of two competing species or strains in a well-mixed liquid culture, such as in a chemostat. Although it provides invaluable information on bacterial growth kinetics in laboratory studies, Monod’s equation may not accurately predict what happens between competing organisms grown in biofilms. Bacteria cannot be viewed as passive nutritional sinks, but rather have evolved numerous strategies to augment their acquisition of resources. Many bacterial activities, including motility, attachment, antibiotic production, and secretion of extracellular polymers, can tip the competition balance, resulting in outcomes that differ greatly from those predicted in planktonic cultures (Freilich et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2007). Particularly, biofilms often form gradients in concentrations of nutrients, oxygen tension, pH, and waste products due to the thickness (Marsh et al., 2011; see Section 22). These factors can significantly affect the outcomes of bacterial competition and composition in a biofilm community. Freilich et al. (2011) explored competitive and cooperative metabolic interactions in assembled microbial consortia. They found that despite high levels of competition between species with mutual-exclusive distribution patterns, bacteria within a community typically formed cooperative loops that allowed coexistence of all species involved in the community. In another study, MacLean and Gudelj (2006) investigated resource competition in experimental populations of isogenic cheater and cooperator strains of yeast with alternative pathways of glucose metabolism. They showed that both coexistence and competitive exclusion were possible outcomes, depending on the spatial and temporal structure of the community. Both outcomes could be driven by trade-offs between rates and efficiency of conversation of resources into offspring (MacLean and Gudelj, 2006). 

## 21.1.3.2 Competition by interfering with colonization

It is well recognized that the indigenous members of a microbial community on the surfaces of human or animal hosts can interfere with colonization by organisms of foreign origins, a phenomenon referred to as bacterial interference or colonization resistance (Brook, 1999). Colonization resistance is not only common but also central to many ways that bacteria affect humans’ health and diseases. The concept that one species can interfere with the ability of another to colonize and infect the host is based on the prerequisite that all pathogens must attach to a surface of the host to cause infectious diseases. For example, the indigenous organisms in the human intestine are largely the primary colonizers on the mucosal surfaces of intestine. Once they are established, these indigenous bacteria can not only persist but also prevent colonization by exogenous species or invading pathogens (Buffie and Pamer, 2013). The indigenous organisms act as natural competitors against invading pathogens, since ecologically, they fit better in their natural ecosystem than any other organisms of foreign origin. Several indigenous Lactobacillus species, which are also used as probiotics, can bind to epithelial cells of the intestine and produce specific glycoproteins that prevent the attachment of potential pathogens, including Salmonella enterica, virulent E. coli, and other pathogens (Reid et al., 2003). Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain colonization resistance, including competing for binding surfaces or nutrients, creating micro-environments that are exclusive to foreigners, producing antimicrobial substances against invaders, and stimulating the host immune response against invaders (Brook, 1999; Reid et al., 2003; Wescombe et al., 2009). More recently, He et al. (2014) used an in vitro model system to demonstrate that social structure of a microbial community also plays a role in colonization resistance of exogenous species. They found that colonization resistance requires the coordinated activities of key indigenous species in the community. Clearly, these mechanisms constitute the rationales to develop probiotics in preventing colonization by invading pathogens. In fact, application of probiotics has successfully reduced the risk of infectious diseases in the gut, urogenital tract, and wound sites (Buffie and Pamer, 2013; Reid et al., 2003). 

## 21.1.3.3 Competition by producing antimicrobial molecules

Microbes frequently produce an extraordinary array of antimicrobial substances that inhibit or kill closely related species (Riley and Wertz, 2002). These molecules include classical antibiotics, metabolic by-products, bacteriocins, and exotoxins, which are all responsible for “chemical warfare,” profoundly affecting the ecology of a microbial community (Czaran et al., 2002; Merrit and Qi, 2011). The ability to produce antimicrobial molecules against competitors is considered as the most intensively studied mechanism of interference competition (Hibbing et al., 2010). To effectively inhibit competitors, however, bacteria must produce sufficient quantities of antimicrobials in the local environment. Otherwise, subinhibitory concentrations of these antimicrobials might induce a physiologically tolerant state of target cells (Davies et al., 2006). How might a bacterium both ensure delivery of an effective dose of an antibiotic and prevent the acquisition of tolerance? One possible mechanism is that bacteria may initiate population-wide cooperation through a quorum-sensing mechanism to synchronically produce antimicrobial molecules (Figure 21.1.2). Thus, the release of antimicrobials may be delayed until a local quorum is achieved, which ensures the presence of sufficient cell numbers and fully inhibitory levels of antimicrobials in the local environment. 

Among many antimicrobials, bacteriocins are one of the most abundant and diverse classes of antimicrobial molecules that are detected in all bacterial lineages. They are potent, often highly specific toxins and can rapidly kill cells that are not immune to their effects (Riley and Wertz, 2002). Bacteriocins can effectively inhibit closely related species or strains, allowing the producers to be successful during competition. Many bacteria have been found to use a quorum-sensing mechanism to coordinate the production of antimicrobials, including bacteriocins (Merritt and Qi, 2011; Riley and Wertz, 2002; van der Ploeg, 2005). It is not surprising that regulation of antimicrobial production by quorum-sensing-mediated cooperation is widespread in bacteria. Cordero et al. (2012) have recently shown that bacterial cooperation is also a major force in antibiotic-mediated interference competition between populations. They have found that genotypic clusters known to have cohesive habitat association act as units in terms of antibiotic production and resistance. Within populations, antibiotics are produced by a few genotypes, whereas all others are resistant. This suggests that cooperation can occur between nonclonal populations, which prevents invasion by non-antibiotic producers and maintains diversity in the community. Thus, antibiotics may mediate competition between populations rather than solely increase the success of individual cells.

## 21.1.3.4 Competition by contact-dependent growth inhibition

Bacteria also compete against one another by a mechanism called contact-dependent growth inhibition (CDI), a phenomenon in which bacteria produce exotoxins to inhibit the growth of neighboring cells upon cell–cell contact, an inhibition mechanism that totally differs from the actions of antibiotics and
